_childDocuments_.review: My humble review after 100% "To say goodbye is to die a little" The Wild Gentlemen, a small and extremely talented Hungarian team, returns with the sequel to Paint It Red.I'm not exaggerating when I say one of the best noir investigative point-and-click adventures I've ever played.The now reformed legendary duo of Chicken (Santino "Sonny" Featherland and the inseparable Marty McChicken) Police continue their lives in a Clawville prey to riots after the fall of Wessler empire, and the hive, the area where the insects are relegated is the heart of this bomb ready to explode.On an evening like many others, a femme fatale from the Hive shows up at Sonny's apartment asking for help in finding her dead husband, whose body has mysteriously disappeared. From here a roller coaster of mystery, intrigue and action will start.Plot that draws from Noir, from the hard boiled so dear to Raymond Chandler and Santino is really a Philip Marlowe, in the feathers of a rooster, in Chicken Police all the characters are anthropomorphized animals. Plot that is never banal, mature and well written,you can notice the experience gained from Paint it Red, and with a good dose of irony the jokes between Sonny and Marty are very funny.An investigative point and click adventure, more plot centric than Paint It Red, more compact, without downtime, by collecting clues then you can interrogate the suspects (less than in Paint It Red but more well structured).Some simple but well done minigames (from hitting a glass with a peanut making it bounce off the bottle to get Douglas the pianist drunk, to a lockpicking, to a kind of autopsy).You can always play with the black and white filter, but in color you notice the extreme attention to details. MASTERFUL voice over work, already in Paint It Red it was excellent, here it is even more good. A gem in all. The Wild Gentlemen is a small team but with every game they show what talent these guys are capable of. So much so that they are creating a real multiverse called The World of Wilderness, which expands the Clawville universe with games of different genres. I can only say thank you guys, it's because of people like you that I love this industry.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicken Police: Into the HIVE!

_childDocuments_.review: This was an absolutely amazing game! It was a great mixture of artistic styles, the music always went well with the visuals, the story was very noir-esque, but what really makes this game great, are the characters, the world building and the voice acting.The minigames were also interesting, the card game really deserves it's own game.A very interesting mix of noir,  neo-noir and noir parody, with a kind-of Bojack Horseman-like world, with obvious parallels with real world history and culture, but there is always some kind of creative twist on them (kind of mixes up Victorian era, and the periods between 1920s-1960s, all the best "detective story time periods"), so it still feels somewhat alien, and always spiced it with some fantasy details of the wilderness.The ending - I felt - was a bit rushed, but still, it was an epic journey.Bigger, better and darker than "Paint it Red!", I really hope that you'll make this a trilogy, even though this might conclude the story.

_childDocuments_.review:
Chicken Police - Into the HIVE! is a character-driven, story-rich, film-noir detective adventure in which you must uncover a complex, world-scale conspiracy by gathering clues, interrogating suspects, and solving puzzles.

Sonny and Marty, the Wilderness's toughest detectives, are about to embark on the biggest case of their lives, which will take them through the insect underworld and force them to face the darkest reaches of their past.

The soul of the game is the characters that bring it to life. There are over 30 deeply fleshed-out characters to talk to, all of them handcrafted and 100% voice-acted. The Wilderness is a world with a history that goes back thousands of years and is full of fascinating facts and mysteries. Explore the city of Clawville and with it the colorful cultures, traditions, desires, and fears of its anthropomorphic inhabitants.

In Clawville you go wherever you want. Alongside the main story, explore a myriad of side quests, pathways, and opportunities, solve problems in different ways, and play the adventure over and over again to unravel every last thread and secret.

You're in for a story that will affect the fate of a whole city, even the whole world, and yet it's also very real and 'human'. Murder, betrayal, conspiracy, loss, friendship, and even love await you in this dramatic and absurd adventure.

name: Arco
detailed_description: Arco is a Mesoamerican fantasy RPG where each fight is a handcrafted bullet-hellish maelstrom that you must solve through clever use of your skills, items, and environment. While exploring the world, your narrative choices affect whether the combat skews more turn-based or real-time. Guide four indigenous heroes through intertwining stories as you battle monstrous creatures, rival nations, and greedy colonizers. Choose peace or choose violence but not all threats can be reasoned with…and all roads in Arco lead to revenge. On a llama. Features: Simultaneous turn-based system that requires tactical planning while staying quick on your toes. Intertwined stories with 4 different characters, each with their own unique skill tree and playstyle. Choices that impact the narrative as well as the gameplay. Handcrafted fantastical world with 200+ locations, 50+ enemies, 100+ items, 100+ skills. 2 hours of captivating soundtrack. It will break your heart and then heal it. Get cursed, run from your demons, slap monsters, and break your neck trying to discover secrets. Llamas.

_childDocuments_.review: I've seen the dev mention that this game, while well reviewed, has not sold well. What a sad state the industry is in when originality, polish, and good writing aren't rewarded. I played the demo for this (an incredibly generous demo in terms of content, and very polished too) a few weeks before release, and after i completed it, I would have pre-ordered the main game immediately had it been available to do so. Nonetheless, I made sure to purchase as soon as I saw it released, and I do not regret it for one moment.This is definitely one of those games which feels like it should have cost more once you start playing it. The story and world-building are rich, the characters are flawed and interesting, and the core gameplay mechanic  is difficult, but not punishing (so far, I have been able to restart or abandon every fight).I want to engage with the world of Arco the way i haven't with a game for a long time. That is a big achievement with an art style as simple as this one (but also the art is incredible in its own special way). Although I'm sure nothing speaks as loudly as money when you are trying to run a business, I hope the devs wont stray too far from what makes Arco, for me at least, an instant classic, when it comes time for their next project. Un-creative companies can make games, but they cant make art.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly? This was at first a pity purchase after seeing an article praising this game, yet pointing out the poor numbers.However, this turned into something I didn't expect.I'd want to play this longer before I leave this review, but this game completely ripped my attention from my current Kingdom Come and Alan Wake playthrough, and I wanna get the word out. It's been a while since I encountered a pixel art indie game that doesn't detract from i's own artistic value by being a low count pixel art game, because the narration does more to add to the characters than any sort of "HD-2D" art style ever could.It's also been a while since I encountered an indie game that so skillfully blends a story driven approach, to a genuinely fun gameplay loop that takes advantages of all the items you find on your journey - whether they're acquired through exploration, or story beats.I'm deeply invested and I hope Arco gets more attention in the future. This is lovely original work that brings me back feelings I thought I'd lost regarding "tiny discoveries", like finding out about Firewatch and Undertale for the first time many years ago.-Post ending edit-Some feedback for the developer in regards to what needs work:UI requires a bit of rework - sometimes the game can't decide whether the player wants to make a move on the battlefield vs wanting to interact with the UI. Some distinction or way of understanding what works/what doesn't in regards to not pressing accidental buttons would be helpful.There are a few dialogue bugs which don't make sense in a "this character shouldn't be here" way.11/28/2024 editCame here to update that among all the games that I FINISHED this year (47 of them), this and Jumping Flash (PSX 1995) are my games of the year.This game is good. Get it.

_childDocuments_.review: I like tactical turn-based games, especially low-randomness ones (favorite: Into the Breach). The pixel art here is gorgeous and the worldbuilding is great. Unfortunately I've bounced pretty hard off the gameplay; I'm not sure I'll come back to it (halfway through act 2).- Maybe I've missed something in the options or tutorializing but there is a lot of ambiguity in the turn resolution despite knowing what each enemy will do. Examples: an enemy is shooting me this turn and I have defensive abilities; will their shot actually reach me this turn? I'm using a "faster than ranged" melee attack but have to close on a ranged enemy; whose attack gets off first?- The "real time" ghosts really drag down the tactical decisions, especially if you're trying to juggle more than one character in combat (which makes commands harder to issue accurately); thematic but increasingly unfun.- Battles can last quite a lot of turns, with a significant chunk of those turns being stalling/defensive turns; retrying longer battles really becomes a drag, and it often felt like there were only a few viable options for approaching them.- Once the gameplay began moving away from ranged skills the combat became even less fun for me.I'm glad the game has an overall positive rating, and I only share this review in the hopes it helps others to cage their expectations. I thought it would be a game for me, but it wasn't quite.

_childDocuments_.review: is a dynamic tactical RPG set in a beautiful pixelated world in which your choices shape the world and your characters.There are three different tales that you experience slowly throughout the game but all three stories follow the same goal: Taking revenge on the red company which has been ruining the peaceful world of  in many ways.All playable characters of  are different and come with somewhat unique gameplay styles. The story itself is straight forward but enjoyable. Is it predictable? Yeah, probably but all the choices you make as a player will have an impact on your character and potentially make the game harder or easier.I was very excited to get my hands on  ever since I saw the first trailers and playing the demo of it earlier this year made me even more excited for it. is a neat game and it took me about 12 hours to complete my first playthrough and I probably missed a few things considering that people on the steam forum talked about something that I wasn’t quite aware yet, also, looking at my achievements after finishing the game for the first time, leads me to believe that  could need two playthroughs to really see and experience everything it has to offer.The combat is one of the main gameplay loops this game has and it’s semi tactical and reminds me a lot of Super Hot. You can plan ahead your moves in a tactical manner but as soon as you move, everyone and everything is moving too which makes the combat very dynamic. Despite the combat being fluent it can be somewhat frustrating – let me explain: You can win most combat encounters by kiting the enemies around since you have to spend mana to attack but you regenerate it by moving around or waiting. Some of the characters have ranged attacks which makes the combat quite easy but some characters have melee attacks which makes the combat a bit harder because kiting without getting hit is a bit harder. This will get better later on because the more experience points you get from combat, or other events that you will encounter while exploring in , the more active and passive skills you will unlock.On the flipside, if you have more characters in your posse, you can move them individually during combat and you can combine some of the attacks with each other which leads to lethal outcomes most of the time.Another side of the combat is the little ghosts that start popping up here and there. Those ghosts are your manifested guilt that move during the tactical phase of the combat which makes it a bit more hectic since they attack you while the combat is paused. The idea of having such a mechanic is nice but there are situations in which having such a mechanic is more annoying than anything else, especially during Act 3. I’m not sure if you could commit to a complete evil playthrough of  because the manifested guilt might just overwhelm you eventually.What is combat without boss fights, eh? Well, fighting bosses are mostly just okay. They are nothing special and that’s fine. Some bosses take a few tries because of the length or because you messed up crucial things but you will be able to beat them eventually without sweating too much.The exploration portion of  is minimalistic but it works well. You move from map to map and most maps have some secret stashes that you can loot. The dialogue is good. The story is decent. The pixel graphics are pretty and the soundtrack is an absolute banger in it’s own way. Is  worth to pick up? I would say so yes. You get at least 12 hours of content for 17,99€ which is a fair deal in my opinion, especially since you can play through it again because I’m sure you probably missed out on a few things in your first playthrough.The story of the game combined with the combat and the simplicity of the movement and exploration just makes this a very nice and special game.  is a little gem with a tiny number of flaws and I’m glad that I’ve played it.“” – UnknownIf you found this review helpful, feel free to visit my  page.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game. Basically impossible to put down. A well-realized South American-inspired fantasy mythos unafraid to confront you with the horror of colonialism. Tight, challenging strategy gameplay. Works perfectly on controller or Deck.(I really really really wish hitting the Select button once didn’t restart your fight with no confirmation. I’ve lost so much progress to this. Disabled gamers may want to know that there’s a later mechanic that makes you take damage if you don’t make turn-based selections quickly enough.)
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: I'm only just halfway through the second chapter, but I already love this game for its unique combat system! It's like if Into the Breach and Enter the Gungeon had a baby, which sounds insane, but it feels just as tight as those two without compromising the strategy or the action of it.The story so far has been really charming, hard to judge so early on but the setting is interesting, mixing different elements of mesoamerican and south-american cultures with a western flavor. Everything is very tactful, I got a kick out of finding accurate depictions of food and naming conventions I know of.Lastly, I want to praise the art direction. The character's sprites are deceptively simple, but the way they animate and how they are put together to populate these grand environments makes the world feel alive in a way that stands out from other games with similar pixel-art styles.All in all, the novelty of everything I've played and seen here makes it easy for me to recommend, and the quality so far has been great.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: Arco is a magnificent game, and you, dear reader, should play it.The fundamental reason is the storytelling: it combines the vibes and pulpiness of a vengeance western with a nuanced and very human look at colonisation and the price of resisting it. It also does it in a world that is not portrayed as a sort of suffering grimdark horror tale, but as somewhere with real joy and hope and silliness and therefore a much more real sense of pain when the story shows how fragile those things are. I laughed at a donkey braying at me when I petted it too much, and a little creature that wanted to make a shop but only accepted sticks as currency, and at digging for supplies and finding an anachronistic toaster... and, equally, it hit hard when major characters died or you saw a burned village that you'd been talking to everyone in not so long before. People in the story are human and treated as such, and that in many ways makes the villains more frightening: the invaders and colonisers aren't zombies or a faceless horde, they're people. Which means they, in some way, and for myriad reasons, *chose* this. It's very good writing.The storytelling is also backed up by absolutely drop-dead gorgeous landscape pixel art. It's genuinely stunning and enormously evocative, and honestly part of me wishes there was a post-game where I could just wander the whole game world as a surviving character to go "ooooh" at the pretty scenery and make some bits of money and chat to the NPCs. Having a setting for a fantasy RPG (including fantasy creatures, ruined temples, quests, the works) that is so heavily rooted in south America is really refreshing rather than another implicitly pseudo-late-medieval-Europe knockoff, and I say that as a professional medieval historian!The combat gameplay is the bit that takes a little time to get used to, especially the meta-level where the expectation is that you might need to "rewind" from failed combats to rejig your inventory and skills before having another go - but the reason it takes time is mostly a good one, which is that the mechanics are very locked into how the game works and work with that. The gameplay is fun once you're used to it and offers quite a lot of pacy tactical puzzling as you go. Actually mechanising the characters' hope and guilt in manifested ways was also really interesting and I liked it a lot.So, yeah. This is probably one of the best indie games I've seen released in the last couple of years, and I really strongly recommend it to anyone who's inclined to have a go.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: Man I loved this game. Totally invested in the story, loved the character design and how each one had their own unique feel and play-style, great balance between overworld exploration and combat. I feel like it sort of ended too soon in terms of story and combat depth, but I can't complain too much, great time.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: Arco is a game that constantly feels on the cusp of being great. There's a lot to love here - fantastic art and music, a truly innovative combat system with an incredibly strong core, and lots of replay value - but the game also is very rough around the edges, from pervasive (albeit fairly minor) bugs and small mechanics that cause the game to go from fantastic to frustrating incredibly quickly.At the time of the review, I've played through the game twice - an average first playthrough probably will take between 8-12 hours depending on how much you want to poke around off of the main story. There's definitely a lot of replay value to this game - many things require two playthroughs to be seen, and there are many secrets and achievements to hunt - but I do wish the main game was a little bit longer. Arco has many clear strong points. Its art is consistently fantastic - another great example of how beautiful 2D games can be when they are made by great devs and a strong art team. Yet again, I'm left wishing that AAA game development would move away from huge, 90 GB games that lag out machines that are even just a little old and towards more of these beautiful, stylish works of art that the indie and small games scene has been creating for years.The gorgeous art is matched beat for beat by some fantastic music. In general, the audio design throughout the game is stellar, from the main OST to the little flourishes that dot the game's menus and interactions. These little details are what separates a good game from a great game, and I'm very happy to say that the devs did a great job with the SFX.Ultimately, these have to be supported by a foundation of strong gameplay, and Arco's is nothing short of innovative. There really is nothing like it - you have to play it to get it. This feels like the first game of a type, a revolutionary way to visualize moment-to-moment combat in continuous space. The game makes use of geometry and travel time to bend the way you conceptualize fights and make it feel as if no matter how stacked the odds are against you, there's always a line to win every fight. The game also pulls a trick out of Undertale's book and starts throwing enemies that move during the planning phase at you as well, so tension is always high despite it being a turn-based system. I hope more games pick up on this type of combat - I think that Arco's abilities explore this space well, but there's so much more potential to be found here.However, this is where some of the issues with the game start to show. While the combat is interesting and novel, it can also be inconsistent and frustrating at times. Especially since the game has a bad habit of just... executing your action immediately instead of giving you some time to confirm a planned move, there are a lot of fights that I had to reset due to the game jumping the gun (or failing to) with regards to my turn. In addition, while the freeform combat is on the whole a welcome change from rigid grid systems of yore, it can also add a lot of confusion based around timing. Too often, I would have no idea if an attack would go off before an enemy's (thus interrupting a lethal attack and gaining the upperhand) or after (in which case I would have to reset the fight) and it meant I would either have to play super passive or risk losing due to not knowing the order that things would execute. Having a way to see this before locking in my move would be incredibly appreciated since part of the upside of a turn-based combat system is actually getting to strategically plan around the enemies' move. I think that these are all things that are very fixable and don't detract too much from the generally positive combat experience.The ability trees are alright. It's a pretty standard progression system without too much to talk about. There are definitely many viable abilities to choose from, although I found myself just defaulting to the most utility-heavy ones since they tended to just be a bit overtuned in my experience. There's 2 bosses in Act IV and I literally never saw either of them attack once since one of the characters comes with an infinite combo at base. Definitely some tuning that could be done there (although an optional side boss in the chapter demonstrates that good fight design can help a lot by rendering the ability to perma-stun just one enemy over and over pointless). The story is serviceable, albeit linear. While I understand that the game has a grimmer tone, the lack of any contrast means that by the end of the story, the tragedy just kind of becomes background noise. I think there are other games with a similar aim in storytelling that do a much better job of making the tragedy hit harder by investing more in giving their characters moments to shine outside of the oppressive system, only to pull them back in harder and faster. Also, for a game that advertises that "Your choices matter (ooooOOoo)" they really tended to not in the grand scheme of the storyline. Compared to games like Fallout: NV where the world is ready to bend pretty drastically based on your actions, Arco's world feels like it converges back to the main story very quickly.While I have yet to do much secret hunting, I'm a little torn on how some of the secret hunting works from my experience going through two playthroughs. On one hand, the game does reward careful observation of background details and paying attention. On the other hand, getting some of the secrets and achievements can feel very obtuse and frustrating. I think compared to a game like Tunic, Arco's secrets feel a little less designed around the player experience. Tunic's secrets are great because as the player, I always have faith that I DO have the tools I need to find something and make progress on a puzzle. With Arco, there are times where I KNOW that I'm close but the game just... doesn't acknowledge it, or generally makes it unobvious whether or not I'm making progress. Maybe my opinion on this will change as I play more and find more endings, but as it stands I don't really enjoy the process of achievement/secret hunting so far.TL;DR - Arco is a strong 7/10 game with a really unique combat system and great art/music. It's a little short for the price point and rough around the edges, but it has a nice core that shines with the creators' passion.

_childDocuments_.review: inventive combat system that puts pressure on the time you spend between moves, resulting in a rhythm that feels less tactical and more like chrono trigger's atb system -- it's like watching a shootout unfold in bullet time. also love the way it handles its setting and themes re: guilt and cyclical colonial violence. cute lizard enemies, too
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: Great game! Buy it if you're on the fence. It's worth full price.Pros:-~20 hours of gameplay for one playthrough-Engaging story-Lots of secrets and meaningful choices-Deep battle system with skill unlocks based on experience gained from battle or story events. Build your characters the way you want to play. You can make some very over powered characters with the right skills and equipment.-Exploration is rewarded and with cool equipment, secret bosses, alternate story paths, and experience-Beautiful pixel art and animations in a minimalist style-Challenging but forgiving difficulty (Use your items!)-Great musicBugs/Issues:-Game stutters when too many elements are around for a battle. This usually isn't an issue, but if you gain a lot of "guilt", enemies and hazards can start to overwhelm the screen causing some lag-Sometimes a communicated hitbox is the wrong size, or an enemy will hit sooner than expected if you're too close. Quality of Life:-The main menu cannot be accessed from the battle screen, so you can't save, load, or escape until the battle is over or you retreat.-Only three "permanent" save files. Autosaves happen automatically at unclear intervals and may get overwritten. IDK if this is intended. It definitely makes you commit to your choices, but I would have liked at least 5 permanent save files. Likely a larger issue if more than one person wants to play the game.I suspect the issues will be fixed soon, but even with the above issues I had a great time with the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: I've only played a little bit so far but I love it already. (Beaten Act 2 and completed the demo. EDIT: Completed the game. It holds up!!) This game is turn-based but it's FAST. Fast combat, fast UI, fast dialogue. It gets to the point. It knows what you're here for.It's also really funny for my battle-hardened rebel with a thick bushy mustache to have a dialogue box that's just ">:(". The writing, for how concise it is, has a lot of humor packed into it just by how it phrases things.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game. Gave it a try after seeing the combat, and it's better than I imagined. Fun, hard and rewarding with a very original turn based system.Also was surprised with a very interesting story with actual dialogue options and different ways of advance and discover secrets. Loved the songs, specially the singed ones.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: Came across this game after seeing an article where the developer complained that having made an original and interesting game that few people bought, he would've made much more money creating a half baked rogue like deck builder game instead. As someone who plays a lot of rogue like deck builders I decided to check it out - frankly hoping that this game wouldn't be anything special so I could leave a snarky review. Unfortunately, I'm disappointed to admit that this game actually IS extremely well made and original. Worse, it's also a ton of fun and has made me realize how unpolished the last couple of rogue like deck builders I've played are in comparison.Quality speaks for itself in the end. The only other game I can think to compare Arco to is Mother 3, with the emotional themes and cowboy aesthetic - and the similarities end there. It's too bad, I wish there were more games out there like this.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: If you really like what you see and Arco is looking like your kind of game then definitely give it a shot. There were some real high moments with the turn-based combat, especially with the more difficult fights.My biggest issue with this game is that I think the writing is just not very good. The prose lacks flavour and the dialogue is extremely dull. The use of language feels kinda 21st century, like the person who wrote the dialogue and descriptions hasn't read a lot of books, which is poor criticism as I can't know how well-read the writer is, but that's definitely what it feels like.I think the story and rpg elements are serviceable, and I think some people would like them. some moments really irked me, such as picking out some gold teeth from a skeleton causing my 'guilt' (a mechanic that causes more ghosts to spawn in combat) to build up, but the story suggesting I be a complete murder hobo to people I don't like doesn't regularly cause my 'guilt' to pile up.Additionally I think the ghosts that appear in combat and act as enemies unaffected by the turn-based system are not a great addition. I'm not sure for what reason they were put in but they force you to make decisions quickly in a way I really didn't appreciate. They also gain gimmicks in the different Acts of the story which make them more annoying to deal with. Luckily there's a gameplay option to remove the ghosts
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: Phenomenal game. It's remarkable how little this game needs to make you connect with it's world and characters. I was on the edge of my seat the entire time. The combat is deep and rich, the characters are engaging, there is a great amount of ludo narrative. A remarkable amount of things that happens in the story is reflected in gameplay and vice versa. In short ARCO is a good game, well worth the cost. I would have bought it for more easily.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: I want to preface this review by saying that this game is not terrible, I was just fairly disappointed with this game, especially the combat and story... or lack thereof. I also wasn't a huge fan of the art style/aesthetic, so I was really hoping that either of the former would carry this game for me. Unfortunately, the combat, story, and just all around RPG elements felt extremely shallow.Combat:The combat system as a whole felt extremely interesting and smooth, until you get out of "act 1", or what is really just the prologue. The skill trees are fairly bland and none of the skills are any sort of flashy. Ranged seems to be the only real way to play the game as melee feels vastly underpowered by comparison. In the tutorial you're taught about interrupting enemies by hitting them.. and then given a simple melee attack that deals a single damage and interrupts for a small amount of magia. This is, in hindsight, probably the best melee attack that the game can offer since any other melee attack either does no damage, or does not interrupt, or costs significantly more magia. Ranged attacks were pretty effective, until you realize that every attack costs a significant amount of magia in order to use, so you either need to run for 3+ turns (the only realistic option), or stand still a turn and get 3 magia back so that you can use an attack once every other turn. Additionally all of the dodge options are interesting at face value, but in practice they're very fringe-case usable, aside from just dash simply because it costs no magia.It was also impossible to evaluate fights before they started. The amount of enemies you fight never matched what was visible before the fight started, and frequently enemies would spawn over the course of the fight, which you have no possible way of knowing will happen or not. Didn't feel very proper for a game that seems like it wants to be fairly tactical.Story:The game felt as if it had no story. You're basically chasing after some bandits that did a bad thing to the village that you met for about 1 minute before leaving it since there's only like 3 NPC's to interact with, and then you're in what feels like an extremely simplistic CRPG, with most of the RPG elements removed. There is no equipment, you pretty much pick up exclusively food and some sellable valuables, and a couple equippable items that aren't really that interesting unless you like using grenade-esque items in games, or extremely lackluster buffs. Small side-note relating to the buff items... most of them work for 3 turns. It's effectively impossible to attack more than one time in 3 turns unless you have an extremely perfect setup, at which case you can only attack twice in a row. Why not just make them work for the next 3 attacks instead of 3 turns? Feels like that dynamic was not thought out well enough.Anyway, the story just didn't feel that interesting. Side quests were all fairly bland as well, mostly just "go kill these lizards" and an escort quest or two, etc. Maybe  interesting quests exist, but I found none of them in my 2 hours of gameplay.Soul Weight Mechanic:If you've played the game you know what this is referring to. This mechanic is interesting in idea, but in execution it didn't feel very well thought out. A "bad decision" is basically anything that might satisfy your curiosity as someone who likes RPG's, or just trying to explore all of your options. The ghost mechanic I actually liked at first, I actually wish it would show up even without you making bad decisions, but it gets extremely annoying as soon as you end up with more part members to fight with.All in all, I can't recommend this game for it's current price tag. I picked it up on sale for around 16$, and I have since refunded it. At 5$ I would say this is probably worth your money, possibly also 10$, but for 25$ it is definitely too much.  The game does have a demo which is good, definitely try that out first to see if the game is for you or not.

_childDocuments_.review: INDIE HIDDEN GEM- unique battle game play- CHALLENGING BUT FUN (I find the mix perfect so expect death but u feel like a bad ass one man army after) - Rich in story and culture- choice feel like they matter alot - Fire ahh soundtrack - The artwork is 10/10- Doesnt feel repetitive as new elements are added in every battle ( I straight up lost all brain cells when i had to control two people as u have to double ur strategy at once but u can do some crazy combos)  - Level up tree for each character, changing their play style
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: Arco is a turn based RPG where you play as multiple characters who end up banding together to take down the Red Company which is a group that are trying to settle in their lands and will not think twice about killing the natives to take their land.The story is engaging and your choices effect the combat as well as the plot, if your character feels a lot of guilt they will be haunted by ghosts in battle meaning that you will have to make the turn quick as the ghosts can move in realtime as you plan your next turn. We get to see the origins for each character and why they set out on a quest for vengeance.The combat is fun and the different characters have different skill trees. When you combine them in battle it's a lot of fun trying to dodge the bullet hell style projectiles and get off combos without taking any damage. Items such as poison and bombs can be thrown and consumables can be taken to give you an edge in battle. The combat provides a solid challenge from the start and the AI are quite strong in fights, this difficulty remains consistent throughout the game and there are no unfair spikes in my opinion.The graphics and art style of the game provide some beautiful environments to explore and there is a variety of different locations all visually interesting and unique littered throughout the game world. The soundtrack is also really good and has some relaxing tracks that play as you travel around the gameworld.The game was fun and there is no filler even among the sidequests. Highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to like this game - the concept, the story, the art are all great. The combat mechanics are unique and interesting, but the execution is poor. You perpetually are bringing a fist to a gunfight. I get that the developers are trying to promote player strategy, but it is like pulling teeth to extract any synergy between moves in the skill tree. Additionally, being melee only is extremely broken, considering there are many enemies who explode on death. Currently I am stuck in the arena because I have no ranged attacks and there's a bug that explodes at the end.Combat mechanic complaints:- Attack interrupts sometimes just don't interrupt. It's not made clear the precise timing around melee, ranged, etc attacks. It would be cool if timing was represented in the UI somehow (e.g. telling you how much damage you will take if you make a certain move).- There's a lot of player nerf. Either that or just lazy mechanics. For example, I got dodge roll thinking I could use that to dodge bullets, naturally. In reality, you quickly dodge roll for about half your movement range and then stand there, exposed, getting shot for 4s. Cool, so that's almost useless. Jump attack is interesting, but often the enemies I want to AoE hit the most are 'damage on touch' enemies (they damage you if you touch them), and yes, when you jump on them you take damage, even if you instantly kill them. Also, jump is not an instant dodge, you can still get hit before you jump. Throw is just about useless. In fact, a lot of stun attacks are often useless because they deplete your magia and you end up waiting out the enemy's stun just to recharge.- For a game that's a western-style shooter, there's almost NO cover for bullets. Every single time your player goes into combat, it's out in a stupid open plain, instead of, for example, around some rocks or interesting terrain (even destructible cover would be very welcome here). I think I saw a rock, like, once.- Barely any companion time. As I said, I'm currently at the arena and they let me fight for a companion for one of the rounds. The companion's moves had beautiful, excellent synergy for crowd control, evasion, etc (a powerful teleport and strong melee combo, as well as another combo that attacks, makes the target stuck, and jumps back instantly). Meanwhile, I am playing as a big punch lady (great character, very boring and unwieldy skill tree).- There's some hazardous plants which are neat except for this one mushroom that constantly damages you if you stand on it and it grows to take over the whole area in combat. I would be fine with this challenge IF it hurt enemies (or dealt only minor damage), but it doesn't! They're ALL immune! So if you have ranged attacks, it's fine, but for the biggest act in the game you are all melee (as far as I've played), so I would often get stuck a dozen turns in and have no way to fight an enemy that just hangs out in the sea of poison mushrooms shooting projectiles at me. Extremely stupid.- Ghosts are a neat mechanic but starting the game with guilt (and without clear ways to absolve guilt) sucks, and whenever you have a teammate the ghosts move even as you deliberate for your teammate whom the ghosts aren't targeting. There doesn't really seem to be an obvious solution, but it is very annoying to have this base penalty in the game and an hp tax for having a companion. Also, the black ghosts are supposed to die on hit, but sometimes, they just don't.- There is no combat log. Often I take damage and I have no idea why, it's unclear who hit me or how they hit me. It would really help to unravel the chaos with just a simple text combat event log, even if it appeared optionally.- Upgrades for attacks don't necessarily improve on the original attack, but are just a different attacks. Have been disappointed by this a number of times, as it hampers progression.Overall, lots of potential here, but unfortunately just a frustrating experience takes away from a lot of the fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: As a hobby game developer, I picked this game up because of its beautiful pixel art and it uses Love2D. I was not expecting one of the best tactics games I've played in years. The difficulty feels great paired with the auto-restart battles upon losing, the skills and dynamic abilities all feel distinct. Fantastic game, might be my favorite game of 2024.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely amazing art, every scenery and landscape is beautiful! Gameplay-wise it's a very fun game, with a lot of variety and different ways to handle a battle, and the story is very catching, with characters you easily get attached to. Overall I really love Arco, a beautiful game with a good, moving story in a very interesting setting!
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: I most likely have nothing to add to the conversation about this game that hasn't been said before, but I feel like I should leave a review anyway, because I really enjoyed playing it and will most likely play it again after some time to get all the achievements and try out any options I didn't pick the first time around.The combat system is incredibly compelling, I never got tired of jumping into fights and trying out new abilities, powers and items, facing off against varied and sometimes rather challenging enemies. The art style is simple yet detailed enough to fully immerse you in the world of the game and convey everything the player needs to know. The mythology is intriguing and is explored just enough to leave you wanting more while keeping most of its mystique intact. The story is strong enough to carry the narrative, and jumping between different characters keeps things fresh and interesting until the end. The music is astounding, clearly a lot of love was put into it and it shows, whenever the singer starts belting out lines about loss and hopelessness you can really feel the pain in her voice.It's just an absolutely fantastic game that excels in everything it set out to do.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a lot of strategic depth. The pause and run mechanic lets you set up actions and combos that are very satisfying to watch play out. Each character you control in your party have very unique skillsets that complement each other, and the skill tree gives you many options to play how you like.I was also really engrossed in the story. I like how each act takes you through a different character's perspective in their relation to the evil Red Company, before bringing them all together in the final chapter. This is a hidden gem, and I hope more people get to hear about this game!
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: I recall briefly checking out this game's page a while ago because I liked the artstyle, and yet when I saw "Turn-based Strategy" listed I was ready to turn away. Not exactly my cup of tea.On a whim I reopened it and saw a demo available- I'll give it a shot, I thought, maybe the art and the story can make up for that aspect and I'd trudge through it.I proceeded to play for 6 hours and finish the demo in one sitting, actively seeking out combat encounters at every turn. I was told the combat is more like 'real-time strategy' which is much more my speed. It is in turns, but things like positioning and timing play a bigger role, making the battlefield feel quick, more alive than I expected.That's not to mention the music and story. The soundtrack is amazing, able to immerse you in the story's grim determination, or blood-pumping action. The story itself has quite the voice, with characters strong and memorable. There's even the occasional addition of humor. The world is vibrant and beautiful as you make your way through, with even the smallest choices impacting the world in unmistakable ways.I'm excited to see what the rest has in store for me! Super cool game.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: Really great so far! I love how novel combat feels, how genuinely big the world seems. A perfect example of what's best about indie game development, why we need to keep exploring new kinds of games and try out new mechanics instead of just making the same thing over and over again. Can't wait to play more.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: Repetitive, frustrating, tedious. There's a lot of potential to the story concept, but I'm not playing any further to see if the story justifies the poor gameplay and unforgivably easy ways to permanently lock yourself out of story beats. Didn't get the lamb the first time before you meet the shepherd? Then you can go all the way back across the map, discover you needed to feed him blueberries, and bring him home, only for the shepherd's dialogue to be permanently locked out. Did you recruit the lamb before? Shepherd instantly recognizes him and brings him home, you get rewards, experience, a new party member! This is such an obvious oversight that it makes the game feel like QA didn't take a look. Did you find the shovel icon in the bandit camp? Well, don't worry - the expensive shovel you can buy later can't be used on it, but you can permanently lock yourself out of interacting with it ever again by having interacted with it once.Other complaints have already noted how the ghosts make playing with party members a discrete disadvantage, or how the fights are more like puzzles that you are obligated to play over and over and over again. Somehow, they offer both no challenge (you can restart endlessly) and ample dread (you have to restart endlessly).It's a pretty game, the music (except the battle music, since you'll hear it - and hear it - and hear it...) is lovely, the setting is appealing. But it's not fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: A very fun 10 hours of gameplay. Combat was challenging without being overwhelming or feeling like I wasn't ready for certain fights. The skill trees leave plenty of room for different tactics, while also having plenty of unique skills per character.Story and dialogue are compelling and I wasn't ready for the game to end.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: ARCO is a game that you start to play casually BUT, when you close it, IT WILL remain in your mind and make you go back and play again. It's not just fun, it's very well done, nice graphics and amazing music. The love poured on the making of this game can be seen/feel every second you spend with it. So, stop reading, buy and play it NOW!
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: A short, sweet game about revenge. The combat mechanics are pretty innovative, mixing real time with turn-based tactics. It's pretty fun, where you have to pay attention to what your enemy is doing but anything can be won with some patience. I hope this game does well. My only gripe is I wish they kept the arena mode from the demo. That would be cool.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: This is a moving story about revenge and its burden and cost. I finished it in 11hrs; currently I'm not sure how much replayability there is in it though a different review mentioned alternative endings and looking at the Achievements I've missed, I can believe it. For example, there is an Achievement for finding all three Obelisks (they're large, out-of-the-way evil creepy things with significant combats associated with them) and I only found one, and given the game's chapter/character structure I'm guessing there's one Obelisk for each of Acts 2-4... finding all three seems like it'd affect the ending. Maybe not. I'm replaying now to find out.Regardless, I don't regret the purchase: even if it's only one story, that story is a good one and you'll be happy you took it in. If I never played it again I'd still say I got my money's worth.The game itself has a relatively clever combat system that isn't terribly difficult if you're tactically-minded; it comes with a combat replay feature for you to try over if you're killed. The music out of combat is good, and the music within the various specific scenes is fantastic. The combat music, however, isn't varied enough and you'll get tired of it by the end. I didn't find the game difficult; rather, I found it engrossing. I played it through in three days and if I was 30yrs younger I could've seen myself doing it in one.This is a real indie gem and a strong reminder of why games like this should be supported. _childDocuments_.review: I just finished playing this game. Here are my thoughts:The Story: This is obviously a story about the gold/oil rush from the perspective of indigenous peoples from Texas and the surrounding area during the gold/oil rush era. The prelude of Act I to set up Act II was phenomenal, but I wish the Sacred Tree had more of a presence throughout Acts III and IV. The story kinda felt like it lost its way through the middle sections of the game, but brought it back just in time for the ending. 7/10The Characters: Teco/Tizo: Fantastic story here from start to finish. This was the only character of the three that I genuinely felt attached to while playing this game, and I wish I had more time with him. Seeing his family decimated and one of the towns he stopped by as an adult set ablaze gave the story the emotional charge it needed. I will say that his abilities felt a bit underpowered compared to the other two, but perhaps that was a learning curve that I needed to adjust to as well as him being the first character one could play as. 9/10Itzae: To be completely honest, I don't see a reason why this character exists other than "I want to kill the Newcomers". I also didn't like how she responded in emotes and had "yas queen" responses (not saying her personality was bad overall, but these responses were certainly out of place). Sure, she fills in the void of "tank" in the party, but I never really understood why she had to be there. Even her ending was pretty uninspiring. Her gameplay was decent, if a bit on the easy side. 5/10Chio: I definitely enjoyed Chio's personality much more than Itzae's, and her banter with her brother was a refreshing change of pace. Being able to teleport alongside Afur made for a very interesting act. However, even though there was a very emotionally charged battle at the end of act 4, her brother's sudden passing at the end felt incredibly shoehorned. 7/10Overall: 7/10The Battle System: Amazing. This was a fantastic take on a turn-based strategy game. The ghosts kept me on my toes and I had to make snap-decisions in order to avoid taking damage. I didn't think many fights were unfair, per se, though my biggest troubles were against the crabs. I also wasn't aware of how short each act would be, so I tended to hoard consumables rather than breeze through them. EDIT: I also forgot to include that the AOE indicators are not a perfect match with their actual hitbox. This aggravated me on more that one occasion, and I think this should be fixed. 9/10The Music: Top-notch. Not much more to say here. Really loved the music that played in the Act IV fight. 10/10The Artwork:To be honest, I wasn't a fan of it at first, but it definitely grew on me after awhile. 8/10All in all, I had a great time with this game, and you should definitely try it if you enjoy strategy games. It reminded me a bit of Frozen Synapse, which was a fun game to play back in the day. Overall: 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Arco feels like a game I should love, but the terrible execution of the combat is the sole reason why I can’t play anything past the first act. It’s a turn based strategy game, but the catch is that turns happen simultaneously a la Frozen Synapse. And actions taken during the game will weigh on your character, and take the form of ghosts that will chase you down while time is paused, forcing you to act quickly. Combine that with a western setting with beautiful pixel art and music, and a compelling story (at least it seems like one from what little I was able to see before giving up), and I should be calling this my Game of the Year. But the combat is an insurmountable hurdle.All actions other than movement cost action points but in order to regain those points, you either need to run around or sit and wait, literally wasting turns. It’s also not clear how much time is spent during the turn actually performing the selected action. Some times it makes sense, like firing a bow and arrow taking longer to shoot a gun; but if I use a dodge roll I expect it to last the entire time, not the first half second and then my character stands there to get blasted for the remainder of the turn. It’s also not clear the direction that enemies are attacking you in, so you can make a move thinking “since this sharpshooter is aiming to his right, I can move to his left to avoid the shot” only for him to whip around and stop you in your tracks. And then some features seem to not work at all. I tried stunning enemies with items and abilities, thinking it would give me precious time to close the gap or line up an attack, only for them to immediately shoot me down on the next turn. The lack of information, on top of enemies often just jumping into fights mid-combat, completely ruins any kind of possible tactics and becomes trial and error. Apparently this was intentional, because the game will allow for fights to be restarted or for you to run away, but that only means you have to do the full fight the next time you come back to the area.Combat arenas and enemies are also just poorly thought out. Gun fights take place in wide open areas with little to no cover, so have fun waiting for the poor enemy pathfinding lead them into your extremely limited range, if they even decide to move at all. All of their guns have infinite range, so they can just sit across the map and shoot endlessly if they want, and some of them will. This bad pathfinding also makes the guilt ghosts a complete non-threat, and you can pretty much ignore them completely unless they spawn in an unfortunate place.As far as the guilt mechanic goes, it feels all over the place too. Instead of being an interesting accumulation of consequences for your actions taken during the game, it really just boils down to a simple morality system where the “good” choices don’t give you ghosts and the “bad” ones do. So you end up with situations like killing poachers and local wildlife that you disturbed with no remorse, but saying the wrong thing or stealing somehow weighing down on your conscious.As frustrating as this game is, I don’t regret buying it. There was potential here, and I hope the team that made this game gets another chance to improve in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: A very lengthy demo (three hours!) got me hooked on this game. If you are a fan of West of Loathing and/or Chroma Squad, those are the games that I was reminded of the most while playing this game. WoL for its sidescrolling "point and click" exploration, and Chroma Squad for its pixels and intricate battle mechanics (although Arco has a unique combat system unlike the other two.) It was also a little bit BG3/DND in it's "every round is 6 seconds", although in this it was more like 1 second per round. I really enjoyed solving the puzzle every combat represented, even when it took me several times to get an encounter right. It's so beautiful, and I had a great time admiring the way they were able to get so much out of such small sprites. I loved every character I spent time with, and the world building was so fun. The story was wonderful, and the music with vocals that came in at key moments was very emotional. Sometimes the battle music was a little repetitive, and there was a moment near the end where a song was playing during an important fight where the song cut out a while before the fight did and probably should have been looped. I would have also LOVED to see a "battle replay" option after combat, where the whole battle is shown without pauses (maybe sped up a bit?). It would be so fun to see how competent you look dodging bullets and hitting people in the midst of chaos. I'm looking forward to replaying this someday and making slightly different choices (and maybe trying to get all the achievements.)

_childDocuments_.review: An honestly surprisingly fun RPG game to play with; the combat is definitely fun with various builds (albeit perhaps not that balanced) and does not overstay its welcome; the story is good even though it doesn't really offer that many distinct narrative choices normally featured in other CRPGs. _childDocuments_.review: I expected a small adventure/tactics game, so I overlooked it initially. That was a mistake.Arco is a reimagined Final Fantasy, in a world founded on ancient Mesoamerican culture. The story is heartfelt and earns the emotions it reaches for by pushing you against a cruel, hard world and having you go through some brutal ordeals. The combat system is easy to get into and addictive. There’s so much to explore, so much charm in every handcrafted pixel landscape.Don’t sleep on it like I did. I highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best indie games I've played in 2024, hell I guess one of the best games in general. Don't let the graphics fool you on Arco, the simplistic pixel characters on the overhead while out of combat add to the charm as the entire landscape and surrounding areas are beautifully crafted to make this game so aesthetically pleasing. There is 5 acts, and each act (minus the first one and last one) took me about three hours to beat and during those acts you are learning the stories of multiple characters while traveling through the world. Choices matter A LOT and this game is an emotional gem while expertly crafting the three stories together and connecting it in the end.The combat and items are also top notch. I'm always hit or miss with turn based combat, but the SECOND I got into Arco I knew I was going to enjoy how it was setup. It's a combination of real time strategy with turn based that makes it so fun, and with that each character has an evolving skill tree to make them slightly stronger with new moves to attack, evade, or or help each other when the time is right. Besides moving your character from one place to the next and trying to find the right opening with your fist, arrow, or gun you also have a handful of items that can be equipped and used in battle with healing items, or items to hinder the enemy. I'm rambling, but this game is incredible. I love the story, combat, dialogue, and every single chapter in this game. I want nothing but success for the dev team behind this, and I truly hope this game gets more recognition, it deserves it.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: Brilliant game, very refreshing concept of the tactical battles which are part real-time and part turn based. I have only one small complain - I wish there was a game mode where I could create character build and take it to the combat without the need of going through the entire story. DOnt get me wrong, the story is awesome with many cool dialogues, but since I am very much into tactical battles I would really appreciate if I could freely experiment with different character builds.TLDR: Awesome game for all fans of tactical battles and pixel art.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: I don't write a lot of reviews, but this game deserves it.In a world of copy-paste, cookie-cutter AAA games, indie gems such as Arco really shine.This is currently my favorite game of 2024. The story is strong and heartfelt, the artwork is gorgeous, and the combat system is entirely unique. I'm a sucker for turned-based combat, but this game cranks the old formula up several notches. I found it to be fresh and exciting in ways that many turned-based games are not. You'll also play as a few characters, all with very different styles of combat and personality.The story is a spaghetti-western revenge tail combined with fantasy elements. It has detailed characters who you will quickly come to love and care about. It's a nice take on a classic trope.I've read that the developers are disappointed in sales, which is a real bummer, because this game deserves recognition and to profit. If we don't support creative indies, that well will eventually dry up and we'll be stuck with mass produced COD and Assassin's Creed clones. Those are fine, but they lack heart and they lack daring.If you like creative indie titles, if you like to support quality work, if you like westerns, if you like fantasy, if you like turn-based gameplay (that can actually be a little sweaty), if you like cute sprite animals, if you like humor, and if you can spare 20 bucks, do yourself a favor a grab this game!Lastly, always pack a shovel.

_childDocuments_.review: Delightful turn-based strategy game where everyone takes their turn at once. The pixel art is lovely, the story keeps you engaged, and I love the way it's presented. Each Act builds on the last not just in the fantastic Western Revenge story, but also in the builds and strategies you can use; You can feel the decisions you make in the story impact the strategic choices you get during gameplay. It's great fun. I'm about halfway through Act IV, and I can't wait for it all to come together so I can play it again and make different choices. Also everyone rides llamas, it's a yes from me.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: I'm halfway (I think!) through Act 3 and rahhh I'm having so much fun! I've followed this game for a while now and I am so happy it's lived up to my excitement for it! As a latin diaspora, I think it's so awesome to have a game with a meso/south american setting in a Western story. While the Western and cowboy genre always have an inherent tension in them due to the underlying themes of colonisation and first nations' genocide, this game subverts that by tackling those themes head on, as the protagonists all have a bone to pick with the colonisers that have displaced them from their homes. It's a really cool role reversal! It isn't just story that makes this game great, it's the gameplay. The game's combat really scratches my itch. It's both very challenging but also very forgiving in letting you try again with different items, skills, leaving the combat encounter with no penalty, and even restarting the fight at any time. It gives the game a very puzzle-like feeling where I will retry battles so that I take the least amount of damage and maximise the use of my abilities. It's both satisfying and addicting.This game has given me multiple emotions already with it's music and graphics. They atmosphere in this game is so beautiful. It's also one I can see myself revisiting again! While Acts 1 and 2 feel pretty linear, in Act 3 it feels like things really split, so I'm excited to do repeat playthroughs of this game to see all the stuff I missed. Especially in spanish! I'm very much looking forward to the latin american translation!Definitely worth the look. PLAY IT!!!!Also TIP: Make sure to use your items and money liberally as they don't carry between acts. Just use the dynamite, bro

_childDocuments_.review: Really lovely game. The setting is very unique for games: it takes place in a magical realist Latin America during Spanish colonisation and plays it as a sort of "inverted Western". The writing is just fair, but the setting more than makes up for it. The combat system also inverts the "real-time with pause" of games like the original Baldur's Gates or Pillars of Eternity and makes it instead "pause with real-time" a la Superhot and it's a lot of fun to play around with (I wish the game played back the combats in real time, which seems like a real missed opportunity. Give it a GIF export button, it'd be all over Twitter!) It also doesn't overstay its welcome, which is extremely refreshing. The weakest parts are the UI and especially the inventory, which feel particularly underbaked. The pixel art almost suits the game, but I also think it would be better with almost any other art style. The music is lovely, though.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the truest examples I've seen of video games as an art form. You can really tell everyone involved with this game is deeply passionate about it. The visuals and sound design are incredible, and the gameplay is a unique take on turn-based strategy that I haven't personally ever seen before, but I absolutely love it.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: Very interesting game. Quite short, but worth the play. Setting, art direction, music, and story are so good and unique: charming glorious pixel art meets bloody meso-american western. It portrays and discusses the evils of colonialism but not that deeply because of its laser-focus on the revenge saga.The gameplay truly elevates this title with how well it's put together. Its approach to the gridless strategy genre is refreshing. You have to carefully consider trajectories, action costs, and the build you made for each character. Very tactical while being very action-y.Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: I was hesitant to play this game because the trailer looked a little slow, but I'm glad I gave it a chance. The gameplay is unique and makes you think.
