_childDocuments_.review: is a brand new game from Coal Supper, creators of The Good Time Garden. Describing itself as a ‘slapformer’ the game sees players explore the Northern English town of Barnsworth, seeing the sights, and taking on a variety of odd jobs for the locals.It is a brilliant game that offers fun cartoon visuals, a nostalgic and evocative soundtrack, top-tier voice acting, well-written dialogue, and non-stop laughs. It has little to no difficulty and maintains laid laid-back, casual feel throughout, prioritising humour and narrative above challenge, which is in no way to its detriment.It was fun to see a couple of easter eggs, and nostalgic nods to the developers’ first game The Good Time Garden. This new title maintains the same level of surreal nature and rude comedy but has a much broader scope in terms of narrative, characters, and playable environment. Coal Supper are establishing themselves as absurd auteurs and their titles are instantly recognisable as their own.I thoroughly enjoyed this game and can see it appealing to a wide range of players. It took around 3.5 hours to complete, is highly amusing and I’d recommend it to anyone looking for a few hours’ worth of interactive comedy.My full review of this game where I go into detail about gameplay, narrative, and styling is available on .

_childDocuments_.review: A slapstick comedy puzzle game set in fictional 1980's Britain, filled with more dry wit than you'll know what to do with. There isn't much in the way of gameplay—it's more like a tool for dispensing jokes rather than something to challenge the player—but the writing's more than good enough to make up for it. I just wish it was a little bit longer, because you're only looking at around a 2-3 hour runtime even if you go out of your way to try and see everything it has to offer.  is a comedy game where you, a nameless and inexplicably tiny salesman, get roped into a series of increasingly odd jobs in the fictional Northern English town of Barnsworth. At its core, it's a puzzle game revolving around the simple game mechanic of slapping things—seriously, like 95% of what you do is just walk up to things and push a button to slap them and see what happens. People, animals, public infrastructure, private property—you name it, you can slap it, and doing so will probably end up solving your problems for some reason or another.The basic gameplay loop is finding a resident that needs help with something, then exploring the much-more-literal loop that is the streets of Barnsworth to find whatever will help them with their request. It kind of gives me point-and-click adventure vibes at times, especially since you can slap almost everything for a silly reaction just like the old Humongous Entertainment games. These puzzles aren't exactly hard, but you'll need to pay close attention to what each character says so you know what you should be doing, because they typically won't repeat their instructions twice.Navigating the town can be a puzzle in and of itself, though not always the fun kind of puzzle. Barnsworth only has a few streets you're allowed to access, and you'll need to visit each one multiple times throughout your playthrough; but the catch is that when you cross into a new street, the path back is blocked and the path forward changes on every visit, so you might find yourself beating your head (or slapping your hand, I guess) against everything to find the new exit since it's not always obvious. The mild annoyance of this mechanic is offset by the fact that each return trip to a street brings new characters and new dialogue so it keeps this loop from feeling quite as monotonous.Those character interactions are where you'll find much of the game's charm as well as most of the jokes. Each one has their own unique personality, full voice acting, and simple but expressive design that feel like they could've been pulled right out of a kid's cartoon. Make no mistake, though: this is  a family-friendly game. There's a fair share of what they call "general mature content", like swearing and copious amounts of pub beer (two of UK's biggest exports, I believe); as well as a few, more egregious things like the crude depictions of one man's haddock and another man's pork and beans, so to speak. It's not exactly  or anything, but maybe don't give it to your kid without vetting it yourself first.The writing involves a lot of cultural references that might get lost on players that didn't grow up in the rather specific time and region this game loosely depicts, so you might miss out on some of the jokes if you can't relate. That said, there's still plenty to laugh at, as much of the comedy revolves around slapstick gags mixed with a healthy dose of dry wit. No matter how absurd a situation may get, there's this jovial but deadpan delivery to it all, as if the ridiculous stuff you're seeing is actually quite normal and you're the weird one for thinking otherwise. That juxtaposition is funny from start to finish, and it's not long before you'll be rolling with the punches like everyone else.Beating the game will probably take you around 2-3 hours, but you're encouraged to explore and interact with as much of Barnsworth as possible to extend your stay, with plenty of optional achievements to help incentivize you to do so. If you fancy yourself an achievement hunter, note that any you miss will require you to replay the game from the beginning to acquire them; and most of them are easy to miss if you don't already know what you're looking for. Just be diligent about interacting with everything and you should be able to find most of them; and don't be afraid to open the hidden achievements to view their descriptions if needed—I promise it won't spoil any big story events for you.Overall, I got about four hours out of it: three on my initial playthrough and an additional hour getting the last few achievements I missed the first time. I wish I could've gotten a bit more time out of it, but at least I can say that time was well spent.

_childDocuments_.review: Many people have compared this game to Untitled Goose Game however, whilst the settings are relatively similar, UGG was a quirky take on the stealth genre with some relatively interesting puzzles. I can't say the same for Thank Goodness You're Here. TGYH has little to no gameplay. You simply walk around a town 5 times slapping things to interact and initiate comedy scenes. There's no puzzles. No game. It's more of a loosely interactive movie. Overall it took me about 150mins to complete from start to finish - including unlocking a ton of secret scenes most players have missed. If you want an interactive movie experience with humour similar to something like Smiling Friends or Don't Hug Me I'm Scared it provides a nice little experience. If you want a something reminiscent of Untitled Goose Game I'd recommend giving it a miss.

_childDocuments_.review: "Thank Goodness You're Here!" is a delightful and quirky adventure that offers a fresh and humorous experience. Set in the peculiar Northern English town of Barnsworth, you play as a traveling salesman navigating a series of increasingly odd tasks assigned by the eccentric locals. The game's unique art style and witty dialogue create a charming atmosphere that keeps you engaged throughout. While the game is relatively short, with many players completing it in under two hours, its originality and humor make it worth the experience. If you're looking for something different and enjoy a good laugh, this game is a must-try.
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: Very much a bri'ish cartoon episode of a game, but that is what I want sooo thank you very much. Oodles of tiny quirks and references to it's island (See it, smell it, sorted) bring a local & regional charm to it - a glimpse of an absurdist depiction of living in some northern town, somewhere in the UK. Adoring the fat mono outlines & bold colors as your circle through Barnsworth as this little/tiny/quite suprisingly average-sized fella through scene to scene as call-backs occur, gags continue on or scenes turn to surreal crazyness. It is with these repeated visits that I kind of adore the game - the jokey writing on the wall, revisiting the oddball cast interacting with one another and seeing the devs comitting to every bit they start - gotta respect the jokster for using the rule of threes whenever they can. The DHMIS-esque crescendo of a song a perfect goodbye-wave to the grinning flavor of a game that is Thank Goodness You're Here.
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a big enjoyer of quirky adventure games and this sure is that. Be a little man. Slap your way through life. Traumatise a man with soot. Giggle when Matt Berry says "peans".This isn't a try-everything-on-everything adventure, nor are the puzzles thinky. The way forward is generally quite clear, but the enjoyment comes from the experience... and from slapping everything possible to catch a few easter eggs. The writing's great, the art style is colourful and characterful, and having it fully voiced really makes the setting. It's a couple hours of solid amusement.

_childDocuments_.review: My initial thought was that this was a cute - family friendly puzzle like game where I had to come help the people in the town. I was wrong. The amount of innuendo's + dark humour + puns, paired with the visual/dialouge - I can't tell what I liked more! The comedy in this game is peak! The artwork is very cute and the expressions are so appropiately paired up with the inappropiateness of the game. This is my kind of humour, like "I'm afraid this isn't a watering can *voice deepens* - it's a watering can't" or the "normal milk" - I had a really good laugh playing this game - and it's simple to play with minimal control usage. My favourite part was Jasper and his tools, but most of all - traumatising the chimney man (ifyky xD). This game was really fun to play!If you enjoy a bit of casual/puzzle games with simple keyboard mechanics - especially a game that's not too long, full of dark humour, sexual innuendo's, puns and whatnot - then I highly recommend this game for you! The artstyle is pretty good, and so is the music/SFX. From facial expressions, tone, dialouge and actions - you'll really have a good laugh. The only thing that traumatised me in this game was the jumpster captain - but otherwise, definitely worth having a look at! :)

_childDocuments_.review: Imagine hearing about a hilarious worthwhile British comedy film that is generally revered - and then watching only half of it. This game has plenty of charm and a cute art style to boot; but generally amounts to being wasted on silly voices and jokes about arse and balls. I will admit my time with this game was enjoyable, but by the time you start actually getting into it, it chucks a long-winded annoying 4 minute musical segment at you and then credits roll.If it had the replayability of say untitled goose game, or actually had genuine laugh-out-loud moments throughout - it would still be a short dissapointment. This is an enjoyable and silly 2 hour story that really should cost 10 bucks at most - but it leaves you wanting more and by the time the credits end, you regret spending money on something as costly as a meal for two; yet it only satisfies as much as an appetizer.

_childDocuments_.review: Not for many years have I ever been so compelled to leave a recommendation for a game so early into its playthrough, but Thank Goodness You're Here! breaks the cycle. TGYH! is a short comedy adventure game with platforming elements, and many visual gags in styles reminiscent of classic British humour.With so many little details present in the world, such as a "Piss Poor" food hygiene rating for a restaurant, or Today's Special for the pub being "Drinks", I've had an amazingly entertaining few hours while playing this through on my Steam Deck.Incredible voice talent is featured across the title, featuring the likes of Matt Berry and many others, including the game devs themselves! There are so many charming characters to come across throughout the game, with elements of progression with things like ongoing dialogues, which adapt and evolve over the course of the game.The game runs brilliantly too, with no issues aside from some delayed subtitles during the cutscenes. A consistent 90fps from start to finish when playing through on my Steam Deck, with a wide variety of resolutions to pick from. I enjoyed the language options between British English and true Northern slang too!If you've a yearning for British deadpan comedy, and multiple subtle visual gags, then Thank Goodness You're Here! won't let you down. While not as long as other people may expect, this casual comedy is an easy 10/10 from me.
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: Why don't more games like this exist. Such a neat and fun experience. Great art style that works perfectly with the humor of the game.I'm not normally someone who cares about achievements, but I had to go back and get every achievement for this wonderful game.I wish nothing but ridiculous success on these devs and I hope they make more titles like this.Runs perfect on Steam Deck too.Still great.
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is full of life. Every detail in "Thank Goodness You're Here!" is immaculately thought out as it invites everyone to fully and authentically join the fun - I don't think I've ever laughed so much while playing a game. Every character has something unique to offer to the inter-weaving stories, whether it's a visual gag, play on words or bizarre revelation. As a person who grew up in a Yorkshire town not too dissimilar to the fictional Barnsworth, there is an additional layer of nods, winks and cultural references to that corner of the world which made me very happy. As well as the characters, setting, gameplay, soundtrack and story all being excellent, the voice acting deserves a special mention. While it boasts an appearance from the multi-talented Matt Berry, the entire voice cast is on top form, delivering lines with perfect comedic timing. "Thank Goodness You're Here!" is a true joy to experience and an ode to cosy, British silliness.
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: As a Lancastrian, the hapless folk of Yorkshire are, of course, my rightful ancestral foes. It was therefore with a mixture of horror and disgust that I saw this game appear, and I think it only fair to give my entirely fair and impartial view.As expected, the game is puerile, absolutely full of innuendo, entirely ridiculous, packed full of absurd dialect, features a cast of ludicrous simpletons with preposterous and almost completely pointless things to ask you to do, and everywhere you look there is some form of reference, pun or sight gag that the devs clearly believe to be funny. I simply cannot properly express how much I resent that they are absolutely right because it is very very funny indeed, this game is brilliant and I am enjoying it immensely. It is frankly a crime against nature that I should be so entertained by something that is so Yorkshire, and I am now in hiding from the Lancastrian authorities who I fear will now strip me of my Red Rose and my George Formby collection. Curse you, Coal Supper, I fear I will now have to monitor all of your future output to ensure you never do anything like this again.
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game specifically because it was mentioned by Lucy on the “Friends per second“ podcast. I’ve never been to the UK, but I am pretty open-minded when it comes to comedy. I still had an absolute BLAST running through this glorious morsel of a game.The jokes, both verbal and visual, Will probably land with more impact if you are a UK native, but I found myself laughing out loud and grinning with delight At the unfortunate series of events that follow the protagonist from the second they leave their office to the roll of the credits. My significant other Couldn’t help but join in the spectacle as she ordered Me to slap every trash bin and pigeon around town, both of us surprised by the amount of variety that can be packed into these few short hours. I absolutely recommend this game if you are looking for something lighthearted, low stakes, low brow, and highly British.  We need games like this to remind us that the industry is not all about million dollar AAA safe bets that push out mostly the same experience year after year. COAL SUPPER likely knew that this game would not be for the majority of gamers. This is something crafted for a niche audience. A specific experience that will mean a lot to a small group of people, and they still chose to develop and publish a game like this. these guys should be praised and supported long into the future. Long live Indies. 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: What do you get when you try to make Viz comic-meets-'Don't Hug Me I'm Scared' but fail? This game. I went in knowing nothing bar the title and some positive buzz, having been kindly gifted the game by a friend. I wanted to like it. I was ready to like it. I played it all the way through. I admired the technical skill and artistic craft that went into the game. I appreciated the archive footage of a Britain I just about remember, the place so perfectly parodied in the Scarfolk books. I went into the game ready to eagerly engage.And I hated it. I laughed - well, grunted - three times, and smiled four throughout the whole experience. By the 2 hour mark I was begging the game to end. TGYH is *very* convinced of its own hilarity and will yell it in your face. It's got comedy music! It's got a cast entirely made of grotesques! 'LOL so random' humour! Animal whimsy! Imagine a papercraft The League Of Gentlemen but with the edgier jokes removed! If the prospect of that causes you to develop a low-level tension headache, you have an idea of how this game may make you feel. It took me about 10 minutes for a weary dismay to set in that wouldn't leave me until the end credits. A whole bunch of the voice acting is horribly overdone in a way I haven't experienced in a game since the atrocious 'Candace DeBebe's Incredibly Trick Lifestyle', and it kills the gag every time. It's the "funny" voice, a kind of strained semi-shout that reeks of comedy stillbirth Bo Selecta. The jokes would have landed better if they'd just got some locals from Ossett or Goole to read the lines straight.Save yourself some time and money and play Untitled Goose Game instead.
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: Do you like quirky, cozy little games with an outstanding, cheeky sense of humor? Because that's exactly what you'll get with Thank Goodness You're Here.While the game itself is only a few hours long, it's absolutely worth the price of entry. I couldn't stop laughing as I played through. Not to mention the fantastic job the game does both introducing the various characters around town, and showing their absurd exploits as you progress through the game. The voice acting is fantastic as well.I would absolutely recommend this game to just about anyone, and hope to see more from the developers in the future! Seriously, try it today!
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: it feels more like an interactive story book than a game. as in the humour is not tied to HOW you interact with the game but WHEN you interact with it and thus the only thing you're actively changing is the pace of the game.an important question comes to mind, does this really need to be a game? i would argue absolutely not. i feel like the humour is not in the interacting but rather the watching. i would have very much preferred to just watch this because half the time it was me wasting time not knowing where to go next. it made me so bored because theres nothing enticing in those moments between jokes that invite me to explore. the game does it feel like you're interacting with the world, but rather just looking for the next silly thing to happen while you aimlessly wander around hitting stuff. it's barebones interaction, you're not really doing much besides observing. like zoo, or an art gallery, but for jokes! i think hitting stuff has so much potential to be funny but most of the time it's just a way to provide dialogue or to just be ocd and hit everything in the world, rather than to set up for a laugh. like i'm genuinely hitting everything just in case i'm missing out on a joke or something, and 99% of the time there is no joke to be told and i'm just hitting stuff for no reason.at the start i was giddy just walking around and hope to do something funny or cool, or to explore and go on little side quests for the townsfolk at my own pace, or to be a nuisance and just hit everyone for no reason other than it's funny and for the townsfolk to have funny reactions; only to realise it's not all there and you can only laugh when the game decides it's time for you to laugh... i think thats a deal breaker for me.however, i really REALLY love the style of the game, using real life imagery to contrast with the cute/silly art-style. it's a fun little experience of doing the mundane and it all wraps up really nicely at the end with the hilarity and absurdity of it all in a song and dance, perfectly encapsulating this fun little ruckus.some of the jokes are hilarious and british humour will always be funny no matter what

_childDocuments_.review: This is not a game. This is more of an interactive animation. It takes anywhere from 2.5 - 3.5 hours to complete. I would not say it is very replayable - I am missing 7 achievements and am not interested in going back for them simply because there is no chapter system or way to go about it without replaying the entire thing. The only reason I could see going back through would be to explore the dialogue/subtitle options, because the devs really poke fun at it. All that said, I really enjoyed the time I spent with Thank Goodness You're Here. I am from the US and I'm sure that I missed a lot of the subtle nuance, but there was enough there for me to consistently laugh and chuckle to myself throughout. You essentially play as a little yellow man completing various mundane tasks for the locals. You have maybe a dozen-ish separate  areas you will repeatedly loop through while completing and picking up these tasks. You have a jump button and a slap button, along with the left stick to control movement and that's it. It's pretty on-rails but every time you loop through, something will be different, whether it's the dialogue, new NPC, or new opening to explore or pass through. If you are here for an actual GAME in the traditional sense, you will probably get bored and/or frustrated by this. But if you are ready to enjoy some good British humor and comedic timing of each set piece then you will be in for a treat. I really can't compare it to anything else, which is exactly why I am happy with it. If, as an American, you enjoy the kind of dry deadpan humor associated with shows like The IT Crowd, Absolutely Fabulous, Taskmaster, The Vicar of Dibley, Doc Martin, Peep Show, The Mighty Boosh, etc.. then you can expect the same from Thank Goodness You're Here, and can judge whether or not you think it's worth $20 to you. The Devs also have a free-to-play game called The Good Time Garden. Played entirely on Steam Deck and worked great with no fiddling.
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: A true piece of art, Thank Goodness You're Here is exemplary is every way:- Gameplay is simple, but engaging.- The art is characterful, detailed and well-made.- Sound design is unmatched (Not to mention they somehow bagged Matt Berry as a voice actor).- Writing is witty, but subtle. Some punchlines only hit me while watching my friends play.Every second of this game has had care and devotion poured into it.

_childDocuments_.review: Thank Goodness You're Here is a short but fun game that takes place in an imaginary northern town in 1980s England. It wears its national character on its sleeve and really soaks in the setting, from everything costing 10 bob to missions involving making pies and fish and chips. Despite its cartoon visuals looking like an interactive version of Mr Men, this game is not for kids! It contains adult humour and even some brief (and in my opinion, unnecessary) cartoon nudity. The actual gameplay is very basic. You run, you jump and you smack things. That is all you can do and the majority of the game involves running around smacking everything to see what happens. This sounds boring but the game is bizarre enough and funny enough that just seeing what everyone does when you smack them is worth a go around. My biggest gripe is that the story involves a fair amount of backtracking - there are a few different locations and the route to get to them is linear, so you'll end up circling around the same few screens several times by the end of the game. Things do get shaken up each time you go around with new characters and situations but it is overall a very linear game with minimal replay value. Once you've seen everything there's little reason to do it again.Definitely worth picking up for cheap; it'll only last a handful of hours but if you like off the wall British humour then Thank Goodness You're Here! is worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: As I get older, gain more responsibilities, and lose more of my brain cells to the impending memory loss from excessive alcohol consumption, it becomes in my best interest to enjoy games that are not thirty-hour, blockbuster spectacles. Most games I start that have long "run-times", my adult-diagnosed ADHD throws a spanner in the works, and I get distracted by the next shiny thing that comes my way.Thank Goodness You're Here! took me less than three hours to complete, and yet it was worth every bob I spent on the yoke. The game is a love letter to northern and midlands England, but even if you have little to no connection to the area, you'll still enjoy the quaint romp through Barnsworth. If you're a dumb yank like me, you might miss out on a few bits here and there, but it's otherwise one of the funniest games I've played. The banter between character, along with their voice acting, is top class. Animation is fluid, and disguises it's video game medium fantastically. Each character is unique, memorable, and adds to the lived-in atmosphere of the town. Cut-scenes are slapstick and brilliant. Gameplay is incredibly simple, and some might call it the game's downside, though I would disagree. If you deconstruct the game at it's most basic elements, it is a "walking simulator" mixed with "light puzzle" themes. Though the city is multi-sectional and is "open-world", the game places plot points and obstacles in your way to lead you on a linear narrative. For some, you could argue that the price-point might be steep if the gameplay is "press X to slap", and it only lasts three hours.But here's the thing: . It's absolutely perfect for me. The entire time, I was entertained, howling in laughter, and enjoying my short amount of free time available to me. I was sitting on the couch, with my Steam Deck, sipping a cuppa, taking in the bants and colorful atmosphere. I was locked in. My stupid short-form-video-scroll-induced attention span was taken away to another world, even for just an afternoon. I could have spent that same money for a takeaway, ore even a film at the cinema that would cost more.And lads, at the end of the day, that's the craic.

_childDocuments_.review: “Thank Goodness You’re Here!” – A Proper Comedy GemAh, brace yourselves, chaps and chapettes! Gather 'round the digital hearth, for I’ve got a tale to spin – a yarn as British as a soggy crumpet on a drizzly afternoon. And what’s this? A video game set in Yorkshire? Well, I’ll be a monkey’s uncle! Let’s dive into the delightful absurdity of “Thank Goodness You’re Here!”The Heroic Quest: Picture yourself – a nameless fellow of indeterminate age and wilfully inconsistent height. You’re dispatched to the fictitious Northern England town of Barnsworth. Why? No one knows, old bean. But fear not! The adventure kicks off with a bang – or rather, a leap out of the boss’ office window. Because doors are for amateurs, right?Barnsworth Bliss: Now, Barnsworth – it’s a proper masterpiece. A hand-drawn fever dream of a town, complete with ♥♥♥-strewn market squares, oozing riverbanks, and more sight gags than a Monty Python sketch. Spiders boing on lampposts, ants shimmy up walls, and scruffy pigeons flutter about. Oh, and the children? They merrily beat each other with sticks. Jolly good fun!Surreal Whimsy: Brace yourselves, mates. This game is sillier than a tea cozy at a royal garden party. From the first “Thank goodness you’re here!” (and trust me, there’ll be many), it’s a relentless barrage of absurdity. But it’s the way it dances with form – manipulating comedy rhythms like a tipsy Morris dancer – that truly shines. Takes a bit to unravel, mind you, but oh, the payoff!Peans and Marrow Songs: Ever heard of Peans? Not quite peas, not quite beans – something delicious in betweens. And the Marrow Song? A bawdy ditty that’ll have you tapping your crumpet spoon. It’s all part of the madcap journey through Barnsworth, where logic takes a holiday and whimsy reigns supreme.Verdict: So, my dear gaming comrades, “Thank Goodness You’re Here!” is a gem – a comedy gem polished with Yorkshire wit. It won’t suit everyone’s taste, mind you. But if you fancy a pint of absurdity, served with a side of chuckles, this game’s your cup of Earl Grey. Pip pip, tally-ho, and all that!

_childDocuments_.review: This is an interactive movie game in the vein of something akin to Kids and Plug & Play. I personally think the developers could've been ambitious and incorporated the occasional WarioWare-esque microgame, as it would suit the absurd slapstick personality. But there's enough simple interactivity here to keep it more engaging than just watching on YouTube; plus, it's genuinely well-designed in that the player retains control as much as possible. Fantastic presentation all around, unironically puts other cinematic games to shame. I normally don't like the bean (or pean) mouths and general flatness of modern digital cartoons, but I can't think of a better art style for this game, and of course the animation itself is fluid and great. Highly quotable dialogue from funny voice actors, and wonderful music. Maybe I like British people now.

_childDocuments_.review: Recently, I was scrolling through my YouTube notifications to see what had been uploaded. I saw that Stumpt had posted a video for a new game called . After watching the video and cracking up, I knew I had to check the game out for myself.Taking on the role of a small traveling salesman, we’re tasked with heading to the strange Northern English town of Barnsworth to meet with the local mayor. But we have to wait to see him. So, we decide to explore the town and meet the locals. However, they ask us to do some tasks all around town for them. That shouldn’t be too hard, right? Now, if only these jobs were regular ones…Even after watching the one video from Stumpt, I still didn’t know what I was getting myself into by playing this and had no real expectations. But I am so glad I went into this generally blind. From start to finish, this game was exceptional and made me laugh so much. The comedy throughout ranges from recurring gags (the man who continually has to clean soot from his living room comes to mind) to more wordplay, wisecracks, and much more (“Reggie’s wife could learn a thing or two”). I don’t know if everyone will get this game’s type of humor. Still, you may like it if you enjoy things like ,  (the wackiness of this reminded me of the show), or other old British sitcoms. In general, the game is pretty straightforward and linear, as things around the town only change once a job has been completed. There was some backtracking to finish tasks, but I didn’t find it too annoying as I had so much fun.One aspect I really liked about this game was the fact that it was fully voice-acted. I especially enjoyed seeing Matt Berry pop up; his voice is so recognizable, and I was surprised to hear him. I also really liked the cartoony art style that the developers went with here. It works perfectly for a game like this. In all honesty, I don’t really have any critiques. Everything that was done for this, the art, gags, voice acting, the writing, all of it, was wonderful.In my humble opinion,  is an instant classic that I recommend in all its absurdity!
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: An absolute banger. Packed with gags - slapstick, surrealism, visuals, great characters -  and properly funny dialogue. The juxtaposition between the bright artwork and the sometimes dark, often mucky humour is ace. They’ve captured that Vic and Bob, Bottom, League of Gentleman strain of British humour. Humour is tricky to pull off in a videogame given how important things like timing are, but they’ve actually used the medium to make the jokes. The comedy’s in the game itself, not just the cutscenes. Avoiding spoilers - humours much better in context than typed into a review - but even the very first interaction you have as a character shows the humour the creators can generate from player interaction, visuals and character. TGYH’s design encourages mischief at every turn. Unlike other games where the central verbs might be "stab" or "parry," here it’s "slap." You interact with everything and everyone with a slap, including dialogue interactions. If you think you can slap it - NPC’s, bin bags, meat -  you can. If you’ve ever bounced off the visual novel genre, consider how much more fun it could be if you constantly had the option to slap. The art and animation style is a perfect match for the game’s daft story and characters, just an exquisite vibe. Bizarre scenarios contrast the mundane aspects of small-town life. The music, from parping trumpet to gently plucked  guitars, and the sound effects are exceptional. TGYH doesn’t hold your hand—there are no quest journals or glowing HUD elements telling you where to go next —but figuring out what to do is never difficult and always fun. And if you do get lost for a moment, you’ll probably find another joke you might have missed. The game’s tightly designed and the lack of explicit direction is testament to that, discovering all the quirky details Barnsworth has to offer rules.At a few hours to run through the story, the lengths is bang on for its content. Feels like bingeing a season of an amazing cartoon. It keeps things pacey and the humour and novelty stay fresh from start to finish, leaving you wanting more rather than overstaying its welcome. It's also dense as a premium pie, packed full of weirdo characters and unique visuals. Massive respect to Coal Supper for crafting such a cohesive, polished and joyously weird experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: My mother nation was ruled by the British Empire, and its cultural legacy lives on in so many ways that we continue to see it with a mixture of both resentment and awe. Those of us with a historical bent might treat a visit to England as a kind of fairtytale come alive.This game gives us a similar deep insight into a certain cross-section of England, and helps us truly understand how these fine people were able to rule us for hundreds of years. One could see the protagonist as a metaphor for Great Britain itself - a blobby homunculus who, through the power of gratuitous violence, bends the huge world around him to his will.Posterity will see this as a work of profound cultural significance. I am enlightened and I think I need a ciggie.
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: A Quirky and Beautifully Crafted Short AdventureRating: ★★★★☆"Thank Goodness You're Here!" delivers a unique experience, despite its short length. The game's whimsical, hand-drawn art style alone makes it worth the purchase, offering a vibrant and offbeat world that draws you in from the start. Every scene is filled with quirky details that give the game its unmistakable charm.I finished the game in about two hours and went back for another playthrough to grab more achievements. The captivating visuals and humor made it easy to enjoy exploring the surreal world again. While the experience is brief, the artistry and atmosphere made those hours feel fully worthwhile.Though I don't see myself returning for another round, I’m happy with the time I spent in this odd and delightful universe. If you enjoy distinctive art styles and quirky humor, "Thank Goodness You're Here!" is a memorable gem that is well worth playing, even if only for a couple of sessions.Edit: I did not refund the game. No idea why Steam thinks I did.

_childDocuments_.review: There's something about this game that's kinda like a warm hug from your auntie who lives up north. Perhaps you don't know her very well, the place is littered with cigarettes and booze bottles, there is the odd cabinet or weird smells coming from random places, and there might be some things that just seem grade A weird.But in the end, when you give her a hug when visiting, it's a reminder from another person that you are loved and appreciated.I love this game because it gives me a nice fuzzy feeling in its comfyness, while being quintessentially rooted in northern British culture. It makes me want to make some tea and offer some Jaffa Cakes or Jammy Dodgers to visiting friends while we talk about all the weirdness that has happened over the last few months since we last spoke.If you're thinking about buying the game, please let this be a vote of confidence that you absolutely should experience it for yourself. There's nothing quite like it out there.ALSO I AM SO SORRY ROY WILL YOU PLEASE FORGIVE ME???

_childDocuments_.review: Thank Goodness You're Here!: A Yorkshire DiamondThank Goodness You're Here! is a right corker of a game, a proper Yorkshire diamond, if you ask me. Set in the bonny town of Barnsworth, players take on the role of a traveling salesman who gets wrapped up in a series of daft and hilarious capers.What sets this game apart: * Unique blend of humor: The game's comedy is a right laugh, a mix of daftness, Yorkshire wit, and a bit of dark humor. You'll be chuckling your socks off as you navigate the town's peculiar folk and their unusual requests. It's like a pint of ale on a sunny day, a real treat. * Nonlinear gameplay: The game's open-ended structure lets players explore Barnsworth at their own pace and discover hidden gems. It encourages experimentation and replayability. It's a bit like exploring the Yorkshire Dales, you never know what you'll find. * Engaging characters: The residents of Barnsworth are a colorful bunch, each with their own distinct personalities and quirks. Their interactions with the protagonist are both entertaining and heartwarming. It's like having a pint with your mates at the local pub, a real pleasure. * Beautiful art style: The game's hand-drawn art style is visually appealing and complements the quirky tone of the narrative. It's like a painting of the Yorkshire countryside, beautiful and serene. * Short and sweet: Thank Goodness You're Here! offers a satisfying experience without overstaying its welcome. Its concise length makes it a perfect choice for players who want a quick and enjoyable gaming session. It's like a quick pint after work, just what you need.Overall, Thank Goodness You're Here! is a must-play for fans of quirky indie games and British humor. Its unique blend of comedy, exploration, and engaging characters make it a truly memorable experience. It's a proper Yorkshire gem, a right diamond in the rough.

_childDocuments_.review: Cute, funny, and full of personality, Thank Goodness You're Here lies somewhere between Untitled Yorkshire Game and point-and-spank adventure game.While there is great humor in the game's objectives - from escaping a pint of beer to visiting a chippy on behalf of a sick cow - much of the game's comedy comes from the eccentric townsfolk and their absurd reactions to the chaos that we create along the way. Without being in the business of tiny pies, I can't confidently say I would react any differently than Tiny Tom to the prospect of a giant one. But I'd hope my response would give others the same hearty chuckle I got on his behalf.Thank Goodness You're Here reinforces its comedy through a clear awareness of the fourth wall. By keeping our protagonist ambiguously small, and inserting Barnsworth commercials seamlessly into what's on screen, the game's scenes are organized like an interactive cartoon. Sometimes you wander into the next scene and catch the tail-end of an amusing conversation, where the ridiculous punchline implies an equally preposterous setup. Backgrounds are filled with jokes that many players won't even notice during their playthrough.The game is short, yet exactly the right size for this type of experience. Its length keeps all the jokes fresh, and makes a great game for a weekend. I'd rather explore the next Barnsworth than keep gu'in in a game that already feels so finished.I look forward to their next game; I'd gladly pay 10 bob.
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: I got it as a gift from a friend and went in completely blind, so maybe id feel different if I'd spent 16 bucks on what is realistically a 3-4 hour experience. _childDocuments_.review: Within the first few seconds of loading this game up (mind you, it asks you a very important question going in), I knew it would be a life-changing experience. You're this little adorable man that goes around helping folks. That's the basic gist of it and yet there's so much more involved. Here are my pros and cons: THE BEST STUFF: Thank you for this comedic genius. - my response to the developers. Timing was on point, I sometimes couldn't even differentiate if I was supposed to be playing or if I was watching a cut-scene. This alone was a perfect setup for the laughs that ensued and I won't spoil it because the ending is a prime example of this. So, yes, humor was sublime, some of the best dialogue I've ever heard and I'm so excited to play this over to get more achievements. EVEN BETTER? The artwork. With each silly or funny thing said I contribute a lot of my laughs to the expressions of these whimsical and amazing characters that I can't forget. Also WOW the innuendos in this were subtle to downright "HERE WE GO." Loved it. AN ANNOYANCE? Honestly nothing really annoyed me, except a bit of the repetition, but it's also integrated into the main story of well "yup, this is where you are." So, kudos it's part of what you have to go through. That's hilarious in itself. Honestly, great game. SCORE: 10/10 - would do again.

_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: This game could have been a cheap pastiche of northern england and still gotten passable review scores, but it is so much more than that. There are many jokes in this game that stand up on their own merits without needing to lean on reference humour, which helps prevent the slice-of-life humour that is there from getting stale for the game's 3 hour run time. It also helps that in addition to the directly presented jokes, there are recurring "joke motifs" that weave their way through the town and help the humour to build into something more substantial, like the way a stand-up comedian will lead the audience on a journey through the course of a set. Stuff like the big pie vs small pie rivalry has so many tiny influences across the game that you can't even tell what the "original" joke is and what is a spin off. It's like joke worldbuilding.The little gameplay there is is frictionless, the platforming is intuitive, and all the object interactions are snappy and satisfying. The only critique I have is that I wish the camera was a little zoomed out, it could feel cramped at times. I loved this game.

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10Oh, blimey, guv’nor! Ain’t it just a proper kerfuffle when the ol’ bangers and mash go all topsy-turvy like a flippin’ dog’s breakfast, innit? Cor blimey, I’m gobsmacked like a fish outta water, what with the blooming ruddy queue down the chippy stretching round the bend like a bloomin’ tangle of brolly-wielding bobbies. It’s a right proper chinwag at the local boozer, with the old codgers nattering on about the Queen’s jubbly jubilee, sipping their pints of bitter and munching on crisps like there’s no tomorrow.Well, blow me down if it ain’t raining cats and dogs, all the nippers jumping in puddles like a bunch of cheeky monkeys, making a right mess of their wellies. Fancy a natter with the lads down the rub-a-dub, have a chinwag about the footie, and then pop off for a cheeky curry? It’s all a bit of a lark, innit, me ol’ mucker? Don’t forget to grab a cuppa and a biccy, keep the cobwebs at bay while you’re having a gander at the telly.Down the road, Mrs. Miggins is having a right old barney with the postie ‘cause her letters got all kerfuffled in the post, bless her cotton socks. Meanwhile, the blokes at the pub are having a natter about the weather, as if it’s gonna change the bally forecast. ‘Oi, mate,’ one says, ‘fancy a spot of tea before the rain sets in again?’ ‘Nah,’ says the other, ‘I’ll just have a pint, ta very much!’Oh, I say, when the clock strikes five, it’s all hands to the pump at the local fish and chip shop. Grab your mushy peas and vinegar, and mind the salt, or you’ll be in a right two and eight! It’s a jolly old time, I tell you, a right knees-up like you wouldn’t believe. Fancy a stroll through the cobbled streets, saying, ‘How do you do?’ to every Tom, ♥♥♥♥, and Harry you meet. It’s the British way, innit? Proper good fun!
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: Very disappointing for the cost.  Like others, fell for the hype and picked it up, but don't see the appeal.  The game is tedious in all senses of the word.  You go round the same map over and over again, and while it does change it up a bit by moving characters around and having some running jokes, the characters and their humor are tedious as well.  I'm not above a dirty joke, I just want them to be funny. The music repeats ad nauseam.  And the end, oh JESUS the end.  I fell asleep during the... song? I guess is the best way to put it?... at the end, and woke up to it STILL GOING so I clicked a few more times and it finally pushed me through to the final minute of the game. Which is just another repeated joke, and then the game ends.  Others have complained about the short play time but all I can say is THANK GOD it's over.My advice: this one's probably best experienced watching someone else play it.  If you're still laughing after looping the map multiple times, then yeah, pick it up.

_childDocuments_.review: Bought this game so my partner could watch me play it.From the art and voice lines I could see that a lot of work and love went into it (even Matt Berry is in there!), however, I would not recommend this game to anyone. Unfortunately, while I did like the small British town setting, I understood only a few jokes so perhaps the biggest selling point of the game went under my radar.As far as gameplay goes, all you ever do is walk around and hit things - a slapformer as the game describes it - which did not keep my brain engaged or interested in wanting to play more of it. While I often compare video game enjoyment to going to the cinemas with regards to cost-enjoyment ratio, I finished this game within 2.3 hours and definitely wasn't left satisfied about my money being spent on it. I think 4 hours is the maximum amount of time you will get out of it and only if you explore every nook and cranny of the game.I would not recommend this game unless you highly value the jokey side of things, in which case you might wanna give it a try on a sale. If you do, perhaps consider turning down the accent (there is an option for that, which could maybe help you get the jokes).

_childDocuments_.review: Thank Goodness You're Here is not a game.  It is definitely not an adventure game. _childDocuments_.review: Of all of the many, many games that I have been generously sent review/early access keys for, Thank Goodness You're Here is a shining badge of honor for me. And for the record, I would've bought this game twice over regardless. Its rare that as you roll credits on a game that you can recognize the fact that you just played the kind of game that doesn't really come around twice. That is absolutely the case here.For something so aggressively British, I didn't feel like almost any of the humor went over my head on lack of cultural context alone. The jokes that I missed were simply because there are SO many jokes at all times that you're bound to go past something and not realize just how funny it is. I went by "Nick's Bricks" store maybe 5 or 6 times before someone in my Twitch chat pointed out that "nick" is slang for stealing, and the "store" was Nick standing in front of a brick wall of a building he very obviously didn't own. There was such a consistent level of silly things for you to be doing at any given point that it never felt like there was really any downtime (in a good way). There was always another objective or another Barnsworth resident to go mess with. There was like 30 running and repeated gags that got funnier and more absurd every time you passed by them or went barreling down their chimney... again. The sausage guy was easily one of my favorite bits in any game I've ever played. TGYH is so heads and shoulders above its contemporaries in terms of comedic timing, writing and delivery from the astounding VA cast that its easy to also overlook the fact that this is an entirely hand drawn/animated game. The art is gorgeous and it is unendingly impressive to me that I didn't encounter a single bug the entire time. The visuals play into the slapstick and comedy just as much as the writing and voice acting does, and your little lemon head main character being this amorphous unfeeling gremlin is so perfect for what they wanted to do here. This is probably going to be one of the best games to come out this year, and easily one of my favorite games that I have played in the past few years. I feel a sense of (definitely misplaced lol) pride on behalf of the team behind this game for being fully committed to making such a weird, oddball game and in the genuine attempt at creating something off the wall they just nailed it. Buy this game, gift it to a friend, for anyone that has ever complained that games are all the same now? Support this title and then leave a review so other people become aware of just how TGYH is.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is good. Its NOT as extremely high-lare-ious as the majority seems to claim, but its still full of, increasingly grotesque, bri'ish charm, dour humor and obvious innuendos.And no, no context here is blocked by not being bri'ish. I am from the continent, as the brits say, and every bit of the specific British wording is easily deductible in its meaning, often alone by context. Although I feel knowing how bad it was on the British Isles during the time that, I believe, the game tries to mimic and parody, it might make more sense why there are cigarette buds everywhere and everything seems to be in a rather severe state of cheapness, disrepair and social disarray. (Thought recent developments kind off threaten to make these parts relevant today.) Now, here is the thing. I recommend the game if you do not mind paying 18 Bucks for roughly three hours of straight forward (if not always straight sane) content with not much actual gameplay. See, you walk and you bash and you jump into things. And while another game could make a lot with that, this one uses it to mainly give you a winding but very linear journey trough this adversity stricken bri'ish community. There is no complexity of gameplay here that goes beyond seeing what reacts to you slapping it and what has changed from the last time you were in the area. So of I were in more dire monetary straights or only interested in active gameplay with ANY complexity to it (like even just "mario jumps on goombas" complexity would be more), I might have my reservations and pick something else that offers mighty more content for nearly the same amount of money. I simply can understand if it feels a bit pricey for what ThankGoodnessYouAreHere gives.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought into the "overwhelmingly" positive reviews and am now regretting this purchase. Why so many people seem to be so fond of this game is lost on me. The hype and praise are absolutely undeserved, in my opinion.First, let me mention the positives. The art-style is interesting, and along with some vintage footage and music, it creates a rather quaint atmosphere that makes this game unique. It opens with a few goofy scenes which lead you to expect a fun journey ahead, but pretty soon its shortcomings become painfully obvious. And it starts with…The gameplay. I think it’s fair to say it’s pretty much absent. Go left and right, sometimes up and down, and jump or slap things. That’s it. The hand-drawn levels offer several places to visit and scenes to witness, but the way forward is always linear. Just go from point A to point B, slapping everything and everyone on the way in hopes to trigger some dialogue or scripted scene. There is potential for branching paths, puzzles or platforming challenges, but the devs apparently decided not to "overcomplicate" their game with things that could make it an actual game. So, instead you’re left with a brainless, linear A-to-B traversal of the same handful of levels, consecutively going through them multiple times with some minor variations.There are no quest markers or logs, so you’ll have to memorize everything offhandedly said to you by NPCs that turns out to be an actual side quest. So, tough luck if you want to pick things up where you left off the day before. But don’t worry, no matter where you go or what you were told by NPCs, you’ll eventually end up where you need to be, because there is only one exit from one location to the next one. It’s just that sometimes you may find yourself aimlessly running around, trying to find where did the exit pop up this time, or who and what needs smacking to make it pop up.As for the humor, if you expect something clever and witty, you will likely be disappointed, as it is largely slapstick, silly and immature, often relying on the use of heavy accents and lesser-known British slang. It managed to get a few smiles out of me, but I didn’t find the game nearly as hilarious as some people claim it to be. You would think that in such case at least younger players would enjoy this, but it’s a miss as well, as the game is packed with sexual innuendoes, has some minor profanity, and a nude character, not to mention several weird and creepy drug trip inspired levels. So no, it’s not a good fit for children either.Overall, given the price asked, the amount of normal playtime (around 2 hours) and level of enjoyment, I would say this game is not only overpriced, but does not deliver neither as a game (or rather “interactive” cartoon), nor as a fun/funny experience, which seems to be its main selling point. Avoid, unless heavily discounted, and even then, don’t expect its humor to sweep you off your feet.4/10

But even that I discourage because none of the humor makes any sense, it just feels like one long list of inside jokes that you aren't part of. Does that sound like a good time? _childDocuments_.review: *Thank Goodness You’re Here* might have seemed like a quirky, fun concept on the surface, but watching it turned out to be a pretty underwhelming experience. First off, the gameplay felt far too chaotic and confusing. Instead of offering an engaging, witty experience, the pacing was all over the place, making it hard to follow what was happening or even care about the characters.Speaking of characters, they were one-dimensional and not at all memorable. The writing failed to capture the humor it was clearly aiming for, with most of the jokes falling flat. What could have been an enjoyable, whimsical experience quickly became repetitive and predictable.Visually, while the game did have a certain charm, it didn’t compensate for the lack of engaging content. There were moments where it felt like more effort was put into the style rather than substance. I found myself bored and uninterested in progressing further after a short time playing.Overall, *Thank Goodness You’re Here* is an experience that promises a lot but fails to deliver. It’s a quirky title that unfortunately doesn’t live up to its potential and ultimately left me feeling more frustrated than entertained.

_childDocuments_.review: Good game on first play through, I like how the environment changes around you. The transition between when paths are blocked off for you to do other things first and when they're open for you to move on is very clean, and it feels very much like watching some weird little cartoon short. I love the art style and I think the jokes are charming. My issue comes with the replayability; If you're following the story, that's great, but if you're achievement hunting like I was it gets really annoying really quickly. A lot of long dialogue sections or cutscenes are unskippable, meaning every few minutes you have to sit through a long dialogue section you've already heard a few times before. If you miss just one achievement section, the automatic saving feature makes it impossible to go back and get said achievement without re-playing the entire game before it, meaning you have to waste another hour or so for a shot at re-doing it. I had to do a third play-through just to achieve one potato achievement, which took around forty minutes. Because of all the cutscenes, I found myself often just ignoring the game to watch YouTube or text my friends while waiting for whatever character I was talking to to hurry up with their dialogue. I know it'd be really difficult to implement a saving feature or some feature to increase replayability due to how intertwined a lot of achievements/parts are, but some kind of skip key or way to go around certain tasks post-completion would be greatly appreciated. Overall a pleasant experience, I enjoyed seeing my favorite 'untitled goose game' characters making an appearance (Herb and the posh neighbor), but the replayability irked me too much to give this game a recommended review.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is horrifying, outrageous and hilarious and terribly, terribly accurate of North England small town culture. I grew up in Batley West Yorkshire, my grandfather put a knotted hanky on his head when he went on his annual holiday to Skegness. My first job was in a pie shop and my parents owned a Fish and Chip shop, and my other Grandfather worked on a veg stall in the local market. I can see all of them in the characters in this game. Be warned there are some um, weird parts to it (Milk Shy was the worst), some strong sexual innuendo (sausage glory hole is an example) but overall I have never had a game make me laugh out loud so much. Make the time to listen to the conversations (don't put your rubbish in my bin was my favourite) read the signs and graffiti because this is less puzzle and more warped Jeremy Kyle soap opera type stuff. Definitely worth the money, but I am finishing the game feeling slight shame (Milk Shy), horror, sentimental and sad that it's finished. Anyway, seethi
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: Comedy games are super rare. I searched Google and YouTube for comedy game recommendation. There were hardly any I would consider comedy. Most of the games recommended falls in par with Mario, Legend of Zelda or just light hearted point-and-click games with minimal comedy element. They sure did not make me laugh and the trailer made it clear, those games were made for elemental school children with elemental school level story dressed as comedy. This makes me wonder if most developer in the gaming world are alien to laughter or the comedy genre. Comedy genre is rare even among the comic industry. I read webtoons. Romance genre is the most common genre in the korean comic industry followed by action followed by thriller/horror. Comedy genre is very rare. In this serious world, a good comedian can do wonder and I am always searching for a good story that can make me laugh. I feel sad that, like laughter has become rare, comedy genre has also become rare. This game is unique and a rare gem. It's the first of its kind and the idea is absolutely original and a pure comedy game in the sense of comedy. If I search YouTube for Hollow Knight inspired games, thousands of recommendation appears. This is not the case if I search, "games like Thank Goodness You're Here". This says how unique and underappreciated gem this is. This game is, in my eye, a masterpiece and I feel nothing but admiration for the creative team to allow us to laugh as we play the game and to think of such an unique game idea.

_childDocuments_.review: You will either LOVE or HATE this game, but it's definitely not going to be for everyone. But if you were someone who couldn't stand those movies - then I'd highly recommend giving this a pass, because you'll probably be regretting it VERY quickly.It took me close to 3 hours to finish my playthrough, which I did all in 1 sitting. _childDocuments_.review: Fair warning to parents out there - the humour pushes the limits sometimes.  Lots of ♥♥♥♥ jokes - you're *almost* jerking off a cow in one scene (you're not, but the joke implies it).  In another scene you're slapping around some fish and it's implied that one of them is a dude's ♥♥♥♥.  Most of the game's jokes involve some innuendo, but some are a bit much.  There are also some off-putting parts that aren't sex related - creepy vegan activism or something?  Kind of weird.  It's fine - it's funny even - but you know... just so you're aware if you're planning on playing this with the kiddo's. Anyway, I'd put the really raunchy jokes at around 1% of the total - most of the humour is tongue-in-cheek and frankly hilarious.  There are tons of little jokes implied by the environment.  Around every corner in the town is rich detail and great little in-jokes.  Even the names of some of the shops and streets are funny just by themselves.  Great game, it's worth your time - 8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: If Monty Python designed a video game after a really weird dream, it would be Thank Goodness You’re Here. This gem flings you into bizarre scenarios without warning, armed only with your wits and a faint sense of “What the heck is happening?” It's a comedy of errors where you’re the star, the fool, and the audience all at once.Expect to stumble through an eccentric town full of characters who look like they escaped a Saturday morning cartoon, only to end up in the wrong dimension. You’ll improvise, you’ll guess, and you’ll laugh at yourself as the game rewards even your worst decisions.Thank Goodness You’re Here is absurd, unpredictable, and somehow heartwarming—a perfect mix of laughs and chaos. It’s proof that even confusion can be pure entertainment!

_childDocuments_.review: Full of Northern charm, whimsy, deadpan, and absurdity not just in its characters, but also gameplay, scenarios, and perspectives. There's so much variety that is used with just the verbs of jump and hit. Very much reminded of Hohokum (Ricky Haggett is given special thanks) with the interactive toybox that is the town of Barnsworth (based on Barnsley, Yorkshire where creators Will Todd and James Carbutt were born). The voice acting across the board (Jon Blyth, Em Humble, David Ferguson, Peter Sutton, Chris Cantrill) is absolutely top-notch and authentic, and Matt Berry as the gardener is more of a smaller role compared to others like Big Ron, Meg, Kerri, Marge, Bish, Rog, Sam, Charlie, and of course the unforgettable Scottish mechanic Jasper. I would have loved in the credits for the voice actors to be put side-to-side to their characters, because they're so important and bring the lifeblood to this game. There are no filler segments or moments, so nearly every scenario in terms of ludonarrative is memorable. There are so many running gags throughout the game that have satisfying conclusions, such as the two neighbours arguing over whose rubbish is in their bins which effectively becomes a weird love story. It's a wonderful idea to have no UI or HUD, because all the attention gets put into the world and interacting with it, rather than menus, and because of the retro 2D simplicity of controls, it's very accessible (even my daughter has been playing it but thankfully she can't understand the northern vulgarity!). I'll try to get as much of my family and friends playing this, especially on the Steam Deck. It's another wonderful idea to be this miniscule salesman character with no voice and ok to be an errand boy, who can squeeze into pipes, hoses, holes, and anything which allows you to explore several levels of Barnsworth from the roofs to underground. The mise en scene is impeccable, full of environmental storytelling and informing the tone and messages of the game. The musical ludonarrative ending is phenomenal, like one of the best endings to a game you'll find this year. When the journey ended, I felt a little sad because it's such a colourful and hilarious 2-3 hour journey through this unique world so I immediately started replaying it to get all the achievements or other interactions I missed.

There is no "wrong" way to play it, as any direction, or any action you chose to do will still lead you on the right path, to the point of *in my opinion* guides being completely useless. It's pretty short, but it makes up for it with its great jokes, casual but enticing gameplay and a wide variety of achievements to complete after you're done, along with multiple optional scenes you can chose to watch or just continue the main storyline. 10/10, best 10 bob I've ever spent.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty funny short game, more of an interactive animated movie kind of feel with the length and linearity of the story, but there are optional things to do so it does still feel more like a game than a movie. _childDocuments_.review: This game is absolutely hilarious. The animation is fantastic, the writing is very clever with a mix of witty and irreverent humor, and the sound design adds so much to the comedy. I laughed out loud many times during this short game.Gameplay-wise, it does get fairly repetetive by the end of the game. You just sort of walk this loop around the town over and over, and while it remains consistently hilarious throughout, I did get a sense of, "okay, can we just wrap this up?" about 90 minutes into a 2 hour game. With that said, it doesn't overstay its welcome by too much, and the ending of the game is quite enjoyable. I will also say that the game, at times, has poor conveyance. You're left objectiveless in an open area wondering what you're supposed to do next with nothing to tip you off, which is strange in such a linear game. The story is far too nonsensical to be able to reliably take context clues from the narrative, aside from the rare instances where a character actually tells you where to go. Luckily, the environments are small enough that if you just wander around slapping things, you'll eventually find your way.In terms of value, it's hard to say that ~2 hours of gameplay (a little more if you are achievement hunting) is worth $20; HOWEVER, if you view this less as a "game" and more as an interactive, animated film that is lovingly hand animated and wonderfully performed by a great voice cast, then it becomes a lot easier to justify the price. And frankly, it's got SO much comedy and so many little background details in every scene that you will want to play the game more than once.Performance was excellent. I played all the way through on the Steam Deck and it ran effortlessly. It could probably be a strong strong option for low spec gamers looking for a laugh.All in all, this is a pretty easy game to recommend for the right kind of player. If you love comedy, animation, games you could beat in a sitting or two, and narrative-focused adventure games with simple gameplay mechanics, then this game is right up your alley.
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: This silly lil' point-n-click adventure contains some of the funniest jokes in video game history, and only gets funnier the more you play it. The spritework and animated cutscenes are also extremely well done, making the game feel like an interactive Adult Swim show. Though it's a bit on the short side (3 hours at most), it more than makes up for it with its hilarious dialogue, in-depth world design, memorable characters and extremely large amount of hilarious background details that encourage you to explore the game's world. Another interesting thing about the game is that whenever you complete a mission, various characters move to different places, and change their dialogue, often having a tiny subplot as well. This not only causes the game's setting to feel alive, but also causes you to feel attached to even the most unimportant characters. Overall, I highly recommend this game to people who enjoy games with a bizarre, often dark sense of humor.

_childDocuments_.review: Played from – to: (2024-09-24 – 2024-09-26) – PC controller.‣ 8/10 – 10 Bob game.‣ Thoughts: I always find it difficult to review or rate games like these. Fundamentally this is a game, but it is so basic that it could’ve easily been an animated show or movie. Thank Goodness You’re Here is a dry British humor title, where you walk around a town and help people out. You mainly achieve this by just stumbling around like a braindead NPC and that is enough for these townsfolk. All you can do is slap. And slap you will, be it an ass, a door or some other questionable object. Surprisingly most people here have teeth which is highly uncommon for UK. Overall, I did chuckle a few times, but I wouldn’t go as far as to call this “the funniest game ever”. Mostly it reminded me of Little Missfortune and that game was peek comedy. I’d say this title is worth your time if you wait for a sale, because I struggle to justify a 2-hour experience being worth 18$, but the quality of the voice acting and visuals is really good so perhaps the price is accurate. All in all, this is an interesting title and the industry does lack games like this.

_childDocuments_.review: What a refreshing game. Good solid British humour, lots of self deprecation, Monty Python style. _childDocuments_.review: A solid puzzle-exploration game that can feel like it is playing itself at times. A very simplistic control scheme of moving, jumping, (rarely) grabbing, and slapping, it is the humor and visuals that keep the gameplay feeling fun and energetic. The music is nice too, but I really appreciate that the game is Steam Deck verified, as it feels perfect for the kind of game that this is.My only suggestions are to add a chapter select or some kind of cutscene skip after beating the game at least once, as it can become a major drag to play through again just to unlock one or two achievements that you missed the first time. Otherwise, this is a fun game to waste a few hours on as you enjoy the sights and sounds of a standard English towne.

_childDocuments_.review: My game of the year so far and not sure anything will be able to knock it off it's perch on the top. A short game, but so jammed full of quality gags and laughs you'd be wanting more no matter the length. It's quality over quantity and the quality of the script is polished to a mirror shine. I laughed out loud too many times to count and the game still gets a giggle out of me just thinking back on it.The game has the framework of an old point and click adventure game, but plays like a collect-a-thon, but where the aim of the game is to collect all the jokes instead stars or coins. I left no bum unsmacked nor object undamaged by my characters puny but powerful punches in a desperate attempt to leave no punchline unheard or unseen. All of this, plus a quick pace and very light and intuitive puzzle design, gives the game a level of interactivity that stops it feeling simply like an isometric walking simulator and into the realms of something else. Something fantastic.If you couldn't guess, I highly recommend Thank Goodness You're Here.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start by saying, if I ever wake up in a small British town where everyone is just a little bit off, I'm going to assume I’m in "Thank Goodness You’re Here!" and proceed to help as many strange people as possible. I’m not sure if this is a game or some weird fever dream I had after too much tea and biscuits, but either way, I love it.The art style looks like a children’s storybook gone rogue—adorable but with just enough weirdness to make you question your life choices. I spent my time helping townsfolk with tasks that ranged from plumbing emergencies (because apparently no one else can handle pipes) to... well, I’m still not sure what half of them were. But when someone asks you to do something in this town, you just do it—don’t ask questions, don’t think too hard, just embrace the chaos.The humor? Top tier. It’s like someone bottled pure British wit, shook it up with a dash of absurdity, and poured it all over your screen. I found myself laughing out loud at situations that made absolutely no sense but were too funny to care. Helping a guy with a moustache crisis or tracking down oversized animals? Sure, why not. It’s 10/10 on the "What even is this?" scale, but you’ll love every second.Pros:Art: It’s like living in a comic book after it’s had a very strong cup of tea.Humor: British humor at its finest. Dry, absurd, and absolutely brilliant.Gameplay: Light, silly, and full of surprises. It’s like someone said, "What if we make a game where nothing makes sense but you’re having the best time of your life?"Weirdness: The town’s weird. The people are weird. I’m weird. It’s perfect.Cons:It’s short, but like a really good joke—it’s over quickly, and you just wish there was more.In summary: I came for the quirky art style, stayed for the bizarre interactions, and left questioning why I now desperately want to live in a village that feels like a cross between Wallace & Gromit and an inside joke no one ever bothered to explain. Highly recommended if you enjoy laughing at things that make absolutely no sense.
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very short, but it's definitely worth it. _childDocuments_.review: "Thank Goodness You're Here!" is thoroughly pleasant, hilariously written and acted, and at times, surreal and dark in the funniest way. There are so many nooks and crannies and little easter eggs to find.You should absolutely play this game. I reached the end of the main game in about 3 hours, but it felt so jam packed, that I could have sworn I spent more time with it. You can tell that this is a game made by creatives. Every part of it oozes personality.

_childDocuments_.review: Lovely game. Bit cheeky, sometimes a bit feverish. Sort of feels like a dream you might have after watching Monty Python or the Mighty Boosh. It is very clear a lot of love and thought has been put into its creation.If you really take your time with it like I did on my first run, it'll take about 3 hours. I played it through a second time just to snag an achievement I missed and got it done in 2. I have seen folks wondering about the price, and though I think it's well worth the cost, at the very least get it if it's on sale some time if that's a consideration for you.Overall, a joyful game where you get to be a funny little guy trying to kill some time before a meeting.
