_childDocuments_.review: Three of the best entries in the entire Castlevania series and a bonus in the arcade game none of us got to play with a remastered version on top? Stealth dropped out of nowhere? FOR £20?!Dawn of Sorrow is the first game that released on the DS back when I was still in school, it's super fleshed out with some almost tech demo tier features that took advantage of the original hardware. The ice one still feels clunky, but the seal drawing in boss fights is VASTLY improved with the ability to input them with button prompts that feel intuitive and fun.Portrait of Ruin is probably the most unique of the three with how much mileage they got out of the partner gameplay. There's plenty of use cases for both characters. Some enemies resist physical attacks, some resist magic, some have different reactions depending on which one you're controlling at the time. There's a truckload of spells and hunter tools to play with, lots of gear and build variety, side quests that range from baby easy to Chinese water torture levels of grind. As a whole, the game's great though with tons of content.Order of Ecclesia was the last real Igavania and has always been my favourite of the three. The difficulty even on normal is definitely its defining feature, bosses will ruin your day if you let them and there's a reward for beating each one without getting hit. The story while simple and sparse is still up there in the upper echelons of the series and explores the idea of fighting Dracula's army without the Vampire Killer in a way that made the experience stand out from most of the other games in the series.Shanoa also controls very fluidly, the MP bar being used more like a stamina bar for your main attacks facilitates fast and snappy combos where you take a few seconds to recharge in between while dodging. The side quests in the village can be somewhat tedious, but it's worth doing them all for at least 2 playthroughs.Konami cooked, it only took a decade but they finally did something so right that it actually deserves my money on release. Now give me SotN, Rondo and Harmony of Despair for the next collection with all the DLCs baked in and online functionality... Maybe an extra chapter or two.This collection is definitely worth a buy, the price is a fraction of what I'd have paid for any of the three DS games and all the bonus content makes it even more worth the price tag. Hell, the OST player has a damn playlist feature! They went HARD on delivering a solid package for these games and it's everything they deserve.
_childDocuments_.name: Castlevania Dominus Collection

_childDocuments_.review: I've put a ton of hours into the original DS releases - these are some of the best metroidvanias out there and I don't see them brought up often anymore. The collection does find a great way around the touch screen functionality (which also kind of improves the seals in Dawn of Sorrow) and even allows you to use your mouse, if you wish. I also love how the original animated intros of each game play in the game select upon highlighting the respected title; it looks cool and new players will know that there are intros (wish Mega Man Legacy Collection 2 did that...). Each game is well presented in this release: games scaled properly, good sound quality, art/music gallery, ability to play any region's version, etc. In addition, this comes with Haunted Castle, the Castlevania arcade game, and an arranged/remade version of that game unique to this release.Dawn, the direct sequel to Aria, adds new features to the soul system where you can buff souls as you collect more of the same exact ones and use excess souls to craft new weapons. Lots of grinding and more potential builds you can make if that interests you. Boss fights are an improvement over Aria too. Only 2 things I have to say I don't like are the new art direction, as I feel it clashes with the narrative they went for, and the last few bosses can be really challenging if you don't utilize the new crafting system as a lot of strong weapons are only available through that method. Seals were improved here in this collection so I wouldn't be worried about fumbling a QTE cause of your bad handwriting. Lastly, Dawn offers probably the most coolest additional mode after achieving the bad end - a what-if scenario featuring, uh, a "Castlevania 3 reunion."Portrait of Ruin gives you to separate characters to work with, Johnathan Morris (yes, John Morris' son) and Charlotte Aulin. Johnathan probably has access to the most weapon types of any CS protagonist. Charlotte doesn't have as many options for melee combat, but she has access to tons of magic and can be pretty strong. You can swap between the two on the fly or set one of them to help you with puzzles or even fights (the latter costs lots of magic iirc). The art direction mostly remains the same here, but I feel like it fits better with the narrative/tone of the story this time around, and I also love the optional dialogue between the two protagonists - shows lots of character. The game is pretty linear compared to previous entries and you'd only backtrack to do missions that a certain character will give you. I'm not big on the endgame and the soundtrack is... just okay. Though to end on a positive note, this game does offer the most extra modes after you are done with the main game.As for Order of Ecclesia, you will either love or hate it. This game is about as linear, if not more than, Portrait. However, I think the level design is a lot more interesting, and the boss fights can be really fun. Game makes a few changes to the combat where two separate buttons are used for left and right-handed attacks and you'll need to alternate between them for the fastest attack speed plus you are given 3 separate build slots for glyphs, which is important to utilize as enemies can be very immune/weak to certain attacks. Ecclesia can and will kick your ass and that might not be everyone's cup of tea. The game has a unique art direction compared to the previous two entries to something that's a bit similar gothic art - it's not the same as it was, but it's good in it's own way. The narrative in this title is probably the best in any Castlevania game, so I will not say anything about it, I feel it will speak for itself. The endgame is pretty cool too, but again, not telling you. Soundtrack is also my personal favorite of the three games in this collection.I'd say Dawn is my personal favorite of this collection, and I do go back to Ecclesia occasionally, but I do need to be in a specific mood for it. Portrait is still really good as well. If you are interested in this series, or metroidvanias in general, pick this collection up. It is worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: So let's get the important thing out of the way, is this collection good? Answer: Yes. Best $25 you'll ever spend.While you are indeed getting what is essentially a DS rom collection, DS emulation is notorious for needing third party material, (like a tablet), to make the more touch screen focused games on it a decent experience, (looking at you, TWEWY).Thanks to the great work by M2, much of the touch screen gimmicks in certain games like Dawn of Sorrow, have been greatly simplified, such as the boss seals using controller buttons now. I'd be the first to tell you it isn't a perfect solution, especially compared to the mod for the regular DS rom version of Dawn of Sorrow, that flat out removes all the touch screen gimmicks. However, I think nobody would disagree with the Dominus Collection being a great 'legal' alternative to emulating these games, (and you can pretend you're funding a new Castlevania title by buying).The DSvanias were always limited by their potential reach. Despite the DS selling gangbusters, a majority never ventured out of the first party sphere of games, Now with exclusively no longer being an issue, I hope the world starts including these games into the conversation of great games, because these games really have some immense passion and soul put into them, especially Portrait of Ruin. There's not a single flat out "bad" title here, even if you consider one of the games to be weaker, it's weaker in the sense of being an 8/10 while another title is like a 9/10. Even the bonus game included here, Haunted Castle, which was very notorious for being a "drain the quarters out of the player completely" arcade title, now has a brand new remake of it that makes it finally playable! If you're like me and love extra stuff that comes with games, like instruction manuals and concept art, this collection also delivers on that front. Every single language these games were released in has both a manual available, and a game version that can be played. Meaning you can play EN Dawn, JP Portrait, and EU OOE, all in this collection, just from the options.This collection is near perfect, with it's only real issue being it's always gonna launch in windowed mode, there doesn't seem to be a dedicated fullscreen option. Aside from that, I have had a couple of weird inconsistent crashes happen twice. I can't definitively tell if they were a game issue, or a hardware issue, but don't let that scare you off, I haven't had any other issues in my time playing,

_childDocuments_.review: Can't wait to 100% souls for the 500th times (Magic Seal was considerably nerfed, so using it is much easier now, thanks the lord)Can't wait to hear "CHARLOTTE! JONATHAN" for the 500th timesCan't wait to die in Order of Ecclesia for the 500th times.Alright, enough jokes, let's get into it.Castlevania Dominus Collection:- What the compilation did right.  + Magic Seal in Dawn of Sorrow: they added button sequence, despite it's awkward, it's much easier to do than dragging a mouse to perform it like in the original, so massive kudos for M2.  + All intro movies are now playing automatically the moment you highlight the game, plus, all of them are upscaled to HD, so more awesome intro movies to watch, which I did enjoy as a kid. Not to mention, you don't have to watch those once you start the game. All of them will go straight to the main menu, so it's much quicker to get into the fun.  + The compilation now displayed all 3 screens instead of 2. In the DS version, you have to press select button to switch the screen between map, and status. You can still do that in this compilation, but not required. It's a matter of personal reference on whether some want the map screen up, or down (at least in my case).  + There's a compendium which compile all the souls, subweapons, magic, and glyphs showcase, so that's cool  + They literally polished the dogtur-, I mean Haunted Castle, and remake it to a better version, holy cow. Talk about bonus.  + There's a difficulty setting for that tur-, I mean Haunted Castle?- What the compilation did wrong.  - The bugged luck stat in Dawn of Sorrow still unchanged, so any gears or souls that only boost luck stat are now useless.  - There's no adjustment to buff those soul drop rate. I'm sorry, I'm not a big fan of grinding. I don't like spending 5 hours to farm for Iron Golem soul just to upgrade my sword or for getting Chaos Ring.  - I can't use WASD movement for Sister Mode in Portrait of Ruin, so I had no choice but to map the button all over again if I ever go through that mode. Meaning it will require one step to play this mode perfectly with kbm.  - The compilation still doesn't give you some location to find item, especially some quest items in Order of Ecclesia that can only be found via rare chest.  - This may not belong here, but from what I heard, if you skip Death's dialogue before fighting him in Portrait of Ruin, your save file will be corrupted, unsure if they fix itsince my draft is very long, I'll make this short:Castlevania: Dawn of Sorrow: Still a fun game, just not as good as Aria of Sorrow, and I still recommend playing that before this just to experience one of the most awesome twist in the series. Though that magic seal can suck my pp, and the grinding is even worse, by nerfing the drop rate, and some are required to craft some of the best weapons in the game, but it still doesn't harm the experience.Castlevania: Portrait of Ruin: one of the most extensive and best level design I've ever seen. Despite it's short, it stressed out very well. Plus, controlling 2 characters at once, while it's clunky at first, it's not too hard to get used to. Don't forget those top-notch soundtracks.Castlevania: Order of Ecclesia: one of the best plot in the game, rival Aria of Sorrow, bar none. The game is really hard, mainly because you have to adapt to a complete different gimmick set apart from the predecessors, and enemies are much stronger than before, meaning some can drain more than half of Shanoa's health with her best gear, and Shanoa, while her stats are awful, her gimmick made up for it, so she's still very fun to play with. I like those soundtracks so much I literally covered some of them in preparation for Halloween in 2024.Just don't play Haunted Castle, it's a pile of turd, go play the revisited version, instead, or adjust HC difficulty to make it "fun" to get tortured with.Overall, get this compilation as you can. It's worth every single penny.

_childDocuments_.review: The Castlevania RPG games are absolute classics. And while many people were upset to see the shift in this direction as opposed to more traditional 2D side-scrollers, as an RPG fan, these games are iconic. Now with the release of the DS games having come out, a new generation of players can experience this incredible package. I'm gonna quickly talk about each game in the order I played them,Dawn of Sorrow is the first game I played and what most people will end of gravitating to immediately. As a follow-up to Aria of Sorrow, it's nice for many players that knew Aria to go on another adventure with familiar faces. The soul gathering is back as is the wonderful soundtrack. However, I found myself questioning some decisions they made. For one, the art style might not throw off many people who never played this. But Aria's art direction was very enjoyable. This is also due, in part, to it being on the GBA, but the DS going into a hard anime direction just feels a little off. The writing is also something I take an issue with. Sadly, I put the writing in this game as 'fan fiction' territory. Even from the beginning, it feels like they didn't have a great direction to go in to make a sequel. I find myself wishing there was more of a narrative push, but instead, it just feels like they threw their hands up, and wrote whatever in order to get Soma back in that castle. The big saving grace is the gameplay though. Just like Aria, it feels and plays incredibly. Like most players, I do have an issue with the seals you have to make for the bosses. However, this package makes them into a quicktime event which mitigates some of the frustration. Not the best, but not the worst.Portrait of Ruin is a game which leaves me yearning for more. A game I think many players may not find themselves drawn to, this is Konami's first shift away from the Aria formula on DS. There is a tie to Bloodlines, for Castlevania fans that know, which is rather nice. But otherwise, it's a journey with a new cast. However, with a new partner system, and the portrait's themselves, I think Konami had some rather interested ideas of this title. However, I think they should have hashed these ideas out a bit more. The partner system, switching between Jonathan and Charlotte, is rather unique. Using them to assist with moving objects, holding down switches, etc. does add some variety in the game. And, as you would expect, their play styles are different. Jonathan is the physical brawler while Charlotte is the mage extraordinaire. However, I wish there was more incentive to switching back-and-forth between the two characters while adventuring and during combat. Instead, I found myself using Charlotte only to cast the spell she had equipped while Jonathan did the heavy lifting. Not bad, just wishing there was a little more. And the portraits themselves is a very interested idea. But I feel they needed a little bit more time to be worked on. It feels limiting and leaves you wanting a little bit more. The visuals are the same as Dawn of Sorrow so, if you weren't a fan before, you won't be now. The music is not too shabby though. The story is, I would say, around the same level of quality to Dawn, though Jonathan's speech can make you want to roll your eyes. I would say Portrait of Ruin is a decent little title with many aspects that could have been better with a bit more work.My bias will be showing completely with the final game on the list: Order of Ecclesia. There is something trouble remarkable about this title for me. The visuals are absolutely stunning, moving away from the anime art style and returning more to a more gritty look. Their is a new array of characters you will meet with side quests to help bolster you and the shop. While Portrait of Ruin had many ideas which needed to be worked on more, Order of Ecclesia does exactly that. The glyph system enables you a wide range of weapons and different abilities at your disposal. You can find these in statues, steal from enemies, or dropped form enemies like a throw back to Aria and Dawn. However, all attacks and abilities are tied to mana. But with mana regeneration fairly quick, it turns the MP gauge into a pseudo-stamina bar. The map system is almost akin to the portrait system, but with some more variety. Though there are some reused assets, I found myself absolutely loving every little area I explored. The music is heavenly, but I do wish there were a few more tracks within the game. And the story is rather good, especially in comparison to the rest of the package. One criticism that is understandable is that, within context of the story, Shanoa does not have emotions. This is expressed throughout in her dialogue as she struggles to understand the things around her. But it helped tie things together and, when her frustrations begin to break through some, really elevates how this must be making her feel since her emotions are supposed to be dulled. This game is truly a marvel.Asking if this collection is worth it is crazy. The answer is a resounding yes. While I do find two of the games to be rather decent at best, I would pay for the collection for Order of Ecclesia alone. And the other two are absolutely worth a playthrough as well. There is not a single bad game in here. The collection translates these DS games to PC absolutely wonderfully and makes me hope that other companies may start looking into re-releasing some DS games onto PC. But for now, this collection is a definite buy! If you're a fan of Castlevania or RPGs, you cannot go wrong one bit!

_childDocuments_.review: This collection ports the three excellent Castlevania titles that released on the Nintendo DS. Aside from Symphony of the Night (which at the time of writing is still unavailable on Steam) these are the best Igavanias by far, and among the best metroidvanias ever made. Originally intended for a handheld, the games are a perfect fit for the Steam Deck. Whatever you play them on, you have options regarding the layout. On the original hardware, the gameplay would appear on the bottom screen, while a map or stat screen would occupy the top screen. Here the default places both of these to the right of the game play, so you always have access to all information bar that of the pause screen. I found this the best configuration but you have other options. The emulation is flawless as far as I can tell. The touch screen elements of these games were pretty minimal to begin with, mostly being a factor in Dawn and one of Portrait’s alt modes.I would strongly recommend playing in release order, Dawn of Sorrow > Portrait of Ruin > Order of Ecclesia. Dawn is kind of the exact mid-point between Symphony of the Night and Bloodstained, it’s the latest game within the overarching storyline but it was made before the others in this collection and I think best experienced first so it’s not overshadowed by the other two games. It is a direct sequel to Aria of Sorrow, which was included in the Advance collection if you’re committed to following the story, though you will be fine without having played it (also a solid game though). While I love all three games Portrait is my personal favourite, with decent variety, a comparatively good story, and a fun dual-protagonist mechanic. Ecclesia has the best presentation of the three and feels slightly more mature, while also being easily the hardest game of the Igavanias (though still perfectly manageable) – so I think it’s best saved for last. All three games feature alternate replay modes that can be played once completed (and in some cases fulfilling certain conditions). For example, you can play through Portrait as Richter and Maria, who are absolute beasts and make for a much more high-tempo replay. This does a lot for the replayability of these titles. Also included are the different regional variants of each of the games, which is nice for completions sake, but I’m unaware of any major differences across these particular titles outside the language selection and a possible bug fix on the European version of Portrait.The bonus game included this time, Haunted Castle, is an arcade game from 1987. It’s quite widely regarded as one of the worst, if not the worst, game in the Castlevania series. While I quite like the presentation, being an arcade game from that era it has notoriously cheap difficulty and just isn’t as fun to play as most of the classicvanias.Surprisingly, the makers of the collection went the extra mile and made a full-blown remake of Haunted Castle, technically the first new Castlevania game in a decade (excluding the Apple Arcade-exclusive Grimoire of Souls). The graphics have been overhauled and look on par with the 16bit-era games. While still not up there with Super Castlevania IV, Bloodlines or Rondo of Blood, its now a pretty good time and at least worth trying out if you like the pre-Iga ‘vanias. As a long-time fan, it’s nice to see an unloved part of the series get this type of treatment.The collection is rounded out with an art gallery, including concept art, scans of the manuals, etc. There is also music player.The Dominus Collection is terrific value even at full price, if you like metroidvanias at all you should be snapping this up, especially if it’s on sale. For me personally, I feel any one of the DS Castlevanias is worth the asking price.

_childDocuments_.review: Pure, uncut nostalgia, delivered with exceptional technical competency.Seriously, I was playing this for the past two days. I can give a point by point of how the emulation/porting work was done well (Though given that Advance Collection was done well, I can't say I'm shocked)1: Responsive Controls - Controls are low latency. I've yet to have any issues with timing.2: Touch Controls - Mouse support means the touch screen stuff is usable (Though I imagine it'd be WAY better on steam deck, because that can do mouse input via touch screen)3: Stability - Minimal bugs at launch: No visual glitches noticed, if memory serves on how this is SUPPOSED to look. No crash bugs. The only issue I ever had with this release was a single audio issue, where the game audio stopped but the UI sounds (from the overlay/collection pause menu/rewind ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥) were still working, but it was probably more to do with Windows Phone Link and swapping audio output than the game itself.4: Value - $25 to buy 3 games that launched on their original platforms at $30 each, and which (in their original format) essentially doubled in price.Konami's track record has been hit or miss at best (almost entirely misses, TBH), but this one's a hit. If these things keep being profitable when they're good, then there's an incentive to make more retro releases of this caliber. TL:DR This is worth it for anyone who remembers the originals fondly, and buying it could improve the likelihood of more high-quality re-releases of classic content in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: The Castlevania Dominus Collection is, at this time, the latest in the series of Konami's anthology series. This collection focuses on the three classic Nintendo DS games and oddly the arcade game Haunted Castle.At the time of writing this I have only played through Dawn of Sorrow and Haunted Castle:Remastered. The fact that Haunted Castle has been remasted shows me how dedicated developer M2 is at their goal of making these games accessible. It's now a much easier game that can be completed in one sitting, instead of the horrible quarter muncher of the original(which you can still play in this collection if you so desire!) Meanwhile, Dawn of Sorrow has had a few changes as well to make it accessible on modern machines. Dawn of Sorrow was an early Nintendo DS title it was hit with mandatory touch screen controls. Instead of gutting the touch screen completely like you would see with some romhacks of the game, the developers had decided to add touch screen functionality with either your controller or mouse. They did remove the touch screen requirement for the magic seal system, now using button prompts that are much easier to handle. Of course there's also extras, such as concept art and promotional material. What I found surprising was that they also included the instruction manuals for the games, and not just one manual but a manual for each region the game was released in. Seems a bit excessive but if you're trying to make an definitive anthology of these games, I guess that's the way to go about it.    The games were always good. The collection just makes them easier to legally get a hold of and play!

_childDocuments_.review: Three great Metroidvanias all in one package for a nice price.  Add on top of that all the Castlevania collection Quality of Life features from the pause menu, and you go up a notch.  While some may prefer the old stylus method, the new quick-time button presses for magical seals in Dawn of Sorrow make this a far more enjoyable game for me.  There's still a challenge, but with none of the finicky unfairness of the stylus sigil-drawing of the original.  Using the right stick is slow, but using a mouse works great for touchscreen actions.  Then as a cherry on top, you get the original Haunted Castle which many fans of the series may have never played, and that even gets 1-upped by having a BRAND NEW old school Castlevania game that loosely follows the original Haunted Castle with more modern controls and feel.  Awesome purchase if you're a fan of the series.  Now, where is Symphony of the Night?  LOL

_childDocuments_.review: Every game in this collection is great, with the exception of the original Haunted Castle game, which is complete ♥♥♥♥.Actually, though, the Haunted Castle remake is fantastic. I'm mentioning this up front because I imagine a lot of people will sleep on this, and there are reviews insinuating that it's simply a visual update, which is completely untrue - this is an entirely new game based on the original's settings & enemies, but with wholly original design. It's a solid classic Castlevania with a low level of difficulty, suitable for beginners who perhaps aren't used to those 8- and 16-bit games but might want to play a game in that style that is more simple to clear. Any skilled player should easily be able to beat it on the first playthrough without even coming close to running out of lives, but there's still enough here to make it worth a play for even the most hardened Castlevania fan.As for the DS games, I played all of them on the DS when they originally released, and have played them occasionally through the years. I consider them to be entirely superior to the GBA games and, controversially, I think that Dawn of Sorrow is a better game than Aria. Aria is just too easy.Curiously, this collection lists the games in chronological order, which is the exact inverse of the release order. I decided to play them in chronological order this time, mostly because I wanted to start with what had been my favourite game, Order of Ecclesia.Order of Ecclesia is still my favourite. The bosses are absolutely the best of any game in the IGAvania set, and I appreciate how restrained they were with the levels, especially with regard to limiting the number of ability-gated items and paths; there's never too much backtracking to do when you get a new power. Enemy design feels better than the other games, and the level & encounter design is more thoughtful, though there are still some areas that have that typical filler feeling that all Metroidvania games seem to suffer from.Portrait of Ruin, in my opinion, suffers from the portrait gimmick, and from an apparent budget deficit? The portrait levels are full of copy-pasted rooms & slapdash enemy placement and, while this gimmick does allow them to portray a variety of locations, the levels themselves feel like a slog to work through. We also lose some of the atmosphere and character that is achieved by having a singular, cohesive environment. (Ecclesia also does not have this, but the environments are consistent and the levels are less tedious to play through.) I also think that the dual character gimmick doesn't work very well - I rarely felt any reason to switch to the second character (I forget her name); her only real use is for enemies that are weak to particular magic attacks, and in that case you can summon her for a special attack instead of switching to her. That said, I will say that this game has the best bosses outside of Ecclesia and, despite my negativity, it's still an enjoyable game. Dawn of Sorrow is more traditional. The main addition from Aria is a weapon upgrade system that involves using enemy souls to upgrade weapons; at first it might seem superfluous, but by the end of the game, you'll need to engage with it to get the strong weapons, and this simply means grinding against one enemy type until the RNG decides to give you the enemy's soul, which is obviously tedious. Anyway, besides this, the game is solid in pretty much every way that you'd hope for in one of these games. The bosses in particular are massively better than previous games.I recommend this collection, obviously. Despite my criticisms, all of these games are very enjoyable.

_childDocuments_.review: The Castlevania: Dominus Collection bundles together some of the most iconic Metroidvania titles, including Castlevania: Dawn of Sorrow, Portrait of Ruin, Order of Ecclesia, and Haunted Castle Revisited. If you’re a fan of the genre, these games offer some of the best experiences available, even if some of the original Nintendo DS gimmicks and limitations linger. These titles were groundbreaking in their design, music, and visuals, inspiring countless games that followed, though few have matched them. A major highlight is that all cutscenes in the collection can be skipped, which significantly improves replayability.Castlevania: Dawn of SorrowDawn of Sorrow stars Soma Cruz, a hero who can absorb enemy Souls to gain abilities. Soma’s combat variety comes from equipping different weapon types, each with unique movesets. The game offers multiple endings, but two are bad endings, and you can't skip the cutscenes leading to them—subtly nudging players toward the better ending.The DS version had some frustrating touch-screen mechanics, like drawing glyphs to seal bosses, but this port smartly replaces that with button combinations, which is a huge improvement. Unfortunately, some touch-based mechanics remain, like tapping ice blocks, though these only appear in a few rooms and feel gimmicky. Another minor gripe is that three optional rooms require a specific amount of money to unlock, which feels like unnecessary padding.On the plus side, gameplay is smooth and fun, with Soma’s Souls being either overpowered or niche in their usefulness. Some Souls can decimate enemies by hitting multiple times, while others feel like novelties. After completing the game, players unlock two new modes: Julius Mode, which offers a multi-character experience similar to Castlevania III: Dracula's Curse, and Hard Mode, which acts as a New Game Plus with harder enemy patterns. Both modes provide ample replay value, though completionists might find the grind for Souls and equipment a bit tedious due to low drop rates, especially on a first playthrough.Castlevania: Portrait of RuinIn Portrait of Ruin, you control Jonathon, a melee fighter, and Charlotte, a magic user. You can switch between the two to solve puzzles or during combat, giving the game a refreshing dual-character dynamic. Each character needs their own equipment and can be customized to suit different play styles. While I enjoyed this flexibility, some of the puzzles that rely on both characters felt more like gimmicks than clever design.The game’s use of "Portraits" to transport players into various self-contained levels is one of its standout features, providing more environmental variety than most Castlevania titles. However, the difficulty spikes compared to Dawn of Sorrow, and enemies dish out much more damage, making the game significantly more challenging. The final boss fight, in particular, is tough, almost disproportionately so compared to the rest of the game.Much like Dawn of Sorrow, Portrait of Ruin has bad endings, and the method for unlocking the good one is far from intuitive. You either need to explore thoroughly or consult a guide, which feels like a poor design choice. Worse yet, the critical moment involves a boss fight where you need to protect your partner while using a slow spell. If your partner gets hit, you have to start over. I hated this section—it’s clunky, frustrating, and mandatory for every playthrough. After that, the game makes you backtrack through earlier zones, now inverted, which feels like lazy padding rather than fresh content.The Quest system is another mixed bag. It provides powerful rewards like new skills and equipment, but many quests involve tedious backtracking and grinding. To unlock the optional and more challenging area "Nest of Evil," you have to complete several quests, which may be off-putting for players who aren’t fans of backtracking. Like Dawn of Sorrow, Portrait of Ruin offers multiple additional characters to play as after finishing the game, which adds replay value, though the repetitiveness of the core game diminishes the appeal.Castlevania: Order of EcclesiaOrder of Ecclesia centers around Shanoa, a protagonist who uses glyphs—magical symbols that act as spells and weapons. This system allows Shanoa to dual-wield different abilities, but they consume MP, which regenerates over time. The combat is slower-paced, and the game leans more heavily on exploiting enemy weaknesses, often requiring specific glyph types to deal significant damage. The game’s gothic aesthetic is gorgeous and adds to the overall atmosphere, though its slower pace may not be for everyone.At the start, the game bombards you with cutscenes and tutorials (thankfully skippable), likely because of how different it is from previous titles. Combat requires more strategy, but the constant need to swap glyphs to match enemy weaknesses can feel tedious. Fights drag on if you don’t have the right glyph, and the randomness of glyph drops from enemies can lead to hours of grinding. The world map is divided into smaller areas, unlike the expansive castles of previous games, but this offers more environmental variety.Revisiting areas to find treasures after acquiring new abilities becomes repetitive, and waypoints are oddly placed, often far from entrances or save points. Ultimately, Order of Ecclesia feels grindy and exhausting, and while it has some redeeming qualities, the constant repetition makes it harder to enjoy compared to its predecessors.Haunted Castle RevisitedHaunted Castle Revisited is the odd one out in this collection, most similar to the original Castlevania arcade experience. You play as a whip-wielding protagonist with powerful sub-weapons. The remixed soundtrack sounds great, though the new art direction can make enemy visibility tricky due to a muted enemy design.The game retains its classic difficulty but is more forgiving than its era, giving you unlimited continues and generous checkpoints. Unlike other Castlevania games, your whip can’t destroy projectiles, which threw me off at first. It’s a fun historical piece for die-hard fans of the series, though it won’t appeal to everyone. The inclusion of this game in the collection feels like a nice bonus for those who appreciate the series’ history.ConclusionThe Castlevania: Dominus Collection is a treasure trove for Metroidvania fans, packing in at least two excellent, if slightly flawed, DS-era titles and a Revisited arcade classic. The games still hold up remarkably well, and while the DS-specific gimmicks occasionally detract from the experience, the improved controls and modern conveniences like skippable cutscenes make the collection worth playing. Whether you’re a long-time fan or a newcomer to the series, this collection offers hours of challenging, satisfying gameplay that remains influential to this day.

_childDocuments_.review: This collection is peak, its probably the best Castlevania collection and its often on sale for $18 you owe it to yourself to try it. My personal ranking is Order of Ecclesia=Portrait of Ruin>>Dawn of Sorrow.  Here are some quick thoughts:Dawn of Sorrow:This is the only one I had played prior to this collection, its fun but a big step down from Aria in a lot of ways, terrible art, awful, awful rng (the crafting system doesn't help it makes drops from enemies and the castle feel worthless sometimes) and a bad story just make this one kind of a sleeper which is a shame because I am a huge fan of Soma and Aria. It's still a great game and worth playing but easily the weakest part of the collection for me, my complaints are mostly that it feels a few steps back from Aria.Portrait of Ruin:The music here is great, Jonathan and Charlotte play completely differently and feel great by themselves or working together, Charlotte's magic is the most fun I've ever had just playing Castlevania and this is probably the most fun Castle to run through for replays in my opinion! Only downsides are once again the character art doesn't really fit Castlevania and the game is sometimes overly easy once you master its systems.Order of Ecclesia:Fantastic art, my favorite Castlevania soundtrack, great protagonist, interesting, if short, story and challenging. My biggest complaints are I feel that there is less replay value than other Castlevania games, the Glyph system is awesome but there are a lot less of them than souls or weapons from previous titles and only a small amount are actually worth using imo. Also the difficulty...im glad its challenging but it sometimes veers into too much, boss hitboxes on attacks tend to linger and can sometimes hit multiple times taking off enormous amounts of health per hit, seriously getting hit once from some of the final bosses takes over a fourth of your hp even with some of the best equipment. Still a wonderful game and arguably my favorite Castlevania title, would love to see the characters and story fleshed out one day in some sort of revisit.Haunted Castle:This was a nice little surprise! A brand new remake! It's cool but I don't have that much to say as, admittedly, I don't really like Classic-style Castlevania titles all that much, but its still a great little bow on a wonderful package!Please give these games a shot! Support high-quality collections like this, I mean how many re-releases like this come along with new content and emulation style features like savestates or rewind?

_childDocuments_.review: didn't realize this game came out alreadyAnyways, this is an incredible collection, all three main games are, as far as I'm concerned, the best metroidvanias ever made. Shanoa especially because of its really precisely tuned difficulty. The games run fine and sound well, so I'll assume the ports are perfect unless something happens, so I'm going to just go to the port. If you haven't played any of the konami metroidvanias, I think these are the best ones to get into them for both their general ease of access and quality of life. If you played the advance collection these are largely improvements upon that format of game utilizing the higher resolution and ability to play video and audio. The extra game (and extra mode for said game!) are also really cool and I'm happy there's a way to legally play them on every system now.More important than the games themselves running correctly, is this port has about everything you could possibly want. The DS features are integrated well, and not only do you get the second screen, you can have your stat AND map screen at once. If that somehow isn't enough, there is an optional enemy and item glossary with little videos of weapon attacks associated with them so you can review the animations. (incidentally, these videos are also on the disk as plain files, along with the opening movies and all audio.)The galleries for the three games seem to cover literally all the official art of the original games I have ever seen, as well as high quality manual scans. The audio sounds great, I assume it's better than the original ds games but I never played them with headphones. There are also higher quality openings available  in a normal 480p-ish resolution. There are even little quality of life things like in-game saves also being expressed as a snapshot in the system's quick save menu. I was honestly a little concerned these would never get ports because the (admittedly pretty small) complications of getting the ds features compatible with other consoles and I figured they wouldn't bother, but I'm glad to be proven wrong.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite not having them currently in my Steam Library (as I have them on PS4), I've been a pretty big fan of these classic collections Konami has been putting out (given that's basically all they really have at this point). I have the other 2 Castlevania Collections and the Contra one on PS4, and when they basically last minute announced this one, the Castlevania Dominus Collection, I was eager to get it on my PC. Why? Because I knew that if there was any chance of the touch screen mechanics being carried over from the DS titles, the PC was the best place to experience them.As stated above, this is a collection of the three Castlevania titles released for the Nintendo DS back in the day, with those games being "Dawn of Sorrow," "Portrait of Ruin," and my personal favorite game in the Castlevania series, "Order of Eccelsia." All of which have been pretty faithfully ported by the folks over at M2. And I gotta say, as with basically anything M2 does, it doesn't disappoint as far as ports are concerned. They even threw in the Japanese Arcade game "Haunted Castle" and a remake of sorts in the form of "Haunted Castle Revisted." I will be fully transparent and say that I didn't play either of these, as they don't really interest me that much, and because I dumped 45 hours into this collection as is getting all of the Steam Achievements. Thankfully, unlike the Advance Collection, I don't have to play what many would consider a "bonus" title for 100% achievements. Besides, I think it's more important to go over how much of the DS stuff translates to PC.The game has a number of layout options for the dual screen elements of the DS titles, but it's something you're going to have to accept as part of the collection no matter what (unless you're playing Haunted Castle/Revisted, because that's an Arcade game). Thankfully, I think the default layout works well, so no complaints there. I also think they did about the best they could with the DS touch controls. Obviously, the mouse can be used for the touch screen stuff when needed, if you want, but they've done a few things to make it less painful a transition overall. You can also control a cursor with the right stick, as that has to be a thing for consoles that aren't the Switch. It works fine enough (I mostly used it for Albus Mode's teleport in Ecclesia), but generally, when the option is there, mouse is usually the way to go for the touch stuff when it's necessary. Thankfully, it rarely is.The collection also features a rewind and savestate feature, but it has some awkwardness in how it works. For controller, you have to hold the left trigger to rewind, but if you don't hold it long enough for the game to recognise it as a rewind, it'll open the collection's pause menu (separate from the game your playing's pause menu). Depending on how often you use it, it may be a benefit or a pain in the butt. I used the rewind a fair bit specifically (mostly for boss fights to avoid having to go back to a save point over Castlevania hitbox stuff), and even then I only started using it towards the end of Order of Ecclesia (as that was the first game I played through, as it's my favorite) to get the game finished that little bit faster. I then used it a little more liberally just to not get frustrated in places where the stiffness of some elements of movement (like turning around) got me hit, for instance.Order of Ecclesia is as good as I remember. I know some people think it's a bit dull in terms of level design, but it is easily my favorite game in the collection still. Glyphs and Glyph Combos work well, and I had a blast revisiting an old favorite. It is notably probably the hardest game in the collection, but it's the best feeling in my opinion. I even played Albus Mode for the first time, and enjoyed that too, for the brisk replay it was.Portrait of Ruin is a game I never got to play for one reason or another, and I really enjoyed it. Not as much as Ecclesia, but still a damn solid game. I do think the anime aesthetic it has works better for it than it does for Dawn of Sorrow, but I still dislike that element in these games, and I enjoy anime a lot. I do have some gripes about the plot of Portrait, namely the way the game poorly explains why Jonathan can't use the Vampire Killer Whip. I know he's "not a Belmont," but given that his family has as much Belmont Blood in it as a "real" Belmont (unless IGA wanted us to think the Belmont family is full of inbred hunters)... so I really don't think it works as well as the game likes to think. I enjoyed the callbacks to Bloodlines (my second favorite "Classicvania" title for me), and I enjoyed Richter Mode. I feel it was a waste to not have a Lercarde mode given the ties to Bloodlines, and I didn't try Sisters Mode. but it was fun.Dawn of Sorrow feels the oldest of the bunch, and that makes sense, since it's the first DS title. It's a sequel to Aria of Sorrow from the Advance Collection, and honestly, it's fine. It has the most intrusive touch screen mechanics, but only one of them (the breaking of iceblocks) is still a pain. They've made the runes a thing where you can just press the buttons in the correct order instead, which is a blessing. I think Aria is just that little bit better, just as a complete package, but it's solid. Julius Mode is a nice Castlevania 3 inspired mode, and is pretty brisk like most of the alt modes.Overall, I enjoyed the collection. If you liked the previous 2 collections, especially the Advance Collection, then you'll probably really like this one.

_childDocuments_.review: "What a horrible night to have a curse. Yet what a good day to be alive!" ~Me finding out the Dominus collection just dropped!Put simply,if you never had a Nintendo DS and want to own these excellent Igavanias legally this is the way to go. There are many ways to adjust your playing experience and if you are an appreciator of art and music this package is chalk full of goodies from promotional and conceptual illustrations to being able to listen to these classic iconic tunes in whatever order you wish.The best inclusion is a complete remake of Haunted Castle done by the same talented crew that worked on Castlevania Adventure Rebirth. It looks breathtaking with fantastically detailed pixel sprites and the gameplay is fine tuned to perfection. It won't take you long to complete but it is so fun and such a loving tribute to old-skool Castlevanias you'll come back to it out of sheer nostalgia!For many (Including myself) these games defined an era of dark fantasy and gothic horror. They were the resurrection of those black & white cinema masterpieces such as Nosferatu and the various incarnations of Dracula,Doctor Frankenstein's Monster,The Creature From The Black Lagoon,and The Wolf-man. More than that they started to tell a complex moving story about generational vampire hunters and all matter of things that go bump in the night. Even Dracula became a more sympathetic relatable figure whilst "everyone" remembers playing as his son Alucard in Symphony Of The Night!My only criticism with this whole collection is it should have come out "sooner". In its' collective absence many developers rose to the challenge and made games in this niche as good if not better in certain respects. Yet these older classics hold up remarkably well with the same timeless quality inherent within their SOTN predecessor. (Or their "Simon's Quest" predecessor if you want to argue semantics! Still,Simon's Quest had a lot of inherent design flaws that Symphony Of The Night addressed and refined. Take that as you will.)Pretty much if you have a child,sibling,friend,lover,parent,or even a grandparent that appreciates Halloween and spooky scary skeletons more than Christmas "this" is the penultimate gift for them. Both it and the previous CV collection are the "best" in the whole series. (Though I wish one of these two more recent collections included Rondo Of Blood and Symphony Of The Night as well!)Pros+Reasonable price point.+The collection "everyone' wanted is finally here!+Various things to tweak to further refine your game-playing experience.+Radical bone-chilling tunes and art galleries included!+ A "paragon of excellence" remake of Haunted Castle!+Each game is a faithful port including those jaw dropping animated intros.+High potential of putting you on better terms with your vampire goth girlfriend!+Recommended for Souls-like appreciators as well as its' glaringly obvious these games were checking off a lot of those boxes before it was cool!+No additional censorship from what I can tell. And the only people whom might complain about this are the small shrieking minority that will not buy or appreciate this collection anyway!Cons-The Igavania DS trilogy in particular are no cakewalks and can be frustrating in certain places. (But not "too" frustrating in my opinion.)-Some may think that the general aesthetics and art directions clash between entries. -I wanted this collection 5 years ago,Konami! (Still,I appreciate cha! For now!)-There have been complaints about the games running slow but for me they run smooth as spider spun silk! This is obviously going to come down to your rig and your specs. (Though c'mon,at this point an i-phone or even a current-year toaster should be able to handle these!)
_childDocuments_.name: Castlevania Dominus Collection

_childDocuments_.review: My childhood. Finally on Steam and other platforms, dropped without any prior advertising suddenly. Easiest impulse buy of my life.If you liked Bloodstained, please do yourself a favor and buy these as well if you haven't played them. You WILL like them if you liked bloodstained. I have played these countless times, so I am giving each one a separate review prior to mentioning the emulation itself.Dawn of Sorrow - 94/100. I honestly prefer Aria of Sorrow, but SOTN is a fantastic entry as well.  The only reason I don't rate this higher is that luck is a bugged stat and grinding to 100% can take a silly amount of time. I feel like Aria also had generally more interesting area design.Portrait of Ruin - 92/100. This one grew on me A LOT. It's one of the most unique feeling Castlevania games, however I feel like difficulty wise its one of the easier ones which holds me back from rating it higher. The quest system in this game laid the groundwork for Order of Ecclessia. Order of Ecclessia - 100/100 - The quintessential Metroidvania game. If you took AOS/DOS, Portrait of Ruin, and Symphony of the Night then combined the best parts of all of them into a blender you'd get this game. The best Metroidvania of all time IMO. It saddens me to know that Castlevania reached its peak before tapering off into nothingness. This game had me wanting a sequel for years. The actual emulator works great, with the touch controls working fantastically and being integrated in a way that I much prefer. While mods did exist to remove touch screen controls, I actually kind of liked the gimmickness of it and have a fondness for them. Instead of drawing symbols to beat bosses in DOS, you simply input it like a quicktime event via the controller instead.The games run at a solid and stable 60 fps, with no lag or jitter. Just like the Gameboy advance collection, the emulator comes packed with a few nice features -- save states/instant rewinding/the ability to change the DS view. Yes. It runs amazing on deck as expected.I feel like the bundle is priced fairly too, going for 100% in these 3 games will take me many hours like they did when I was a kid. If you like Metroidvanias, Castlevania, or just...games in general do yourself a favor and please buy these. Now we wait for SOTN+Rondo Of Blood+Harmony of Despair :)

_childDocuments_.review: A welcome addition to the previous Castlevania collections, showcasing the last and (in some respects) most experimental of the series' Metroidvanias. _childDocuments_.review: I'm gonna go ahead and give this a positive review because these are my three favorite Castlevania games and I am SO ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ecstatic that they are no longer relegated to being stuck in Nintendo DS Limbo and barely functional emulators, but there are some QOL things I am hoping they add (but I'm not going to hold my breath), such as full mouse + keyboard support. Right now it is very basic and minimal and you have to do the old school two-handed keyboard approach where you move with the arrow keys and everything else is done with letters. It just feels clunky and it's made worse by the fact that there is zero instruction manual from what I can tell, so you just kind of have to mash keys until you figure out what does what. I would really just love for keybindings to be added, I would probably not mind the keyboard controls as much if I could move with the traditional WASD scheme, but moving with arrow keys, jumping with Z, attacking with A/S, etc., is very unintuitive. Mouse functionality is also limited to certain things only, like navigating the maps on the right side of the screen and typing in your save file name. More settings would also be nice; unless I'm missing something, it appears that right now the game can only be played in window mode, not full screen, which I am not a fan of.Besides these minor quibbles, I am very happy with what I have seen thus far and am honestly just thrilled that Konami is FINALLY doing something with these games. I hope this means that more are to follow (LAMENT OF INNOCENCE AND CURSE OF DARKNESS, PLEEEAAASE KONAMI 😭😭😭) and that maybe there is a chance we will finally get more games in this legendary series.

_childDocuments_.review: It's rare that a franchise meets their heyday on a handheld console of all things, but that's absolutely what happened with . After finding their footing on the GBA, Konami produced three extremely strong Metroidvania titles for the Nintendo DS: [i[Dawn of Sorrow[/i],  and . At long last, Konami has lifted these games off of the veritably ancient handheld and ported them to Steam, making it possible for new players to experience the highest quality games in a franchise of bangers. The  is yet another old game port job, but with some additional bells and whistles that make it worth picking up. It's probably best to give three "micro reviews" to each game in the collection, before then evaluating the package as a whole, so you know what you're getting into. *****A direct leadup from arguably the best game in the franchise,  follows highschool student and reincarnation of an ancient evil Soma Cruz. Following an attack from a cult seeking to revive the Dark Lord, Soma pulls up his big boy boots and dons yet another sick-as-hell coat to stop them.  is a solid metroidvania in it's own right, building off of 's design ideas... along with some missteps. The map design and general gameplay is great, and the soul system returning from the prior game is wonderful. Enemies have a chance to drop "souls" on death that can be equipped for passive bonuses or as subweapons, giving Soma a ton of attacks to use. There's always a giddy rush of adrenaline when you see a soul pop out, and get to experiment with how it might work. Souls are diverse and add a lot to the basic gameplay, especially once you kill a boss and get its soul. The major problem with this is that  introduced a crafting system that uses these souls. Players must abandon strong, fun-to-use souls just to keep up their DPS with weapons, which feels bad. Couple this with poor drop-rates on some really useful souls, and  can be very tedious to play. The low drop rate does encourage replaybility through randomizing the souls you end up getting by playing casually, but ultimately this is the weakest game of the trio. Still, it's a highly competent game with great pacing, lots of content, and a killer soundtrack. ***** is the second game in the collection, and probably my favorite. The story follows vampire-hunter-apprentices Johnathan and Charlotte as they venture into Dracula's castle to fight... not Dracula! They go up against a mad artist named Brauner, who has the ability to create magical paintings that lead to other worlds. Ditching the soul system completely,  chooses to instead work in a dual-character mechanic. Johnathan is the traditional warrior hero who uses swords and whips, while Charlotte is a mage type character who slings magic. The game paces out character upgrades for both protagonists very well, and it feels great as both characters develop into independently-strong beasts. While the soul mechanic was dropped for this title, there's more than enough variety between both characters to make up for the loss. The game uses the dual-character mechanic quite well, with lots of fun puzzles, but the star of the show is the potrait system. The portraits let the developers introduce new environments to Dracula's castle, like ancient pyramids or a downtown city. This gives the game some much-needed variety, though the game faces pacing issues in the back half due to re-using these locations. There's also a sidequest system that is a little tedious, but thankfully the rewards are very much worth it.  sounds like a gimmicky mess, but in reality is probably the best game in the collection and one of the most underrated  titles on top of that.*****The weirdest game of the bunch has to be , if only for how transparently this game would be the inception for the  games. Starring a witch named Shanoa,  follows an order of anti-Dracula agents trying to stop his resurrection. Shanoa's gameplay is unique in that she not only re-uses the soul system from , but doubles down on it! Shanoa can equip no less than four souls at once, though some are clearly just weapons for her to use. Souls still drain from the mana meter, now functioning more like a stamina meter, which slows Shanoa's damage potential by a huge amount.  As a tradeoff, Shanoa's spells are powerful and offer her mobility and utility that the other protagonists could only dream of. Accordingly to this increase in utility, this is the toughest game in the package, with many levels that are linear combat gauntlets. While not nearly as savage as the older games,  does not mess around, and can be a surprising shock coming from the earlier two games. While that might sound annoying, fret not-  is a late-stage DS title, meaning it is packed full of some of the best sprites, stages, and animations that the DS could produce. The game boasts an excellent art style and the story is actually really good for a game of this type. Though the linear gauntlets might wear you down, once you get past the early stage,  becomes a traditional Metroidvania, and has some great level design to support it. Even still, the linear gauntlets are good fun and provide a nice break from the dungeon-crawling of the prior two games before diving back into it. One of the most experimental  games, and maybe one of the best. *****So these are three great games, but why not just emulate or grab a cheap copy online? Simply put, this is a great package. It goes on sale for around 20 bucks, and comes with loads of extras. Not only do you get all three games, but subtle changes have been made to each for a better experience. The game offers a solid way to use the touch-screen mechanics from the DS with your analog stick, making it much easier to tap specific things with precision. The irritating Magic Seal system from  has been heavily neutered, several bugs have been squashed (with the fun ones left in) and all three games allow you to display the game, map, and equipment screens at the same time. Coupled with savestates in each collection for fast farming, and this makes the collection the singular best way to play all three of these games. Plus the collection comes with Haunted Castle  an HD-remake in the style of  or . Altogether, this is a pretty solid package.Normally, I don't recommend these cash-grab rereleases. I feel that they're cheap, poorly-made hackjobs that exist to sucker any consumer who doesn't want to touch emulation. This package is not one such deal. It's a fairly priced, well-constructed collection that contains three excellent Metroidvanias. The additional bells and whistles push this over from "cheapo rushjob" into "well-made tribute". If you want to try , love Metroidvanias, or just enjoy beating skeletons so hard they explode, then you really can't go wrong with this.

_childDocuments_.review: Missed opportunities with dawn of sorrow to actually correct the broken luck stat and make the game much more enjoyable without having to deal with 1% or less then 1% drop chances for souls. The glyph system for killing bosses should have just been removed like many romhacks of the original DS classic do because nobody likes that ♥♥♥♥. _childDocuments_.review: Definitely worth having if you are a castlevania fan! I believe Konami is doing the right thing by releasing these Castlevania ports...First Collection we had was a nice boost, the Advance Collection was a great addition and now they did this, I was totally taken surprise by it and just saw it appear out of the blue! The Dominus Collection! This is by far the best DS games you could enjoy in the Castlevania franchise. Touch Controls can be done with the mouse, however with most of the touch mechanics are now done with the controller button presses. (For example, Dawn of Sorrow you simply press A, B, X, Y, etc to auto-draw the symbol during its phase) I love these type of games! Soundtrack is perfect, controls are nice and tight, and the graphics HD update makes it even better! Now if they overhaul the N64, Ps2 Titles we would have nearly a complete Castlevania Collection on our system!

_childDocuments_.review: Really happy to have these games as a collection (also they fixed the fullscreen issue from Advance).  The price for what you get is absolutely worth it.  I think the layout for DS games converted to PC are as about as good as it's going to get in this.  In fact, when using emulators, you wouldn't be able to have the status screen and map up at the same time, so that's a pretty great addition.  But you still get all the layouts that you have in emulators anyways, so this really is the definitive way to play these games.Now can we please have a game for what happens in 1999?  Or at least a localized version of SotN from Sega Saturn?

_childDocuments_.review: Huge fan of the classic metroidvanias and this does not disappoint.  Played through these before and the emulation on this port seems to be top notch.  I did have the issue where my system was not set for 60hz and it was very slow, but after adjusting my setting in Windows, no issue whatsoever.  Only thing I don't like about these games is that in order to get the "true" or "real" ending, you'll probably have to search to find what you're missing out on.  Without spoilers or hints, I wish there was some more obvious clues as to how to find what is needed to progress to the final boss.  However, pushing 15-20 years old, info is available everywhere.  If you're like me, be ready to waste pointless time and energy to get near that 100% completion!Enjoy, worth every penny.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my GOTY after Elden Ring SOTE, it's an incredible game preservation collection with a lot of QoL add-ons, not to mention the DS games are fantastic; I've fully completed all of the games including the modern remake of the Haunted Castle, all of them are amazing; a must-play for all metroidvania fans.I'd recommend starting the Haunted Castle Remake first as it is an hour or so long! If you care a lot about the story and lore in these games, it's recommended to play Castlevania Bloodlines before playing Castlevania: Portrait of Ruin, as these two games are connected. Same with Aria of Sorrow and Dawn of Sorrow, but you can pick any game and still have a lot of fun!
_childDocuments_.name: Castlevania Dominus Collection

_childDocuments_.review: The franchise that gave its name to an entire genre, in a complete and feature-rich package. Konami's best product in recent years and honestly one of the best retro game collections in the technical department. The biggest red flag these types of collections usually have is the input delay, which is not a problem in this case. Other features like the rewind mechanic were really good and welcome against OoE's obnoxious game design and difficulty spikes. The games themselves are amazing and really fun to this day; most of the soulless Metroidvania clones still fail to grasp the gameplay, atmosphere and feeling of these games. I experienced two random freezes/crashes and saw some other reports in the review section, so I think that Konami should look into and address these types of problems. On a final note, I think more screen options would be welcome, like a main screen focus with the other ones even smaller.
_childDocuments_.name: Castlevania Dominus Collection

_childDocuments_.review: Another great Castlevania collection.Games are mostly unchanged from the DS originals - IMO they are not as good as GBA ones or SoTN but still very good metroidvanias nonetheless.The only thing that was changed that I noticed is that in DoS seal drawing was removed and instead changed to QTEs - which is positive change as doing stylus movement with mouse or analog stick would sucks and even with stylus was arguably the worst part of DoS so I like it that it was removed.The only gripes that I would have is that this is the only stylus functionality that was changed. Albus mode in OoE is still awkward to play due to that, destroying ice blocks in DoS with stylus could have also been removed to work like in Julius mode. But other than that games are still great and worth playing.For bonus content there are once again galleries, jukebox and ability to switch to JP and EU versions of the game which is great. The best addition is - finally - Haunted Castle arcade game and Haunted Castle revisited. Having easy access to both of these games is just great treat for people that want to see the series roots.So yeah - another great collection that is worth playing and having in your library. Hoping for SoTN + Rondo collection soon.

_childDocuments_.review: The three main games here Dawn of Sorrow, Portrait of Ruin, and Order of Ecclesia are masterclass examples of what a metroidvania should be. I would recommend this collection over most games and definitely over any other metroidvania game.If you like these types of games and dislike the Hollow Knight esque games in the genre, as I do,  I recommend Valdis Story, Deedlit in Wonderlabyrinth, Astlibra, Afterimage, Timespinner and of course Bloodstained Ritual of the Night.

_childDocuments_.review: God tier collection, I 100%'d all achievements in about 70 hours, so for the asking price of $25 before any steam deals, that is  INSANE.if you're buying this, you probably already know Castlevania and have played a game or two. I had only played Lords of Shadow and Symphony of the Night (the greatest 2d RPG ever made).The games all play flawlessly, let's just begin with thatI played 3 brand new games to me. Here's my breakdown from the perspective of someone who 200%'d Symphony of the Night.Order of Ecclesia: The hardest game in the group, but maybe that's just my return to Castlevania is general, you gain abilities by getting stigmata drops from enemies, fairly straight forward, maps are smaller and area based.Portrait of Ruin: Definitely the best game in this collection and it aint close in my opinion. Much more casual experience, perfect amount of difficulty, grind, and puzzles. gameplay is based off of having two mcs alternate abilities, and/or having both on the field at once for strategic damage.Dawn of Sorrow: Probably the weakest experience in the collection, not bad, but the map has a very confusing path progression and it had an annoying DS mechanic where you had to draw seal circles to kill bosses and if you don't get them right you have to fight the bosses for a bit longer before it gives you a hint on how to draw the circle, very honestly, you don't draw the circle enough to remember, kind of annoying. HOWEVER, the soul system in the game is pretty awesome if you're a grindy person. you can grind up to 9 souls for each enemy souls and increase their ability power and some are just rediculous, makes grinding rewarding and fun. Bonus Modes you get achievements for:Albus Mode: Order of Ecclasia -> Piss easy honestly you are so OP, you have a machine gun pistol.Richter Mode: you are FAST, bro zooms around and does rediculous damage, finished this mode so fast on normal, heard hard more is much more awful, so good luck.Julius Mode: After beating Richter mode moving this slow killed me inside, however you get several characters to play as, map progression is just as confusing in this mode somehow lol. not much to say here, except good luck with the grasshopper boss and the final boss without rewinds. Then of course you get the Haunted Castle Revisited, which is just a bonus mode better graphical version of the arcade game. no achievements, no saves, just classic arcade gameplay.finally you get concept art and the music soundtrack of every game.BUY BUY BUY

_childDocuments_.review: On the one hand, dawg this is an emulator. It's not as overt as some companies' re-releases, but you can save and load states independently of saving and loading your files in the games.On the other hand, I'm more than happy to give credit to big companies for making their older titles available again. People won't rom stuff they can actually buy, and re-releases like this take the pressure off of fan communities who're trying to do video game archival work, freeing them up to focus on more obscure stuff.As far as the actual games in this collection, they're good ones. Ecclesia in particular is so close to wrapping back around to early Castlevanias, or to innovating a whole new microgenre.If you like oldschool vania rpg jank and you want to play a bunch of influential titles from a few consoles ago, I'd strongly recommend grabbing this. It's a lot of hours per dollar, the quality is consistent throughout, the spritework is good, and the soundtrack bumps.No buyer's remorse here, just brain off, number go up, and item grind begin.Edit: It does randomly crash sometimes.2nd Edit: Okay, the crashes are pretty easy to trigger. Jumping at the wrong angle into a wall in Ecclesia does it. This isn't great.3rd Edit: It do be crashing frequently for no reason. Making it worse than emulation. Konami why are you like this.4th Edit: I guess I should also review Ecclesia as well as this port. It has some neat ideas and is an interesting fusion of old and new vanias, but wow the grind is obnoxious and the difficulty feels wildly inflated in a way that isn't fun. I'm glad Bloodstained refined this gameplay, even if I like Ecclesia's aesthetics more.5th Edit: Crashing, visual glitches, ungainly save states. I'm glad there's versions of these games available for people to buy again, it's just a shame that they run worse than the ones the fan community kept alive in the meantime.6th: That's probably the least enjoyable dracula in any game, castlevania or otherwise. The scuffed hitboxes and juggles are bad, but having a second phase with a repeatable attack that you can only pass if you have a specific shield glyph (otherwise the second it catches you it juggles you for full bar) is really interesting and unique design. I wonder why more games don't do design like this. Could it be because this design is bad and makes the game worse. Surely not.

I've played all of the Castlevania series on GBA, so I'm glad they revived the DS games for the PC.

_childDocuments_.review: Dominus is easily one of the best combo packs I have ever purchased. You will get your money's worth! Music, game play, story, everything is polished. _childDocuments_.name: Castlevania Dominus Collection

_childDocuments_.review: This collection is really well done - I especially like being able to hold down L2 for the rewind feature. Order of Ecclesia is my favorite and it played great. Having both sub-screens viewable at all times was really handy as I could see the map and the beastiary at the same time.
