_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Same great Yakuza game formula. If you're a fan of the series and the developer, RGG Studios, you already know what to expect in terms of presentation, execution, humor, combat, minigames, gameplay mechanics and so on. If its not broke, why fix it, right? If anything, you can expect some innovations such as (but not limited to) the 'Agent' style with its variety of gadgets, going into this game. A must buy for any Yakuza fans, especially if you're a diehard fan that has played every entry because this game panders to people like us with multiple callbacks (moreso than any other previous titles) to previous games. Its like a RGG Studios love letter to their fans, in the form of a game. Story-wise, this takes places during Yakuza: Like A Dragon and you will see references to parts of that game here.This is likely going to be the last game we will see the legendary Kazuma Kiryu in a good ol' Yakuza beat-em-up style game and as the main protagonist as his appearance in the upcoming mainline entry, Infinite Wealth (which will primarily star Ichiban Kasuga and co.), is going to be his last appearance (heavily implied from the trailers). RGG Studios have gone on record to state that mainline entry games are now going to be turn-based only moving forward, meaning this game is a side entry. Plus Gaiden translates to 'another tale' so that's a fun fact for you. Like any other previous Yakuza game entries, there are numerous callbacks to that have happened in the previous Yakuza games, so if this is going to be your first Yakuza game, expect to be confused.The game's engine is amazing. This is definitely the same game engine that will be running the upcoming mainline entry, Infinite Wealth. Faces (to an extent, NPCs as well) and facial expressions are amazingly detailed. Lighting and textures has been improved, I dont know how RGG Studios do it, every game they release they just one-up themselves in the graphics department. Simply amazing. Performance-wise, its great too. 4k60fps without DLSS gave me no stutters or performance losses on my 3060. Shame that this has to be pointed out as numerous modern game releases have been plagued with performance issues.Gameplay-wise right off the bat, even without upgrades, Kiryu feels much more agile akin to Yagami from the Judgement series in his new 'Agent' style. The 'Agent' style battle stance and moves are even similar to that of the detective's. Kiryu is also much faster and lighter hitting and he comes equipped gadgets to play around with, like the wire thats showcased in this game's store page. The legendary Dragon of Dojima fighting style that we all know and love, dubbed as 'Yakuza' style here, makes its reappearance too. Although in this game, Kiryu does come with more baseline moves such as being able to charge your attacks from the getgo rather than needing an upgrade like in the previous titles. He's a also tadbit slower than the  'Agent' style but hits harder and can now, for the first time in the series, counterattack right after getting hit with either a headbutt, a quick punch or a quick kick. This is exclusive to 'Yakuza' style and it essentially allows you to trade blows with enemies. Kiryu naturally has this new ability without needing an upgrade though its not stated anywhere in the game that he can do this so I'm making a point to mention this in my review. You can also later, get an upgrade to charge these counterattacks. Almost all of the fighting moves and heat actions we know and love are back in this game, like the repeating knee to the face, mashing punch that will lead into a heat action, finishing holds and more. Understandably, some heat actions have been omitted as it wouldnt have fit Kiryu's current personality, such as the heat action where you were able to scrape an enemy's face on the ground in Yakuza 5.Mortal wounds from the Judgement series are not present in this game. Furthermore, both the 'Agent' and 'Yakuza' styles have their own unique BGMs that will play during a fight, much like Yagami with his various styles having unique BGMs in the Judgement series. Picking up items overworld that are elevated off the ground have been made much less tedious here with the wire too as opposed to how tedious it was back in the Judgement series. Also, finally, you can now smoke on demand as Kiryu (no, the smoking taunt in Yakuza 5 doesnt count) at any of the designated smoking areas just like Yagami can.For the first time in the series, you are now able to customize Kiryu's outfit as well as equip him with various accessories and not just change into preset outfits (which were only available during post-game in the previous titles)! While technically you could already do this in Yakuza 6, your choices were only between the full iconic grey suit or ditching the coat and just the red shirt with sleeves rolled up. In Gaiden, you are given a wide variety of outfits and accessories to pick and choose from to completely dress Kiryu up in fashion, head to toe.The Sotenbori locker and finding the respective locker keys to unlock each locker from Yakuza 5 returns in this game.One of the biggest changes to minigames is the change to the Cabaret hostess club minigame. The Yakuza series has always found a way to incorporate interactions with real gravure or JAV actresses, such as the live chat minigame in Yakuza 6, into one of the minigames but it has never been done with the Cabaret hostess minigames. In the past, the games would have Kiryu interact directly with various actresses with their likeness rendered into an in-game model using their faces as a reference. In Gaiden, this has been replaced with a VR-esque styled gameplay where the hostess addresses you as Kiryu while directly looking at the screen/camera. Personally, this change felt really jarring to me since you could even see the ringlight in the actresses' eyes. It certainly wasn't my cup of tea, though your mileage may vary, depending on if you're into this particular style of interaction.

_childDocuments_.review: Gaiden's events happen alongside the events of Yakuza Like a Dragon, here telling the story of a Kazuma Kiryu trying to erase his name under the codename of Joryu. Gaiden relies a lot on Kiryu's past, so a little bit of warning it has all sorts of minor and major spoilers from many games, and also spoilers of the one that happens alongside with it, so do be aware of that. WIth all that said, I was not ready at all for how hard this story would go, main story doesn't beat any longer than maybe 10-12-ish hours but they still manage to pack a whole lot of drama and feelings into this one small package, all of the new characters are memorable, and obviously some good old Kiryu coolness as we love itCombat throws back to the hack'n slash formula, bringing Kiryu a bit of Judgment influence which is great. Agent style is nimble and tactical, full of gadgets and technical combat, and the Yakuza style brings back the street fighting dragon, full of heavy power and strong strikes. You can't go wrong with either style honestly, both have their unique shine in the right time, combos feel awesomeSide content also goes hard, the Coliseum is the big attraction of this game and the main moneymaker, spending time here experimenting with teams and even playing other characters is mighty fun. Akame Network is quite bulky and important to upgrade abilities, the return of Pocket Circuit is a welcome funsies add, show your charm for the girls in the Cabaret Clubs (this time in live action), visit the Boutique to customize Kiryu's clothes and face, and of course all the usual gambling and sports minigames are present as well. Also, big props for bringing an arcade of Sega Racing Classic 2 (renamed out of Daytona USA 2 due to licensing), that's a first ever PC/console release for that game and I was really excited for itDragon Engine had great graphical ugprades, more specifically to lighting, reflections and colors, everything is so much more atmospheric and colorful I love it, and once you have a taste of the Infinite Wealth demo you can tell they meticulously upgraded these departments thinking of this game to deliver a very lively and colorful Honolulu, definitely the peak in graphics for the seriesAnd speaking of, Like a Dragon Infinite Wealth Special Trial is an extra gift you earn after beating the main story of Gaiden, packing a short story demo and an exploration demo, it's similar to the same event demo you've seen a few times on youtube but here with even more content and no time restrictions (thankfully!). Needless to say this game is looking and feeling awesome, I could fill another half-review with how many cool details it has but you've read a lot of text at this point already. Can't wait for it now, fueled my hype that was already skyrocketedGaiden only has one DLC. Not a huge impact in this one it's more for fanservice funsies, you get three legendary yakuza for the coliseum, obviously they're awesome and strong but if you want to spare some money it's okay, not that much to be lost in terms of contentAfter you beat the game you can still enjoy Premium Adventure as you always do in the series, but Gaiden unexplainably lacks New Game+ for you to replay the story carrying over your abilities. My theory is that it maybe just maybe could have to do with how Akame Network works, but it's just a silly little theory of mine we never really got word on why's NG+ just missing, but yeah that has to be my only big complaint about this game

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly this is a DLC quality game being charged at nearly full game pricing.  While the story itself is good and it can keep you entertained for a while, I cannot in good faith recommend this to anyone but hardcore Yakuza fans at the current pricing and even then its with the caveat that its story really feels like there was about 5 additional hours potently cut to make the game available before LAD8 releases.  I just dont understand why RGG would decide to charge 50 bucks that you can beat in around 5-6 hours when the Kaito Files is 30 bucks for a very similar length experience.And that's the key phrase i will use here.  the Experience is the same as almost any other RGG game just compacted into the most bizarrely paced story imagineable.  there's periods where it feels like the story is barely crawling and then periods where everything happens all at once at the same time.  Its all over the place and frankly while the ending was a great catharsis, I cant get over the story told up to that point.  Even a key plot point is barely talked about and is seemingly swept under the rug late in the game, almost as if it was just dropped to give long time fans of the franchise something to discuss and freak out about while having almost zero relevance to the actual story.Combat feels so pointless too even playing at the profesional difficulty.  Agent style is borderline useless outside of 1 or 2 spots in the story and requires skills (which are gated by 2 different currencies) to actually feel where Yakuza style actually starts at.  Most encounters feel reletively non-threatening as money is plentiful and health items are cheap, and boss encounters feel more like a QTE to land Tiger Drop once you have unlocked it.In short, if your a Yakuza/LAD diehard who loves the franchise, this is more of the same that you love but in a condensed form that left me wanting much more for the price.  I honestly cant recommend it to newer people to the franchise because this isn't representative of the usual length and story telling that RGG usually does.

_childDocuments_.review: [Y6 spoilers]This is probably one of the most refined Yakuza experiences you can get. They trimmed the fat majorly, and it's to the game's benefit.  Minimal padding, fun and exciting combat and a story that'll hook you despite its smaller scale than the numbered sequels of the series.  I would recommend buying this if it's on sale, as the game is pretty short. I clocked in at 12 hours on Professional Difficulty. I paid £25 and for that, I'd say it's worth it, especially if you liked 0, Kiwami 2 and 6.  The final boss alone feels like an apology for how much of a pushover Iwami was at the end of 6. Likeable characters, memorable soundtrack, pulse-pounding combat and fun minigames are abound in this DLC-sized entry, and I'm sure you could extend the playtime even further if you went for all the sub stories on offer. Performance-wise, this runs like a dream. On my RX 7800XT I was running 1440p at 120FPS with no drops, even during set pieces with dozens of enemies. An exemplary PC port, if ever there was one.

_childDocuments_.review: The Man Who Erased His Name is another entry in the long running Like a Dragon / Yakuza series of third person action games. This is a sequel to Yakuza 6, and features a new playable character called Joryu.When a powerful Yakuza clan believes that Joryu’s true identity is actually the legendary Dragon of Dojima, Kazuma Kiryu (despite the fact that Joryu wears glasses, while Kiryu doesn’t wear glasses, and he’s definitely not the same guy wearing a terrible disguise), Joryu is drawn into a plan which could define the future of the Yakuza.•	Writing is good, and contains the usual dramatic scenes, twists, and betrayals that the series is known for. This is also a story about how much someone will sacrifice to protect their family.•	TMWEHN also connects to the later chapters of Ichiban Kasuga’s story in Like a Dragon, which means we already know how this part of the story ends, however we do learn more about Joryu’s role in those events.•	I really like Joryu, so I hope we see him again as the main character in another game. There are also a few other interesting characters, including government agents and Yakuza members who want to use Joryu for their own agendas, and a young woman called Akame, who runs a network which takes requests to help homeless people.•	Cutscenes are cinematic and have good graphical quality.•	I played with the Japanese voice acting, which has good quality, but only the cutscenes are voiced, with in engine conversations during both the main quest and substories, being text only. Yakuza 6 was fully voiced (I can’t remember if this was also the case with Like a Dragon), so this is a backwards step.•	Most of the action takes place in two main locations, Sotenbori (previously seen in Yakuza 0, 2 and 5), and an amusement park for the rich, known as the Castle.•	Fight against gangs of Yakuza and other thugs in real time combat, using a combination of punches, kicks, and various melee weapons, while building up your heat meter to perform powerful finishing moves.•	Joryu has a new “agent” fighting style which allows him to use various gadgets during combat. The spider can trap enemies in webs, but I didn’t find the others that useful, so I preferred to use the classic Yakuza style.•	Boss fights are fun, mainly thanks to the responsiveness of Joryu’s dodge move allowing him to quickly evade their attacks, while also setting up opportunities for a powerful counter attack. I was actually able to win most fights through skill, instead of relying on drinking the drug store’s entire stock of toughness z’s to stay alive like in some of the older games.•	Besides the main quest, there are various activities to keep you busy.•	Akame Network involves stopping groups of thugs from beating up civilians, and simple fetch quests (mainly to buy food or medicine from shops). This is basic copy and pasted content similar to what Ubisoft fill their open world games with, but they do reward you with cash which can be used to buy ability upgrades.•	Substories – the best one features a cameo appearance from a familiar character, but unfortunately most of them lack the wacky tone of the previous games, and can also feel a bit repetitive, for example three of the substories ask you to defeat gangs of thugs, but each gang involves the exact same sequence of 6 fights.•	Fight in the Castle’s coliseum against single opponents or larger groups for huge cash rewards. Many of the substories allow you to recruit allies into Joryu’s clan, which can take part in team fights. However, I don’t like the time limits, especially at platinum level, where you have to fight 15-20 enemies who all have massive health bars. Winning is less about skill, and more about how much money you’ve spent upgrading your damage to KO enemies quickly.•	When you want to take a break from the action, there’s also the usual wide selection of minigames, including darts, pool, golf, karaoke, sega arcade, pocket circuit racing, poker, blackjack, mahjong and shogi.•	It took me just under 30 hours to complete the story and most substories and coliseum fights, which is a decent amount of content, but still shorter than most games in the series.•	Controls worked great on my xbox 360 controller.•	I didn’t have any problems with bugs, crashes or framerate.•	I recommend using DLSS to clear up some distracting edge flickering, which can be particularly noticeable on Joryu’s glasses.Like a Dragon Gaiden: The Man Who Erased His Name is a good game which existing fans of the series should enjoy. While the gameplay feels like just another Yakuza game, its definitely worth playing to continue the story. However I would advise waiting for a sale due to this being a shorter game.As the story directly follows the events of Yakuza 6, this wouldn’t be a good place for new players to join the series. I would advise starting with Yakuza 0, or the Judgment spinoffs which have similar gameplay but a separate story.

_childDocuments_.review: This stems from playing Yakuza 0, Yakuza Kiwami 1, Yakuza Kiwami 2 and Yakuza: Like a Dragon.As far as story telling goes, it not very exciting. It really doesnt get exciting until Chapter 4 (out of 5). Of the games in the series I have played, this really felt like a DLC - A Colosseum game with quests and a lot larger gambling space really is what this game sums up to be. Youre mainly stuck in Sotenbori. Have little to nothing to do in Ijinjo and you dont even get to touch Kamurocho. They do tie in their Yakuza Like a Dragon game and the upcoming games in the series and it does cover the tiny interaction Kiryu had with Kasuga and thats it. They bring back some of the  references and players from their previous titles which kind of gets me engaged just a little more, but the face value it brings falls below my expectation. In perspective, I spent more time finishing the Cyberpunk DLC alone at 100% achievement than this game also at 100% achievements. Ill get more into the game details towards the end. Fighting feels a little sloppy. Im glad they brought back the button mashing brawl way of fighting. He doesnt really reach to hit the next enemy so there is a lot of air combat. You get 2 fighting modes: Agent mode where you can use your weapon arsenal which is great to use for anyone who is not a boss. Then you have Yakuza mode that is good for bosses which is pretty much it. As far as using or finding weapons, you cannot keep or equip any weapon. The weapon you use in that fight only last until the end of the battle scene, until you use a heat action or until you are knocked down. \Unlike other Yakuza games, you can stack similar items and have compounding stacks. Here, you cannot. They got rid of the food combos for more effective healing and they also removed item sets for boosted stats. When youre swapping out gear, the equipment screen does not tells you what stats the current item gives, but it will indicate what stats will change when you swap it out. They dont show duplicates which makes equipping gear much simpler and easier, but its also very limited and shrunken down. Im so glad that the golf mini game has gotten so much better to play. The golf mini game is actually fun to play and enjoyable. The Karaoke game feels like an actual rhythm game now because the buttons match the beats but you can only sing with Akame- no one else.The achievements are realistic to accomplish. Unlike the Kiwami versions of the game, the achievements are impossible feats of perfection. This one at least, you dont have to play the game up to a certain level to be able to get the achievement to pop. Its cool that there are quests you can do depending on the outfit youre wearing. I would like to see more of this in future titles, but make it where you can change your outfit in your home base or even use your Colosseum outfit out in the open like a regular costume. It also shows the change of outfit during the cutscenes. This game only allows you to change outfit in one place, and its troublesome to access sometimes.POCKET RACING - even with guides, you really have to work for your wins and you do really have to utilize your boosts and stabilize abilities at the right times. Its so much more fun. They did try to do something unique with their cabaret club interaction where they make it more like an interactive movie instead of the usual game graphics. Its unique; like the photography studio sidequest on Yakuza Kiwami 1. As for the overall game, the writers did a great job with the ending. It portrayed very strong emotions and does tie in Kiryu (in this case, Joryu) with the whole reason he had his name erased in the first place. Its just THAT ending scene alone is what makes playing thru feel a little rewarding. Still, all things considered, I still felt more disappointed than satisfied (or even just ok) with this game as a whole. its really difficult to justify paying for this game at full price. Its fun, but it just felt lacking - unfinished even. Im really hoping that they get to add perks in the next game for people who bought this one because it really doesnt feel worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Kiryu's Last Stand? Unveiling the Shadows in Like a Dragon Gaiden: The Man Who Erased His Name! (ฅ'ω'ฅ)In the gritty underworld of yakuza lore, the latest addition to the saga, Like a Dragon Gaiden: The Man Who Erased His Name, brings back the legendary Kazuma Kiryu for what might be his final dance. Developed by RGG Studios, this side entry offers a fresh take on the familiar Yakuza formula, introducing the enigmatic Agent style and weaving a tale that unfolds between Yakuza 6 and Like a Dragon.The game's engine, presumably the same one powering the upcoming mainline entry, Infinite Wealth, showcases remarkable graphical improvements. Faces, especially those of significant characters, are meticulously detailed, and the enhanced lighting contributes to a visually stunning experience. Performance-wise, the game runs smoothly at 4k60fps, a commendable feat considering the performance struggles seen in some recent releases.Gameplay innovations come in the form of Kiryu's newfound agility and the introduction of the Agent style. The combat system, though reminiscent of the classic Yakuza beat-em-up style, brings a new layer with the Agent style's high-tech gadgets. However, a few players note that the combat doesn't flow as seamlessly as in previous titles, and there are concerns about potential rushed development, with typos, localization errors, and lingering elements from Lost Judgment.The narrative, set under the pseudonym Joryu, thrusts Kiryu into a gripping action narrative, navigating a web of intrigue created by a mysterious figure attempting to draw him out of hiding. For devoted fans of the Yakuza series, the game provides a satisfying continuation, filled with callbacks to previous events and characters. However, newcomers may find themselves lost amidst the intricate web of Yakuza lore.The game's length and pricing have stirred mixed reactions among players. While some praise the approximately 35 hours of content as enjoyable and worth the price, others feel it falls short in side content compared to previous entries. _childDocuments_.review: First off I wanna start off with the positives of the game before I talk about whats bad about it. On my account I have played all yakuza games but not 7 (I don't really enjoy turn-based combat) so take this with a grain of salt.Pros:-Despite its shortness, a brilliant story that is told surprisingly well.-I love that they copied a few things from Lost Judgment (the best combat in the franchise) like the mortal reversals.-Coliseum being back is great again (although it has its issues).-Amazing action scenes, martial arts is on point and it really sets a new standard.-Villains were brilliant probably the best even though the story couldn't show them off more.-Great references to characters from previous games except missing Y3 and Y4 which is upsetting because Y3 had a lot of good characters that they had to throw away due to the old quality of the game which deterred people.-Side stories were funny as usual and did not miss.Now the flaws...-HEAVILY downgraded combat from LJ. It is still quite good standard but on professional difficulty the gameplay was sometimes an utter chore. The AI was tweaked differently in order to balance Agent Style but giving enraged enemies ultra instinct and bosses a mountain of hyper-armour while making yakuza style slow af was definitely annoying. Whoever decided to make story bosses get enraged, I hate you with a passion. Heat builds up way too slow that it came a little close to giving me yakuza 3 flashbacks. Extreme heat was given less emphasis yet they gave it lots of extra moves but then it comes with having to pick extreme heat mode for extra moves rather than for heat actions and vice versa which just doesn't feel right, AND heat drains way too quickly its annoying. I don't know how much time RGG had with this game but they could've at least added some kind of hidden arts. Agent style is both good and bad, its rush combo is overly long making it hard to utilise without being hit from bum♥♥♥♥ nowhere and the combo being abruptly ended. Lock-on was actually a bit strange and didn't lock onto the enemies I wanted to, I have no idea if its just me but I have no idea how RGG (again) broke something that was already established in LJ. I hate that the gameplay was tailored more to casual players who just mash the attack button than the OG fans who love the combat because they can't find it anywhere else. Its a case of RGG fixing a lot of what isn't broken (all they had to was copy and paste Lost Judgment combat).-Missing character development between a few characters. Sometimes I felt that Kiryu (Joryu) kind of needed more time or backstory of why he is good buddies with certain characters. This is only just a minor nitpick not a deal-breaker.-Story should've been a bit longer. Paying £10 less for such a cut in story length doesn't really seem like a good deal. Obviously I would've preferred not being side-tracked to do fetch quests or whatever but maybe something to fill the gaps as it is fairly short.-Quality seemed to be worse than its other dragon engine games, must be due to its short development time but RGG should've delayed the release to polish up on its looks. I must note that characters have more jagged edges and enemies look especially bad when they pull off their mortal attacks.-Game kept freezing in odd parts, it might be my computer on my end but I have never had any freezing issue with any RGG game ever. My specs are also quite good so it cannot be that.-Reusing old assets like enemy movesets from LJ (they sucked because kiryu literally has barely anything to work with), pocket circuit racing (im kind of glad its back but at the same time it is blatantly lazy). But also they forgot to reuse other things like the ally movests for coliseum which makes no sense. Why give enemy AI a full expanded moveset but then proceed to take away all of its features when the player uses them (Kaito was a ♥♥♥♥♥ to fight in particular even though he is basically the same from Judgment, goes to show that judgment's combat is better despite being 4.5 years old).-Coliseum being time based than skill based (crowd pleasers) shoes the devs attitude to the combat. Having a set time means that the devs mainly wanted damage output to fix all the flaws the game has so battles don't drag out long and aren't difficult which I think is stupid. I try to play with no damage upgrades to make the game challenging and fun as it pushes me to style on enemies rather than mash one button or heat action spam. However the coliseum makes it almost impossible as damage output at base level is just not enough to keep up. I don't think any yakuza game has made it timed before and when its timed its for ultimate battle so it makes perfect sense.In conclusion maybe get this game if you are a yakuza fan, IT IS GOOD but I am leaving a thumbs-down as RGG shouldn't EVER use this game as an example for brawler combat in future it is bad. I do regret pre-ordering and I must emphasise to get this game at a heavy discount as its not really worth its high price. Really? £45 for a rushed RGG game. (Anyone who disagrees with my opinion on the combat probably think that ishin's combat is good).

_childDocuments_.review: When  was announced back in 2016, it was described as . And sure enough, a new protagonist, Ichiban Kasuga, would take over as the new face of the franchise during the next game, . But as it turns out, Kazuma Kiryu’s story wasn’t quite over after all, as he even went on to re-appear as a protagonist during . To bridge the story gaps between his (re)appearances,  was released - a spin-off that’s also offering a return to the real-time action combat of the older  games.Bluntly speaking,  is a game with a clear target audience in mind: Players who’ve played through all mainline  games before – or at least the most recent ones. It’s not meant as a character introduction of Kazuma Kiryu for newcomers to the franchise, who might’ve started with . I can’t stress this enough:  features heavy spoilers for  and , as it assumes that the player is familiar with the events that conspire in these games. If you’ve yet to play these games (you should!), don’t start with  until you’ve done so!As for the actual game,  is a surprisingly short entry in the franchise. If you’re just going for the main story, you’ll spend about 12 hours finishing the game, though a completionist playthrough clocks in around 32h according to . If we’re only going by a main story-focused playthrough, this actually makes  the . While I don’t the game being shorter as it leads to a more focused story, I do feel like the current asking price (49,99€) might be a little steep for what’s on offer here and I highly recommend waiting for a sale instead.That’s not to say that  is a bad game but despite it’s shorter length, it also uses it’s ties to the recent  games as an excuse to recycle quite a lot of content as well as locations. Now, reusing old content is hardly new for the franchise and not necessarily a bad thing. But as the game , it’s fair to say that the content recycling went even a bit further here than what we’re normally used to. There’s only one new (small) location in the game and there are only 34 substories to complete – and while the story is obviously new, a lot of the remaining parts of the game are minigames you’ve all seen before. Again, these minigames are just as much fun as they were in  for example, but it does not really make the 49.99€ price-tag seem good.Still a lot of fun is the return of real-time action combat. This time, Kiryu got access to two fighting styles: “Agent” and “Yakuza”. The latter one is focused on slower, heavy hitting strikes and consists of moves you might’ve seen in past  games (e.g. a “breakdance kick” once fallen to the ground). The “Agent” playstyle is focused on gadgets instead, like flying drones or a combat wire, which can be upgraded separately. Personally, I stuck to the “Yakuza” style through almost the entire game since it seems to fit Kiryu more, though I was sad to see that the amount of heat actions including objects are quite limited – most of them resort in the same animation (Kiryu bashing his victim’s face in with the object he’s currently holding) and only very few objects received the special animation treatment (e.g. pliers).But generally speaking, beating dozens of enemies up is still as fun as it ever was, no matter the fighting style you might choose. As usual, you can purchase different upgrades, which either increase your stats or allow you to perform new moves in combat. A good way to earn money is the “Akame Network”, a level system that’s basically tied to almost all side content – do side content, level up the network, which results in new side content. Almost all substories in  are unlocked this way instead of encountering them on the streets like in previous  games.Thankfully, levelling up the Akame Network isn’t required for the story after the initial introduction, which means you can just play through the story without any grinding roadblocks (like the 3 million yen story requirement in ) in your way, if you want to. And considering the story does quite a good job of showcasing Kiryu’s new situation and his mental state, I can understand not wanting to stop for billiard of golf.A few of the plot points might come up a little too often but generally speaking,  is one of the better paced story in the franchise that offers the usual mix of twists and turns one can expect by now. Thankfully, due to a smaller cast of characters, the story is also quite easy to follow and doesn’t become as convoluted as some of the other  games did. But while some of the events that happen are quite foreseeable thanks to the intersection with , it was the bittersweet ending that really took me by surprise and made me shed more than a few tears. Without spoiling anything, if you’ve been on the journey with Kiryu as long as I’ve been, you really don’t want to miss the two final cutscenes of this game.Concluding,  can best be described as a bite-sized  experience. It got everything one expects from the franchise, from the flow of combat to silly minigames and even sillier substories, and does give players a better understanding of the new chapter in Kiryu’s life. However, it’s also a shorter game with a lot of recycled content that can’t really justify the high price-tag of the game, since it doesn’t really bring anything new to the table. It’s quite clear that it was originally conceived as DLC but as long as you don’t expect anything else, you can’t go wrong with this game if you’ve enjoyed what came before.

_childDocuments_.review: Weird how I seem to be playing Like a Dragon games more often than I’ve ever played the typical Ubisoft games, but the burnout is far less noticeable… Seriously, though, RGG Studio has been putting out games set in this universe not just annually lately, but often with several games coming out the same year. And in situations like with this game, I’m not sure if there was the point. Not that I disliked Like a Dragon Gaiden, quite the opposite, but it does feel almost unnecessary at points…Like a Dragon Gaiden: The Man Who Erased His Name is a new entry in the long running series of titles that erased their old international name (which was Yakuza), but remained mainly open world action adventure titles with beat ’em up combat and cinematic stories. This entry, as the title itself says, is a side story that is set during the events of Yakuza: Like a Dragon, but despite the short visit to Isezaki Ijincho (the main setting of that game), most of the events happen in the classic Sotenbori that was originally seen in Yakuza 2.At this point I usually write that the “open world” section is not big but is otherwise dense with stories, but it isn’t exactly the case in this game. It’s not fully embracing a typical open world onslaught of icons pointing to busywork tasks, but for whatever reason the substories do go in this direction this time around. Not that there are no longer more deep side stories for you to explore, but most of the optional content this time around is far closer to how substories were in the earliest entries, with simple “bring me X item” tasks. While the longer more involved substories rarely do anything interesting even when their premise is good. There’s one wonderful crossover exception, but apart from it, the substories are pretty weak in this one.Same goes for the main story, really. You do get to learn more about some secret agent-like society that was first hinted upon in Yakuza 6 and some of the characters shown there seem to be set up to reappear in a later game. But as far as the current story goes, you get some minor details and some new emotional scenes talking about things you already knew from other games and it’s not particularly fulfilling. Some of the new characters are really nice and Kiryu, for a change, has more range in his personality, but it’s not a game that will interest anyone with its story but the biggest fans of the series.So what did I like about Like a Dragon Gaiden: The Man Who Erased His Name? It plays really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ well. Just like with Lost Judgment, combat controls are extremely fun and better than they’ve ever been in the series. Every fight just flows well and provides enough challenge (on a highest difficulty) for those who like it, while providing a perfect amount of challenge (on other difficulties) for people who just want to have fun. Granted, some mini-games still go really unfair, unless you grind or look up best solutions, but those are an exception and most of the time this game is just really fun to play.Yet it puts it in a weird spot. If you like RGG universe games for gameplay and it alone can interest you, this is a good game for you. It’s unlikely to become your favorite, but it’s really really fun. But if you like the RGG universe for the story, you really can skip this one and not miss out on anything the games won’t recap if needed later on. I liked it, but at the same time, it was a rather forgettable even if enjoyable time.

_childDocuments_.review: A very nice conclusion and wrap up of Kiryu's story at least until Infinite Wealth hits. The story is easily right up there with Yakuza 0 with a very good mix of comedy and serious moments that everyone has come to love. The quality of cut scenes and cinematics have improved so much and it was an absolute joy to watch.Combat feels nice although it definitely feels a bit lacking when compared to previous games. There's a smaller variety of heat actions which is a shame and combat is significantly easier as extreme heat mode is a very easy way to cheese most fights. Boss fights are definitely much less fun than compared to previous titles where each boss has a quirk; most of the boss fights in this game feel the same. However, the introduction of Agent style more than makes up for it. I've had way more fun beating people up and throwing them all around than in any other previous game. Coming from Yakuza 7, it was great to beat people up in the combini again.Another change from previous games is that substories are all now triggered from a "HQ" location which is kind of neat as it is easier to clear through all of them rather than hunting them around town. I can understand why some people might prefer the older method though.The coliseum was pretty cool but kind of underwhelming due to the ability to cheese fights with extreme heat mode. The team fights also felt kind of forced in and at some point, they become very annoying due to the insanely high health pool of some of the "boss" and "mini-boss" characters can be.Overall it was a really fun game and well worth it's full price. Steam Deck compatibility from launch was also a really neat bonus.

_childDocuments_.review: As a reminder: This game is a conclusion of all the Yakuza games released to this day. Playing this first would be the same as watching the final Season of Attack on Titan or any other good series before Season 1-4. You would ruin your experience.Now for the review:Kazuma Kiryu is back, for better or worse, depending on how you see it, but on a technical level, this game takes everything that made Yakuza 6 and Kiwami 2 amazing and improves it quite a bit:Kiryu keeps his Dragon of Dojima style, which is now called the Yakuza style, but it’s slightly nerved in comparison to Y6 and K2. They made it slightly slower and took away two of the side-steps, you can only do one now (and you get a roll upgrade later) otherwise the moveset is mostly unchanged.The star of the show is the new Agent style. It’s mixture of Yagamis Crane and Kiryus old rush style with some new gadgets, which are really fun to use.Gameplay wise Agent style is superior, especially on harder difficulties, due the nerving of Yakuza style and it generally being faster.One of the biggest changes in terms of combat is the number of enemies you can fight at once. Some battles (mostly in the Colliseum) makes you fight up to 20 enemies at once. After this game, One Man Army Kiryu definitely deserves his title.The main story might be shorter but in terms of minigames and side content, Gaiden has almost as much content as a normal Yakuza game:Additionally, something, that doesn’t really fit into any of the Subcategories: Some outfits from older games return or you can just dress him up as a clown, and it will affect almost every cutscene!Now for the most important part of the game:In terms of story writing, it's kind of amazing to think that the entire situation of Kiryu, where everything started to go downhill for him, begun in Yakuza 5 or more specifically it's ending.Before that, all Yakuza games had it's of own concluded stories without any big impact for it's successors, but with Yakuza 5 and successor Yakuza 6, everything changed:The entirety of Yakuza 6 and Gaiden could have been prevented, if Kiryu would have been there to protect Haruka. The decision Kiryu made at the end of Yakuza 5 to go into prison were the trigger for everything that took place afterwards. You could even go further back and say that Kiryus decision to let Haruka pursue her dream of becoming an Idol let to all of this, which is impressive to think about.You could say, that this is all an one big arc and it's still ongoing for 11/12 years now.If the writers of Yakuza, or Like a Dragon, how it’s called now, planned this from the start, it’s actually really good story writing. Now we will have to see how it continues in Like a Dragon Infinite WealthThe sum it up, without spoiling the game, this game has definitely the most emotional scene in the entire franchise with one of the best voice acting pieces I’ve ever heard, which would even make the toughest Yakuza cry.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon Gaiden is the first mainline "mini-game" in the Yakuza/LAD series, taking place right before and during the events of Yakuza: Like a Dragon. Starring Kazuma Kiryu, who hasn't been playable since Yakuza 6 back in 2016, masquerading as Joryu as we get a peek into his life as a Daidoji operative after his supposed "death".Getting some of the obvious out of the way, this is not a full experience Yakuza game. Only sporting a total of 5 chapters, where most other Yakuza games boast an average of about 13, rushing through the story won't give you as much mileage as before. Alongside this, this mainly takes place on two of the smallest free roam maps in the series: Sotenbori, which has very little new areas to explore, and the Castle which is essentially just Purgatory 2.0. Don't expect a full series game out of this, but there is still fun to be had.From a gameplay perspective Kiryu's styles seem to take a page from Judgment. Agent, the new style tempered around fast attacks and crowd control, ends up feeling underwhelming outside of extreme heat mode and it feels significantly weaker than Yakuza, the slower single target style that focuses on single target damage. While Agent is fun, especially with how much crowd control gadgets have, it feels significantly weaker than Yakuza style outside of extreme heat mode, which mainly powers up the gadgets to an insane degree where you can just nuke enemies without much thought. Alongside these changes are the re-introduction of deadly attacks, press dodge to counter them before they hit for a large amount of damage. This mechanic was copied and pasted from Judgment/Lost Judgment, but with the added caveat that enemies cannot be killed until their attack ends, meaning you're better just waiting the attack out to counter than to beat them to the punch, adding this weird combat pace at times where you'll wail on someone, they'll almost go down, but then they deadly attack and you have to wait for a short time. Then, onto sidestory content. This game's sidestory is Coliseum where we get a return and improvement on the Kiryu Clan/Majima Construction minigames with Hell Team Rumble. You choose a character to lead, either being Kiryu or another character that's part of your group, and build a formation where you go head to head with AI. Unlike in their previous renditions, you actually have a hand in the fight outside of just pointing out where your troops go, making it feel more natural for a Yakuza game. Pair this up with how insane the fights can get, Hell Team Rumble is a huge highlight of the game that I hope comes back in some capacity in a future game. Coliseum outside of Hell Team Rumble is still very fun as well, as it actually pays out well and has progression that doesn't require a massive amount of grinding. To top this off, you can only go into certain VIP areas after completing a certain amount of fights, so you're encouraged to complete these to open up the Castle further. Pocket Circuit also makes a return, but is just more of the same, with the only difference being that most parts can no longer be bought outright for cash and has to be earned with Circuit Points that come from finishing a race, completing a time trial, or beating a rival. Hostess clubs make a return as well, but this time somewhat downgraded. This time it incorporates FMV instead of in-game models, which feels very bizarre and takes me out of the game, despite in-game most of the NPCs state it's "Immersive". Alongside this, Hostess affection is harder to get, and major details about them are actually missable due to the new question structure. In other games, Hostesses will ask you questions that relate to their personality and substories, and anything that's important to their substory is unmissable. In Gaiden however, you can choose between three different questions, but some of them have no bearing on their personality and don't help towards learning their interests, especially since now the final question events to up their affinity can have wrong answers that, while neutral and doesn't lose any meter, will require you to re-visit them. Their max affinity dates are also underwhelming as since there's no in-game model, we just get dialogue over screenshots until we reach an unskippable FMV of the hostesses trying to be sexy. Hostess club was tedious before, especially if you were aiming for Amon, but now it's made worse due to odd structuring.Story wise, it's so compacted that saying anything past Chapter 1 is a pretty big spoiler. It's quite good and is fairly standard for a Yakuza story. He really is the man who erased his name.Now for everything else: Soundtrack is pretty good, feels like a mix between Like A Dragon's more dubstep style and a blend of some of Lost Judgment's themes. Graphically the game looks great, especially with the lighting in the Castle. Voice acting is also top tier as usual.TL;DR A good, but short Yakuza game that could have used a little more polish for combat, but is still very fun.8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I was initially apprehensive of this game, because Yakuza 6 was such a good ending for Kiryu's saga. So when I heard this game will have Kiryu as the protag again I was worried that it would take away from the ending of 6. But this game helps bring closure without diminishing Yakuza 6's ending. The final chapter is one of the best in the series in both hype and emotional impact. The game is much shorter, about 1/3rd of the story length of a mainline game, but it feels well paced for the story it tells.Gameplay is a step up from Yakuza 6, the combat feels less "floaty" and the new gadgets spice up the gameplay we're used to at this point. Overall, Like a Dragon Gaiden is another great entry into the series. A great companion piece to 6 and a bridge between 7 and 8.

_childDocuments_.review: Even though Gaiden is a side game with a main story and side contents roughly half the size of the usual RGG games, it still delivers on pretty much most of it. The biggest strength in Gaiden is how it bridges between Yakuza 6, 7 and upcoming Like A Dragon Infinite Wealth. The story revolving about Tojo and Omi's dissolution and how the aftermath of 6 made Kiryu a Daidoji Agent are handled really well. Even with short runtime, all the major characters are well written and have their own story arcs. The final boss symbolizes perfectly well about how the dissolution won't be easy for lots of the yakuza, how times are changing and some of them are desperately clinging to their old way of life. It's tragic but also handled with an intense and cathartic action sequences that is both entertaining to play through and make you feel for the characters.And then the ending, one of the, if not the saddest moment in the series. It's moments like this that make Kiryu feel believable throughout the games. Beneath his stoic demeanor hides an overwhelmingly warm heart to his family. Gaiden is ultimately a direct continuation of Yakuza 6 and that feeling of parenthood and sacrifice echoes throughout the game and especially in the ending. Combat in Gaiden feels great and the more aggressive enemies make for more challenging fights. It just feel and play incredibly well in every situations. The side contents, although small in variety, still manages to entertain. Some substories are among the best in the series and tackle Kiryu's past events, some are about current technological dilemma and some are just really funny. The live action cabaret hostess minigame is actually enjoyable, even if it's shorter than the previous games and lack depth that Yakuza 6 had. The fact that you can't ask them out for Karaoke is also a bummer but the live action videos itself are acted well enough, some are sweet, some are seductive and some are funny to watch. Pocket Circuit is back, still great as ever and it does have a callback to previous Pocket Circuit. The Boutique is great, although a bit barebones compared to other games with similar feature. The Castle Coliseum is the best version of the series coliseum to date, it can be challenging, chaotic and just really fun to fight.Gaiden is mostly about quality than quantity. It comes with smaller package than the previous games but still manages to be one of the best RGG games, especially for longtime fans. Coupled with varieties of great soundtrack, the updated gorgeous visual, the beautiful locations and its attention to details and generally just how much optimized the game is, it's made in less than a year  but still a quality game through and through.A perfect bridge between previous games and Infinite Wealth that not only concludes one of the series' story arc in a beautiful way but also genuinely telling an engrossing and emotional story.

_childDocuments_.review: Story (no spoilers):Definitely conscious of the character. This game does justice to Kazuma Kiryu's past, ideals, burdens and history.It does an excellent job at feeling as a perfect focus for him, with its occasional callbacks to past games, with it not being too little, but not too much either as not to feel like complete fan service rather than a well founded game. So yeah, if you want a game, even if short (5 chapters in lenght only) that gives a gives a more proper send off to Kiryu, this is a entry you shouldn't skip by any means. (Why would you want to skip it, anyways?) Kiryu has much more attitude than in many previous games, too. The ending made me drop tears of both sadness and joy.Gameplay: The gameplay is, to put it simple, fun. Agent, the new fighting style, is presented as a more tactical one, being able to overwhelm hordes of enemies. However, as you progress through the game, it becomes less than that to become more of a quick, easy way around finishing fights. And no, it's not because the character being bound to get stronger as the game progresses, but rather than it not being as tactical as presented, but more of a silly mix up of gadgets that justify the name of the fighting style, some of which are of quick and of more slow use, but all of them being able to finish the battle in a minute, or 8 seconds in most cases. It doesn't mean it's not fun, because it's the complete opposite, but it's definitely not a before and an after when it comes to battles styles in the series either. Kiryu's signature Yakuza fighting style (now being the fighting style that you unlock as you progress a little further into the story) has some minimal changes that might not be for the convenience of the player too, like it being powerful at the price of being slow, and the beloved ¨finishing hold¨ move being stuck behind Heat Mode. Even so, this is the most fun it has been playing with Kiryu in the Dragon Engine so far, to say the least.Duration and side stuff: The main story is around 12 hours, but that was no relevant for me because of how the side content of the game does a wonderful job at stretching the game to around 30 hours. Side missions. Customizable clothes. Minigames. Immersive hostesses. Pocket Circuit Races. Colisseum fights and the entirety of the Castle. Even being able to play as any of the characters you recruit to join your side at the colisseum.All of that felt like a fitting part of the main story as I went through it. What I'm trying to say, if you want the game to be longer and more enjoyable than what only 5 chapters sound like for a Like a Dragon/Yakuza game, all you need to go is to go out of your way and have fun. I cleared all of the colisseum fights with a S Grade and reached rank 30 in the Akame missions, and it was like having a buffet served in front of me that left me with a smile and conversations topics for the future.DLC: Owning the Legendary Fighter Pack DLC is fun, but definitely not a must to overcome the colisseum. In case you think it will be defining to your enjoyement of the game if you don't own it because of how the characters there are some of the glorified cameos of the series. (Looking at Majima still spinning as the fight ends is fun, though).Conclusion: Akame is very cute. Having the game's duration in mind might help you savor and enjoy the game and its events more. Buy the game on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: This is meant to be just a short game, to fill in the gap between 6 and 7 in regards to Kiryu, and i expected to finish it in just one or two evenings, but i found this game has a lot more to offer.LEGACY:It pays proper homage to previous entries with mini-games and substories. Fans of the series will appreciate numerous easter eggs dropped in the form of text or quests. Those subquests are bite-sized but i wouldn't say they are short, it's definitely not "bump into a scammer" sort of thing. They explore some topics that never got much attention in previous games which i love.COMBAT:Absolutely fantastic, with TWO GLARING FLAWS(more later), but still i never get tired of it. This game makes you feel extremely powerful and gives quite a bit of exploitable abilities and playstyles, but at the same time it can be quite challenging(at least in the arena but we'll get to it). My favorite has been using the payback ring and indra's amulet to blast through arena bosses as quickly as i can. The GLARING FLOW i was talking about, however, is related to the juggling limit. When you bounce an enemy off the ground, much like in Lost Judgment, you can keep them in the air by dealing damage and thus creating combos. The problem is that this game limits HOW LONG YOU CAN KEEP IN THE AIR. A completely unnecessary limitation, coupled with inability to quick-cancel out of Agent Style finishers, despite it being supposedly a faster, more evasive style than Yakuza Style. It is quite difficult to play evasively in this game in general because of how slow Kiryu's attacks are, and Agent Style could have been his saving grace, but alas. Another thing is i was hoping that you'd bring back wall-bounds. It seems you have something similar where the enemy can be pushed into a wall with a finisher, prompting them to bounce off of it, but nothing else can be done about it. It's not a flaw, but i wish you could bring back this mechanic from Yakuza 3 and Yakuza 4.PLOT:I don't want to spoil much, it stays true to its original vision, while also freshing things up. I've never seen Kiryu this expressive before, much of it is thanks to Kuroda Takaya's stellar performance as his voice actor. And while the story is not very long, it is extremely rich with events, 1 chapter may feel like 2 or 3 chapters! And the side activities help you thin it out and be prepared for the next emotional rollercoaster.DLC CONTENT:This i feel deserves a special section because i was very let down by the special fighters Majima Goro, Saejima Taiga and Dojima Daigo in the arena. They don't have even half of their moves from previous games, it's fun to play as them for a bit...But nothing more. It's a shame, because i was really looking forward to it.OVERALL:I feel like this game is well worth its price. I know it could have been a lot better, but for a short game this is an amazing result and i hope they do even more Gaiden games, so we can play as our other favorite characters someday. If you feel hesitant, then i implore you to give this game a try!

_childDocuments_.review: Again a hard to not recommend game in the Yakuza series. But I'm still going to, here's why.As is the case with most Yakuza games, the world within the game doesn't follow its own rules. This makes following the story silly and frustrating. First your character is plowing through enemies as if they were cardboard. Next you'll watch a 5 minute movie about your character struggling with a piece of said cardboard. This is supposed to create tension and motivation for the story, but since the world already lost most its believability, it's hard to keep invested.Next we have what's actually happening in the story. Well... not much really?! The main story is very simple and short. There are side missions that you mostly plow through, and as usual they don't have much story to them. They work as an excuse to beat up people but that's it.The coliseum fights are somewhat fun, but there's only so much of those until you've seen enough. Maybe some more variety would keep things interesting? The fight system also feels somewhat more limited and boring compared to previous titles. Things are mostly smooth but it's just very repetitive even with full abilities. With only two styles and quite clear use cases for them, fights start to quickly repeat the same pattern.One of my surprising personal favorite features in previous titles was eating at the restaurants. It brought my mind back to Japan (where I've visited a couple of times), and I always got very hungry watching and listening to Kiryu eating. Unfortunately that feature has been basically removed, as you don't gain any experience from eating anymore and the eating animations aren't that delicious anymore.It's not a bad game at all, but unlike Yakuza 0, I don't think I'll remember or miss what happened in this game after a few years. And hence, I'd only recommend this to people addicted to Kiryu beating up people.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon Gaiden is an enjoyable experience that acts as a homage to past Yakuza titles as well as a bridge between the end of Yakuza 6 and the beginning of Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth. This makes it a must-play for long-time fans of the franchise despite being short-lived in terms of story length. New fans will probably need to play or be familiar with the major events of Yakuza: Like a Dragon beforehand, as the story of LaD Gaiden's plot revolves around some major spoilers for it. Some knowledge about core events of Yakuza 0-6 pertaining to the main protagonist are recommended as well.Completing all story and side activities will take roughly about 40+ hours or less (minus idle time). If you played and enjoyed any of the Beat'em games made by RGG Studio previously or simply a fan of story-driven action games, then this is definitely for you.  :)* The good old beat'em up styles of game protagonist Kazuma Kiryu (from Yakuza 0?) got remixed into two distinct fighting styles. One of which includes the use of spy gadgets to add a new flavor to the combat, and each style has its advantages depending on the situation* Adequate amount of sub-stories that does not feel bloated, and plenty of mini games that can keep you hooked for a good while* Grinding level is pretty adequate compared to some of the past titles in the franchise, and 100% completion is not required for full Steam achievements (more like 80%, and you can actually skip Mahjong and/or Shogi if you're bad at them and still get all achievements :D)* Customizable character appearance that persists even during cut-scenes after it becomes available (except for Karaoke scenes)* Inclusion of graphical settings like DLSS that boost overall fps for smoother experience* A trial version of the upcoming sequel "Like a Dragon: Infinite" is included with the game for players to get a feel for the game* Certain mini games can be a hit or miss with the players, in my opinion* Certain Coliseum fights can be ridiculous in difficulty even at full personal and team upgrades, and some races in Pocket Circuit mini game feel dependent on RNG to win* While not a con, the game finale fights may feel too underwhelming (that is, enemies are as weak as paper) if the player has fully unlocked & upgraded all abilities :DStory: 9/10Gameplay: 10/10Visuals: 10/10Soundtracks: 9/10Overall Score: 9.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: A GREAT KIRYU COMEBACK AND FAN SERVICEI am a big fan of the Like A Dragon series and although initially excited, was also skeptical of this game since LAD Gaiden follows a more different structure than other mainline games and follows similarly, according to some developer interviews, to The Kaito Files, a special DLC for Lost Judgment. I actually like these shorter Like A Dragon experiences since the mainline LAD games, even the old ones, are very lengthy and have so much stuff to do. So this is a nice break and spin of the usual formula and opens more potential for more stories that can be told in the LAD universe if the devs wishes to do some.Like A Dragon Gaiden: The Man Who Erased His Name is a LAD game that focuses on an undercover Kiryu Kazuma being an agent of the Daidoji faction, assuming the name Joryu. This game being a Gaiden (side-story) tells a fun and simple and somewhat interesting tale about this new side of Kiryu Kazuma. Being an agent means he will always fight and do combat (as he always do) and enables him to have a very new and unique style which is Agent Style that gives him alot of spy tools and gadgets.The story is okay and simple but I will say my criticisms for the story is that there are really no stakes. This is mainly because the game takes place at the same time as Yakuza 7 and the whole goal of Gaiden's story is to reach a crucial moment that will impact the overall story in Yakuza 7. So any moments where Kiryu and his friends are in danger, never really feel like actual danger since they all are in Yakuza 7. Another criticism I'll give is on a certain antagonist that I was kinda hyped due to how much backstory he has but ultimately, he's just another generic villain that is evil.I will say that this is the most chill Yakuza or Like A Dragon game. Kiryu in this game is somehow the best he has ever been. Kiryu Kazuma has always been a very interesting and very well-written character starting from Yakuza 1 to Yakuza 6 with the sixth game being tying a neat bow to Kiryu's saga. That's why I was skeptical towards this game's release since for me Kiryu's tale is already done, but fortunately Kiryu has a great comeback and he comes hard. While there's daddy Kiryu in Yakuza 3, depressed Kiryu in Yakuza 5, and angery Kiryu in Yakuza 6, LAD Gaiden has peak, Dragon of the Dojima Kiryu Kazuma.In some way it is brilliant to have Kiryu being an agent to showcase his pure intelligence, raw skill, talent and charisma, that really presents why Kiryu is the Dragon of Dojima since in the past games, there was never really a moment of that part of Kiryu's life other than being mentioned and told by characters countless times. Even Yakuza 0, the prequel that shows his origins, only presents the period before his tenure as the Dragon of Dojima. All the characters in LAD Gaiden are likable as there always banter between Kiryu and them. I really love the more quiet moments where they are just chilling out eating, or just complimenting each other, or just..... talking. Although Kiryu and his peers are mostly out of the norm, being a Yakuza and all, the writing and the dialogue makes them all very grounded and very relatable.Combatwise, it is okay. I am still getting used to Agent Style and found myself using it when fighting larger crowds, but ultimately all the tools you use as an agent like whips are very fun and crazy as they always been. Kiryu has two fighting styles with the other being Yakuza Style which is the classic traditional Kiryu combat from past games. There's also the juggling system from Lost Judgment so Kiryu can finally juggle enemies too. I'm not an expert when it comes to Like A Dragon combat but I've lot of fun with it here.Being a shorter Like A Dragon game like Kaito Files, this game is obviously short. I finished the main story in 20 hours and there are two big side-content which are the classic substories (but in a unique spin) and the fighting arena (which also has unique spin). My only criticism is only on the substories with the gang related substories being very repetitive and tedious as hell. But that's just my only main complaint since the other substories are bangers as all things should be.Music for me is also kinda okay. There some bangers that kinda mixed in with not so banger ones. Some of the not so bangers are kinda generic, trailer musicish, but the banger ones are great like Deadly Struggle, Un Altro Appasionato, and the Yakuza Style theme.When comparing between Kaito Files and LAD Gaiden, I ultimately prefer Kaito Files first mainly because of how high the stakes are there. Not to the discredit how high the stakes can be in LAD Gaiden, but LAD Gaiden is also a fun time with Kiryu and I'm kinda glad he's somehow back. Comparing to the mainline games isn't really fair since this is a much smaller game and different direction, but LAD Gaiden does takes elements from mainly the Kiryu Saga games and offers abit of homage to them.I recommend those who have played the Yakuza games to play this. For newcomers are also welcome since this game is great at recapping some aspects but mostly in Kiryu's backstory.Overall, a solid and short Like A Dragon experience.4/5

_childDocuments_.review: Gaiden is Gaiden. A short spinoff you can call Yakuza 6.5. Its a very short game, only 5 chapters, but those 5 chapters are pretty solid. The mini games are pretty good, many returning from 0.Gameplay feels like Judgment with two fight styles. Dragon, and Agent.I dont need to explain Dragon to you, so lets talk about agent.Agent is very fun, a very fast swan like style. It comes with much fun abilities like holding square to throw bomb cigerattes, holding X to dash around and run over people with rocket shoes, holding triangle to send in drones that attack people over time and circle you while blocking, and of course the string which you can use to pull enemies, items hidden around the map, and weapons to you. It was a very fun style to pair with THE DRAGON STYLE. The unlock system is money based like 0.The core side missions are little missions you take on for an intel woman. This woman provides many pretty good mini games from what I have played. you will unlock points for her, which allows you to get awards, upgrade your abilities. Not a huge fan they tied this into the upgrades, but fair enough. The upgrade screen is very similar to Judgments also.THE CASTLE. What a grand and amazingly crafted location that is beautiful to see. Its a major plot point of the game and holds many gambling mini games and the wonderful coliseum you fight in. The coliseum mode is pretty awesome. You can fight as many different characters you recruit into your team, among some being very prominent characters from past games if you got the dlc preorder, as well as a suprise Judgment reference if you accomplish a certain side quest. I thought it was fighting arena done best its ever been done in the series, so if you like that you will like this. There is team battles, your team vs others, 1v1s, 1vgroups, and SPECIAL battles that usually involve weapons and special fights like certain types of bosses.So, the only downside to this game is its incredibly short, as I said the campaign is 5 hours long. The only thing holding this game back. Idk if its fully worth 50 dollars. I would say more 30 or 40. It definitely shouldve got cut in half Id say. The story was pretty solid and well done despite how very short it was, with an incredible tie back to the moment (you know the one) in Yakuza 7 where kiryu shows up. The story ties it all up in a bow for 8 coming out the beginning of next year, and it was a pretty good experience despite how small the game is. It had a very beautiful end and truly made it feel like this is the last game Kiryu is the main protagonist in.8/10 - JIRYU WICK.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon Gaiden is unlike previous LAD games more of a side story like experience, but even then it's still a LAD game. With beautiful visuals, it still has the classic vibe and side stories/minigames but with a much more compact story. And man, what a story it was! Also my personal goty. I'm going to keep this very short considering that the story isn't all that long eitherso I'd rather want you people to experience it yourself. But man to me this was the game everyone (me included) neededthat weren't agreeing with the way Y6 ended and used some of its characters.Overall the story is great man, lots of intense and crazy moments happening, with some fun stuff as well. But I am gonna tell you this, this game broke my soul man :')This game also overtook 6 as my favorite Kiryu game. Yeah, it's that good! Gameplay is crazy, the fact that Kiryu has more than 1 style again and for the fact that we can JUGGLE as well in this game. You start with the new style Agent, it's the style that you acquire from the Daidoji, it is basically a mix of Yagami's Crane style with a more Agent like vibe I guess??Either way it's more fast-paced compared to the second style as that is more for a brawler and street fight type way, the move style for agent is more of a martial arts tactical fighting style.Both styles also have a color, for Agent being the color blue and for the other red. Agent style is also a great way to start juggles when going in heat mode. Overall, you're gonna get a lot of Judgment/Lost Judgment vibes when playing the game. But Agent style is not only fighting no, no, you have like 4 gadgets you can use, a spider-man like web/string that comes out of your watch to pull enemies to you or push them away, a cigaret that's basically a bomb. Freaking rocket boots, and drones that can chase enemies.Agent style is crazy hahaha there is so much from it. And of course for the second style we have The Yakuza Style as the game names it (normally being dragon style but oh well). It is vastly improved from the versions of Y6 and Y:K2, being overall much smoother and fleshed out with some changes, new move sets and finishers, he can basically do his iconic kick pose as a finisher. But dude do you kick the ♥♥♥♥ out of enemies when upgrading it oh man enemies went flying hahahahah.I do gotta say this in all honesty, this is I think is the only game where I haven't relied on heat moves as much compared to the other games, I was really mostly just fighting with juggles and charged attacksso that did kinda surprise me a little. Overall the combat in this game great, although a combat speed could have been nicely added, It's good but not LJ level good as that one still takes the cake for best RGG combat let's say it's better than K2 and 6 and on par with JE combat considering that one also has 2 styles. However, one huge new thing has got to be the feature that you can actually personalize Kiryu. That's right full on character customization, I freaking love this feature in this gameand I really hope it doesn't just stay in Gaiden, but actually carries on to other games as well. LAD Gaiden still has the side stuff like Substories and Minigames, as they will always be a core piece of these games. this time you have something called the Akame points, in order to get those Akame points you'll have to do Akame missions/substories, as in this game substories are actually a checklist that you do in order to gain more bonding with Akame, it's kind of unfortunate that it's not randomly like the previous gamesbut as for Kiryu being an Agent like person, it kinda makes sense that he is doing it this way, and either way the substories are still fun to do, especially for some! But you'll have to see it for your self.Mini-games, oh man POCKET CIRCUIT IS ACTUALLY BACK, I love this minigame man, one of my favorite things to do in Y0 and K1, and I'm really glad they brought it back one more final time, aside from that another mini-game that returns to the Dragon Engine is Pool, yes that was missed as well for some odd reason and that is also still fun to play, one other new thing is that some point you'll unlock a hideout that has an actual Sega master system which is pretty nuts, has around 12 games in it, tho some you got to buy at like ebisu pawn something close like that.Also, later in the game you'll unlock a new play environment called The Castle, there it has the casino/Japanese gamble games, a cabaret with LIVE ACTION performances yeah it's super weird honestly, and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ does it take so much space around 28 GB????? (0_0?). Outside of that you also got the place where you personalize Kiryu, The Boutique which has all kinds of clothing options.Enemies are your typical street guys or yakuza like the previous games and not the unique types like in LAD7. However, they are very advanced like the enemies in the Judgment games, so when you have a low upgraded Kiryu, be tactical as to how you fight them because lots of them fight back hard. A returning feature to the game is The Colosseum, which also is featured in The Castle, but man is this the best version of the Colosseum we all know.... EVERY FIGHTER IS PLAYABLE, and no I'm serious every fighter in it is playable, if you preordered the game you get playable  (or if you buy it separately as DLC). But ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ actual playable Daigo is nuts, lots of the fighter have their own move sets alto some also have move sets from previous bosses and enemies, pay close attention, and you'll see it. The rest you'll have to see for yourself, as it's too much to say about it. Now, then, the other thing this game does great are the bosses. Every, and I mean every, boss in this game is just great. You do have some mini bosses, but they are also good. But the main bosses? ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, very fun to fight to and to some degree quite challenging, also there is a returning feature that the enemies will use Mortal Reversals, as they were first introduced in LJ, Gaiden also has them for some of its enemies and all the bosses. Now I will stand on this with all my heart, this game has the best final boss fight in all LAD, yep there I said it! Overall just the final boss fight was peak LAD moment it has 3 action phases with the last one having a different OST.... ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, I loved this boss fight. The soundtrack is quite a take cause holy damn this ♥♥♥♥ good! What's surprising is that most of the composing was done by a lot of new people and by some returning composersthat did the OG Y1 and 2. The boss fights, fantastic osts, the battle themes for both styles are really great, long battle themes also great, personally the main theme Fading Away hits in every spot for me that's some tearjerker stuff right there if you just even read the lyrics. The third phase of the final boss really nails it for me man, I've been constantly listening to the soundtrack a lot! It really is still something that RGG studios does for every LAD game of theirs.Having an absolute banger of a soundtrack!That concludes my review for Like a Dragon Gaiden: The Man Who Erased His Name.Even though it's shorter, this game was very much quality over quantity to me from the gameplay, the great story and characters, and even the side stuff.I really hope we get more Gaiden games, maybe for other characters like Majima or Akiyamathere are tons of options! I also hope this is really not the last Kiryu Action game...Cause if so, I'm really gonna miss it :'((9.8)
