_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon Gaiden feels to me like the perfect distillation of the best parts of modern Yakuza games, compressed down into a package that's much more compact than other recent entries while still providing the same mix of compelling story, incredible combat, and wildly varied mini-games and side content. As a companion to Yakuza 7, it provides a wonderful feeling of familiarity, and as a standalone entry in the franchise, it stands tall among the better entries in the series.By nature, Gaiden is a much shorter game than 7 or either of the Judgment games - it's designed as a side-story, returning to Kiryu to fill in the gaps in his narrative between his exit in Yakuza 6 and his small side-role in Yakuza 7. Despite clearly being a shorter narrative, though, I found that it felt plenty meaty, moreso than several of the pre-5 entries in the series. I think a big part of this is that its story is split across just five chapters, making each of those chapters quite long compared to how these games are usually structured. The end result is that the narrative has very little downtime, with only a few periods where the story gives you the time to poke around and do whatever you want for a little while. The story is typically split between serious, heavily-written drama and absurdity, centering Kiryu's struggle to continue on in a life that, in his perception, no longer has meaning, and this narrative thread carries him through to where he seems to end up in Infinite Wealth. It's well-written and feels like it does Kiryu much more justice than 6 did, while setting him up for a potentially perfect true departure from the franchise with the next game.The combat is not quite peak Dragon Engine combat - Yakuza Style still feels weird and retread-y even with the tweaks to combat borrowed from the Judgment games, but Agent Style is an absolute revelation and completely justifies the weird narrative framework of the Daidoji faction. Seeing Kiryu shoot out Spider-Man webs and whip people around relentlessly, zip around on rocket boots, summon literally fifty drones to irritate every enemy in sight, and blow people up with explosive cigarettes is both hysterical and deeply satisfying. The group/1v1 split in the styles is still clear, with Agent ideal for clearing out large groups of enemies and Yakuza best suited to one-on-one showdowns, but it often felt like a necessity to switch to Yakuza rather than a choice I was glad to make. On the whole, though, it's still modern Yakuza combat, and it still just feels great.On the whole, Gaiden is another worthy entry in the Yakuza franchise, far more essential than its side-story nature suggests. As a brawler-style palate cleanser between the turn-based 7 and 8, it's extremely fun, and it provides a great mix of connective tissue between the games and standalone entertainment and intrigue. Pick it up.

_childDocuments_.review: The story is pretty darn good, the combat not so much. It's buggy, the cheap-looking animation and camera work as well as snapping from early Dragon Engine games is back, and a lot of the heat actions feel impactless.Agent style is unfortunately terribly undercooked; it's limited, stiff, and buggy. However, the sound design is really satisfying. Tiger drop sounds everywhere, it's great.Yakuza style is just, ugh... it's strong stats-wise and it "works" better than Agent, but it's honestly not fun to use. It's basically Kiwami 2 DoD again. The combo animations still look and feel really disconnected and samey.It just seems like so many of the advancements to the Dragon Engine that Judge Eyes and Lost Judgement have made, have got thrown out again or forgotten about. Even the UI looks like it got downgraded. It was neat getting another chance to play as Kiryu, we got some amazing match ups for him this time around, but the fighting and overall feel of the game just was incredibly underwhelming and I think it wasted heaps of potential.

_childDocuments_.review: Allow me to give you a different perspective that you won't often encounter. I love Yakuza 7. I love the character of Ichiban. I also love the Judgement series with Yagami. For the games with Kiryu as the MC? I've not been as enthusiastic. I've tried multiple games with him it, including Ishin....but I wasn't able to get "in" to previous games with Kiryu as the MC, because of how stoic he is as a character. I bought this game as something to hold me over until Y8. THIS game? I'm starting to like Kiryu. Is he stil stoic? Yes, but this time it feels better.First things first, the "movie" cut-scenes?  *chef's kiss* It's amazing, and considerably the best that RGG has ever made. It doesn't take very long in order to get to the action and getting you invested on wondering what's going to happen next and why people are trying to get Kiryu back into the fold. Kiryu's fighting is smoother than ever and "secret agent" style is definitely my go-to choice when in combat. At first glance, you might think the blue rope attack is stupid.....but on the contrary....it's very useful at times and somehow never loses it's appeal as you progress through the game. Speaking of progressing, you may notice that in chapter 1 that your exploration in the city is limited to the direction of the next cutscene. Don't worry, this is done away with by chapter 2. The story introduces a new character to the Yakuza franchise. This character is the one that offered Kiryu money to "die" at the end of Y6. He is back and he is Kiryu's handler. On top of that, he seems to be a pretty honorable guy. I've not yet finished the game, but I hope he stays true to the end. If there is one thing that I DON'T like about the game? It's that to get new moves or to increase your health/stats......it's not done by experience of battle, but by money. What this means is that when you are spending money on clothes/armor, food, etc....you're also having to use it to upgrade Kiryu. This will mean that you will need to grind more than ever to improve Kiryu. What would I rate the game as of now? Without even getting into everything the game has to offer? I would give it a 9 out of 10.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a veteran to yakuza games fighting will feel janky. Gaining heat feels harder than other games and there are not that many heat actions. Yakuza style just felt broken and it was the only style I used after mid point...Ok let me get this out of the way, if you're a new player this game is not for you. This is where it feels like the story ends. Every other game we played so far was building up for this. Kiryu finally going on a break after all those adventures. Bosses feel like bosses we fought in older games, especially final boss. Game does an amazing job at ending the story. I teared up and was just staring at the credits scene like I watched an old friend go away.Fighting is bare bones, but the story is just amazing. Not for new players, and definetly older players that played all other games will like it.

_childDocuments_.review: Heads up, I will spoil some gameplay related stuff, I won't talk about what happens in the story itself. - is one of the shortest games in the series that's more of a setup for an upcoming adventure while showing stuff that happened in 7th entry off screen along the way. Despite being advertised as a bite sized RGG title and having a good time all the way through, I still can't help but feel like I've been overcharged considering the amount of content this game provides. I am not talking about the story length, that was to be expected to be short, but I was hoping they'd make up for it by having a decent amount of side stuff and extras. This game does not have NG+, Legend difficulty, or any sort of Gauntlet/Climax Battle challenge mode, so once I was done with all side stuff I could possibly do, I can't find a good reason to ever return to it. So what unique modes are there?Yeah its not really a unique game mode, but the gimmick of this one is that you have group fights, your teams and you can play as a whole bunch of characters. That sounds all well and good until you realize majority of characters just kinda suck to play as. Even characters that used to have hype move sets have been bastardized, and I will never forgive RGG for what they did to Higashi from Judgment series in this game. Kaito is also there, but you bet he's nowhere near as good as he was in Kaito Files DLC for Lost Judgment. Sugiura is there too, and unfortunately, Yagami is too expensive so he's completely absent.When you finish the game, you will be granted access to the upcoming LAD 8 demo, This demo is fairly lengthy and lets you explore a lot more than I'd normally expect with a side story or two being available. This is cool and all, but in the future I doubt there'd be a reason to ever look at it for what it is so.... enjoy it until the real thing's out I guess?If I could give it a mixed rating I would, I did have fun with it but its not an easy recommendation unless you're really into the series. I am sure I'd be way, WAY more forgiving if the damn thing didn't take 100GB of space, but as it stands, I see no reason to not uninstall it now.

_childDocuments_.review: *Like a Dragon Gaiden: The Man Who Erased His Name* dives into the life of Kazuma Kiryu, the iconic yakuza, as he navigates new dangers in a fresh chapter. This installment delivers a rich story paired with the gritty action gameplay the series is known for, set in the familiar yet evolving underworld of Japan. Returning with a refined combat system, *Like a Dragon Gaiden* blends Kiryu's classic moves with new techniques, enhancing his signature brawler style. The game encourages a balance of strategic and direct action in encounters, with unique mini-games and side missions adding depth. The combat feels visceral, with engaging mechanics that keep fights fresh and satisfying. The narrative picks up Kiryu’s story with complexity and gravitas, exploring themes of redemption and identity. The storyline delves into Kiryu’s life in hiding and the struggles of living in the shadows, set against a meticulously detailed urban Japan that reflects the series' attention to atmosphere and culture. The visuals shine with detailed environments, character expressions, and immersive lighting, bringing the bustling cityscape and quieter, moody locations to life. The voice acting and soundtrack are equally impactful, enhancing the experience with emotional depth and adding weight to Kiryu’s journey. *Like a Dragon Gaiden: The Man Who Erased His Name* is a solid addition to the franchise, combining refined gameplay with a powerful storyline that honors Kiryu’s legacy. Ideal for series fans and newcomers alike.

_childDocuments_.review: Probably the most well-tuned brawler produced by RGG using the Dragon engine I have personally seen. Runs exceptionally well on AMD hardware. The story is a little faster paced compared to other Like a Dragon fare, though this isn't a bad thing since the story itself is said to be shorter, and it doesn't bog the player with exposition that they either should already know or be able to ascertain themselves. The emotional beats are on point as always. It is very much a Like a Dragon game for Like a Dragon fans.Special mention to go the music. Whether it is the 007 style jazz for "Agent Style", the amazing karaoke tracks (both old and new) or the creeping 80s synth when Kiryu wanders the neon streets of Sotenbori, the soundtrack lives up to the bar raised by its predecessors. While if you are new I would recommend playing the other titles first in order to appreciate the full story of this game, if you are familiar or especially a fan, both young or old, Like a Dragon Gaiden is a masterful chapter in the saga of Kazuma Kiryu.

_childDocuments_.review: This game originally was going to be DLC, but it ended up becoming its own stand alone title. You can honestly finish this whole game in 12 hours if you just rush the story. So the game is obviously in the short side but I really think this is one of the best games in the franchise gameplay wise. Story itself without going into spoiler territory is a bit slow at first however it then kicks into high gear in the later chapters. Normally I would have a problem with that style of story telling (Kingdom Hearts 3 left a sour taste in my mouth) but considering the length of the game, it's not horrible to deal with. Side content there's a shocking amount of stuff to do. Substories wise they're a treat as usual with some great fan service. The Colosseum is easily the best it's ever been with the ability to also play as every single ally you recruit into your team is also really awesome, despite the lack of heat actions for them. Gameplay as I mentioned is really REALLY good, It's Lost Judgement combat with even more juggling, and the style switching for juggle combos are really smooth. I'm not claiming to be the sauciest or best gamer in the universe, however I hit some saucy ass combos on some bosses and it felt really satisfying. Agent is a really sick new style and the gadgets are pretty funny to mess around with, and the traditional Dragon Style feels at its absolute best in this game, really shows RGG is improving the combat with every new game they make. TLDR tho, I would honestly still wait for a sale, despite all the praise I've given this game. cuz you're paying for a 12 hour game featuring a demo of Infinite Wealth.

_childDocuments_.review: Consider Like a Dragon: Gaiden to be something of a "clip-show" episode in the grand scheme of Yakuza/LAD. The main purpose of the game seems to be to remind you of key moments, and activities that Kiryu has engaged in throughout the series, framed under the guise of explaining why Kiryu appeared in Yakuza 7/Like a Dragon. Does it succeed in this case? I would say largely yes.The two combat styles are both very fun, although the "agent" style does take some getting used to for it to properly click. The plot of the game is ...fine. I don't feel like it really told anything that was needed from a narration standpoint, but it does allow for us to see a more fragile side of Kiryu near the end, so you could argue that everything depicted in the game is just appetiser for that "moment". Still, I would say the journey is still worth it for fans of the franchise.You'll get to see a few fan favourite activities and character cameos (albeit some in not the original form you remember), but the story is very short and to the point. Despite the price of the game you should very much consider this game a "tide over" until Infinite Wealth releases. It makes no attempt to try to be as elaborate as the other games in the series and you can basically completely platinum the game in around 20 to 25 hours if you're not taking your sweet time.Of course, I can't ignore the price either. Here in Australia this game is 82 dollars. 91 if you get the version with the DLC included. Now, consider that this game is only 5 chapters rather than the usual 14 to 15 and the price gets a lot harder to justify. Still, the game is fun to play and it has a lot of good ideas like the character customisation options. It also has a demo for Infinite Wealth if you're curious to try it and don't care much about spoiling stuff in advance.I'd say the game is worth it ... but I'd also suggest maybe waiting for a sale to actually buy it. 90 bucks is a tall order for essentially half the experience you'd normally get. I was lucky enough to have gotten gifted the game by a friend, so I had little complaints but I could see the price point being a major complaint for others.

_childDocuments_.review: Additional Info:Once again, we slip into the suit of Kazuma Kiryu, the former Dragon of Dojima. In an attempt to protect himself and his past, he faked his own death and went into hiding under the alias Joryu. In true Superagent style, he hides his true face behind a pair of glasses and earns his yen in Sotenbori as a henchman for the local Daidoji gang. Naturally, though, Kiryu—er, Joryu—can't escape his skin either and soon finds himself entangled in another conflict once again. Ultimately, the incidents create unrest across the yakuza as a whole.Right now, I don't want to reveal too much. In the spin-off, a young all-around player named Akame is introduced as the new sidekick. With the aid of the local homeless, she has amassed an information network. She is not just a client but also a vital point of contact for Joryu, providing him with direct access to the underground. Like A Dragon Gaiden relies on bigger, freely accessible sections rather than a true open world. Since Sotenbori is where we spend a significant portion of the game at first, there are plenty of eateries, shops, and places to relax and build strength in addition to an entertainment district and leisure areas.The streets are crowded with people and have vivid colors that give off a typical Japanese flare. But here, too, the issues are apparent and, more importantly, visible. We frequently encounter homeless people on the streets, as well as wandering gangs who we would gladly punch. Then there's the castle itself, a massive cargo ship used by the underworld as a home for chaos, the expression of evil forces, and bizarre dreams. The Colosseum, a significant new game element, adds a nostalgic touch to this otherwise amusement park-like location. We can establish ourselves as prize fighters here, move up the ranks, and get large paychecks. We have the option of fighting as a team or as individuals. This allows us to enlist additional teammates and use them in our squad through side missions.Akame's talents advance as we acquire network experience, allowing us to hold tournaments with progressively larger awards. The Hell Team Rumble competitions offer chaotic combat entertainment. We can choose the fighters starting positions and the order in which they will compete using the team screen. Though, to be honest, this strategy quickly evaporates in the chaos, group activities and intense fights make for an enjoyable game.Like A Dragon Gaiden Is a well-bred action game with a strong emphasis on the intuitive battle system. With just a button push, we can switch between our two available styles whenever we want. We can use a variety of technical aids as agents, such as the spider, an electromagnetic lasso that we can use to bind or throw opponents. In true James Bond fashion, we can even call in drones to assault our targets and set off a device akin to a cigarette that explodes. We can also turn on a tiny jet engine beneath Joryu's shoes and use it to surf around rather than running. As an agent, we often hit targets more quickly and precisely, but our single hits deal less damage.This mode's opposite is the red-colored Yakuza mode. We deal greatly more damage in close quarters and during charge-up assaults when we're in this state. You learn new moves as you advance in skill and with various Heat Actions; however, you must hold down a specific button to use the Agent devices. It can be irksome when, as it frequently happened in my case, I created a Heat Action in place of using an Agent device. Control and overview are frequently lost because the camera is unable to keep up with the fast-paced action. The intense fight scenes elevate the Yakuza series despite these flaws. The addition of weapons and items adds to the appeal of punches and kicks, which feel incredibly forceful. We can build up heat energy through effective attacks and counters, which we can then release in a sort of fury mode. Joryu is less vulnerable to hits and does damage very swiftly during this phase.The game allows for some free time in between all the fighting and gory killing. And as anyone who has watched the Yakuza series will attest, hilarity and seriousness go hand in hand. This is also the case in this spin-off, where we practice golf, play darts or pool, and complete laps in pocket circuit racing. Alternatively, we have the option to play renowned classics like Fighting Vipers 2, Virtua Fighter 2.1, and Sega Racing Classic on nearby Sega Mega Drive systems and at arcades. We also comb vending machines for adorable plush toys, and these can then be given as presents to the local nightclub's hostesses. The interactions between the scantily clad ladies are presented by the developers with subtly obtrusive live-action footage. However, despite their humorous sound, the flirting attempts are actually pretty unsettling. The unflattering camgirl attractiveness of the scene is accentuated by the easily identifiable ring light reflection in the woman's eyes, which regrettably creates a weird lasting memory.Following the original series, the spin-off also doesn't take itself or its characters too seriously. In my opinion, the peculiar and distinctively Japanese humor could have been somewhat more prominent and exerted a more significant influence on the adversary design. The criminal adventure occasionally becomes bogged down in monotonous ranked bouts and the required elevation within the Akame network, despite the thrilling plot and intriguing characters. To put it simply, this means that we must finish the side missions and engage in combat in the Colosseum whether we want to or not. There are a few notable exceptions, but there are nine (!) substories alone that only feature gang battles, hence why I would have preferred more variation in the missions itself. At the end of the day, all of the missions are ultimately about brawls, sometimes bigger and sometimes smaller.Like A Dragon Gaiden took only six months to develop and was initially intended to be a DLC for the upcoming Infinite Wealth which even suprises me more. It possesses all of the series hallmark qualities, including an engrossing plot, peculiar comedy, a ton of side activities (even though they're somewhat repetitive), and a ton of minor surprises to discover. The only catch is that you must be familiar with the series in order to really enjoy this game. For those who are unfamiliar with the series, Like A Dragon, Judgement, or Yakuza 0 would be a better choice. Nevertheless, I can heartily recommend this espionage spin-off to enthusiasts. Particularly for fans of the Yakuza: I swear, the conclusion will make you cry.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game overall that'll appeal to anyone who has been following the Yakuza series but a few downsides that are unique to this one. On the good side, the combat feels so much smoother and fast paced than previous titles. There's essentially two stances - Agent mode and Dragon. Agent mode is a mixture of gadgets and fast paced moves from Kiryu that aren't "light" attacks by any means. It feels fantastic and I did most fights in this stance because you could quickly evade and follow up which was something I felt lacked in past games. Dragon stance is more of the older approach of brute forcing attacks with block penetration and immediate counters. Overall both are great. The gadgets are more of a gimmick than anything so 90% of your damage will come from actual attacks. Downside is the path this game takes to get you from start to finish. There's a huge block that comes in the middle of the game that forces you to do sub stories and arena battles. In other games, these were totally optional and at no point did I ever feel forced to do a bunch of sub stories that I wasn't interested in. It's not the case here and I'd say half of my playtime was being forced to grind through them with a relatively short main story line. The story itself was alright. It ties into the other yakuza games by portraying yakuza in general as degrading into a bunch of common criminals exploiting regular people who are being phased out from society. It runs largely parallel with LAD with Ichiban so unless you've played that you might not know what's going on. There's a montage that tries to inform people who haven't played it, but I thought it was way too fast and insufficient if I hadn't already played that.Overall, worth a buy if you have time. I think this might be the last game we get with someone stoic like Kiryu running as the lead--I'm not a fan of the naive/energetic Ichiban who seems to be the new lead of the franchise. It's a little darker than the other games, but I actually liked that part and felt it fit well. I just wasn't a fan of the substory grind, but I could get over that.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very good its worth your time if you have played the other games connected to Kiryu (Yakuza 1 through 6). This game feels like they tried to make a better conclusion to Kiryus story then yakuza 6 as well as kinda leading into his story in 8 (Ill mention the "kinda" in the spoiler part). Gameplay is solid as usual and the minigames are just as strong as before. The Agent style as a fighting style is the fast style of this game {most comparable to Crane in the Judgements), but with a more defensive profile (kinda like Snake from LJ but in role only) and has gadgets to mix it up and make groups easier to fight. _childDocuments_.review: The latest spin-off in the Yakuza series, Gaiden expands on the story of Kiryu Kazuma following the events of Yakuza 6 and through Yakuza: Like a Dragon. There are two fighting styles available to Kiryu, both of which are satisfying to use. Graphically, this game impresses on a 4K display at max settings. Performance can be saved using DLSS or FSR. The story is rather short compared to recent entries in the Yakuza series, clocking it at about 15 hours. The story pacing is broken up with a significant amount of side story filler, which will be appreciated based on your enjoyment of that type of content. I enjoyed this title as a fan of the Yakuza series but I could understand if it underwhelms newcomers. 7.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: It's like a dash of Judgment in your Yakuza(/LAD) and that's not a bad thing (such as the strong enemy attacks you can interrupt and follow up with hard-hitting counters and bleeding from bladed weapons). The game is short (by comparison) if you're looking for the usual Yakuza experience but if you are invested in the story of the games, if you want some more context behind a certain character's arrival in Like A Dragon, if you are invested in Kiryu and what he has gone through in his life then this story is really, really good. The ending tore my soul apart in the best way. It really is a must for fans.You will find a some fun references to Yakuza 2 as well as one or two Yakuza 0 callbacks and while it is easy to become overpowered in combat it does, at least, make clearing the street trash rather quick. There are some fun attacks that combine with the agent style but you will find yourself feeling familiar with the style if you've played Judgment (it is not outright copied but has the same tight feel as Yagami's tiger style). Among some incredible cameos I won't spoil, there is a Judgment character who shows up in a really great sub-story. In fact, I'd say the sub-stories in this game are almost all fantastic and worth the time.The arena allows you to play as many different characters (including three from Judgment). The coliseum really does feel like the big showpiece of the game and it's a really is a spectacle to be introduced to. Akame, a new character, is also a fun addition to the cast.Problems:Your mileage may vary but I found the hostess stuff absolutely weird and uncomfortable (but if you're a fan of Kson, that might be different?), two of the four gadgets feel as if you really could just ignore them outright. While there are many options to fight as in the coliseum there is, unfortunately, no real contest between Kiryu's strength and playing as someone like Daigo, Majima, or Saejima (which, while fun, does lack the upgrades Kiryu has). While the group battles in the coliseum are really fun it does bring out a bit of a grind to level your team which might extend gameplay for some but was not quite for me. I also found the omission of some classic heat actions from Kiryu's Yakuza style to be a disappointment. Also, if you happen to be a fan of grappling attacks in combat you can expect to be frustrated as almost all enemies but the weakest will quickly break free. While the agent style does have a fun way to snatch weapons from enemies or the ground there is something lost in not being able to actually carry weapons on your person like previous titles (though you will be familiar with this if you have played the Judgment games).Conclusion:All in all, if you're a Yakuza fan (and have played Yakuza 0 and Yakuza 2 or Judgment) you will find a lot here to like. There are some really great moments where you finally see Kiryu losing his composure and usual cool with where his choices in life have left him and the pain it is putting him through. It's a must for following the Dragon of Dojima and his story and leads into an explanation as to why Kiryu will be found in Infinite Wealth. While it might not be worth full retail price right now, the english dub might be enough to warrant it (if you prefer not to deal with subtitles) but I don't think it will hurt to try and get this game at around 40 or so. If you love the Yakuza storyline, however, the price of admission is worth seeing the emotional ride Kiryu goes through in this title.Quick edit: As for long-time Yakuza fans? You can FINALLY WEAR DIFFERENT OUTFITS WITHOUT HAVING TO BE IN PREMIUM ADVENTURE!

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished the game and got my last achievement so I'm going into this review pretty fresh. Like a Dragon: Gaiden is an absolutely phenomenal entry in a series that I've grown to adore. The gameplay continues to be refined with each entry, and I'd say this is about on par with Lost Judgement in regards to combat. Though there are only two stances, the insane gadgets you unlock for Agent stance more than make up for it. The extreme variety of side content is here as always, with most everything being an iteration on existing minigames to make them a bit more engaging, most notably the clan battles from Yakuza Kiwami 2 and Yakuza 6 are actual battles you participate in instead of that weird tower defense thing. On that note, this is one of the best iterations of The Coliseum in the entire franchise, though there is one specific substory fight that you'll need to level up your clan for. The map size isn't particularly large, roughly the size of the Majima Saga from Yakuza Kiwami 2, but there is considerably more content and variety packed into here than you'd think. If you're a fan of these games you can buy this with no worries, you'll be satisfied for sure.Story is shockingly engaging for something that's filling the gap between Yakuza 6 and Like a Dragon, I genuinely wasn't expecting to be as interested in anything outside of Kiryu himself but that wasn't the case at all. Akame is an excellent addition to the cast and is a joy on screen, pretty much every character punches well above their weight in terms of what you'd expect from a spinoff entry. I cannot recommend this game enough if you're a fan of Yakuza and Kiryu in particular, longtime fans will have an absolutely ton of references that they can pick up on. On top of all of this, there's a demo for Infinite Wealth included so you can get your feet wet for that entry. RGG Studios has turned into one of my favorite developers to watch right now and this game is a testament to their skill. It's absolutely unbelievable that this was made in six months.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely loved this game. Its events occur at the same time as Like a Dragon's, so it's quite a self-contained game story-wise, but it still took me 20+hr to beat the game and side content (notably, substories and arena, didn't quite never got into Pocket Circuit racing).As Kiryu's last dance approaches (presumably), we get to see him in action again from the ending of Y6 until the ending of Like a Dragon. This time around, Kiryu's some kind of secret agent with gadgets and all, which give some variety to the combat gameplay. First few hours of combat fell a bit stale and lack options, but variety quickly grows and combat gets funnier very soon as you start unlocking new moves.We get the same old Yakuza Style, and the brand new Agent Style, which is a more swift, agile combat approach in which you can use Kiryu's gadgets. Some of them felt pretty useless (cigar and drones), but thread and rocket-powered shoes felt like they added variety and added some strategical options, so a nice change of pace. It's not like fights are very difficult anyway, specially since this game allows us to unlock Tiger Drop as early as chapter 1...Music and voice acting are top tier as usual and the graphics are the same formula as ever: gorgeous for main character models, more modest in environments, and some PS3 sprinkle for NPCs...If anything, I would complain that unlike in Y6 or LaD, Gaiden's new characters didn't really leave a mark on me. Kiryu and the old dogs steal the show, really. Though I would like to see Akame back, she seems qualified to take over as a new kind of Florist of Sai.All in all, if Like a Dragon franchise is the kind of game you enjoy, this is close to the greater ones, so don't hesitate to give it a try. Solid 8-8.5 for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Like A Dragon Gaiden is such a huge disappointment. I can't stand playing as this Joryu guy, he's by far the worst protagonist RGG has ever made. He doesn't come anywhere close to being as charismatic and endearing as other protagonists, like Ichiban and Kiryu.Speaking of Kiryu, it's wild that so many people in the story keep thinking Joryu is Kiryu. _childDocuments_.review: *Some Minor Spoilers*Like A Dragon Gaiden: The Man Who Erased His Name is a conclusion to a Saga that should have definitively ended in 2016's Yakuza 6: The Song of Life.Yakuza 6 is by all means not a “bad” game and definitely not a terrible conclusion to Kazuma Kiryu's story. Instead, it is remembered as a game that didn't have the proverbial guts to end the Dragon of Dojima’s seven game journey. Yakuza 6 did numerous things correctly by establishing Kiryu as a grandfather and introducing us to a new cast of supporting characters in Onomichi, Hiroshima.  Unfortunately, The game seemed allergic to using legacy characters in the Saga and relegated most of them to the wayside in favor of a new supporting cast.  In consequence, Kiryu's final game feels smaller and intimate, for better or worse. If this truly was the end of Kiryu's story, then Yakuza 6 should have been a celebration of the same. Instead, The end product was just another mainline Yakuza game and not the emotional climax of the journey. As we watch Kiryu walk down that street, fans are instead teased for more. The Dragon never dies. And the tease bore fruit. Kiryu returns as the sole playable protagonist of Like A Dragon Gaiden. Once again described as Kiryu's send off, Gaiden is set with the task of providing its audience with a smaller, intimate, and emotionally satisfying ending for one of gaming's greatest protagonists and it does so successfully.Gaiden's story places Kiryu in an interesting setting, practically divorced from his legendary life and past relationships. Over the course of the game, Kiryu forges new bonds, fights against a new bunch of baddies, and eventually enters an ideological battle for the future of the Yakuza. In the midst of all this crime ridden chaos, Kiryu's emotional journey remains at the forefront even if it doesn't seem obvious. Kiryu doesn't show a lot of emotions in the story, the logic of its plot makes it necessary to do so. But when Kiryu's stoic veil falls, the writers really make it count.Takaya Kuroda brings his performance of Kazuma Kiryu to new heights, delivering a beautifully human performance for a historically stoic character. For the first time in years, the writing truly allows Kiryu to become incredibly vulnerable, giving Kuroda a chance to show us a side of Kiryu never seen before. At one point, I was convinced that there were no stories left to tell with this character until Takaya Kuroda proved me wrong. There is much to tell with this character, even if this is the final stretch. It's one of the greatest voice acting performances in the video game canon and leaves its ending as the best in the series. Kudos to the facial animations as well, the emotional scenes would have been hollow without the fantastic work behind them.Speaking of the ending, I can definitely say that the final chapter is an all time great experience. Upon its arrival, the game fires on all cylinders to deliver a climactic and emotionally resonant experience filled to the brim with fist fights, team ups, hype moments, climatic showdowns, and a greater degree of emotional vulnerability for Kiryu. It’s seemingly the end of a Saga until Infinite Wealth finds a way to top it. While I cannot say much about the ending, what I can say is that it is a fantastic ending. An explosion of emotions built up over several games. Jacob Geller in his "The Best Games of 2023" video, once called the final hours a “transcendent experience.” I am inclined to agree. This is amazing stuff and they saved the best for last.If it's not obvious by now, the characters are the biggest strength of The Man Who Erased His Name. All of them are memorable in their own right, even if some are more developed than others.  Within the short runtime, the story is able to develop its cast of new characters with varying degrees of success. Characters like Akame and Shishido are standouts and have already become fan favorites. This is thanks to the lovely character writing and great acting from their voice actors, delivering the human qualities this franchise is known for.However, other characters such as Hanawa are written in a strange way. Hanawa typically doesn't show much emotion, but he does reveal some humanity in rare and interesting moments. Upon further examination, this is by design. But you would have to play the game to see it yourself. Despite the interesting writing and time spent, it was hard to fully invest into Hanawa. A true shame as the character makes a substantial appearance in Infinite Wealth.Unfortunately, Gaiden has pacing issues in the story. The game mandates the player to engage with the game's side content such as The Akame Network and the Coliseum before moving onto the main story throughout the various chapters. This results in an inorganic and frustrating introduction to side content that takes away the narrative momentum of the story.The strangely slow pacing is saved by the fun of Gaiden’s combat that I absolutely loved. This is the best brawler combat the franchise has ever done. It’s smooth, responsive, and incredibly fun to play. The game provides the player two fighting styles to toy around with. The first is the Agent style, which turns Kiryu into a methodical and elegant fighter and provides him with gadgets such as Flying drones and the Spider rope. His movement is swift and can transform a battle from a brawl to a fluid dance if done right. A far cry from the destructive, forceful, and familiar Dragon of Dojima fighting style that is also provided as the second fighting style in the game. The fighting styles serve to show Kiryu’s development as a character, that he has become refined and patient as shown with the Agent Style.While some of its plot elements remain underdeveloped, some characters aren’t that interesting, and its pacing is somewhat of a mixed bag, the story of The Man Who Erased His Name remains to be a good and rewarding experience. The focus on Kiryu pays off spectacularly and the Saga is capped off nicely.  The gameplay may be typically “Yakuza”, but it remains fun and polished to play. 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: As I am awaiting the release of , to my surprise  released . This takes place after the events of  and during the events of the 7th game. This title uses the action beat-em-up gameplay that the previous games have done, rather than the turn-based RPG mechanics that were used in . is now putting his  life behind him, assuming the name of  and effectively becoming a dead man to everyone he loves and the world. However, one night during a mission he was assigned to someone seems to know what actually happened to him and wants to bring him out of hiding.  must find out what is actually going on and take down whoever is trying to expose him but it also seems a lot more is going on than it seems. The only issue I had with the story in this game, is that it’s really short. I completed it in like 6-7 hours at best. The story for this game is honestly fantastic, it fills in some gaps that  had and the characters are overall amazing. It will also showcase some events from  as well as some of the characters making a cameo appearance. To top it all off, the ending to this game actually made me shed some tears which is one of the first and only games to do so.The gameplay is very fun, and I enjoyed playing through the beat-em-based combat as always. This is also the first game where I played on professional difficulty, which was manageable for me. You have access to two fighting styles,  and , each having its own set of skills and abilities for  to utilize.  style allows him to use the  specialized martial arts. It’s a fighting style that is very fast-paced, with fast punches and kicks.  can also use special gadgets in combat, including a grappling hook called the , AI drones to home in on enemies called , Jet engines on his shoes called , and  - a bomb disguised as a cigarette.Then there is the  fighting style, which is more mixed with the  and  style used in the previous games. It now has triple finishers and a new red aura so your enemies can know you are a threat. All of his heat actions are back, from all the way back to the first  game, with two new ones added to spice things up. Overall, the  style is a slower fighting style and the one I used the most during combat, as it was my preferred choice.There are also times in the game when enemies do a special attack that will do massive damage.  can counter these moves with a counterattack and deal some damage to the enemy while doing so. The  has also changed - if you take damage the  will no longer deplete, the only attacks that can make it deplete are ones that use electricity.While in  any damage done to  will be done to the meter instead and will keep doing this until it’s depleted or shut off. There is also gear you can equip that will help you out in combat by providing state buffs.To get upgrades in the game, you can do side content to get money and . The latter are given to you after you are done with a side quest. You can get stuff like new moves, health, attack damage, etc. There is a ton of side content to do and I did a bunch of it throughout my playthrough to make sure I got enough  to get some upgrades. I never had an issue with getting enough , though I did have an issue getting money as that is also used to get upgrades. However, there are ways to get money - it’s just that I ran out most of the time getting upgrades and buying healing items.As mentioned before, The  has a few side quests for you to complete that will earn you money and . There are also  missions for you to complete that will give you the same rewards. This can raise your  and the higher it is, your rank will go up in the , which is a secret area you can visit that has a colosseum for you to fight other people.However, I do have one issue with the gameplay and that is with the  style; it’s underwhelming. The issue comes with the fact that the  style is better for taking out enemies as a whole. While the  is useful for crowd control and there are upgrades to grab more enemies with it, that also has an issue. To use any of the gadgets you have to hold down the button. So, for example, if I want to use the , I will have to hold the B button on my controller and this applies to the other ones as well. To get them out is a bit slow and you are kind of a sitting duck while doing so.Except for the  gadget, that one makes you move and it seems to be quick to activate. I wish I could have used  more but besides the delay of holding X and the time it takes for the smoke to explode, it's not worth it as sometimes it will be out of range of enemies and can hurt you and your allies.The graphics for the game are honestly beautiful with some of the scenes being simply breathtaking, all backed up with a fantastic soundtrack.I tested the game on an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1060 3GB, AMD Ryzen 5 1500X Quad-Core Processor 3.50, and 16 GB of RAM. I experienced no issues while I was playing, and the game ran fine for me. Although there were some drops in my frames a few times that may be due to the fact I need new PC parts, only time will tell if I can run the next game.I had a ton of fun with , but I need to mention that if you are someone who is starting out with the series, I'd avoid this game for now, as you won’t understand the story of this game all that well. Also, the game is only 6-7 hours long. There is a lot of side content but that only brings it up to about 20-40 hours in length. _childDocuments_.review: Another minted entry in this beautiful series of games. LADG: TMWEHN gave me an enhanced view on life, the choices we make, and how they can open/close door into the future. This game focuses on Kiryu and the direct consequences of his actions in the previous Yakuza entries (Y0-Y6). This isn't just an epilogue to those games previous games, but a tie-in to LAD: 7 and a transition into the future of the series. Game has improved beat-em-up combat, excellent cinematics/acting/music.graphics/style, and a slightly convoluted but intriguing and emotional plot that keeps you hooked till the end. Also has some great new side content and epic nostalgia filled side quests. Characters new and old are also top notch (especially Akame <3). Last of all, the final chapter has one of the most epic moments in all of gaming, and the final few fights are peak Yakuza/LAD. And once all of the fighting is done and dusted we are treated to a final cut-scene 20 years in the making that could bring any man to tears. I am not crying, you're crying D; 9.3/10

This game has SO MUCH STUFF to do. Like all the other Yakuza/Like a Dragon games you can literally spend all your time (and yen) faffing about doing NOTHING. It's amazing. I'm a big fan of the LAD/Yakuza games and whilst I was iffy about this one, the references, callbacks and little nods to previous games is quite charming. Definitely recommend to anyone who is into these kinds of games.

_childDocuments_.review: List of things that could to be changed to make the combat better:-Base combo speed and style switching could be quicker-Grab needs to be buffed and made faster, it lacks I-frames and way too many enemies resist it -Mortal reversal lacks I-frames, this is a problem in group fights with boss enemies-Heat gain is too slow without booze or low HP-Heat actions are very unbalanced, some delete a full boss health bar, others do ♥♥♥♥ all-Status effects, especially bleed need to be less of a pain-Long getup/stun animations after being hit with big attacks kill momentum -Bouncing of the enemies guard and slowing down your combo is still problematic-More context/enviroment based heat actions-QTEs for bosses and action sequences, what happened?-less focus on extreme heat mode, right now it's just a win button since there is no cooldown for heat actions and all of the ones in ex-heat deal tons of damage-Komaki Parry?I would have prefered it if the devs focused resources on one great game instead of releasing three in such a short timespan. To be cynical: This and Ishin just feel like content to bridge the gap until the next "big game".

_childDocuments_.review: Never have I ever thought this day would come. The day, when I'm gonna post Negative Review for Like a Dragon/Yakuza title.I'm not a newcomer to the series by any means. Just checked my game time and it's at least 950+ hours in RGG studio games.A very humble message to Sega before we begin. ♥♥♥ you, greedy ♥♥♥♥♥. Why ? A) Intentionally locked Pre Orders for several developing/"poor" countries and THEN proceeded to sell the game at release day, thus depriving fans those silly P/O bonusesB) The most disgusting price tag across the series in terms Price:Content (Quality + Amount; we'll talk about it later) and the absence of adequate regional pricing. Ukraine, LATAM, MENA, India; you can check and compare prices here if curious:I've bought Y:0-6 for full price. Every game. 7 and J games with a small discount. Can't anymore, because Sega decided to raise the price 2-3 times.C) Sega's support didnt bother to answer a single ticket regarding locked Pre Orders, just marked them as "Solved" and closed.If RGG had a say regarding pricing and pre orders, I, honestly, wish them the same.If you wanna know a bit about my "taste" in these games, here's my Top 3 without specific order:- Narrative-wise: Yakuza 0, LaD (7), Judgment- Gameplay-wise  Yakuza 0, LaD (7), Lost JudgmentFrankly, whole game felt just like an advertising campaign for IW. With a price tag 50$.What I disliked the most ? LaD Gaiden is a big DLC rather than a separate game. A huge fan service sinkhole which appeals to nostalgy of the fans.Game surely looks and plays like a LaD title. It has the "shell" of the series, but I didn't feel the "soul" inside that shell. I wasn't hooked on the story. Guys, I loved babysitting at Y:3, Haruka's part at Y:5, but again, this game just didnt click with me.I also have my doubts regarding writing. It didn't feel like Yokoyama wrote this story. Made some edits - maybe. I'm aware they develop multiple games at the same time and Gaiden was meant to be a small game. It seems like this project was given to junior team/employees.Characters were okay. Voice acting is top notch as always.They recorded 30-ish compositions for this one, but the other half of the music - the same tracks from previous games. I wanna stop here for a moment. Music has always been a very important part of narrative in LaD games for me. It dictates the mood and sets the atmosphere for the events we participate in. And RGG always wrote a new tracks for each game with small exceptions. These are Yakuza Kiwami re-made tracks from Y:1, alterations of Kiryu's and Majima's theme Receive You and maybe several more less repetitive examples. Never bothered RGG reused assets from time to time but this title is the one big half assed repeat.Chapter 2 (was it ?), when Kiryu arrived to the Castle was a cringe fest as well as amount of Ryuji Goda (at this point I dont even know what to call it) references. From my point of view, RGG didn't wanna put more original content in this game or I dunno. What I want to say is that for the first time I'm genuinely scared for LaD series future. This title is theirs first "new" project (Ishin is a remake) after Nagoshi left the studio.I'm freaking out not because it's something huge. On the opposite. It's a sum of many red flags.One guy said that nowadays big companies mostly ride on the success on some old titles and almost never develop something new. This is my exact thoughts regarding Gaiden. Too many Y:2 stuff.Last nail in coffin was the last unlockable Coliseum fight - Minamida GrandPrix. I guess many reckon it was cool, but combining everything said previously - I think not. You will face robots that mimic movesets of all final bosses from Yakuza 6 to 1 in reverse with their music themes. I already had a bad taste in my mouth and now just remember the emotions every previous title and corresponding battle and the character brought me, only to see a metal piece of crap in front of me - a reminder that the devs are slacking off. This one really controversial for me. On the one hand it would've been fun idea if not all previous fan service in one small game, but on the other, yeah, that and text above.They also tried to ride on success of previous banger tracks like Pledge of Demon (0) and Theory of Beauty (6). Check tracks Hellish Octagon and Psycho's Anthem and tell me you dont hear the "resemblance".Whats new ?Well, 1 new Combat Style; 0.5 new mini game (It's called Hell Team rumble and since it's still in Coliseum...see for yourself) + "biggest" but idk if best addition - Akame Network. Shortly, Substories were mostly converted into requests in here plus you have a lot of mini requests and brawls across Sotenbori. Complete them, earn Cash and Akame points to upgrade your skills, buy new gear. Substories mostly bland and boring in Gaiden. Ai app was okay, Judgment crossover too. At least half of them - eliminating three gangs. First Summer Uika's play as Akame was good. Fun fact, her surname is Dojima :DThe rest is familiar to the fans. Same mini games, same bullies on the streets, eateries, shops, lockers.There are very few Dynamic Intros we all love, and maybe one was good.No NG+, no Legendary difficulty. Fifty Bucks. FmL....LaD 5, 6, Gaiden SPOILERS AHEAD !I wanted to talk regarding specific topic, which caused a lot of confusion for me. Idk why I include this to be honest.Since we talked about the story, my favorite part, hands down - Kiryu watching recording on tablet in Finale. That was strong, that was good, that's what we love in LaD games. Strong emotions. But again, almost everything else - meh.Had no issues with Performance. Rtx 2060, Ryzen 3700x, 32GB Ram. 1080p high settings, DLAA, no DLSS - 80-90 FPS.It was the first time, when I considered viewing cutscenes on YouTube and maybe reading a bit after, instead of buying the game. And my guts told me to do so. But constant possibility of a rocket coming into my window (greetings from Ukraine) told me "You only live once and life is too short" so I bought it. Which I, honestly, regret.If you're on the fence regarding this game - don't buy it until -75%. Not worth it. Not buying similar project in future.Platinum is very easy.And regarding future of LaD series and my concerns, I, honestly, hope I'm wrong and everything will be super great, in terms oа quality. Less than 3 weeks until Infinite Wealth release. Oh, and one more f u for Sega - New Game Plus in IW locked behind a paywall in a Master Vacation Bundle, available as a part of Deluxe edition. Pre Orders locked again for several countries.Couple interesting tracks from OST:Wait till 0:40, trust me:It's a very chaotic review, but I've tried. If you've read it all - thank you.

_childDocuments_.review: So - yes, I recommend it with hesitance.  I got it on a very steep discount.It's a decently good story - if you ignore the final sequence before the ending.   It's a bit difficult to follow what's going on, because it assumes that you are intimately following the story from all the way back to Yakuza 0.  There's even an intersection with Yakuza 7 (the first Like a Dragon), all the way to a specific set of cutscenes, and it'd been so long since I played that game I didn't remember the segment was there too until I looked it up on Wikipedia.  I did remember the homeless camp where Ichiban goes after he gets injured, but that's all I'd remembered. That's not to say it's a bad story, it's just that the subsequent games don't do a good enough job of revisiting older segments.  There's too much assumption about how closely you follow this stuff.Final Fantasy X did so good of a job with its world building that by the time you played X-2 that came out years later, everything was 100% recognizable; that's how it should have been done here but wasn't.What I REALLY liked though?  This fight engine is how Street Fighter should be like.  I absolutely loved pulling off counters and neutralizing baddies with a smoothness that I've never experienced in any game before or since.  It's also a generally visually impressive looking game over all (lip sync is a bit questionable, but don't really care about that).But...- Akame should have been a love interest.  Period.  She came across like just a helper, and that's nowhere close to what she really is/was.- The excessive "stab with knife, cut with sword, smash with bricks" mantra only to have guys constantly come back over and over and keep on fighting (via cutscene).  I would say more, but it would spoil things.  Bottom line: it suffers from the "Kingdom Hearts" syndrome.- This is an EXTREMELY short game.  The core gameplay itself - with no side content - can't be more than 10 hours.  My playtime is rushing and purposely watching the full cutscenes when they played; the cutscenes have to be half of the playtime.  It's ridiculous (and I LOVE cutscenes).So I recommend it...but NOT at full price.  It's a generally fun game, but it's simply not a $60-70 game.

The biggest highlight of the story comes during Chapter 3 and 4.Overall, this is a "highly recommended," title for the franchise. (It's going to be confusing calling the series Like a Dragon in English when every game before 7 was just Yakuza.)Now, let's see what the Infinite Wealth trial is like...

_childDocuments_.review: it's hard to compare this game's plot with other games in the series because it was created to be a short, contained story between two mainline games. however, the plot of gaiden was fairly straightforward and was relatively tame. it definitely did its purpose in introducing where kiryu has been and those who want to disrupt his life, and wraps it up in a nice bow at the end, also adding some needed family elements and emotional beats. it's filled with fanservice which i'm not complaining about in the slightest, and was short but sweet. a fun time! oh just simply amazing -- every character introduced was absolutely perfect for what their role is relative to the story, and they're somewhat complex for such a short runtime. you like the characters you like, and hate the ones you hate (with some outliers of course). shishido was a standout for me personally, and i'd love to see akame come back from rgg jail please yokoyama  not much, but that was expected. i didn't jive with the interactive cabaret club, or the short street missions but the minigames that reappear from other games are improved upon in the new engine. the coliseum was a blast to playthrough, definitely improved from past games with a fun twist. being able to dress up kiryu not only just around town but also the outfits being featured in cutscenes was some of my favorite parts of the game.  it's pretty custom for an rgg game to have amazing voice acting, but this game really didn't hold back. kuroda kills it as always, and deserves some sort of trophy for best delivery on some of these lines, especially near the end of the game. not a single voice actor let me down!!!  genuinely one of my favorite osts out of the entire series. its more slow and emotional songs are standout to me, and fading away is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the catchiest song of all time. i loved all of the bosses' themes, especially the leadup to the final boss. not a single track that disappointed me.  absolutely stunning visuals and shadows!! everything was very fluid and very sleek looking, which is welcomed considering the spy-esque theme of this game. needing to use both akame points and yen to buy skill upgrades was definitely a choice, but whatever makes the boys upstairs happy i guess. i really had no complaints about the way the game ran at all.  it feels so good to fight in this game i swear!!! it's second best in terms of combat feel (first being lost judgment) and the two styles is such a fun balance of play style. agent style is so refreshing with it's goofy gadgets and methodical punches, while yakuza style is rough and powerful. juggling is beyond easy in this one, and each punch is base boosted with the loudest thud so you really feel the impact. not to mention, heat mode is super overpowered and was almost outright comical at times, and i love it.  this was truly such a fun time with lots of peak moments. i still think about some scenes in my daily life, just because it was that impactful for me. i cried harder at this ending than i did at 8's ending, if that tells you anything.  this is basically a yakuza fan's wet dream!!! if you're already a fan, definitely play this and go have fun, but if you're new to the series DO NOT!!! play this one until you played the rest of the series. its best moments are based on important events in the past games, and would genuinely make no sense without context. such a great game, shame everyone seems to be changing their opinion about it after infinite wealth's release.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing all Yakuza/Like a Dragon games that are available on Steam, I can't say either this is a must play or a skippable entry.Like a Dragon Gaiden: The Man Who Erased His Name takes place in parallel to Yakuza Like A Dragon (Like a Dragon 7) and you play as Kazuma Kiryu (now using a fake name "Joryu"), the classic protagonist of the series. Planned as a DLC package for Like a Dragon 8 Infinite Wealth, Gaiden is shorter than most entries and feel like a lot of its parts are made with less budget and time.That being said, this is still a very entertaining game from RGG. These guys know how to make the most out of a small open world and the grounded setting. Plenty of minigames, progressions, and side stories that are worth sinking your time into, not only because they're fun and have depths beyond the surfaces, but they also give you resources to unlock upgrades for Joryu in combat. And trust me, you'd want to have some upgrades.The combat system in Gaiden is somewhere between Judgement, Lost Judgement, and Yakuza 5. Joryu has 2 fighting styles, Yakuza and Agent. Agent is a brand-new style to the series, it focuses on fast and long combo string, 3 consecutive side-stepping, and sci-fi gadgets like drones, Spider Man web wires, rocket-powered shoes, and cigarette bombs. Yakuza is a combination of Dragon Engine Kiryu's Dragon of Dojima style and some moves from his older games. Yakuza style's attack speed can feel quite slow, but not overly clunky like Yakuza 6, similar to Judgement. This game also features enemy-juggling, which was first seen in Judgement and streamlined in Lost Judgement. Joryu's combat rhythm and capabilities can open up even the stronger foes for some nasty juggling combo. While juggling and gadgets sound fun and powerful, enemy AI in Gaiden seem tampered to be more aggressive and opportunistic in their strikes. Lost Judgement (the latest Dragon Engine game) seemed to have AI's that are afraid to hit the player and often leave you alone while you combo attacks either regularly or while juggling. Meanwhile Gaiden's enemy AI doesn't care where you are in the arena or what you're doing, they will try to hit you and get you off a combo. So most of the time while you're fighting multiple foes, you'll have to utilize everything to create yourself some space or dispatch the weaker enemies quickly. The Heat mechanic also returns, but it is nerfed pretty harshly. The Heat bar that allows you to use Heat actions or activate Extreme Heat goes up rather slowly in Gaiden. So, either you have to stock up on heat-regenerating items or use it very sparingly, either way you cannot spam it like in the older games. is highly dependent on a player's investment to the series. I'd say that if you only played 1 or 2 Kiryu games, then Gaiden wouldn't be as worthy to you. But if you're invested in the series, the story, the gameplay, and universe, I'd say this is a must-play, implying you haven't played it already. This game tells a very interesting and emotion part of Kiryu's life story but not necessarily required to enjoy future or older games.One more thing I find weird (and noticed when it got worse) in this game is the lighting. Most RGG games are fine with their lighting, even with Kiwami 1&2's green filter, scenes from those game don't look out of place and offer a consistent imagery experience throughout each one. But Gaiden has a focus on darker shadows and overall color level contrast of the image. This might be to some people's preference but I just find it a bit jarring. Seeing bright particle effects over a dimly lit environment, while contact and cast shadows are sometimes too dark and sometimes too bright that they don't seem to exist, threw me off from the experience a bit. Some scenes nailed the high-contrast lighting perfectly, such as the prologue scene with blue and red lights on each side and the shadows are dark and threatening. While some scenes like the final boss fight has less detailed lighting, overly reliant on baked and static textures and colors. It's a good game for screenshots sometimes, but not most of the time imo.I still give it a 7.5/10, a good Yakuza game, through and through. Even with shortcomings from short development time and branding as a side-game, it still offers a completed Yakuza experience through good story, memorable characters, cool set-pieces, abundant side activities, soundtracks, and satisfying combat system.

_childDocuments_.review: This game does not at all let you know it was made in the span of 6 months in parallel with 2 other games from the studio.    As a Like A Dragon entry, it's well paced and punches way above its weight with a very cohesive narrative that still has its classic mood swing charms, yet it avoids the messy plot webs of the PS3 era games that might make it too nauseating for less committed fans. Kiryu's characterization is even stronger than it was in the previous games, but it still finds time to explore and discuss the formerly-titular organisations that this franchise is actually about.    As a standalone game, it is one of the shiny gems of 2023 with a characteristically strong desire to make an enjoyable product and tell a compelling story. The downside i can see in playing this game as a person unfamiliar with the series, however, is that structurally, Gaiden is heavily reliant on callbacks and references to at least 4 previous titles, from characters that are mentioned to events that are retold, which can leave a new player with gaps in the understanding of the overall story.    The $50 price tag, though, might just be a bit too steep for a game with about half the playtime of a mainline title, especially considering that most of the secondary content is reused from previous titles.    Overall, this is one of the best entries of the franchise, and its a fairly high bar.

_childDocuments_.review: When the Joryu man said "I am like a dragon and you are facing the man who erased his name!" before he proceeded to gaidEND everybody, I literally cried :(Like a Dragon Gaiden: The Man Who Erased His Name is a fantastic video game and a game that I believe went beyond my expectations.  I expected a short video game that wouldn't really have much in terms of stuff you can do outside the story. In other words, I expected Gaiden to be a short game to snack on as we anticipate Infinite Wealth's release. Even though I didn't have high expectations for Gaiden, I was still excited to play the game. Safe to say that my experience with the game has been very positive.Story is very short. In fact there are only 5 chapters which is less than half the number of chapters in a typical Yakuza game. Nonetheless, the story really hits well and had lots of interesting twists. I think it was great to see some additional context behind the events that unfolded in Yakuza: Like a Dragon. Nishitani III was a really good addition to the story and a character that I think is pretty cool.  Finally, it is very refreshing to see RGG use new and original characters to be protagonists. Joryu is pretty badass and resembles a lot like Kiryu. In fact, I think it was neat for Joryu to have the Yakuza combat style since it is a great tribute to Kiryu. Overall, even if the story is pretty short, it is well done and fun to experience.I've seen a lot of people have different opinions about the combat, but I think the combat is great. I think what makes this game's combat so great is how much they have improved the dragon engine combat since Yakuza 6. The combat in that game is alright but definitely a little janky. Judgement and Lost Judgement definitely helped to improve dragon engine combat and make Gaiden's combat more satisfying. In fact there are elements of Gaiden's combat that got inspiration from Judgement and Lost Judgement. Onto the actual combat style. The Yakuza combat style is definitely a step up from Yakuza 6 and Kiwami 2. The combo finishers are so satisfying when you land them, and it makes for a really satisfying combat style. Plus they added the funny yakuza kick into the game so it definitely gets a thumbs up from me. Agent style is also so much fun to use. The style definitely goes up there as one of my favorite styles to use, simple because of how much fun you can have with it. There are so many gadgets to use and it makes fighting enemies so much wackier. Gaiden has lots of side game content which is definitely something that is needed for a story that is so short. Sure, this game may not have as much side content as a typical Yakuza game but the side content is really fun. The Akame quests are pretty interesting and serve as a great distraction from the story. In fact, I was stuck on Chapter 2 for a few days because I was just doing the Akame quests to obtain new abilites. You got also your standard minigames like karaoke (which has Baka Mitai so it's already good), arcade, golf, MAHJONG, darts etc. Gaiden has these minigames plus other minigames with major updates to them like Pocket Circuit, the Hostess minigame and the Battle Coliseum. The return of Pocket Circuit is a great addition and nice to have again. It's really funny seeing Joryu get so upset at losing the race. Pocket Circuit is also pretty hard. It starts off simple but then  you get the really challenging races and the difficulty ramps up. It's definitely keeps the minigame interesting to play. The Hostess minigame has also seen big updates with the fact that the hostess is now real. Not much I can say about it but it is definitely the minigame of all time. The Battle Coliseum has recieved lots of updates and it has improved a lot. What I like about it is the fact that it is so chaotic. So much happens and it makes the fight so interesting. This is definitely what I wanted in a coliseum minigame for a long time. Plus, I got the legendary fighter pack which includes Majima, Saejima and Daigo. These three definitely make the coliseum minigame a lot more fun and the DLC gives you a way to finally play as Majima again. Safe to say that the minigames are very fun in Gaiden.In terms of other things I liked, the combat upgrade system is definitely a big step up from Kiwami 2 and Yakuza 6. I really disliked the EXP upgrade system in Kiwami 2 and 6, and I'm finally glad they decided to just use money to upgrade your combat styles and unlock new heat actions. Music is also very good. I know the Gaiden OST is on Spotify so I'm gonna listen to it more. I guess the only complaint I have is the price. $50 is a bit much for a game that can be completed in a short amount of time. It really boils down to how long you will play the game and if you will continue to play the game after finishing the story. For me, I will definitely keep playing this game, so I think I got my money's worth for this game. Like a Dragon Gaiden: The Man Who Erased His Name is a really good game and went beyond my expectations. Definitely get this game when it goes on sale in he future.

_childDocuments_.review: LaD: G is the 'Gap' episode between Like a Dragon 7 and Infinite Wealth and it fills in a lot of little plot holes regarding Kiryu's story as well as the people and families around himIt's a smaller story than the normal Yakuza game, but it's generally engaging, fun, and emotional. It's a really solid send-off for Kiryu in my opinion, and has some of the most bombastic character arcs and boss fights I've seen in the series. The fighting mechanics are mostly enjoyable however the general movement feels insanely sluggish in the beginning. Kiryu's dodge doesn't seem to cover any ground and he has next to no reach when attempting to hit anyone. It must be for balancing reasons but either way it takes a few hours for the combat to actually feel good.Overall despite the slightly low amount of content (for a yakuza game) I really enjoyed what was there. Everything was polished, there were a significant amount of new mechanics to toy with (Coliseum battles are a blast), and the story felt extremely meaningful. This might be my favorite Yakuza title behind 0. Well done RGG

_childDocuments_.review: The Man Who Erased His Name (will call this Joryu-game from now on) is a spin-off of Like a Dragon Gaiden that takes place in parallel to Yakuza: Like a Dragon or Yakuza 7. Joryu-game expects you to know the story from the main game, and will talk about secret reveals from Y7, and will show you quick flashbacks from Y7 to keep you up to date where the story is. So if you haven't played the Y7 you'll either be lost or spoiled. Joryu-games returns to being a brawler game, and follows the story of Joryu, which might be very similar to someone you know is really not Kiryu. He put on shades and different suit, so you will never recognise him. Like superman, alright? It's Joryu. Whole 2 different letters in the name, so you won't ever get it's the same person. And Kiryu is dead anyway.As far as Yakuza games are concerned this is a minigame. The story is pretty short, and even doing all substories and side activities will clock you at less than 40 hours. The game is being sold at a lower price than full entries, so that's fine. And it also has tons of Sega retro games included, so in theory you could spend hours upon hours just played the emulated games.Joryu gets two battle styles in this game. Brawler/Yakuza style that is similar to red styles from the older games. Hard hitting, counter attacks etc. There's also completely new Agent style, where Joryu uses Bond-esque gadgets as part of his arsenal. You start with spider-man-ish web slinger that allows you to disable opponents and throw them around, or steal their weapons. But as the game progresses you get 3 more gadgets. I found 3 of them to be very fun to use, but the cigarette bomb took too much time to explode, and as such was a pain to get working properly. This time the action takes place in Sotenbori, and while it reuses the old map you get it with ray traced shadows, and man, Sotenbori never looked so good. There's also completely new map that takes center stage in the game, and you get there pretty early on, but that's as far as I go.I didn't like what they did with substories. Usually they would jump on you naturally as you walk trough the streets. But in this game you have central hub where an informant will tell you about all the requests that people have. Then you go to the place and get trough typical substories. That makes them feel much less natural, and honestly a bit less fun. It doesn't help that there aren't really that many of them, and most of them are related to gathering party members for one of minigames.There are also exclamation points tossed all around the map with people wanting some small things from you. Usually short fetch quests. Things like "bring me tissues" were thrown into this category too. It's pretty similar in quality to the mobile app micro-quests from Y6, but a bit better and less repetitive.The story is, as always, a strong point. Not gonna lie, a grown man is gonna cry at the ending. That's what Yakuza does to you. You would think the story of spin-off would be weak, but I really liked it. Being short and moving at fast pace only made it better. It also made more sense for me how name-erasing thing works for Joryu. In Y6 it felt a bit far-fetched.Most of the side-content is tied to battle arena, where you have a lot of matches to go trough. As you go trough them you will also unlock some boss battles on the arena. This means that for most bosses you won't be able to use items in-battle. Though that is not a problem, as it's probably the easiest Yakuza game I've played. Even the final secret boss is mostly a pushover once you get their attack pattern... and you'll get it within the first battle and win this first battle most likely. It's easy in this game to get 2300 or so defence and be invincible, and your blows can one hit KO most of the enemies even with pretty mediocre attack scores. That said the arena battles are pretty fun, but I think the most advertised team battles are least fun out of the bunch. All in all very decent entry into the Yakuza series, and closes the story of Kir... Joryu much better than Yakuza 6 did. If you're enfranchised player you probably already bought and played it anyway, but if you're new to the series you should start with Y0, Y1 Kiwami or Y7. This is best played after Y6 and Y7. Still, recommended, just be sure to do your homework before playing.
