_childDocuments_.review: This is a deck builder game where your goal is to beat 8 levels (antes) of 3 rounds each, where the score requirement grows exponentially. You'll lose a lot, but you'll gradually unlock more "jokers" which alter the game's rules or provide multipliers and points under certain hand/deck conditions, where some unlocks have a strong advantage to beating the first 8 levels (and then progressing into the endless mode challenge). There are many game altering cards to explore, many types of challenges/bosses, deck types, etc. that can keep you entertained for quite a while. As you play, you are constantly weighing your choices to mitigate risk and alter probability to work in your favor, even when you manage to build a seemingly broken deck (which is often quickly destroyed in endless mode).Also always check the boss rule on the start of a new level so you can hopefully prepare and say "nah, I win" or "it's so over" with confidence, instead of being blindsided and definitely losing.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really fun when it's new and you're getting your feet wet, but the later difficulties almost instantly become nothing but an RNG fest. Oh, you didn't get a xMult Joker? New Game. You're supersuiting Diamonds and then the Ante 7 boss debuffs all Diamonds? New Game. You've got a perfect build but lose the Ante 8 Boss because 13 out of the 16 Aces in your deck SOMEHOW magically ended up all stacked in the bottom quarter of the deck and you can't dig any further? New Game. You're $1 short of buying Throwback right before the Ante 6 Boss? New Game. Got dealt a hand with three Pairs in it for the fifth time in a row, defying all odds and statistical probability? New Game. You literally just keep restarting the run until the game decides it's time to hand you the things that it needs to hand you in order to win the higher stakes. There's no engagement. There's no planning. There's no strategy. There's no forethought. Just click the cards and pray. And it's a real shame, because this game has such an amazing foundation and sound and art and concept that I would love to just put 5,000 hours into this thing, but I've Gold Stickered like five decks at this point and I literally feel my blood pressure start rising when I even think about sitting down to play.If you're curious and don't mind throwing the money away to play this game very casually here and there, you'll likely have a great time.But if you're like me and many other people that want to see every corner and collect every collectible from the roguelikes they play, avoid Balatro. You might as well just go to the casino and try to win some actual cash, because high stakes in Balatro is nothing better than a glorified roulette machine.

_childDocuments_.review: A roided-up, roguelike amalgamation of online Poker, Space Cadet Pinball, and Spider Solitaire. Balatro has the air of a generic preinstalled game on Windows XP but also has clear influence from the modern deckbuilder roguelike genre. Manipulating your 52-card deck to extreme lengths to get the most out of the various Joker cards is a lot of fun. Or vice versa, finding the right Joker that pops off with your deck gives Balatro a real explosive feeling. Things fall a little flat though because it all goes towards getting a high score and that's it. Yes, there are deck modifiers and difficulties and challenges and bosses which are just modifiers, but all the variation just obfuscates the initial path to getting a high score. It's a fun puzzle a lot of the time, but it also wears thin when played at length. All in all, Balatro is a unique, polished, roguelike deckbuilder with explosive potential.

_childDocuments_.review: A very solid rouge-lite. If you like deck builders then you will likely enjoy it. It does differ from other games of its kind in that there is generally more of a focus on adding external "powerups" (jokers, tarot cards, planets cards) rather than the actual playing cards, which I think helps it stand out. And since there are so many different tactics to try it takes quite a while before it really starts to feel repetitive. The stakes and challenge runs add levels of consideration and play around with the base premise of the game in a very fun way.I will note that despite being someone who is VERY into this exact kind of game, it did take me a bit of time to get used to the flow of it, and that made it initially very frustrating. I think that it's because there is some muscle memory that deck-building veterans need to put aside when playing Balatro (as an example off the top of my head, it can often actually be very useful to add a lot of cards to the deck, rather than thin it out like you would in other games). But once it hits, it H I T S. I love it, it's definitely a game I will continue to come back to again and again.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's not belabor the point. Balatro takes the gambling aspect of the roguelike formula and cranks it to the extreme. It's not just aesthetic. The shop is a gamble, the card effects are a gamble, the attached card game is a gamble every time you click discard.The genius is that Balatro then demands of you the exact opposite of wild variance - consistency! Hit this steadily increasing score target, or it's back to deck select with you and your sorry mug. Each run is an exercise in pulling order out of chaos, and putting together a combination of cards, jokers, and planets that will get you the score you need every single time. If rigging the odds and flattening out variance in your favor gives you dopamine, you'll enjoy playing this game. But, be advised, this is a numbers game - if you refuse to engage with the mathematics behind your actions, expect your skill to hit a natural ceiling.10/10.

_childDocuments_.review: After sinking some time in this game, I can say without a doubt that this isn't a very good game. The amount of things out of a player's control is to be expected in a game about poker, but it isn't at a level where a player's skill or knowledge can really help runs. It's all luck, which isn't a very fun mechanic. A lot of other roguelikes/roguelites I play use player skill/strategy/knowledge in combination WITH luck to make a game fun. Good runs in Balatro feel pretty good. Not *too* great because the post-win rounds scale WAY too much. The bad runs feel like -- and ARE -- massive wastes of time. Hours and hours spent on runs that were going okay until the game **purposefully** creates a perfect adversary for. It happens so often that it simply can't be bad luck. The game makes itself worse artificially if you're doing well, which sucks for the player. Playing different decks (characters, in a way) doesn't feel different enough. Eventually, they all tumble into the same formula for a win. Focus on one hand and have the mult and mult mults for it. It gets boring incredibly fast -- making it feel like even MORE of a waste of time.I was on the fence about getting this game initially and it was basically for these reasons. Safe to say that I had a little fun, but I probably would have had more fun playing anything else. It's really just a way for me to procrastinate at this point.

_childDocuments_.review: I’m no poker aficionado. My knowledge of the game is mostly gleaned from casual observations and snippets from TV shows. I couldn't identify a Royal Flush if my life depended on it (I've got the achievement for discarding/ruining a royal flush in-hand...), but I know it's something you want. Balatro, despite its poker facade, isn't really poker. It's the first game that’s made me understand and love the core mechanics of poker, and it's easily one of the most engrossing titles of the year.Calling Balatro a poker game is simply inaccurate. There are no opponents to play against. Instead, it's a poker-inspired roguelike deckbuilder. The real poker aspect lies in learning to assemble hands like a Flush, Straight, or Full House. A handy glossary illustrates these hands and their scores, which helped me, a poker novice, finally memorize and enjoy the game.Balatro’s design makes it incredibly addictive. The fast-paced, snappy gameplay allows for quick sessions, yet it’s deep enough to occupy entire afternoons. Even when the game doesn’t go your way, you’re compelled to try again. The music, though limited to a single track, is highly engaging and adds to the game’s hypnotic appeal.Balatro is a must-play. Dive in and experience it for yourself. I could easily write another thousand words or more, but I think you should enjoy discovering it on your own. Explore the 150 unique jokers and the myriad of other cards that make this game a true gem. Priced at $15, Balatro offers immense value. Get it, get it, get it.Oh also - I could listen to the main audio track for hours and hours. It's delightful.10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Pure distillation of why rogue-likes can be addictive. The aim is to modify the rules, the deck and the hands themselves to try and break the game and get BIG NUMBERS. Big numbers good. This is not a poker game, it is a single player rouge-like where you play poker hands to hit a target score per round. You have a number of hands and discards allowed per round in order to try and hit that score. At the end of each round you can buy packs and modifiers to juice the rules and the deck. You try and get as far as possible, trying to hit bigger and bigger numbers, and to try and beat 'boss' rounds that hit you with a debuff. You have various decks you can play with, each of which modify the rules or deck in different ways (+1 play/-1 discard, +1 discard/-1 play, only hearts and spades, etc.). Incredibly simple, incredibly malleable, runs take about 45 mins. Pure crack, perfect on steam deck.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel obligated to provide a dissenting opinion to the unanimous praise this game gets. There's fun to be had in the early stages of the game, and in the silly and wacky automated builds that make big numbers, undeniably. When things are working out, Balatro provides a fun sandbox. The problem is when things aren't working out, which is the statistical majority of the time if you're playing it seriously. Beyond a basic level, there's very little skill expression in this game, leaving you victim to the whims of the random number generator to lose constantly and unavoidably. The game is addicting and provides a compelling player fantasy in its early stages, and this is a problem because it makes the mindless slog that is the later difficulties actively frustrating, but hard to walk away from. If you're a rational individual who can play till satisfied and put it down when it stops being fun, then it should be a pleasant and rewarding experience. Otherwise, be warned.

_childDocuments_.review: It's Balatro.In all seriousness, it's an amazing game and a supreme example of how great aesthetic and game feel can carry a simple premise all the way until the end. But, that's the entire point of the game, whether you like it or not. It's brutally unfair and extremely rewarding. Getting a high score has never felt so good. The soundtrack is mesmerizing. There's a reason this game has become such a viral hit, and when you look at the negative reviews here on Steam, you'll see that most of them still have dozens of hours logged despite leaving a negative review. Balatro is one of the few "Must have" titles on Steam, and at this price, who can complain?

_childDocuments_.review: This isn't my typical type of review, but I have to tell someone about Balatro. So imagine taking a game of poker and blending some roguelike elements, add deck building mechanics then sprinkling a synergy system that rewards you for thinking outside the box AND now imagine that game only costing $15? Well, that's Balatro in simplest terms, See guys, I like a game of chance, I love to gamble & this fills my body with endorphins without having to go into crippling debt! you start the game off being essentially berated by a Joker card, and it quickly shows you HOW to play Balatro which is at it's core Poker but with the aforementioned elements.You start by choosing a deck, in the beginning only a few available but as you play you'll unlock up to 15 different decks all with v. Points scored will be dependent on the level of your hand, for example if you play this hand Aces will equal 11 each and 4s will be 4. So that score of 30 will be added to the blue margin and then multiplied by 2 (if you dont have any jokers active). It's possible to level hands up using Planetary cards which is how this flush is level 2 and you'll see the transformation to level 3. I'll show you as I play this flush how it all adds up for you- and baam that's pretty much how you win a blind. You beat each "blind" or level by playing Poker each "ante" is 3 levels- small blind, big blind & boss blind- each with varying scores you must beat with the added difficulty of the boss blind having an adverse effect such as diamonds not counting towards your score, only being able to play a certain hand like two pairs or flushes, having no discards etc etc, surpassing the Blind score will have you win a certain amount of money AND if you beat it in fewer turns the "hands" you didn't use will add up at the end of each round (usually $1/per hand) then you're taken to a shop where you can buy Joker cards, there are 150 of em with varying effects, Vouchers that can add for example an extra Hand or Discard or make the rerolls cost less, planetary cards that can level up a certain hand, tarot & spectral cards that can add bonuses to your playing cards & booster packs where you can ADD playing cards plus any of the aforementioned cards like jokers, tarot, spectral & planetary.the objective is to beat 8 antes each ante with a set of 3 blinds, but it is MUCH easier said than done. ive had some of the most ridiculous combos like look at this synergy right here, my Business Card Joker has a 50% chance of scoring me $2 when I play a face card + it's a Polychrome so it'll tally at the end of the hand a 1.5 multiplier, my space trousers adds 2x to every Two Pair i play (which includes full houses) my Scary Face joker is a boost for face cards that adds 30 chips  aka the blue score to the left of the screen that then gets multiplied at the end by the red margin my Rocket joker adds 50 chips PLUS after every blind, I get $3, but are you ready for the KICKER guys? You know how I said that the Business Card, and the Scary Face adds only to FACE cards? Well Pareidolia Joker MAKES ALL my cards "face" cards. Playing this straight you'll see all the added bonuses I get. 10k in one hand. But because I   of the SHOP if I wanted with all the money I keep receiving. and it gets me thinking for sure I'm winning this game. NOPE. Prepare to lose A LOT. After 8 hours I thought, I may not win one of these then it all clicked and I cheesed it HARD I mean HARD. And I scrounged up a win... in normal difficulty with a basic deck... I realized this game was meant to be beaten over & over, it has me convinced that if you're thinking of buying this game- you need to be a masochist because PAIN YOU WILL FEEL and I want to both hug & kick the dev only known to me as Local Thunk- because I KNOW he has got to be a sadist, getting off on our pain.... but in conclusion, if you're thinking about getting this game. BUY IT NOW! If you haven't heard of this game because gaming is having a hell of a year, check it out. It's so simple to pick up and just play for a few mins or sink a couple hours into it. Oh and if you have a SteamDeck? This is where Balatro shines, playing it on the go on my lunchbreak or in bed? *chefs kiss*

_childDocuments_.review: Balatro is a deckbuilder game where you play poker hands to reach the highest possible scores, while only being allowed to play a few hands and redraw cards a few times. The game allows you to buy all kinds of passive and active upgrades to cards, and you need to keep up with the rising stakes of the rounds. I can really recommend the game for anyone who likes deckbuilder game in general, it's easy to learn, there is a ton of variation, every run feels totally fresh, your strategies will be compeletely different from run to run, and you will end up with a few really fun and totally overpowered combos. It's really not as luck-based as you would expect a poker game to be and the artstyle, music and level of polish make Balatro a really well-rounded experience!My only criticism of the game is, that I think it's possible to have runs that just aren't all that fun because the items you get just dont work together at all, and sometimes you can't just really "go with" the setup you've been offered and it makes you be "underleveled" for the current run really quickly. But that aside, there is really only positive stuff to say about the game! Really, if you need a casual game to spend a bit of time with, I can totally recommend playing Balatro!

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this on a whim because a reviewer compared it to Slay The Spire.  It's good, but it's not as good as Slay The Spire in my opinion.  It is a fun deck building game with a short learning curve.  Like Slay the Spire, It has all the bells and whistles of the genre, and I recommend it, but with a few caveats:- The pixel font is annoying and only serves to make it harder to read.  It can't be turned off.- I'm not sure how much development is going into mainting the title. I had accidentally exited out of the tutorial, which took a considerable effort to remove my saved games so I could re-enable it.  When I searched for an answer to this problem, I saw people were requesting a UI fix for this half a year ago.  It may not a priority for the developer, but being able to return the game to predefined state seems like expected behaviour.Ideally this would be a great mobile game (and it appears it isn't--I checked).  I could really see myself playing this I have 15 minutes to kill.  However, if I have to sit in front of my PC, I would prefer more in depth games to make it worth my while.That said, its an interesting concept and its a fun casual game.  For those reasons I don't regret buying it and would recommend to others.  I would however wait for it to go on sale--Its pricing is a bit steep for what it is, IMO.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely devious, basically takes the fun parts of poker and strips out the boring nonsense like waiting for other people to play or losing all your (real) money and lets you focus solely on weighting the deck and strategizing your setup. The sheer number of interesting powerup combos you can string together really gets you thinking about strategy and how to optimize your run which gives it that great "one more turn" feel. The fact that it's based on pretty well known card mechanics means it's really easy to pick up too, and the game gently reveals its various modifiers at a pace that never feels too slow, but also lets you realize their implications at an approachable speed. Kind of surprised it's taken this long to do a deckbuilder based on traditional card-decks but the mashup is perfect.

_childDocuments_.review: A good roguelike is like good coffee. It should be bold, unique, and satisfying. Both are best enjoyed in copious sips, and if you have enough of either, you’ll want more.It’s not an exaggeration to say that Balatro is the best deckbuilding roguelike since Slay the Spire, which is the most vaunted example of the genre. Balatro’s gameplay loop is compellingly simple: make poker hands from a standard deck of playing cards worth an increasing number of chips. Sounds simple, right? Except you can add or delete cards from your deck, collect Jokers that have multiplying and stacking effects, upgrade specific poker hands using Planet cards, and more. Stack the deck with Hearts to increase your chances of a sweet Flush, or fill your deck with Jacks in combination with a joker that rewards you for playing face cards. Do both. And a dozen other things, and then try something different. There’s no end to the combinations you can conjure to keep adding to those all-important red and blue numbers that calculate your chip total, and if you’re like me, you’ll just keep coming back. The game’s subtle soundscape and psychedelic visuals are icing on the cake. That Balatro is able to take something as simple as a deck of playing cards and turn it into a game with such scope, appeal, and replayability would be an accomplishment in itself. But there’s also what Balatro *could have been*. It could have been a ruthlessly addictive, pay-to-advance nightmare mobile game, and it would have been savagely good in that role. In other words, with playing cards as the star attraction, it *could have been* what it appears to be from afar (and apparently to the South Korean government): gambling. That the developer decided to make it a single price roguelike for PC shows either an inherent integrity or a missed opportunity for profit that makes me as grateful as I am impressed.Balatro is about as close to a perfect game as they get in these tortured days of late capitalism.

_childDocuments_.review: This is something I need to get off my chest, because I've never managed to play a game for several hours before without enjoying even a second of it.Steam asks whether I recommend this game to other people and I'm thinking I have to write this from the perspective of whether I recommend it to people who are like me; Balatro clearly strikes a chord with most players that it doesn't with me and I'm not sure what it is, but it might a certain thrill of gambling, which I personally don't experience.I've only played four runs total which could mean I'm missing the bigger picture, but based on what I've seen myself and what I've seen and read from others I am pretty sure there is no point for me to continue playing.To sum up the issue, I believe the RNG forces the user to play to a very boring and same-y strategy every run if they want to win. The store page advertises endless possibilities and that it'll put you in a hypnotic state, but the game's mechanics are such that if you just go with the flow, pick synergetic jokers and build your deck accordingly, then you're gambling away your victory. This is because there's so-called "boss blinds" of which I seem to have encountered various new ones every run I've played so there could be tons I haven't seen yet, and it seems there is always one that completely nullifies your current setup, ending the run. For example there are jokers that enable their multipliers when you keep playing the same poker hand a second time in the round which is great in most cases, except then the game shows you the middle finger and gives you a boss that says you can't play the same hand twice, meaning the joker or several jokers don't work, meaning the run is most likely dead. Or, if you've been struggling to receive synergetic jokers from the shop at all due to rerolls eating up all your money, you could still win with multipliers and other upgrades on cards, except with that you're truly in gambling territory where if you don't draw the right cards at the right time you just lose. There's also a ton of boss blinds that disable cards anyway, it's just too risky a strategy. One run I had a joker that gave me multipliers per card of a certain suit each run, so I had a flush synergy going, and then I got a boss that just so happened to disable that exact suit the joker expected. Or let's say you played to your economy so you could buy good jokers for the late game, then you might get a boss that reduces your money to zero or even to the negatives.Due to this, I haven't felt like I lost because I didn't strategize properly, I lost because I got unlucky. And likewise, winning would feel empty because I know no matter what synergy I piece together, I just got lucky that a boss didn't kill that exact synergy. One might think the solution to this would be to NOT rely on a single way to get multipliers, but that's not exactly possible due to bosses that quadruple the minimum chips you need to reach. Splitting jokers between different synergies does not seem consistently possible while also making it past the high chip demands. You could also when you see a boss that kills your synergy sell off your jokers and try to get different ones, if you get incredibly lucky to get a good set of jokers in two shops max. Or you get so lucky you get a reroll boss blind skip and the new one doesn't also screw you over. It just always seems to come down to luck.After reading through and watching several strategy guides it seems the only true consistent way to win is to first play to economy and slowly start acquiring jokers that synergize with each other so that low cards, even a single high card is enough to consistently get a ton of points. Tarot cards, planet cards and such are virtually never worth spending money on. That seems really boring. But if I play the interesting way with different ways to rack up chips then it's a gamble on whether I get just the right bosses to screw me, or whether I waste all money on rerolling for jokers that aren't straight up garbage, because a ton of them seem completely useless for mid and late games. Building a deck that already has 52 cards and hope to have the right ones drawn most of the time is far too risky without also being super lucky with jokers to better control what cards you get on hand and have in your deck. Is it even a deck building game at that point when actually building decks is just a gamble on whether it'll work out or not?______Aside from the gameplay, there's some issues the game could fix to make the experience better. First of all, the tutorial sucks and doesn't tell you anything. You need to have a basic understanding of poker, and assume that you are meant to play actual poker with yourself, because the tutorial absolutely does not even inform you that different hands have different chip and multiplier bonuses.Second, a majority of my frustration early on came from the fact that the game doesn't aptly convey information to the player. For the first two runs, I didn't know you could rearrange cards to change the order of multiplication and addition. I didn't know the Discard counter would only go down by only one point per up to five cards each instead of one point for every single discarded card. On the first run I had two Tarot cards permanently stuck in my inventory because I couldn't figure out how to use them; the use button was greyed out and I genuinely assumed I had a debuff. I wasn't told I had to select applicable cards first and then go back to my inventory to use, which seems counter-intuitive, but could at least have been explained at all. I ignored a lot of cards and jokers because I couldn't contextualize what the descriptions meant – e.g. "what is a Trigger? What is a Full Deck?" When a card tells me "adds the number of times poker hand has been played this round to mult", I absolutely have no clue what to do with that information as a new player: I don't know what "poker hand" is (I don't play Poker and English isn't my native language) and even when I found out what that term meant via the wiki, I thought I just had to play any poker hand at all and that would add to the card's own counter. Instead, what it means is it keeps track of individual, different types of poker hands and how many times those have been played, and when you play a specific poker hand it checks how often you've played it this run and adds that count to the multiplier. So card descriptions are often very vague or too jargon-heavy. I also ran into a boss that would not "allow" me to play less than five cards, but then it did allow me. I assumed it was a bug but then it discarded those cards instead and removed one hand from my counter. That's not what people think "allow" means, this description borders on being intentionally mean-spirited.The UI could be a bit more user-friendly as well. I accidentally sold a joker because I put down my Steam Deck against a wall and it hit the left shoulder button. That's a pretty stupid button for a selling action, but there should also really be a confirm button for this case. Also, I appreciate a lot of the accessibility features, like you can check what cards are left in your deck so you don't have to have spreadsheets open for card counting or have the memory of an elephant. But for whatever reason there's no option to pre-calculate a possible score, which may be because some effects are random and so there's no elegant way to show this. But it still means that sometimes, early on or during an awful boss I have to whip out a calculator to see if I can make it or not.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the essential video game. It's a roguelite deck-builder based around standard playing cards and poker hands. _childDocuments_.review: This is a great game. A very interesting twist on Poker, with a deck-building and rogue-like (repeatable) aspect to it. Each game consists of 24 rounds. Those 24 rounds are broken into 8 sets or levels of 3. You start with a standard 52 card poker deck. You get 4 hands per round to draw 8 cards and use 5 of those 8 to make the best poker hand to beat the set score limit. You also get a few chances to discard up to 5 and redraw. Two Pair is worth 92.8% more than One Pair is. Three of a Kind is worth 58.3% more than Two Pair is. A straight is worth 40.3% more than Three of a Kind is. A full house is worth 25.0% more than a straight is and so on. Playing a bunk hand (just high card) is practically useless. One Pair is worth 300% more than just a high card hand. And the cards played matter too. King, Queen, and Jack are all equal (Aces are worth 10% more than face cards), but One Pair of KQJ is worth 50% more than One Pair of 5s is. And One Pair KQJ is worth 114% more than One Pair of 2s is. To start round one you have to get at least three hands with Two Pair, fairly easy to do at least 81% of the time. After each round you can buy either upgrades that increase your hand value based on certain conditions (or sometimes just all the time) or additional cards to add to your deck of 52, or effect cards that can change cards in your 52 card deck to either be worth more, be different cards, or be altogether destroyed. By round 3 you have to score 100% more than you did in round 1. By round 6 you have to score 33% more than you did in round 3. By round 9 you have to score 400% more than you did in round 6. By round 12 you have to score 150% more than you did in round 9. By round 15 you have to score 120% more than you did in round 12. And the difficulty stays like that all the way to round 24. I have only beaten round 24, heck I’ve only even ever made it to round 22, once, one single time. It is challenging, but it is definitely very fun. If you enjoy poker and aren’t afraid of a deck-builder, you should definitely try it out!

_childDocuments_.review: So when i first approached this game, I was like WTF. To be fair for a new player it is hard!!! I recommend watching some of the 10000 you tube videos if you are struggling as that is what I did.BUT, once you understand the flow and mechanics, there is a lot to love about this game. How is it that a game from a solo dev crosses 1M users in such a short time - like a month i think...It proves that if the game play is great, the pixel graphics and repetitive music, few will complain. To be fair, if you want a casual clicker poker game , this is NOT FOR YOU. If you are an RPG gamer like me that loves the whole min/max cycle, then this will be your favorite game after a few tries.I cannot fathom a solo dev having such a solid game with no crashes, with such a huge variation  in cards types and their effects. It boggles my mind.  I play AAA titles made by 100 people and they have way more bugs!!!AND!!!!!! Now there is MODS!!! The dev left the game open for the modding community, and that will likely get the next 1 M players... It is amazing how many devs of single player games oppose mods. Shameful!If you have any interest in poker OR deck builders give it a shot. _childDocuments_.review: Balatro is a great little rogue-like poker-like game that is surprisingly addictive. I did not expect to like this game as much as I do, and can't wait to see what the devs do with it next. If you like simple and snappy gameplay, are looking for something new to pick up for your steamdeck, or wish poker was more interesting thanks to magical jokers, then this is the game for you. The only thing I wish it had was a stronger sense of permanent progression. Outside of gathering a stronger sense of understanding and overall strategy, your fiftieth run feels pretty similar to your first run. The different decks can offer some interesting twists, but I'm still missing the sense of gradual progression and accumulation of abilities that are present in my favorite rogue-likes. Even with that, I still highly recommend picking this up.
_childDocuments_.name: Balatro

_childDocuments_.review: Cleverly designed and dangerously addictive mashup of the roguelike and autochess formulas with a memorable presentation/soundtrack (even if it is only like one song on loop). Perfect casual game with lots to do/unlock--absolutely worth the asking price.Having already beaten most of the higher difficulties and gotten completion marks on most of the decks (analogous to characters/classes in a roguelike), I can tell you that this game does suffer from some balancing and difficulty issues. Runs will often be crushed in the first couple stages if you don't get the right RNG, especially brutal on higher difficulties. A relatively small class of top-tier jokers (passive items) utterly dominate the tier list and you'll likely find yourself using many of the same ones in repeat wins, as the far larger library of more situational jokers often prove straight-up unusable by comparison unless you get a very particular set of synergies. It's closer to Slay the Spire than something like TBoI in this way, as the lack of skill-based mechanical gameplay underpinning the build system can make it feel a bit one-note and helpless on many runs.With all that said, there is plenty of fun and variety to be had here--it's a fantastic product well worth playing made particularly impressive as it has all been put together by an inspired solo dev whom I fully expect to support the game going forward with balancing updates and more content.

_childDocuments_.review: Here's a bit of a hint.For joker bonuses, a pair counts as any hand that contains a pair, like two pair, full house, and three of a kind on up to five of a kind. Likewise for any joker that buffs a three of a kind hand will count for any of the previous hands aside from pairs, and so on. Planet cards are exempt from this, as they only buff the individual hand type, which can make a massive difference when even a pair of cards can be stronger than a full house.Work around your strengths, and don't fear losing, sometimes just getting something you haven't acquired before may help for future unlocks.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is excellent. Despite having a very simple game and progression structure, it is extremely easy to dump multiple hours in one session on this game. It is sad for me to say that I have dumped 25 hours in this game in the past week or so, it's that addicting—except it's not, it's dedication. Overall, the premise is simple, you are playing poker hands to gain chips and beat the required chip counts of each bind. Better hands give better chips in addition to a higher multiplier (mult). But then the twists come in.In addition, there's even more content. You have multiple decks that give you different advantages in-game such as an addition hand or discard, or additional money, or have you start out with particular vouchers. Once you beat the game, it's not over. There's numerous more stakes that only make the game more difficult and more addicting. There's a common theme with this game, it's addicting, and it's deep for the price the devs are asking. 25 hours in so far, and while I've collected most of the cards, I have barely gone through the challenges, all the decks, and all the stakes. While at times, your RNG might be frustrating—especially at the beginning with little content unlocked, there's plenty of times where I can just sit down and enjoy playing poker, or have your monkey brain lit up with dopamine as you hit 100,000 or 1,000,000 chips in one hit.Aside from gameplay, the older-style pixel graphics look great. It's simple and give the game a unique flavor. I also haven't experienced any bugs—the game runs great both on my PC and my Mac (so I can gamble instead of focusing on my bachelors). The only issue I have is the fact there is only one soundtrack, but it isn't enough for me to really gripe—I can turn on Spotify and listen to my music.Overall, for the price of $14.99, buy this game. It already is overwhelmingly positive! This is my first time playing a rogue-like deckbuilder, and I am not disappointed. I had a friend who at first thought this game was going to be boring after a couple minutes, and is now DEDICATED, not addicted to playing. If you are one who wants to gamble without the crippling debt or busted kneecaps from loan sharks, this is a great alternative. Overall 9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I've certainly had fun with Balatro. It's a cool idea, and exploring the huge range of jokers and crazy combos is interesting and exciting for a while. I'd say this is enough that I feel like I got my money's worth, hence the thumbs up. However, there is one major issue holding Balatro back. It doesn't have the staying power I hope for from a good roguelike deckbuilder because the balance on higher difficulties is way out of tune.At the highest stakes, I feel pretty confident that most runs simply aren't winnable. The scaling penalties (especially the -1 hand size from gold stake) nerf your ability to play straight poker quite hard and the chips you need ramp up fast, so you need to find a strong joker early or your run won't make is past the first few antes. You only have a few chances to look in the shop (and need to get money first anyway), and many of Balatro's jokers are situational or long term plays that do little to solve your immediate problems. So most runs consist of grinding out the first few hands (or lucking into good skip bonuses), reaching the shop, finding nothing that can help you in the short term, and either restarting or quickly finding your run is dead on arrival.When you do get a strong enough start to get out of the early game things are a lot more interesting. However, you still typically need to find powerful jokers that enable multiplicative scaling (and enough utility to consistently play the necessary hands) to actually win your run. Again, sometimes you find what you need, sometimes you don't. The RNG isn't quite as bad here since you get more chances to shop at least, but there are still runs where it feels like you never had a real shot because Balatro never gave you access to tools strong enough to overcome the endgame. Conversely, sometimes you luck into a run where you start steamrolling early and never stop. Winning is more fun than losing certainly, but these runs feel more like good luck than strong play.The dev has a balance update planned that should substantially change how the game plays at higher stakes, so maybe this will address some of these issues. I hope it does and that I can spend more of my time with Balatro engaging with the interesting and fun part of the game and less at the mercy of RNG.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing video games for almost 25 years now. Every once in a while, you get a game that reminds you that you are human. And humans are ostensibly, at the end of the day, animals. And like all animals, we humans have primal urges in order to satiate the basic needs to maintain our survival.Through these carnal needs comes vices. Sometimes we revert the growth and development from our hippocampus in order to quench the primordial thirst within us. We do things not because we are proud, but because we exist. And through those things, we become alive.Balatro is a rogue-like, deck-builder that uses the casino card game of five-card draw poker as a basis to it's gameplay core. Because it uses a standard, well-known game to build off of, the barrier for entry is low, but the skill ceiling is high. Even for a smooth-brained marsupial like myself, the dumb country bumpkin in me knows how to play poker.But Balatro isn't just about poker. It's about the numbers.  Watching the numbers, the multipliers, the stackers, the juicers, the hot digits. As you learn to make friends with the jokers, the planets, and the arcanas, they help you on the path to watching the numbers go up. You build joker decks inside your decks, increase your main deck, and then you watch the numbers go up.The minutes turn into hours working on your antes. You don't skip the antes because you need the interest to buy your planet cards to get the hot stacks. Or to make friends new joker buddies who want to make your life even more miserable.I wake up, I think of Balatro. I commute into the city, and my brain craves a fresh ante like a college student needing a Zyns. I'm at work, I think of juicy plays to get the numbers higher. I go home, and my Steam Deck starts crying because it knows it's time for numbers. There will be no rest until the mults are high, as will I.Overall, Balatro is very good and I recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Is the game fun? Yes.Is the game addicting? Yes.Is it worth $20? Absolutely not.The premise of a poker roguelite is definitely an interesting one, until you remember that "oh yeah, the entire point of poker is that it's luck based." And even though you know that going in, the fact of the matter is that once you start getting into the higher antes, whether or not you lose in the second round or beat the final boss by 500k points comes completely down to luck, regardless of how well you can mitigate it. You are most of the time forced to one trick pony to have the raw numbers needed to complete the higher levels, and oftentimes your score is more determined by random secondary effects applied to your jokers rather than the jokers themselves. Some jokers are also just disgustingly overpowered and singlehandedly carry runs or so underpowered that they might as well not even exist.Don't get a good joker by the 2nd ante? You lose.Don't have most of your jokers as polychromes, foils and holographics? You lose.Don't get a focused build because the shop keeps feeding you trash? You lose.Get 4 bad hands in a row that your one trick pony build wasn't equipped for? You lose.The long play time comes from bashing yourself against the wall over and over again until the game finally feeds you all of the overpowered stuff at once to the point where you then effortlessly trounce the run. There isn't really even an actual progression system like other roguelites, as adding jokers and vouchers to the pool still requires them to randomly appear and for you to be able to afford them when they do appear.Every single one of your many many failed runs are also basically indistinguishable from the last. The game has one (I repeat: one) singular song that plays throughout, the visuals are just a wavy synth clown vomit that sometimes changes color and nothing else, and there is no story, no rhyme and no reason to the game in any capacity. You play poker to win and then you start over or you lose and a sentient playing card insults you. That's it.So to summarize: is the game as fun and addicting as everyone says? Yes. Is it worth $20 to sit and wait for the game to finally allow you to win for 50+ hours? No.

_childDocuments_.review: Truly, truly excellent. There's not much I can say that hasn't already been said by other reviews. It's a poker-based roguelike. Even if you don't know anything about poker (which I don't, by the way), the game has all the information you need to figure things out.It's way too fun to see what kind of nonsense builds you can create. On one run you might end up with a really powerful straight hand that also gets buffed by how many diamonds you play, on another you might focus on two pairs with a multiplier that gets more and more insane the more consumables you sell. The Jokers you unlock can do all sorts of crazy things, and just seeing all the new discoveries is fun on its own, but before long you'll start seeing the Matrix or something, thinking "okay, if I move this King to the right of my hand, it'll apply a x2 multiplier on top of the bonus multiplier that I get from playing these other even-numbered cards, which also get retriggered by this one particular Joker that I have..." you get the idea. There's so much potential.Balatro is very easy to pick up, and equally easy to get absolutely engrossed in. Highly recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: When I first saw this game getting popular, I glanced at it and my eyes glazed over thanks to the poker aesthetic.This was a mistake on my part - this is a fantastic deck-builder with a surprising amount of strategic depth and play variation.The poker base mechanic I'd brushed off as a chintzy-looking gimmick proves an effective on-boarding tool - even the most casual card-slinger likely has a decent understanding of traditional 52-card probabilities, which makes for quick adoption of familiar early strategies leading to deeper exploration of the game's more unique mechanics.  Highly recommended whether you're a casual card player looking to explore an accessible entry point to a new genre or a hardcore fan of deckbuilders.
_childDocuments_.name: Balatro

_childDocuments_.review: I guess I can recommend this game, but don't expect it to be some great achievement in the modern roguelike. Sure, its got some cool features, and there's alot you can get out of playing it, but if you want to play a game that operates on RNG for pretty much 90% of all wins, that's all you dog.It wouldn't be so bad in that regard, if the house wasn't so stacked against you. You get piss-poor points by doing anything that isn't a flush or straight variant (aside from a couple good Two-Pair runs you can get going, if you invest the early game into doing so). Three and Fours of a kind upgrades are thrown at you alot, regardless of the fact that getting those off are EXTREMELY rare conditions (shoutout Straight Flush for being pretty much as useless as upgrading High Card). Most of the jokers are kinda run-specific, and the game doesn't do a great job of rewarding you for trying to narrow your deck towards a certain goal, whether that be a particular suit you want to focus for flushes, or if you wanted to do the opposite and focus on getting rid of everything except the top 10-->Ace cards, it doesn't matter. The game will give you completely random ♥♥♥♥, so you can't commit to a single thing until about halfway through your run (and even then, it likes to fill your options with stuff that just flat out is not compatible to what you're going for).Which again, would be fine, if there were more optimal options instead of the same 3-5 hand types/builds that actually get you to a dub. This game rewards you for going with the flow of each run, never really thinking about the past other than what cards to ABSOLUTELY avoid across ALL builds (yes they exist for some reason lmao). This "flow-focus" has it's own vibe to it, and that's not going to be for everyone, but in my case, I keep teetering between "nothing matters, so just play whatever you can, whenever you can" and "man I REALLY want to get the face-card build going this time since I've never done that before" only to get to the higher rounds, have a boss blind that completely counters what I've been building towards, and just throwing my hands up like "oh okay! That's how it ends, gotcha!"These frustrations are only further expounded upon with the higher chip levels you unlock from winning on a particular deck. The higher the chip level, the less time you have to build anything that can adapt to whatever is in front of you. Having a better multiplier scale for lower hand types would make the game much more enjoyable, without completely abandoning the "randomness" that comes with playing games like these, in my humble opinion.Sidenote, I also wish there was more to unlock as a whole. Once you get most of the jokers in the game (which isn't hard to do, its just about the amount of runs you do), there isn't much to go for afterwards, kind of makes the "gambling addiction" meme of this game feel a little more real and less of a joke.Also good luck voicing any complaints or comments that are negative towards a game like this, your friends will already have the "Get Good" responses ready to go. And they'll have a point, I was pretty much done with this at around 30 hours, but persevered for another 20 because I didn't want to believe the game was poorly designed, I wanted to get better! Turns out, its a video game, and if its not fun, why the hell are you playing it?---- 50 hours later ---Ah Balatro, you old so and so! I could never stay mad at you :)

_childDocuments_.review: Developed by LocalThunk and released in 2024, Balatro is a rogue like deck builder with a Poker theme. Using the card combinations from Poker, customize your deck to better suit your playstyle and bend rules to achieve great scores. The basic mechanic of the game is simple, play poker games until you win. Games are presented in “antes”, groups of 3 poker rounds where the third round has special conditions and modifiers. The modifiers present part of what makes this game unique. Between each round, the player has access to a store, where a number of cards can be bought, which can also be altered. Cards can be bought as booster packs as well as Tarot cards, Planet cards, and Jokers. Each of these booster packs allow the player to select different cards for their decks and customize not only the score of specific card combinations, but also card modifiers, score multipliers among other things. The amount of customization possible in this game really transforms what could be an addicting, yet simple, deck builder into a complex rogue like, where rules are bent and almost all can be modified.  Another notable feature this game brings is the little details. From the effects in the cards, to the small screen shake when points are added, all details that are so well made and implemented an already impressive art style and game. If deck builders are something you already enjoy, I highly recommend Balatro, even if you never played Poker before, it is truly a fun addicting game. If you enjoyed this review, I would like to invite you to visit  my curator page for more recommendations and reviews.

Play your hands to unlock Joker cards with various powers to push farther and farther into the tourney.  Collect Tarot cards, upgrade your decks and smash through boss fights (yes, in a poker game) to unlock cards and achievos on your profile. _childDocuments_.review: It's got a curve, especially if your unfamiliar with poker hands in general - I know I was - but god it's addicting. Runs that "win" are short, but you can take any deck you win with and continue on into an endless mode, while not forfeiting the win unlike other roguelikes.The premise is simple - form poker hands to score points. But you have other things that can affect the score - Jokers that multiply the score if its certain suits, Tarot cards that modify cards to be Glass, Planet cards to buff the base level and base score of your hands - that you can really build any way. Decks themselves are different - some remove all the face cards ( Q/K/J ), some completely randomise the contents of the deck, and others just give you one extra discard.When you get past the initial curve, it's fun. It's very fun, and if you ever get stuck on remembering what Hands do what, or their scoring -- there is a button that shows you the hands, their base scores, how many times you played it (which does matter for some cards!) and other important stuff in the run.Big recommend :>

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an exercise in frustration. You need a very precise set of types of jokers and if you don't get all the pieces (+Chip, +Mult, xMult) in sufficient quantity by the sixth ante or so, you are doomed. The nature of poker means you are at the mercy of the cards sometimes, and the hands themselves don't really scale very well past about the third ante so even if you farm planets of the appropriate type with Telescope that strategy doesn't work. The game feels very unbalanced with exactly two viable strategies (the joker combo i outlined earlier is one, score triggers is the other) and if you aren't on either strategy you will not have much if any success. I commend the developer for the attempt at making a deckbuilder out of poker, but the end result is an exercise in frustration as the antes climb regardless. Of particular annoyance is the need to clear every stake on the way to the high stakes in order to unlock the last deck - it makes it where you can't just switch decks to try out a new deck for unlocking things, you have to grind all the way through every deck you want to try to use against the higher stakes. Absolutely miserable. I can understand making people do it for the highest stakes but the stakes that unlock decks should really let you use any deck once you've cleared the preceding stake with any deck. In any case, the game is more frustrating than fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't think a game about poker could be turned into a roguelike with fair, controllable RNG, but here it is.Initially the game just seems like simple Poker, but you'll quickly realize that the game is not REALLY about getting good poker hands; it's more about vital roguelike decisions, like gaining immediate power boosts to survive the next round and ruining your late game, or getting a scaling lategame powerhouse only to die in the next round, or gaining an early gimmick card that shapes your entire game plan from then on. Even if you draw Royal Flush every hand somehow, if you can't build around it, it will significantly underperform compared to a well built deck that just throws out a single 2 all the time. In that sense, the RNG is surprisingly fair and manageable. There's so many tools available to you that you really should be able to get really far, once you're beyond Ante 1 or 2. Unless you're playing a gimmicky deck that only does one thing and a Boss stops that deck from working (and you also didn't get the boss effect reroll), you should be able to win MOST of your games. It's all very unexpected from a game with the frame of poker.My only complaint is that the game does lack the more powerful tools (Jokers) unless you spend time unlocking them-- which does make this a subtle meta-progression roguelike game, rather than you having the same power as someone who played for many hours. Also, that Gold Sticker achievement is absolutely bonkers.

Even just looking through the large variety of Jokers and playing around with the foil patterns when they appear is very fun. (My favorite is Smeared Joker--so pretty.) _childDocuments_.review: Pretty good rougelite deckbuilding poker game. Lots of creative ways to build your deck, with the main goal being to beat increasingly difficult scores and conditions. Pretty high replayability and it's fun finding combos and getting all the secret unlocks. Highly suggest trying the demo or watching a short playthrough to get an idea; you do not really need to know how to play poker to enjoy this.My personal gripes:It is lacking in atmospheric depth, just video poker with no lore, characters, motivation surrounding it. You're not even playing against a player or enemy, just a score. So it does feel like playing solitaire in a way.The game doesn't have consistent problem-solving card text so effects can be very unclear. For example some cards give you "+1 hand", but some cards say "+1 hand per round" which is functionally the same, but because its described differently its easy to assume it does something else like maybe its a temporary effect or that the effect is reapplied every round instead of one time permanently. Some cards have unnecessarily long text that make it more confusing than it is, such as "all cards you play gain +10 multi if they score", obviously if a card scored then it was played, and there's no need to specify "all cards" because there's no exceptions or conditions. So it couldve just read "scored cards gain +10 multi".Completing the ascension system requires you to beat the game with every deck with every difficulty. This feels excessively grindy having to go through all the easier ascensions with every deck multiple times just to reach the more difficult fun stuff. There is an "unlock everything" button in the options menu to skip it, but this also skips all the unlockable cards and secrets. It would be nice if this grind is reduced to beating each difficulty with any deck, and/or there is a separate unlock all button just for the ascensions.

_childDocuments_.review: Addicting and frustrating. I cannot find the fun part of Balatro, only the addiction of gambling.Balance is out of whack and there is no good feedback on your deck's power level. You end up losing a lot of runs out of nowhere due to bad luck or a small miscalculation. When you win a run you are 10-100x too powerful. From what I am seeing only "small hand" and flush decks work well due to their consistency.In short the gameplay is not tactical but more random and "win more" which does not lend itself for a fun and exciting gameplay loop for me.The UX could use a bit more work, there are small inconsistencies here and there. For example looking at the current Ante is behind too many clicks (considering how often one needs to do it) and the "hover over deck tooltip" only works when you are playing a hand (although you need to look at your deck during many other times too). These issues are not a gamebreaker but are the surface of the real issue deeper within.Will I still continue playing this and did I think it was worth my money? Possibly.It's just hard to recommend this when Slay The Spire exists, a quite different but in all possible ways a superior game.Hopefully after a few rounds of balancing and polishing Balatro will be as good as it deserves to be! If Steam supported a "Neutral"/"Maybe" recommendation I would give that instead.

_childDocuments_.review: okay so i've been trying to get into a bunch of games recently. played baldur's gate 3 for about 25 hours before running into some weird storyline stuff that gradually wore me off it, tried starting bioshock and had some fun but couldn't really get into it, played a decent amount of ghost of tsushima because i was watching a lot of kurosawa films but then this game came along. i've only had it for about four days and i've already somehow sunk 20 hours into it, and feel like that playtime is just going to balloon more and more.on the surface it's fairly simple, a poker based roguelike (roguelite? honest to god i do not understand the difference) deckbuilder with no story, multiplayer, or really anything going on outside of the main gameplay loop, but my god is that gameplay loop fun. i like poker quite a bit to be honest (though i'm not much of gambler) but this is barely even poker outside of the hands and the aesthetics, instead it's much more of a luck and math based puzzle game. trying to give yourself the highest possible score by building your multipliers and sprinkling your deck with cards that have a variety of different enhancements. one run you can be scrambling to get a flush or a straight on the last hand to desperately beat the boss and the next run will have you just cruising to the end playing pairs the entire game. you can write it off as "addictive" or "mind-numbing" but to me i just find this game so pure, so raw, about engaging with simple systems to create astonishing results within strict confines. usually have found myself incredibly bored with roguelites (likes?) but this is the first one to really sink it's claws into me and i think i'll have a hard time letting go. it's over for me once the mobile port comes out.also want to just quickly praise the art direction which is simultaneously charming and psychotic in the same breath. all of the unique joker cards have great designs, some merely being beautifully rendered pixel art, others drawing their influence from other cards (baseball, pokemon, credit, etc.), many of them drawing specific influence from clowns in pop culture (juggalos will love this game, woop woop), but all having their own unique charm that makes some legitmately hard to not buy even if their effects will just tank the run. also love the swirling backdrop that really makes you feel like you're succumbing to madness as you accidentally enter your fourth straight hour of play, and the great punchy sound effects are sure to provide the pure dopamine hits any gambler craves.i swear _childDocuments_.review: The demo was fantastic, chiefly because of the limited selection of jokers.The full game turns it into a RNG-fest, because it adds so many utterly worthless things to the shop pool that you simply have to hope you get the right ones. Did you roll the right jokers and planets on this seed, at exactly the right times? You win. Did you not? You lose. There's very, VERY little decision-making involved, you simply have to hope you get exactly the right sets of items.And then you have the large number of boss blinds that remove even the few aspects of real logical decision-making from the game entirely. A boss that prohibits you from playing multiple of the same hand kills deckbuilding in one direction, and a boss that prohibits you from playing anything but one hand kills deckbuilding in another direction, while bosses that cause cards to be drawn face-down eliminate the only possible strategy you can be asked to employ. Couple those with a boss blind that permanently destroys your (hard-earned) ability to earn more points for hands, and you just have an exercise in arbitrary luck.All in all, a very disappointing full release of an exceptionally promising demo.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Overall really fun and addicting game that is affected more by RNG than other roguelikes, causing you to often lean on easier builds/stronger decks to guarantee a win instead of shooting for builds that are more complicated or higher risk (i.e. more fun).The core gameplay loops is fun, simple, and very satisfying. You play Antes that consist of three rounds, 2 unconditional blinds where you just have to meet a minimum score and a conditional boss blind. You score points by playing poker hands and earn money at the end of each round to purchase power-ups, modify your deck, or strengthen specific playable hands. It's pretty neat to see how everything comes together, and you'll soon be racking up tons of points and cash and, like other roguelikes, you soon push toward a refined strategy that centers on your playstyle or synergy among the items you've been offered.Sadly, RNG seems to affect runs in this game more than other roguelikes that are more skill-based, which I suppose plays into the playing card theme. It can add to the thrill, but more often adds to the frustration of having a great build and just not drawing the cards you need despite high odds. That or you just end up getting screwed by a boss blind that completely trashes your deck. That's where the other problem lies with build RNG. It's often a good idea to have a hand or strategy you can fall back on if you catch a bad boss roll (there are also somewhat rare opportunities to re-roll bosses), but with limited opportunities to modify your strategy, it's often better to go all-in (no pun intended) and strengthen a single build than to hedge. Again, these could be viewed as just roguelike things, but you'll feel it more in this game than something comparable like Slay the Spire because of the limitations of the mechanics and the inability to overcome build weakness with skill.(EDIT: The RNG issue is exponentially worse on higher difficulties. Subsequent difficulty levels add negative modifiers that can be so restrictive that you're almost entirely relying on good RNG to even get a run started. Bad boss rolls, bad tag rolls, bad shop rolls, bad draw rolls, these things are all issues you have to overcome in a normal run, but they are just stifling on some of the higher stakes. And again, I can't help but compare it to something like Slay the Spire where, while you could sometimes hit a brick wall on higher difficulties with more modifiers, you usually felt like you had some kind of chance, if even a slim one, to play your way out of a situation or turn around a tough run.)Another issue that is common in roguelikes but more frustrating in Balatro is the relative strength of certain decks and builds. I played the demo extensively, so by the time I got to playing 1.0, I really wanted to move away from some of the flush and full house builds (two very easy hands to build around) that I had leaned on during the demo period. Let me start by saying that it should be harder to create builds that revolve around higher risk/higher reward hands, but sometimes even getting the ball rolling on these kinds of builds is next to impossible with what you're offered or what you draw. I could go into more detail, but it's not an issue that will affect everyone, so suffice to say that people who play roguelikes for build variety will need a lot of patience.Still recommend this game given the amount of playtime value you can get at the price point. Even through the course of the demo period, there were a number of significant updates made. So I imagine LocalThunk has got plenty of ideas in mind to keep this game fresh for a long time.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a really fun game to discover. I certainly get all the hype around it. But it also turns out to be very superficial.Contrary to most deckbuilding/deckbuilding-adjacent roguelikes, where you have to make concessions and constant adaptations to an imperfect build in order to win, Balatro rewards you for being single-minded.You only need a little flexibility in the beginning, until you figure out what hand and/or couple jokers will carry you, at which point the best and only move is to tunnel vision really hard into it, and just play the same hand over and over again, until you win. A process which starts very, very early in a run.Basically, it lacks a whole layer of complexity to keep it fresh in the long run. That, and endgames are super redundant.Worse, the formula for a winning run rarely ever changes. At least a joker that gives chips, at least a joker that gives +mult, ideally a joker that gives xmult, at least one of which has to be a strong-scaling one, and then whatever you can fit in how little space you have left that can complement it. It doesn't matter what kind of hand you play, as long as it fits your joker line-up and you manage to make it spammable (and despite timid steps having been taken in the last update, high card still is the most reliable hand by far).So it feels to me that not only you play the same hand over and over, you actually , over and over, barring edge cases.You always need the same couple of things, and there just isn't that much variety in how you can gather them. Somehow, it makes sense. After all, you rarely get to make really game-changing tweaks to your deck, and even then, most of the work comes from the jokers, which you only get to carry 5 of, and whose effects very rarely reach beyond a "will reward you X for playing X type of hand" level of complexity. Kind of feels like playing Slay the Spire with only common cards and a hard cap on relics.On top difficulty, while smart thinking obviously does help, the game is primarily won by finding something worth committing to early enough, and then getting lucky enough to find stuff that complements it, or the other way around. And, if you're doing decently, but didn't get offered the boss reroll item, you might still end up losing at the very end, to one of the 5 possible final bosses, that takes 3 times as many points to defeat. 3 mostly uneventful bosses, one that can occasionally be a challenge, and then one that will automatically end most runs. And I mean,  runs. Do the math, 1.2 million really takes a lot of luck to be theoretically doable. That's some fine design right there.The game also suffers from a lot of pointless content that doesn't add much to the experience but makes completion more grindy than it needs to be (like, 5-ish starting decks - the equivalent of playable characters - making somewhat significant changes to the gameplay, and another 10 that pretty much all play the same way).Finally, some minor nitpicking : at least one mechanic feels like it was just copied from other popular games without understanding why it belonged there (and not here) : the interest system.While it made a ton of sense in TFT, for instance, it brings a false sense of depth to the game, and turns out to do the exact opposite of that, as it further incentivizes you to think in black and white (if this isn't a perfect fit for my build and I don't need it to survive right now, here's another excuse to dismiss it). Essentially a way to take away some liberty from the player, while tricking them into thinking they're getting more of it, and again, rewarding single-mindedness.I suppose certain folks will be happy with it, as it does very much have that power trip aspect that I've seen lots of people complain is missing in StS/LBAL/other similar games.As far as I'm concerned, though, having to make concessions to make an imperfect build work is what keeps me entertained - and occasionally surprised - in the long run, as opposed to just dismissing everything that isn't a perfect fit. There's a certain kind of magic in these games that I don't see in Balatro.(On a sidenote, there's a lot of micro-managing to do, so if you don't like that, by all means, stay away.)Edit after 40 more hours : I waited a few months before playing it again, and having little recollection of some things made it enjoyable for a while. I tried to keep an open mind, but really, I stand comforted in my views. The game promotes dichotomous thinking, and the impact of strategy vs. RNG (strict sense, not a comment on difficulty) is much lesser than standard in this genre.It's not bad, or stupid, or wrong. But if you like digging into games even a little, there are much better options out there.Edit after another 80 hours : Since I was getting close to all achievements, I gave it more time. Done with that now. Unfortunately, it only threw light on more issues, which I added to the review.

_childDocuments_.review: Man I want to like this game but I just get too frustrated at the sheer randomness to seem to ever have fun. It feels like my decision making has a fraction of the impact that the RNG has, to the point where the line between playing the game myself and watching someone else play it is nearly non-existent. In other words, the game pretty much plays itself and you're just a spectator that has to click a few buttons. My decision making doesn't change much (and in theory if it is changing it should be improving as I play more) yet I'll spend 40 minutes not getting halfway to the end of a run before failing then suddenly break ante 13 despite the fact that I'm not fundamentally doing ANYTHING different. Not only does it make the 5 runs that end early because I got a series of unlucky draws that has a less than 1% chance of happening or I run into the one boss blind that makes half my deck entirely useless even more annoying, it makes the one run that went really well entirely unsatisfying since I don't feel like I really did anything but get lucky. Then there's the balance issues. There are SO MANY jokers that are 100% worthless unless you're building a deck around that specific playstyle. So many jokers you would basically never take unless you needed a TINY boost to survive the next blind and a handful of jokers that you would almost never pass up regardless of what kind of deck you're running. It hints at the broader issue with "generalist" cards (those that are good with any kind of hand, any other jokers, etc) vs specific cards (things that only trigger when you play a certain kind of hand, or a specific suit or value of card). Consistency is King in games like this and in any given run you will be shown dozens of cards that are inconsistent with your deck at best and can't even be conceivably useful with your deck at worst. When you've got such a near indescribably massive gap between the best and worst RNG outcome and every aspect of the game is determined by RNG the game ceases to be something that required strategy and becomes a slot machine. When there's a joker that gives pairs +50 chips, then another that gives pairs +10 mult, then another that gives pairs x3 mult, and that pattern repeats for every single type of hand, you end up with a game that is overwhelmingly populated by trash you're unhappy to see, and that just isn't a fun or engaging way to play a roguelike for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Can you guess where I first got interested in this game? Were my friends playing it? Did I see a YouTuber pick it up? Did I read a gamer magazine? Nope, it was the store page. This game managed to draw me in, before the release of its first demo, just from some screenshots on this very same page that I'm now posting the review. And I'm so glad it did.It's pure dopamine. That's all I can say. Find the right joker? Hit Wheel of Fortune? Get an outrageous score? It keeps you coming back for that. There's only a few games that consistently bring me back for another round, no matter how hard they are (Peglin is one). By far the best feeling is trying out a new strategy and discovering it's better than you expected (I always use Chariot now). And no decision paralysis either! This game is fairly intuitive and easy to pick up, which also makes it quite relaxing. I cannot guarantee that it will actually cure your gambling addiction, but it will take up an hour (or 35) of your time.There's so much content! 150 jokers, tons of extra cards, 15 decks times 8 difficulty levels, add on some challenges and extras and that equals a lot of variety for just $22 AUD ($15 USD) which you might lose in just one game of poker. Then there's the task for the truly dedicated of beating the highest difficulty with every single joker - if there weren't an unending number of cool seeds to try first.The only frustrating part is luck (which is what all the negative reviews are about), which is unavoidable in a game based on cards, but bad luck is definitely not the only factor if you lose a run. It is overall a strategy game with about 20% luck, which might increase at higher difficulties. 's endless mode also hits the nail on the head. Because the scaling is so intense, it succeeds at asking "how far can you get?" rather than "can you go infinite?". In some games' endless modes, you know can keep your run going indefinitely, so there's no need to keep playing if the gameplay itself isn't really fun. In , the game keeps throwing challenges at you, so you know you're going to lose eventually but you want to keep pushing the limit. When I get a really good build, I just have to go endless - and that, if not anything else, is the sign of a good endless mode.This game is a V I B E . The pixel art is delectable and seamlessly mixes its pixel sizes (unlike  games I won't mention). The theming is very clever, and I would especially love those cards as a physical deck. The sound design is incredibly tactile and the music ties it all together to complete the stylistic fusion of an ancient but much-loved PC game and the world's weirdest casino. This game is instantly recognisable from any of its assets, much like others in its genre. So much love has been poured into the game's style, and the result is a complete feast for the senses. has a huge Discord server where we share art, discuss balance, make in-jokes, and get hyped for future content. LocalThunk has iterated on the game extensively to keep making it better (and will continue to; there's still post-release content planned), and gets input from the community. I was even part of a repaint called  that you can mod into the game - I didn't even mention the modding support. Even if there were no more official content, the community would keep this game alive for decades.This has been my dump of thoughts. There's nothing more I can say about  that would do it justice. It simply ticks all the boxes. Anyone with any positive impression of small stackable rectangles with markings on them will enjoy this game.  isn't just a poker roguelike, it's  poker roguelike. Try it. You'll be glad you did.
