With one mission you can barely get two "low grade" batteries.Scaling is abismal. "Low grade" batteries have 100 charge, cost 500; "Middle grade" batteries have 150 charge and cost *1000* and finally; "High grade" batteries have 200 charge and cost **2500**. So for TWICE the charge you pay *FIVE TIMES* as much. And you can't even buy a "high grade" battery with one mission.When you are in a shop/whatever, and you click back, you are in your seat and there is no other to get back into the store without getting out of your seat, walk to the airlock and reenter the shop...Systems drain too fast, circuits break down too fast.The game becomes almost unplayable after rank 5...Edit: I found the custom Settings option.Now we're cooking with gas...

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very unique game, but you should properly adjust your expectations. And don't even think about playing it without a controller.Is Star Trucker a ETS 2 is space? Hard no. Not even close. It's more akin of Everspace 2 in structure (closed areas locked behind jumpgates) and of Elite Dangerous in spirit and fully realized 3D-movement with a pinch of a Classical mechanics.You basically haul around things, maintain your rig (huge part of gameplay is resource management even on very easy) and try to navigate fully realized 3D space without bumping onto things due to inertia and momentum. That includes very precise docking procedures that can turn off many people, who bought the game thinking that Star Trucker is a 2D car game with a space skin.I really love the flow, the style, the navigaton and the gameplay loop, but I really think that the publisher sold the wrong game to the wrong people. Star Truckers is Elite Dangerous trader's path minus the combat, bloat and always-online shenanigans. It's compact, cozy and possess a very unique atmosphere of a space Texas Highway with great soundtrack to boot.It's a very solid game, but once again, adjust your expectations accordingly.

_childDocuments_.review: The GoodI like it. The controls feel great, It has just enough cockpit activities to feel like a simulator and the VA is good. Its basically American truck simulator Lite in space. Have not experienced any bugs and the tutorials are very clear. I can see myself sinking at least 20 hours into this. Voice acting is great too.The BadComing from other truck simulators, the hauls in this game are very short. It took me about 10 minutes to do a medium distance haul. I feel the map is rather small as well. There are a total of three jumps to get from one side of the map to the other (about four to six minutes real time). I feel this game really needs to improve on its scale. I want hour long hauls in the future with many pit stops and landmarks to look at. I want to have the sense of being out in the middle of nowhere. Planetary travel zones would be cool too. Arriving in the atmosphere and traveling through the clouds of a planet.I also feel like the AI is pretty bad. The other drivers seem to not care at all about you. They do not avoid you at all... in fact, I was trying to dock at a station and one traveled right between my and the dock as I was backing into it. The AI cars need much work.Final ThoughtsTo me this feels like a complete early access if that makes sense? Everything works, there just needs to be more. The price is fine for what it is... but I just want more. More trucks, more (and BIGGER) systems, more variety of missions, paint jobs, truck flair, truck stops etc.I am really looking forward to this game growing and hoping the devs add much more content.

_childDocuments_.review: The game has its charm. I really enjoy it so far, and probably will for a couple hours more.Before you buy, be aware what this game really is.It's not really Euro Truck Simulator in space. The economic side of the game is quite limited, as of now, but the gameplay loop is enjoyable.There is some sort of a story going on in the background, you can engage with it at will, whenever you fell like it, apart from doing normal deliveries.I cannot really put a finger on it, but the game is somewhat confused about what it wants to be.The driving/flying part is okay, much more comfortable on controller (also, runs great on SteamDeck), but manageable on PC. Interacting with the rig howewer is cumbersome without a mouse (there is no dedicated button for cruise control, responding to radio calls etc., you have to point at the button/radio and interact with it. It often leads to crashes, as you are not looking at the road).Navigating space is also strange.There are many systems you can travel to, but only Atlas Prime seems to be well thought out and organised. In other systems the game turns into a Rock Dodging Simulator, as there are no highways or they are not well marked.On Altas Prime you just follow the road to the nearest station and then choose another road to the next station etc.Some tips before you play:a) DO NOT choose the predefined difficulty levels. They are crazy unbalanced and DO NOT match their descriptions. The "Driver" difficulty pays you pennies on deliveries and any scratch to the rig is REALLY painful. You can either go into the custom one, or try the game out for about 20-30 minutes to understand what settings mean what and start over. The game is rather linear, unlocks come from the story, so starting over is painfulb) Delivery docks are usually short for the station names, use it to navigate betterc) Invest in a different figure at the front of your trucks. Seems cosmetic, the wings threw me off sometimes when I was aimingd) The rig has a lot of inertia. The steering changes whether you are cruising, accelerating, slowing down or on cruise control. Be aware of that.Some things I would love to change about the game:a) Make navigating the systems easier. Finding a proper road to use, or finding the road at all is unwieldyb) Rebalance the difficulties or at least provide more description as to what they entailOverall the game has its charm. The soundtrack is awesome. When you get a hang of driving it's really enjoyable and the story elements provide some nice variety for the gameplay loop. The visuals are also great, but are rather generic.The game also lacks in tutorials and explanations about how everything works.Would definitely recommend, but make an informed purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: Overview: Star Trucker is an interesting survival space trucking game with an interesting story a colorful cast and challenges along the way. With highly customizable difficulty you can set the game that's just right for your intentions. Its sound and visuals are also quite good. It is an incredible game from a person team who carry a positive tone in their interactions with the community and work to make the game even better.Additional information: The game is not A/ETS or even ATD. Understanding that is key to enjoying the game. While you can play the game in a delivery loop like A/ETS or a delivery survival loop like ATD, it differs in small yet challenging sectors and fast traveling time. From my perspective, it's a single-player story experience of a new trucker who then works with the trucking community in the new sector in various missions that all converge into one final mission at the end while trying to survive the hostile space.

_childDocuments_.review: I waited a year for this game and it has absolutely not disappointed. This is not a game for everyone, but if you are just looking for a relaxing time and a very customizable game play experience, then you will get many hours of fun out of this and it will be well worth the price. I am not really a truck sim kind of person, but you put anything in space and I am there to at least try it. I don't really know why this game caught my eye, just something about the idea of a big rig in space scratched an itch I didn't know I had. The actual gameplay is top notch imo. Yes, it is repetitive, but I don't really think that's a bad thing. This is not a game for the hardcore truck sim fans, or the pain-loving Souls-like fans. This is a game for someone who is looking for an immersive vibe. And this game nails that. The controls take a good hour or two to learn, and another several hours to really start to master. Even at almost 20 hours I would say I am at like a 5 or 6 out of 10 when it comes to the driving. You do start to get the feel for it though, and eventually it will stop seeming weird and you will want to test out different ways momentum, speed, and angle can change your direction. You can also sort of drift, it takes a second to get there, but it feels pretty cool once you do it.There is a story, it's more like a bunch of side quests, but more like AC Origins side quests where they are very fleshed out and have a solid start, middle, and resolution to them. You really get to know the side characters through the dialogue (which is actually great, the VAs actually brought some top notch performances to characters you mostly listen to, but don't see) and nothing in the game ever feels unnatural as far as that dialogue is concerned. The side quests are also never forced on you, you can start one, half way finish it, go do something else, and then go back and finish the quest. It is very much a "make your own fun game."The gameplay itself can also be heavily customized. My recommendation is to play through the first hour on the Recommended difficulty, and if you like the game, figure out what you like and don't like about each of the game play systems. Then, start a new save and make a Custom difficulty and change everything you want. You can also skip the tutorial using the custom settings and that's a big W on the devs for that option. Speaking of, and I have to mention this no matter how many times people have said it. This game is made by TWO PEOPLE. It is actually insane what they were able to create and package into a 1.0 full release. Not to mention they plan on continuing to update this game and to add more content down the line. I'm not gonna say you should buy it just because of that, but, if you are the type of person this appeals to then keep that in mind when you see some of the crazy stuff they were able to create together. It is truly a testament to what indie gaming is in the modern era. Overall, I believe Star Trucker is, at least for me, an absolutely amazing game that is well worth the price tag and that I cannot recommend enough. I will continue to play this game and rack up hours, possibly to an unhealthy amount, and I hope that everyone this game is for finds this and loves the hell out of it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is about constantly micromanaging the truck's various systems with a little driving on the side.  There should be a way to recharge batteries from docking with stations, and having the ships systems repaired from the stations instead of having to  replace batteries and computer chips, and air filters every 5-10 minutes.  When you aren't replacing components on your truck, you're climbing out on the truck to patch an air leak because of random spawning debris that your clunky ship is unable to avoid unless you're crawling at low speeds.  Systems don't have redundancies, gravity goes off and all your cargo flies around the cab regardless if you are moving or not.  There's no cargo net to keep cargo in place and bumping anything devalues the cargo making it next to worthless for resale.  What truck driver doesn't secure his/her cargo, especially fragile cargo?

_childDocuments_.review: This is a no brainer if you are a fan of ATS/ETS2. It's really cool because it adds a whole other dimension to that formula, up and down. I am much more impressed with this game than I thought I would be. It is quite well fleshed out, with many systems to monitor and interact with. I took the advice of others and made a custom game so that I could turn down the battery drain, which I had heard was quite aggressive, and I'm having a great time with it. The graphics are just beautiful, and I do not thing I have seen a single bug, nor have I seen a single frame drop. This is damn impressive guys, well done! This would be incredible in VR.Here is some feedback for the devs.....One thing I would like to see is Hotas support. If I could use my dual sticks would be awesome. It would be nice to have some more songs for the radio, but I enjoy the ones on offer now. It would be nice to use the CB without losing full control of my ship somehow. Maybe a long press of a button? On a spacewalk, when I open a box, It starts spinning, and makes it difficult to place things inside the box. All in all I think this is a really chill and polished game, and it gets a thumbs up from me. I am glad it exists, and I look forward to updates and dlc's.

_childDocuments_.review: I love so much of this game. Once you get the hang of the flight model, it's fun to zip around corners like an insane person. It's fun to run on a single engine through a sector to give the other one a chance to cool down. I love setting myself on a course and disabling the assist so it's just a drift. This game has been one of the most technically spectacular feats that I've ever seen come out of a two-person studio. It runs well, and I've only become aware of a single bug in the whole time that I've been playing it. It's perfectly scratched the itch I've had since I first stumbled across it in August of 2023.I can't recommend this game because some of the interactions between core gameplay elements turn it into an anxiety generator without a mechanism for rewarding the player for living through that anxiety. While I hope that the game receives updates that remedy my intentionally nonspecific issues, it's not an Early Access title and it is likely exactly what Monster and Monster envisioned.My current save is in pretty dire circumstances, so I think I'm going to start a new custom difficulty game when I play next instead of trying to continue it. I want to switch this review to recommended, and I feel like that'll give me the best chances of reaching that goal, even if I have to explain that I don't recommend the recommended difficulty.

_childDocuments_.review: I've not gotten too far into the game but this scratches  every itch that I have in this kind of game.The Cons:I come from Space Sims. This game isn't one, its not trying to be one either. Getting used to not having lateral and vertical thruster movements takes some getting used to. This quite literally is a Space Trucking game in that sense.The economy can be pretty harsh. Some of the essentials you need to survive can cost multiple trip's worth of pay to buy, and while you can find them in beacons sometimes, this game more than any other requires you to play the early game right to not get yourself into a death spiral you can't climb out of.The Pros:The reason why I play games like Star Citizen is because I want as much as possible to move away from the idea of inventory screens. I like it when an object has a physical presence in the world. All of the supplies you're going to need for your truck are going to take up space, they need specific storage to not get damaged. This interacts with the rest of the game too. If your gravity goes out, your cargo will float around in your truck. If you stop too suddenly or get in a collision, your cargo will fly out your shelves. You can even die if you have things laying around your truck and they fly in your direction.All of the maintenance aspects that the game has aren't just busywork. Outside of the resource management of power cores and the durability of internals, you can fly in bursts of acceleration to not overheat your engines if they're too hot, or turn on cruise control if they're getting too cold.There's "roads", but roads make you take longer to get around, you spend more fuel. You can drive offroad, but then you will have to dodge space debris which if it hits you makes you have to spend money on repairs, time repairing hull breaches, and may even damage your cargo. And this is before I get into all the biome specific hazards. I just unlocked an area that has electric storms.I got this game, started playing, looked at my clock and 5 hours had passed. So far, its really really good and I highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: like star citizen except 40,000x better, 40,000x more released, and $40,000 cheaperno fr this is the best job sim i've played yet and it's a complete experience at release. haven't come across any bugs yet but the settings are somewhat limited (ie. no keybinding yet, unsure if HOTAS is supported either).+ats/ets style jobs+ats/ets style cargo type unlocks+salvage (get out of the ship (bring a container so you can just load it up quicker))+maintenance is engaging+off roading because space+good views, +good fps for me on mid hardware+good music, good radio+good controls and good feedback from the dashboard (ie. directly telling you miles til empty, good cameras, good status information to know when you need to replace power cells) - and you have to actually click switches on the dashboard which feels great for jump gates.+NO LOADING SCREENS once you open your save. menus are immediate in/out (even faster than loading out from ats/ets garage) so you are constantly in game unless you are viewing the map or looking at jobs, skill tree, etc.+you can upgrade your hull and crash through an asteroid field and still get paid+interesting environmental hazards that require you to pilot in different ways, keeps contracts engagingplease continue updating this, would be great with multiplayer for convoys.haven't come across anything negative at all to say, honestly.e: after unlocking every feature - it would be nice to have more out-of-ship content. still strongly recommend for how solid the gameplay loop is.e2: also let us change the horn sound...

_childDocuments_.review: /10Without a doubt one of my favourite space trucking games to ever have been released in the year 2024.I have sunk some hours into it, and I only have plans to sink even more hours into it as it is. Yes, I say this as someone who has played space combat games before, but there are times I'd like a break from combat games as well.It's nice to see how dedicated & passionate the 2-monster team (Dan & Dave) really are.I appreciate their hard work, as I patiently wait for every game update that only just keeps making the game better & better overtime.Sure, at first, the game didn't even have custom keybinding available as an option, but as the time goes on, eventually custom keybinding was added as part of one of the game updates Star Trucker has had.It just goes to show that good things come to those who wait, so if you're patient like me, and have waited for the game to be polished more, then we're on the same boat.There's plenty of difficult options to choose from, one of them being a custom mode, where you can tweak & change the difficulty settings to your own liking, which is pretty neat. Once you learn the basics of the game, you'd find yourself to be able to do more than just doing jobs all the time, as you can even buy goods from one system, to later sell in a different system that pays a higher price for 'em.I haven't had any major issues, other than salvage beacons spawning in buildings (uhh... pretty sure that's a bug that will later be patched out), and a lag spike in at least one system. Maybe it's something to do with my graphical settings, but other than that, yeah.I'd definitely recommend this to anyone who would want to relax taking it easy on more relaxing difficulty setting, or/and for anyone who would like to challenge themselves by playing on "Well-Rounder", "Mechanic" or even "Hardcore" difficulty. I have faith that "Hardcore" is actually doable, even if the pricing of these air filters is ABSURDLY high, like that is honestly my only complaint about hardcore difficulty, as I have managed to survive for longer than just 3 real-time hours on HC alone.If it weren't for how expensive the air filters were, then Hardcore may be more enjoyable, but then again, the difficulty itself wasn't even designed to be remotely fair in the first place, so I suppose that's very reasonable.But yeah, whatever you're looking for, let it be a relaxing experience or a challenge, and you like space games, then this may be the game just for you.

_childDocuments_.review: For everyone who wants to buy it: it's not a game about long rides in space, it's a game about managing your truck and delivering cargo between small hubs by jumping through warp gates. And every 15-20 minutes you have to dock at the nearest station to buy new batteries (you can't recharge them,  you have to buy new ones, and that's expensive). The skill tree is about getting new types of jobs, nothing that gives you anything useful for your truck. It's still fun, but it's not what you can expect from this kind of game. Most of the time, you have to manage your truck (buy new power cells, new filters, parts, fuel, etc.). Forget about long trips, you just drive from one warp gate to the next and that's it.

_childDocuments_.review: You're a trucker, in space! Its pretty straight forward, going from point to point, maneuvering your truck and trailers. There are character quests to progress the story and freight jobs to make money, plus little salvage opportunities and potential to smuggle different types of contraband. You also have to maintain your rig which consists of swapping out power cores and circuits when they are expended. Overall, I'd give it currently a 7/10, its fun, it looks great, its simple to start but has a decent amount of depth. I feel like 10 hrs in I have a good grasp on the gameplay but I have a couple new regions to unlock which if anything like the 2nd region, will introduce new gameplay mechanics. Looking forward to seeing what they do to build on this game. That 7/10 has a lot of potential to go up if they build on it in meaningful ways.

name: Ultros
detailed_description: ULTROS: DELUXE EDITION Enhance your somatic sensory input with the Ultros: Deluxe Edition – including the Ultros Digital Artbook, showcasing the psychedelic world through never-before-seen imagery from the visionary El Huervo, and the Ultros Original Soundtrack, blending Peruvian instruments with classic orchestral themes, lovingly orchestrated by Oscar “Ratvader” Rydelius. About the Game You wake up stranded, after seemingly crashing your ship on The Sarcophagus — a giant, space-drifting, cosmic uterus holding an ancient demonic being known as ULTROS. Trapped in the eternal loop of a black hole, you will have to explore The Sarcophagus and meet its inhabitants to understand the part you play. Are you the gruesome breaker of this cycle, or can you become a link from destruction to rebirth? ULTROS is set in a multifaceted realm - a vast alien landscape teeming with life. Grounded in science fiction, ULTROS comes wrapped in an eccentric art style and a mystical soundtrack from the visionary El Huervo, renowned for his work on Hotline Miami. ULTROS explores meta-themes of mental health, life, death, and karmic cycles through deep lore and environmental storytelling. Experience brutal, intimate, close-quarter combat with cosmic lifeforms, driven by a sense of urgency – where precision is paramount and every cut of your blade counts. Yet this intense combat is juxtaposed with cultivating the greenery and tending to plant life in The Sarcophagus, providing precious moments of contemplation and peace. In turn, this grants deeper access to obscured paths. The rich world of ULTROS holds many secrets for those curious enough — and fearless enough — to seek them out. A unique loop-based mechanic will allow you to start over at key moments in the story, providing opportunities to unfold such secrets, unlock different areas of the world and new abilities on a branching skill tree. Experiment with and master your own specific fighting style as you explore the world of ULTROS. Each loop brings you closer to the truth...

_childDocuments_.review: looks like a metroidvania, but is not entirely one. You get double jump relatively early... and soon after that it's taken from you. Yeah. It's a time loop where you're constantly thrown back to square one — which includes losing your abilities and even your weapon, so you have to get them again each time.It feels disempowering, to say the least. So much so that I considered refunding when it happened for the first time. But the game's acid aesthetics convinced me to push on, and in the end I think it was worth it. The game is visionary and has a bunch of unique ideas. Just don't go in expecting a classic metroidvania.It's also a roguelite — in that "the cycle starts anew" and your progress is reset after killing each boss. Except not really: each cycle also changes shortcuts and generates new events, and the level design around the zone you begin in is nothing but stellar, skillfully guiding you down a different path with each cycle despite the world being technically open. It's one thing to design a metroivania around the player having or not having an ability; it's a more daunting thing to design it around juggling abilities and constantly getting and losing them.Much more unexpectedly,  is also a sort of Farmville-like sim. You can plant and grow trees in the game. They produce healing items, but each of them also has an ability — like creating ledges over time or breaking through walls. Choosing the right trees to plant in the right places is your key to accessing every room on the map. Growing them takes time, but you can use compost to speed the process up. And also you can dig seeds out and re-plant them...Another incredible challenge the game throws at you is the Living Network. You will at one point find a net that can connect buds that are close enough to each other. When connected, they bloom, and when connected to save points, they make them teleportable. The game then suggests you connect all the map — which means going through it via unique paths, finding shortcuts and growing the right trees. The trees part was too much busywork, but generally it's an incredible idea for a metroidvania, making you look at the map with different eyes. I hope more games do that.The fights and levelling system are also unique. You heal by eating various fruit and body parts, each of them nourishing you with some of four imaginary substabces. When you get enough of which, you can unlock skills. By finding Mnemonic Mycelium, you can lock a skill in for future cycles.As for the fights, they're very easy. It's hard to die in this game. But they do things like reward you for using unique attacks instead of mashing the same one. And did you know you could tame some opponents by feeding them? Yeah.Overall, I applaud a game that isn't one more Dark Souls/Hollow Knight. It's unique and bursting with original ideas. Not all of them are executed perfectly, but they aren't annoying either. So I think  is worth buying and playing to support the future development of these ideas, if nothing else.P. S. A friend of mine asked recently if "casual metroidvanias" exist, as he doesn't like hard challenges and action-packed combat.  was the closest that came to mind. (You can make it harder for yourself, but overall it's chill.) And that too is unique.

_childDocuments_.review: Perhaps I went into Ultros with misguided notions. Perhaps I just wasn't patient enough with the inversion of genres and mechanics the developers were going for. At any rate, Ultros turned out to be a game of diminishing returns for me.The psychedelic art is certainly one of the game's initial draws, as is the fabulous music, which can easily evoke harmony and folly within a few note changes. Upon reading that the game could be played as a pacifist, I instantly became keen on a game I had otherwise been holding off on for a few months. After all, I had several new metroidvanias to consider in 2024. Perhaps I misread the article because upon starting Ultros, I was surprised that combat was seemingly the only way forward... at least for a time. Once a few loops are completed, the gardening mechanics begin to unfold, and your non-combat options with it, but this comes late enough in the game where I wasn't all that compelled to utilize what remained an clunky system till the lackluster end.  For a metroidvania that ultimately wishes you to eschew combat and instead garden, the controls are passable. I never felt that many of the skill tree items truly served a purpose for platforming (looking at you wall slide). To achieve the peaceful ending with the titular cosmic entity, you must connect a living network of plants. This map-wide puzzle of dot to dot is essentially the true core of the game, or said another way, the hidden game underneath the seemingly basic metroidvania. Problem is, once this became clear to me, I simply had very little goodwill left towards the game to play it this way. I just wanted to be done with it, opting for the easier violet ending. A sad notion since I had been so keen on this game being pacifist. It's clear people really like Ultros for the gardening and living network. But after so many hours of wandering the wrong way, or trekking through the same mundane area after another loop began, I simply wasn't compelled to play any more than I had to. As I trudged through my final two areas, I wondered how a game I was so jazzed about for the first eight hours or so now felt both tepid and like a teeth-gnashing chore. Some of this chalks up to time and circumstance, and inevitably, comparison. Perhaps that's unfair to say, but when compared with the puzzles and secrets of Animal Well and the combat of Blasphemous, both still fresh in my mind, Ultros simply felt okay most of the time. With the emotionally rich science fiction of 1000XResist still beating in my heart, Ultros' hands-off lore-approach to story simply made me shrug. At the end of the day, I simply wasn't compelled.Had the gardening mechanics began a few hours earlier and not remained so opaque for a total of 23 hours of play, or had the game ever hinted in the direction forward just a smidge more at times, perhaps I would be in a different place with Ultros. Perhaps. But probably not. You see, I'm learning something about myself as a gamer, which is that unless a game is sheer fun - like Nova Drift, Minishoot Adventures, or Vampire Survivors - the immersive factor of a game for me must come from either excellent and/or innovative mechanics and puzzles and/or character and story. It could be literary like Norco or Citizen Sleeper. It could be exploratory and tactile like Jusant or Sable. It could be mind-altering like Cocoon or Fez. But lore alone does nothing for me. This penchant in the medium to sprinkle lore about does not make me want to complete a game. And outside of a few lackluster plot points, Ultros hinges a lot on lore and some curious mechanics that I never really clicked with. A shame, but at least some folks are digging it.

_childDocuments_.review: Ultros is a solidly built, and interesting, take on the metroidvania genre - combining the familiar exploration, puzzle, and combat aspects with an almost roguelite loop system and its connected plant system, it's something I honestly am enjoying a ton.Pros -- Beautiful art and music style (while the screenshots look chaotic, it is actually super easy to follow while playing)- A proper story told in a mix of dialogue and illustrated cutscenes- Combat is fluid and easy to learn (though the gameshow segment can get a bit fiddly - won't say more than that to avoid spoilers)- There is a lot to explore and experiment with, even though the map is only about average size.- Never was left wandering aimlessly, if I was going a direction I hadn't gone somewhere before, there was always something there.- Has better roguelite progression than most roguelites these days (you unlock items to keep your skills run to run)- I tried a few times to intentionally get softlocked (such as not getting my tool that provides my movement tech, when going to a new area) - and there was always a way through, even if a bit more difficult.Cons -- Keyboard controls feel clunky, even though they're rebindable, this is definitely a controller game (works near flawlessly on controller)- The flying mechanic needs some more time in the oven for controlling it (though this won't fix some of the 'you may not pass' type things that keep you from shortcutting or getting soft locked)- You generally need specific plants in specific locations for a completionist run, so it will take some guessing in certain locations.Overall, I enjoyed my time with it, and can wholeheartedly recommend it to fans of metroidvanias - even though it is on the easy to moderate end of things in terms of difficulty, even without accessibility features turned on (yes, it has visual and difficulty accessibility options for players that need them)Want to watch the gameplay, and get the full review? You can find it on youtube @

_childDocuments_.review: A very interesting take on metvan I've never seen before. For those saying that it's a rougelite or rougelike, they haven't played the game or played it enough because it's not. It has some elements with it's cycle loop that plays into the story but I would say it's almost genre defying in this sense because it doesn't fit a traditional metvan progression system but also is certainly far from a rougelite... if anything it has a carry over story similar to that of story driven rougelites like hades, but it's mechanics and progression are very different... in a very good way. A very unique and fresh twist on the genre, it's certainly made for people that love the genre and have played all it has to offer, in terms of creativity, ultros completely kills the competition. Simply put, i have never seen a game with so much debate over it's genre and progression where almost nobody really knows what the game has to offer, its completely unique and you will probably never play anything like it---except for maybe future clones of this style because of how cool and fun it is to play. The art style, i think, is a big selling point to the experience. The game is handcrafted excellently. I was originally gonna play the game on shrooms with a buddy of mine but decided against it as you are almost looped into the phyc experience while sober. Really does feel alien, especially with the text, story, and gameplay feeling so different and un-understandable, it really does immerse you in a different world. It feels like the devs were able to pull the dimension from an acid trip and put it into visuals, really great work on the art. Something else I've noticed with regards to the handcraftedness is how everything feels so meticulously thought out and planned. For example, when planting a tree and coming back to that location for a new cycle, it now perfectly unlocks the next area, or not having the extractor at a specific part, everything is catered to different mechanics and no double jump---i never feel stuck or lost and the large map makes it so exploration is constantly at the front end of the game, and the environment feels like everything was thought of in making that experience feel organic. As for the characters, I really like a lot of their personalities, and the way they play into the broader ecosystem has the npc elements of the world really come to life. You aren't just a brute mindlessly killing, as you advance the story you can cultivate the environment, leave food in soil for compost for new exploration, tame various alien pets---capturing a lively ecosystem in 2d games is a task for sure, since you lack a lot of the "realistic immersion" so coveted in gaming. That being said, i find 2d games often more immersive and ultros is no exception... it actually might be an exception in how well it pulls off the immersion. In very few games do you not feel like the agent of interaction that the world revolves around, in very few games do you actually feel like a part of the ecosystem in a real way. Their are certainly broader themes of environmentalism throughout the game, and the way the mechanics don't shy away from it either is important to! Making sure to kill the species around you in a specific way, or making sure to plant a specific kind of tree to get an item or faster route, or anything like this---its a game that rewards the player for taking care of their environment. Nature isn't simply a tool for your exploitation, where you run in and kill everything in site and burn it all down, it's more so something that you need to interact as a part of and give back to if you want to progress (great game design in that aspect). A critique that I've seen levied at the game is the lack of mob variety, but I completely disagree with this in the context of the game. First off, their is a decent amount of mob variety, but a look at the design of this game makes it obvious that it wants you to be a genuine part of the games ecosystem and handle every mob in a unique way---knowing this makes it obvious why there aren't just randomly genned slightly different critters to be mindlessly killed, because you need to recognize and form a connection with each unique monster type, some of them you need to use a specific mechanic on, some of them you can feed and they'll be your friend, most of them you can do a lot of unique things with, keeping the variety low makes each one actually have personality and makes them feel special. Overall, I think the major thing that ties the game together as that the devs actually gave a ♥♥♥♥ about the environment crafting... when building metvans i think the immersion, ambience, and "vibe," of the game are the most important elements, and in this way, the unique art style, creative game mechanics, world interaction, cycle loops, mobs, and gameplay come together to make an extremely tightly knit and cohesive experience. I would recommend this game to anyone that likes 2d games, metvans, rougelikes/lites, or any isometric type genre as I think it excells in everything it attempts to create a great player experience.

_childDocuments_.review: It's really an arborvania - a large chunk of your tools revolve around planting and cultivating things and it goes hard on the depth surrounding them. _childDocuments_.review: Ultros is one of the most intriguing games ever, not only from a narrative perspective but also in terms of gameplay and how the two are intertwined. Completing it 100% is only for the select few but in my opinion Ultros is a must play for metroidvania lovers, atleast up to the first ending. As many of the reviews point out though this may vary depending on the person. Reason being the sort of reset mechanic that happens several times throughout the game. This initially worried me greatly so i sorta rushed the start to get a feel for this mechanic within the 2 hour refund window. In hindsight it is not that bad at all, especially because by the 3rd loop you know when and more specifically where a reset happens. . The fun thing about this is that the game opens up new pathways every loop so it really doesn't feel that samey as people make it out to be. These new paths do a good job of guiding you through the game's substantial map, which features a set of varied and unique biomes. Most areas play pretty differently so there's a lot of variety in that regard. You can discover most of said biomes on your first pass through but like any good metroidvania there's some stuff for later. Level design is pretty solid in general so exploring each area is pretty fun the first time. On loop resets your map discovery is kept, but unfortunately broken barriers also reset. This is the one thing i would have loved to see handled differently as it's a bit of a headache sometimes. There are other things that do persist though mainly the things that you plant. Because other than a metroidvania with roguelite elements this game is also a farming game??!This caught me pretty of guard initially but by the 3rd loop it became clear how much this would change the map in future loops which is super unique and also kinda fun (for the most part). It also ties into the games' narrative and symbolism super well so i must say that it worked for this game. The unfortunate thing though is that seeds get lost upon resets but luckily there's always the right ones nearby. These plants play a MUCH bigger role in the post game to get the true ending but at this point the mechanic becomes very convoluted as it's no longer as straight forward which plant to put where. There's tons of soil patches, 10 different plant types and the matter of composting it or not. To save yourself a headache i'd suggest using a guide after you get the first ending as that's still possible at this point if you're interested in getting the proper ending.I got about halfway this true ending when i decided that i was no longer enjoying the mechanic. Even with the proper plants in place there's still some fiddling about with your gardening tools and i felt like i was fighting the controls a bit. Up till this point the controls had been super smooth though, not only for the platforming but also in combat. The platforming is a bit basic but the environments add fun obstacles like scaled that tip or jumping pads. In combat it also responds quickly and while combat as a whole is rather quite easy there's still enough going on to be engaging. Bosses were fun and unique too, although not as hard as most other MV's. You can make it easier yet by spending points in the talent tree. You unlock these by eating your enemies' remains, with cleaner kills (using different moves rather than button mashing) yielding better spoils.These upgrades also get lost upon reset, except for when you use a special collectible item to lock these memories. These as well as lore bits are the games' true collectibles and finding enough of them to lock the whole skilltree was one of my primary motivators to progress in the game. Other than exploring the map and unveiling the story ofcourse! Said story is just impeccable. The way it ties the central mechanic into it as well as the environmental storytelling on display is just amazing. Your starting location tells something the game never explicitly mentions but which the eagle eyed players will soon pick up on. Most metroidvania's go light on story but this one i'd say it's the focussing point. And they nailed it, not only in the overal story but also the backstory of each character/zone.Speaking of zones the visual variety is great, you have gardens, luxury districts, living quarters, temples and even a distillery. The overal game is just beautiful but that's something nearly every person agrees on and is apparant from the very first time you see a screenshot or boot up the game. What you don't see initially but will hear soon enough is just how utterly INCREDIBLE the soundtrack is. The song 'broken promise' which plays in the rotten orchard especially is just downright beautiful. I'm picking up a copy of the game's OST which i'm listening to as i'm writing this and will continue listening to for a long time. In some ways i'm even happier i played the game because it introduced me to the OST so even if you don't plan on playing this game, do yourself a favor and give it a listen.Finally there's performance which at this point was spotless. I also had no bugs, like at all... I'm actually suprised about this given how many systems the game has to keep track off in terms of physics and all the different plants. At first i thought these were static in their growth but with the later tools you can manipulate these quite a bit so the fact that it worked as well as it did was suprising to me. I had no crashes either or any other technical hickups and loading times were super fast. So technically the game is incredibly polished. It's a super unique experience that is super enjoyable untill the first ending. After this engaging with the more finnicky gardening mechanics became more of a chore but not enough to leave a sour taste. I'm perfectly happy where i left it off and may revisit this title some day to finish it up.
_childDocuments_.name: Ultros

_childDocuments_.review: Every time I shut down this game, I need an hour or so to touch the ground again, and uhh... I am trying to write a review after having finished it.This game is extremely unique. I love the bizarre and ethereal music, the beautiful and alien art, the central concept of connection and gentleness, and just, this amazing and intriguing world teeming with life. Trying to make a Metroidvania with new ideas is a gargantuan challenge, and I honestly believe that the gardening system in this game is one of freshest, most brilliant puzzle mechanics I have seen in several years. Initial impressions can be confusing, but rest assured, there is an answer to everything if you keep pressing forward. There is a surprising number of combat moves, which makes sense given how the game's hunting system works. However, the combat challenge is actually very, very low for the genre - and that is okayI have no complaints worth making about the game itself. I did experience some programming bugs that hindered progression (ie. soft-locking because I entered a save capsule and the game didn't load the menu, or doing so because it can't load the next screen for some reason). I also don't appreciate that the frame limiter doesn't kick in until you get in-game, nor do I appreciate the game turning my DS4's light green or yellow for some reason.This game is something truly special, and it is absolutely worth picking up if you are interested in Metroidvanias, psychedelic imagery, or planting gardens. You won't find the next Hollow Knight in here, but you will find whispers of a future we have yet to attain
_childDocuments_.name: Ultros

_childDocuments_.review: A psychedelic surrealist metroidvania that tries to do a lot of new things in combination with a stark and vivid art style. While I was initially excited to delve into the game I quickly found myself bouncing off it.The art style is probably what stands out most about the game and granted it is beautiful, with vivid colours and creative animations all blending biology with technology. Unfortunately the game lacks an understanding of contrast. There is so much detail and colour that it's difficult to tell what is foreground vs. background. Interactive vs. inert. The visual language games have - colours that communicate qualities and mechanics, sparkles and particles that denote interactivity - all become lost in this haze of overwhelming colour and movement.The combat itself is trying to stand apart in a few ways. Your first sword has very short reach and you are encouraged to pull off a combo with minimal repeated moves - though it doesn't specify what actions count as repetitive, and this early on I only have two attacks so it seems obtuse to demand variety. Equally the combat is very rigid with a dodge-and-counter approach that requires you to learn to 'dance' with each foe - learning the patterns in a very structured way that feels at odds with the ultra natural and flowing world. The limitations end up feeling like enemies have a 'correct' way to be killed in spite of your options.The skill tree also feels very messy. Killing enemies rewards food items (portions of their body) and the quality depends if you killed it 'elegantly' or not. Food items fill some amount of the four bars that represent your nutrition, and these bars can be emptied to learn new skills. It's a nice idea albeit convoluted, with quantities being very imprecise so you can't plan ahead (maybe I'm being too rigid now). In the first hour I unlocked maybe 5-10 of these upgrades but they were for small granular things I hardly noticed or for features I hadn't even learned to use a 'normal' way yet so my choices didn't feel very impactful or meaningful. Not that the upgrade tree seems to have any coherent structure either.In the same way my first hour of play didn't feel like I was really accomplishing anything. Part of this is contrast again - the signal to noise ratio on all of the dialogue is mixed. Everything is intentionally obtuse and seems to be style at the expense of substance, you just vaguely understand that someone needs to be killed because they're preventing you from leaving. Even item descriptions are surrealist contradictory nonsense - things 'taste of time' and 'smell of Elysium'. Part of my attraction to the game was that it seemed to have a detailed and cohesive alien world to learn about, but it feels more like everything is being made up as the artist goes. The detail is there because it looks cool not because it's functional, the writing is flowery nonsense because it sounds cool, not because it means anything.In conclusion, I get the feeling Ultros is a result of inexperience. Not that it isn't an impressive looking game - but the level of presentation betrays a lack of fundamentals. There are essential game design elements that are missing or roughly hewn, it's not unplayable but certainly sets up some expectations that miss the mark. I'm sure some folks will get everything out of this they want, but for me it just hit all the wrong buttons unfortunately.
_childDocuments_.name: Ultros

_childDocuments_.review: I'm quite mixed on this one. This game has an interesting take on the metroidvania genre, but it suffers from requiring a lot of patience in order to be able to do actions most metroidvanias already have given you.Experimenting with plants is a brilliant concept, even more interesting when they can be used to create new platforms, allows wall running, or going to a higher areas by attaching a plant head that launches you far away on a tall tree. There are so many things you can do, granted if you have a lot of patience and plant seeds in your disposal to experiment with, and this is where the issue lies.Some plant seeds are located at remote areas, and due to the game's time loop nature, if you forgot to use those seeds, you have to go back collecting them at their respective areas. Some walls are only breakable from plants, but the question is, what plant should you use? You have to consider the geography when choosing the plant; which requires you to understand how the plant works and interacts with the environment, and these requires a lot of patience and experimentation. The one I hate the most is in Greggamoja Refinery, where you have to use a spray ability to bend the stem of a plant so they grow along the flow of water, and it becomes tedious when the gimmick of this region is doing this across the entire region.Other mechanics that require you to use plants are unlocking mechanical doors and allowing current save point to be fast-travel-able. A lot of areas don't have any soil to begin with, but you can feed the enemies so they can tender the soil or even generate new soil in that location. You have to do a lot of work just to be able to fast travel, which is insane really. Games usually reward you with fast travel so you can backtrack for collectibles, but in this game you backtrack to unlock fast travel primarily, then the collectibles.I can see the whole focus of this game is about the nature; hence why a lot of mechanics in this game are tied to the plants. The story is also related to the nature, where you become one with them. You care for the soil, and the nature will reward you. It is an idea that I really liked, but perhaps done too much to the point the gameplay hampers down my enjoyment towards the whole narrative.
_childDocuments_.name: Ultros

_childDocuments_.review: It took a little getting used to post-demo, but I dig it a lot. The gardening mechanic is very cool, but I will be honest that I was a bit put off the first time I got time looped (if you played the demo, it's directly after the end of the demo).Disregard the reviews with one hour of game time pegging this as a rogue-lite. It surely is not.There is a re-birthing time loop mechanic, but it is not on death, and the progression is not rogue-lite esque. It IS a metroidvania with some unique twists- and it is possible that not everyone will like all of them. But if you only gave it an hour, you didn't give it a chance. Your map and exploration, as well as your gardening, is persistent between loops.With that said, you do need to re-learn skills that you've unlocked- done by hunting and harvesting the enemies for different flavors of experience. It is quick to do, and fairly fun. It was a bit off-putting to me at first, but you can 'lock' favorite skills before you time loop, thus increasing your ability to explore and fight each time.
_childDocuments_.name: Ultros

_childDocuments_.review: It took me a while to get into it as it starts slow and unimpressive, not taking into account the dazzling colours. This game is honestly one of the most vibrant visual feasts out there. I wasn't a fun of the it being yet another exercise in loops and rogue mechanics, but good news is, it's short and sweet, therefore, you don't get a chance to get tired of it.When it comes to combat, there's not a lot of it as the variety of enemies is low. It's the bosses where it gets fun. It's surprising as you get a big variety of attacks, but you'll find out why in due time. The controls are responsive, but the aerial combat is hit and miss... mostly miss.As with most roguelikes, there are plenty abilities to unlock and lose an hour later. Thankfully, if you look around, you find a way to memorise them. Very soon losing them is not a bother. Some I never used as I didn't fully use the mechanic to grow food. I can imagine it's essential for the full experience though. Eating is how you regain health and unlock abilities, as each plant has different nutritional values. It's a neat idea.Metroidvania shows it's face by introducing you to an expansive map full of secrets and hidden passages. Exploration is, therefore, a big part of this game. That and platforming. Ultros generally balances multiple genres well and presents some unique an wacky ideas. It's little shocking it seems not that many people finished it.Last thing I want to mention is the music. Simply amazing and different then anything else. When it goes full on jazz at some point, I'm not sure why I'm still surprised.
_childDocuments_.name: Ultros

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to love this game. At first glance and for the first couple hours it seems great, but once you've made it through the first couple cycles the glaring flaws start to show. The devs made some serious design flaws when making this game that really hold it back. For example having to do the combat training sequence every new cycle if you go through the area, which you don't even get to until your third cycle anyway. Why would you have to do a tutorial every new cycle? Being cut off from previous areas with no apparent reason why. The skill tree is 50% useless skills/perks you will never use. And the bosses are extremely ez. I'm on cycle 5 and I've died once. Game is very easy especially if you've played a lot of Metroidvanias.The worst thing about this game though is the exploration. That's one of the best qualities of a gear Metroidvania. In Ultros, all areas look more or less the same with the same color scheme and aesthetic making it really annoying to trying to remember if you've been somewhere or not. You pretty much just have to memorize the layouts or go off landmarks.Hate to give this a thumbs down because it could have been a good game, but due to some severe design flaws I can't recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Ultros

_childDocuments_.review: Ultros has plenty of charm and interesting things going on compared to your typical metroidvania.  It’s a fairly good game with a bit of a niche.  Being underground exploring and dealing with plant life vaguely reminded me of an adventure/exploration game from 2012 called . The first few hours of my playthrough had me quite confused.  I was concerned that I’d find various aspects of the game frustrating, but I just went with what Ultros was throwing at me and things progressed very smoothly.  I’d start each new loop with no idea as to what I should be doing, but the way that the game pushed me in different directions despite me feeling kind of lost was quite clever.  The sound/art is nice, I really dig the colours and art style.  I didn’t find it difficult to distinguish backgrounds from foregrounds and enemies, nor did I have any difficulty tracking my character amongst it all.For better or worse, combat is on the easier side of things. For the most part you just time a dodge (feels like timing a parry in other games), and attack with X + direction, kinda like in Smash Bros.The game wants you to use different attacks on every enemy to be rewarded properly for killing them.  Fortunately you can pretty much do that just by pressing X + a different direction each time.   Bosses look nice enough, but they are total pushovers.  This isn't a game that you play for the combat.As far as the concern from players that hate roguelites (And yes, I'm aware that this game isn't one!), the looping didn't feel repetitive in the way that a roguelite sometimes can. I didn't feel as though I was repeating the same stages over and over.  I felt like I was going in new directions in a persistent world, the feeling is far more what you'd expect from metroidvanias. When I started a new loop, I didn't feel as though I was enduring a great deal of repetition in order to find new ways.As well as acquiring a set of metroidvania abilities, killing enemies nets you plants which you can eat to unlock skills from the skill tree.  ..It is a very small and basic tree.  I think of it as some extra sauce, and not as anything too important.  After the first couple of loops you’ll pretty much have this maxed most of the time without needing to give it much thought.  When you start a new loop, you won’t lose many skills that you care about because you’ll have locked them in with your.. ‘brain thingies’.  You probably won’t have enough ‘brain thingies’ to do that for the first loop or two, but you quickly pick up so many enemy parts to reacquire your lost skills that it hardly matters.  Also on a new loop, and separate from these skills, the main metroidvania abilities need to be reacquired from a specific room on the map, which isn’t much of a hike and didn’t bother me in the slightest.The gardening is an interesting part to this metroidvania, overshadowing the combat and platforming.  You'll grow various plants that can open up paths to new areas.  Each plant is a little bit different, some sturdy ones acting as platforms, others as vines that you can swing on, and so on.  Unfortunately your metroidvania abilities are mostly gardening tools to aid with this.     In the later parts of the game the gardening becomes kind of a finicky puzzle.  You'll need to work out which plants you can manipulate to expand across the map further. It’s tricky to differentiate the plants from one another as they look pretty similar in your inventory.  It actually became too much of a nuisance for 100% completion for my tastes, so i stopped after getting the first ending. _childDocuments_.review: I don't recommend this game but that doesn't mean it's not necessarily a good game. For me, the visuals are a bit over the top for me and make it actually challenging to play to a degree. You can get used to it over time so it's not impossible, but it is a lot - borderline overstimulating, though I do admire the ambitious art.For me, the reason I don't recommend it is because I thought this was going to be a nice metroidvania but it's a roguelike + metroidvania with loops of death and redoing stuff from scratch and replaying the same parts over and over to progress the story. I just am not in any way, shape, or form, interested in these roguelike formats that make you live in a time loop to stretch gameplay and as soon as I realized, after just under an hour, that this was going to be a game where you're reborn and retrace your steps, I was done and refunded it. Not a fan, but good luck if this is your thing.
_childDocuments_.name: Ultros

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, it feels like the combat system would've been incredible if the dev didn't try to force variety down the player's throat. Giving a ton of combat options and letting people experiment with what they prefer (with no penalty) is almost always the best option.I truly wanted to like this game. Despite my short list of good traits, the game really seemed promising, but it fell flat on the most important aspects: the gameplay. A flawed game with beautiful graphics isn't a good game. A game with poor graphics and excellent mechanics will get people hooked. I unfortunately didn't even launch the game until two weeks after purchase, so by the time i tried out the game and realized its shortcomings, I was outside the refund window. Even though I'm stuck with it, this game isn't worth completing, given how many good metroidvanias and roguelites are on the market.

_childDocuments_.review: Ultros is not the easiest game to explain. Not only because it takes its psychedelic identity to heart, even during the few crumbs of exposition; the gameplay is similarly baffling at first glance. You might not get it in the opening hour. Is this a metroidvania? Okay, makes sense. The skill tree is a bit quirky, but interesting. Oh, here's an upgrade. I think I'm getting the gist of it.And it resets. All of your stuff, gone. And that's puzzling, because not only the game is most definitely not a roguelike, it also keeps pulling the rug from under you in terms of gameplay. The loops aren't identical. New mechanics keep getting introduced, upgrades you had on previous loops are given to you earlier or in different locations, and it might take quite a few loops for you to finally start finding your footing on what the game is, what it expects you to do, and how it's all going to play out. Oh, and then it introduces another huge mechanic that will slowly change the way you go about the game.And frankly, as frustrating as it might sound (and is), it's part of the beauty of Ultros. It's a puzzling game. I like puzzling games, sometimes. Especially when they have beautiful artwork and soundtrack as this one does, together with a vision for what it wants to be. How it presents itself, the story it tries to tell, all of it is coherent and alluring in equal measure. And I have to say, the ending is nothing short of beautiful.But it also has to be said that Ultros is not the most tactile game I've ever played. Inputs often feel less than tight, and plenty of its mechanics require a precision that borders on frustrating. The skill tree is reductive and, due to the loop gameplay (and upgrades that let you keep the skills between them) are so easy to unlock it becomes almost a small inconvenience.The major mechanic of Ultros involves planting seeds and waiting for them to sprout. This is important both for traversal and for another gimmick that gets introduced later in the game. This, while innovative and (to me) kind of addictive, can be extremely frustrating because first, you need to have the seed you want in your inventory, and second, you need to use the correct one (or a good enough one) and fertilize it if need be. This will have you running around the map for seeds, resetting loops, working towards making garden spots appear and sometimes wild guessing on what could work in this particular spot. Busy work.This can be satisfying, but if all you want is a relaxing metroidvania with regular incremental upgrades to give you that dopamine rush, Ultros is not it. Ultros is demanding, taxing and sometimes monotonous. You know, like gardening.And like gardening, if you put in the time, you'll see it bloom. There is something amazing about the way it subtly, but definitely, makes the player change the way they play the game. It's not forced on you; it evolves naturally from understanding it. Mindlessly beating the flora and fauna to a pulp is never the best option, as the game looting system demonstrates from the get-go; but eventually, violence itself will be a last resort. You'll find yourself much more concerned with more peaceful endeavors, something that beautifully echoes the message of the game.I heartily recommend Ultros. It is a game you'll remember, if you have the patience for it. Just be prepared for less than satisfying gameplay and more than satisfying most everything else.

_childDocuments_.review: I was absolutely enchanted by this one. The orchestral soundtrack, the vivid colors, and the cosmic mystery provided a unparalled, captivating experience. While there were many QOL and mechanical frustrations, I navigated past those thorns to enjoy the delicious fruit at the center of this game. The best video game ecology I have experienced by far.

_childDocuments_.review: It is with a heavy heart that I give this a thumbs down. It's absolutely gorgeous and has some truly inventive ideas, but they never really jell into a complete experience.Combat is fussy and unsatisfying. You've got a huge arsenal of moves to learn, but enemies are either practically or actually immune to all but a handful of them. I never felt masterful, but I also never felt outmatched; fights have a kind of graceless, flailing quality to them. You fight less and less as the game advances, and enemy spawns can even be removed from future loops with the right tool, allowing you to remove combat entirely. Managing nutrition was interesting and clever, but with the mycelium I could just save my favorites and not have to worry about picking them up again. This whole constellation of systems feels vestigial, like the game used to have a bigger focus on battles but didn't have the heart to remove them as the focus changed.Gardening is a fascinating idea, but fiddly in its execution, and it comes too late in the game to feel like the core part of the experience it wants to be. Plants and flowers don't always grow in ways you expect them to. Compost to grow them further is a limited resource and can't be recovered if you find that it doesn't fix your problem. Grafting and bending is incredibly slow and tedious. I wish that these mechanics were available closer to the start of the game and more central to the gameplay; relegating so many interesting mechanics to late-game completionism is a truly tragic waste.I admire the craft that went into the visuals and sounds. The illustrations are unique and compelling, and the live orchestrations set the mood flawlessly. There isn't another game out there that FEELS like this one. Unfortunately, the half-baked gameplay got in the way of appreciating the art for the whole time I was with it. I can't even recommend that you just buy it and try it because the experience you'll have in your first 2 hours is completely different than your experience at the end of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Ultros

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game more than I did.I'm a big-time Metroidvania player, so this game held a lot of appeal to me because it offered some unique takes to the genre.  The beginning of the game is the strongest aspect - it has a certain focus while encouraging exploration, sort of like a Castlevania game. As metroidvanias go, the early combat is tame, almost relaxing. But... as this game goes on, the combat becomes entirely de-emphasized, and exploring becomes more and more convoluted and aimless. The idea of connecting a network of trees is unique and cool; but, the execution is less than I'd have wanted. I got about 10 hours into the game before I got so bored that I just quit playing. I wish I could've stuck through it, but frankly, I just didn't have fun.Pros:+ Great and unique artwork+ Great soundtrack, it sets the atmosphere perfectly Cons:+ Lacking focus, changing genres essentially once you hit the mid-point of the game+ Connecting the network becomes a tedious chore+ Combat can be clunky, but is generally overly easy+ Doesn't quite feel like a true Metroidvania
_childDocuments_.name: Ultros

_childDocuments_.review: This game is one of the coolest things I've ever seen. The art direction is pure genius in every aspect - visuals, writing, sound design. The art is just absolutely stunning, the writing is a word salad of technobabble that usually means nothing at all and somehow that just *works*. There's plenty of unique and interesting concepts in the game design as well, from how you level up by consuming nutrients you get from food harvested from enemies, how that food degrades in quality from hitting the same enemy with the same attack more than once, how the back-tracking inherent to a metroidvania is rephrased as a loop mechanic... I think this is an instant classic, it's amazing, and I honestly can't wait for people to start speedrunning it.

_childDocuments_.review: I HIGHLY RECOMMEND ULTROS.DO NOT i repeat DO NOT listen to any 1 hour reviews of the game claiming its a rogue lite/rogue like. the art is absolutely breath taking and yes, it has SOME features that are common in rogue lites but this is a metroidvania through and through. exploration, is fun and unique because of the loop system, every loop opens up much more of the map, and if you pick the correct upgrades you can even explore places you wouldnt be able to without otherwise mandatory abilities.  fun game, dont listen to uninformed reviewers.

_childDocuments_.review: The demo was great. The second loop was not great. Exploration is directionless and every room feels the same. I have no idea what to plant in any particular spot and the game isn't giving me any clues, environmental or otherwise. This is a problem when there are limited resources. Combat is poorly implemented. Dodge windows are very inconsistent and there aren't nearly enough combat options to justify the "variety" system. The game gives you no feedback on whether your attacks are varied enough until the enemy is dead. I wish the devs had leaned into the gardening aspect and skipped combat entirely. There are so many ideas here that it feels like five games jammed together, but none of the concepts are fleshed out enough to be compelling.

_childDocuments_.review: The art and soundtrack are definitely the highlights. Probably not a game for everyone, but I had a great time. I got both main endings in about 24 hours- and this included me wasting time. I've gone back for a couple achievements and might try to 100% it someday, but it has a satisfying ending that doesn't require you to get 100%. I found the way it blended roguelike and metroidvania elements interesting. The combat is ok and stops being relevant about halfway. There is a big shift in how the game plays about halfway through which isn't like either genre. Because of this blend it doens't really feel like a roguelike or a metroidvania to me. If you're ok with a game that has very little explanation and want a unique experience then I recommend it. If you go in expecting certain traditional metroidvania or roguelike standards it might be disappointing.

_childDocuments_.review: While Ultros’ visuals are beautiful and music outstanding, the gameplay didn’t hook me. The games combat is satisfying, but the lack of difficulty and enemy diversity doesn’t sell me on it. This issue compounds as the story requires you to loop over and over, going through the same areas and fighting the same enemies, and re-earning the same abilities/perks. To try make up for this they have a farming activity, where you find seeds that grow various different plants, each plant opening up possibilities for shortcuts upon every repeat. However if you plant the wrong seed, you can’t dig it up until later in the game, meaning early game you’ll find yourself wasting these seeds over and over. The farming system feels tedious in design. You can also lock in a small portion of your abilities/perks (to keep them on reset), but neither this nor the farming system mitigates the tedium of restarting. Backtracking/re-exploring feels even worse due to the movement system; there isn’t really any fast way to move through the map, with sprinting tied to continuous running, and all momentum being stopped as soon as you bump into anything, or roll. It’s not even strong as a platformer, with little to no environmental hazards (none that I’ve see so far).None of this is to say Ultros is a bad game, just that it’s not for me. If you’re going in expecting something akin to Blasphemous or Hollow Knight, you’d be sorely disappointed. The movement/combat in those games feels a lot tighter, and there is more emphasis on platforming. Ultros feels more akin to an experience, as you take in the music, atmosphere, world and its unique visuals, and is best treated as a casual game. If that appeals to you, I heavily recommend it, it’s just not for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Ultros

_childDocuments_.review: Metroidvanias are one of my favourite game genres. Roguelikes have never really appealed to me as I don't like the idea of restarting over and over again. Ultros, however, piqued my interest due to the visuals, the good reviews, and the rogueLITE element, which I thought could be a good middle-ground for someone like me who loves metroidvanias, but has never played a roguelike.Unfortunately, this game just wasn't for me. I did power through and complete the game up until the credits rolled (took me around 11 hours), but I just can't recommend it for those who like metroidvanias, but don't like roguelike/roguelites.First the positives. The visuals are soooo good! The trippy colourful world is so fun to move through. The plant life pops and the changes to the world that slowly happen every 'cycle' are always fun to notice. The score in certain areas and during certain boss fights can be really cool too. I did like the overall idea for the story, even if it was a little confusing and not amazingly executed in the end.So on to what I didn't like. Part of the issue is that it's not reeeeally a true metroidvania in my opinion. It definitely has metroidvania elements - progress, get something new, unlock new area etc - but it's only a metroidvania in that very basic sense. There aren't really abilities to unlock that make game play more interesting, or traversal more fun, or make you want to backtrack to find new things. There are unlockable 'talents' but these are very basic in nature and make very little difference to the overall game as a whole. There are also no in-depth choice mechanics like charms/gems to alter game play or upgrades to weapons/skills so generally feels pretty shallow. In addition, the lack of things to collect makes it feel like there's no benefit to exploring.The game is also very repetitive in premise. There's a central area where Ultros is located, and your objective is to destroy 7 incubators throughout the world and return to Ultros after destroying each. Every time you destroy an incubator you gain something that usually unlocks the next area/incubator, however you need to return to Ultros first, and every time you do it 'resets the cycle' (basically turns back time) and you effectively restart the game and lose all your items and abilities. You then need to return along the same starting areas, fighting the same enemies, regaining the same abilities... it just feels very tedious. The 'resetting' mechanic, whilst making sense for the story being told, really adds nothing to the game in terms of fun or interest.The main issue of this for me is that it just felt hard to get invested in character progression when every 1-1.5 hours your character gets a hard reset.There's also a major mechanic of the game when you need to plant seeds to grow plants. The type of plant that grows is dependant on the seed you plant and you need specific plants to overcome certain obstacles or progress in certain areas. These seeds however are not always readily available, meaning you may need to do a lot of backtracking and searching, especially since you lose these seeds every cycle. You may also need to use compost on these plants for them to grow better and some take more than one cycle to grow. It's just very tedious and in the end I just couldn't be bothered with them, only doing what was absolutely necessary to progress. I just didn't enjoy this mechanic at all.Combat is very basic too. There a sort of interesting mechanic, where if you kill an enemy with different combos they drop better loot/items, but after a while you just ignore it and hack your way to victory spamming the same button - it makes minimal difference - meaning combat leaves a lot to be desired. It's also compounded by the fact that the enemies are far and few between with no real interesting mechanics to counter or adapt to.Anyway that's my two cents. If you're in the same boat as me - you love metroidvanias, but aren't a fan of roguelikes/roguelites - then this won't change that and I can't recommend it.
