_childDocuments_.review: It is now almost 10 years since this game released and it still holds up.I played the game from day 1 and it has been a refreshing concept back then and somehow still is.The idea of parkour + zombies works really well, mix in a good enough combat system and you got yourself a game that can be enjoyed for hundreds of hours, it somehow does not get old.Graphically speaking it still holds up, the game looks pretty good to this day, however I would have loved to see some more graphic options to disable certain parts without editing the "video" file (if you do this then the game will not allow you to join VAC secured lobbies iirc)The Nights are actually difficult, since you are not expected to fight, but to run. And if you do decide to fight, you'll most likely end up dead before the sun rises. Where in Dying Light 2 you can just waddle on and on in the night and kill Volatiles with ease.The Story is not bad, but it felt longer when I first played it xD It took me roughly 20 hours when replaying the game, yet it felt like maybe 7 hours max lolThe character development of Crane is decent, going from a corpo ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to being on the side of the survivors and doing what helps the locals.However I wish his infection would have played a bit more, kinda like how Dying Light 2 does it.Controls feel better than in the sequel, however you will sometimes fall to your death and think to yourself "I should've hit that.."Not to mention being downed in this game, if you get stunned on the ground by a bigger enemy you will lay there for like 3 seconds, which allows you to get combo'd like hell.Zombies can be very tanky in this game, surviving like 3 shotgun shells to the head for some reason, they also are super aggressive with grabbing you, something that is handled much better in the sequel imo.Another annoyance is how grindy the skill tree can be, having 3 skill trees is fine, tho by the time you reach lvl 25 in one of them you will most likely already have completed the game and a good chunk of the side quests.Weapons having durability is fine, it makes sense considering they made Dead Island before, however they do break very easily, even with the perk to make them last longer. The game has a variety of melee weapons and ranged weapons to choose from. Guns are loud and attract runners, but can save you in a tight spot, or being stealthy with a pistol equipped with a silencer, melee weapons can be upgraded and modified which gives a lot of combinations to slice through hordes of infected.Or maybe you wish to go in with a bow and arrow to take them down, whatever floats your boat!Dying Light 1 is better than Dying Light 2 in my opinion, it plays better, runs better and the scenery is much better than "2 destroyed places"I know that Dying Light 2 plays more in the future, but I would have loved to have more than just "destroyed city" and "destroyed old town"Dying Light 1's Slums and Old Town look great and - while both being a little small - are fun to explore and re-explore.Not to mention that Dying Light has a brilliant expansion; "The Following", which is a new map, story and amazing ending(s) in the size of a pretty big DLC, the map of The Following is amazing, I love the buggy and the upgrades to it, etc.

_childDocuments_.review: The game has much going for it; you can make the experience your own. Blast your way through hordes, sneak around and snap some necks, plant traps, lure your prey into them... or just drop-kick them... I like to drop-kick the zombies... Story-wise, there is nothing groundbreaking here. It's really just your typical zombie outbreak where further mutations have created a variety of threats for humans to deal with— think "Left 4 Dead."There's a lot of DLC for the game, and it may be tempting to pick up the whole shebang, but I can only speak to some of that. I've only played the Bozak Horde DLC, and it was more of an interesting challenge than anything else. I've heard that the DLCs, in general, aren't anything to run home about, but I'm only 30 hours in and have just cracked the surface of the base game — though I've beat the main story and some side quests. You may want to get the base game first and see how far you get and whether or not you enjoy the game enough before deciding if you will expand it further. Overall, if you're looking for a zombie game that gives the player freedom in how they want to play the game and don't care for innovative storytelling (just average storytelling), this is worth a try.  Rating: 8/10P.S. I have never played the sequel, so this review is influenced by nothing other than the original game.

_childDocuments_.review: I slept on this game for far too long. Wife and I have been playing nonstop, it's such a good co-op game. You follow the same story, but can easily split up for side quests or just to mess around for a bit. Just enough looting and crafting to be fun, without really being too much of a distraction.The gameplay wasn't quite what I expected, it's a lot of platforming, melee combat and a truly compelling story. As you progress in the game, there's a lot of shooter elements and the DLCs are fun distractions (e.g. a timed dungeon). You can approach some quests/puzzles in different ways, which can be fun.If you're on Linux, don't bother with the native binary and enable Proton Experimental instead - this will install the Windows version, which is actually kept up to date. A bit unfortunate that they did originally ship a port, but it's performance is terrible and it's not kept up to date with the DLCs etc. However, once you swap to Proton it runs really well (6800XT, Debian 12). Also, I play with a PS5 controller and it feels really solid.Overall, this game has been a ton of fun so far (I'm about 30% into the story).

_childDocuments_.review: What a memorable game! Just finished it together with The Following expansion. I can't believe I've put this game on hold after buying it on release, because it scared me a little bit too much at that time (I'm not an horror, jumpscare, type of guy). What a mistake! Yes this game can scare the ♥♥♥♥ out of you sometimes, but everything else is just too good to pass on. So here I am in 2023 playing this game and being amazed.So many times I told myself : "what a game, and it released in 2015?!", and "wow, this was so ahead of its time". Honestly it will probably end in my top10 games of all time.- It is made with pure love and passion, with so many attentions to details be it visually, sound, atmosphere, characters, lightings... some examples: ambiant noises inside houses (wind going through, wood cracking, steppings on materials, opening fridges), or in cities with screaming pain, wind going through trees, water waving, ...- The sound design is AMAZING, it contributes a lot to the immersion,- The gameplay is so smooth and fun, jumping, gliding, sliding, climbing, slashing or shooting... it's done exceptionnally well,- The story is great especially if you're doing all of the quests, honestly it might be one of the few times I have been doing ALL of the quests without being bored, as the lore expands through it and you get to know what are these survivors doing, even with some characters connections you learn about,- Scavenging is fun because exploration is greatly rewarded (rare enough in games nowadays to mention it), usually open worlds are filled with junks everywhere just to articially increase game-length,- The views! So many times I have enjoyed the views on top of building, truly again, it's due to the game atmosphere and attention to details,- Zombies actually feel menacing and going out at night will prove to be a BIG challenge (it's dark, zombies are tough and numerous), planning is key or you're out for troubles, it's one of the better Zombies games there is,- The support from the devs years after release, releasing most of the updates for free or super cheap,- The Following settings are great and again, you feel the love the devs put into their game, the plot is so good and ends very well the chapter of M. Kyle Crane, I have loved how they've told this story more than the main game. Honestly it's been so greatly written. You get everything from the main game minus the constant parkour & big city layout,- The musics are beautiful, intense and memorable. The main theme for both, the main game and the expansion gives me chills,- The game is smooth, running at high FPS, and I had 0 crash.- Honestly sad about the expansion's car / lack of buildings. It's the parkour that made the main game more enjoyable. Luckily the settings and the stories(not just the main plot) of this one compensate. But I didn't really enjoy having to ride a buggy, I felt like playing another Far Cry :D- Some jumpscares made on purpose. Yeah I know that's not really a bad thing to some people, but it's the only bad thing I have to say ;)It's honestly a one of a kind. I don't think I have ever played a game with so much attention to details. In this type of game where the immersion is key, it is so important. It is definitely not a zombie shooter as I have seen people judge this game harshly for what it is not.

_childDocuments_.review: Got this game when it was around 18$ for both the game itself and the DLC, and played both single player and 2-3 people in the entire party.It's only worth that price tag, and nothing more in my opinion- it has the polish of a good game, but the gameplay is frustrating as hell.If you have motion sickness, this game is your worst nightmare. It gets super grindy at times, and the level progression is so absurdly slow that you WILL most likely look up videos of how to cheat the leveling system. Parkour makes no real difference to the game once you get the grappling hook. As you can save yourself mid fall or legit hook yourself from building to building like Batman. Why parkour up a building when you can look up at the edge and Batman yourself up to it, skipping the entire experience. (These aren't normal buildings either, these are near 5-6 story buildings).The parkour mechanic is also wonky as hell, sometimes you grab a ledge on the top of an office building, only to turn around randomly and leap right the hell off. Having the grapplehook can save you in these situations. But its a system you really need to get used to, as you need to aim your camera straight at what you intend to grapple, making for frustrating gameplay at times.Combat. Is. Frustrating.You will learn to despise Virals (running zombies) with every ounce of your being, as they flat out prevent you from using guns outside. Your guns are restricted to areas only containing human fights or inside buildings where you know they don't spawn, because outside- they spawn infinitely, spawning 3 every time you shoot a bullet. Not only that: They. Can. Dodge. Melee. Attacks. CONSTANTLY.Zombie grappling is the most unholy mechanic they made for this game. I understand why zombies would need to grab you, but they can latch onto from clear outside your melee range, and they do it so incredibly fast that you will always instantly lose health because of it. Your weapons can also permabreak. You have a machete for example, but when it loses full durability you have 3 points to spend to repair it 3 times, but once you run out of repair points, that weapon is flat out useless. It makes it difficult early-mid game to find a weapon that reasonably does enough damage to last you a long time. Why farm for good weapons when they will break an hour or two later and you can't repair it anymore? Plus the weapon upgrade is perma as well, meaning if you get a mod and apply it, you can't remove it. So unless you save your best weapon for those 3 super upgrades, your going to be running with a high-tier weapon that only does a fraction of what it should.----Minding this though, there are some good points. Crane as the main character is the single best thing in this entire game. He is single handedly the most relatable character in all of gaming, not caring who he's talking to and even telling annoying people to f-off and shut up. It makes for a great character with and awesome personality, making the story worth playing and listening too.Late-Game combat is rather fun. Swinging a Katana and chopping off 3 heads at once is super fun, and eventually you get enough money and ammo where you can freely use guns (even when virals keep coming) in most situations. Overall the more powerful you get, the game goes from frustrating to actually playable. Overall, its a 3-4/10 experience for me. I got half way through the story before I was so frustrated with this game that I flat out just grinded the rest of the story and DLC (which has disappointing endings by the way) and immediately uninstalled.

_childDocuments_.review: I completed the entire Dying Light story via "other playable means" - I got this copy during the free weekend just to see how well it has aged. Not disappointing, but not exceptional either: 6.5/10.DL is your ye ol' zombie chompie game, with unremarkable hordes and horde kinds, shoot-em-up expectations, and a heavy focus on stamina-based mechanics and an unsurprising skill tree. However, the parkour - oh I could hug and kiss and spoon the parkour all night.First person parkour is the most exhilarating experience you can gain from being a dude in a game. Prototype? Bam, alien-bite superpowers make it go from nyoom to nyoooooooom. Uncharted? Bam, a single grappling hook is sufficient for the experience to go from a cover-based shooter to a rope-based shooter. Spoilers: this game  because it is a good game.With world models being used alongside first person cameras, DL goes from excited dogrunning to excited dogrunning with weapons. And flying! But not a lot. But still. Meh. I mean I ca-Dying Light is a well-crafted first person experience. Be THE generic dude to save a city by being an errand boy. Encounter a generic bald-headed antagonist that is crafted like the blend of Far Cry 3's Vaas and  Metal Gear Solid V's Skull Face. _childDocuments_.review: ~~RANT, NOT REALLY A COHERENT REVIEW~~Dying Light starts off as an interesting take on actually being afraid of zombies but having the advantage of mobility over them. For the first third of the game, it uses this idea really well and makes you feel like you're playing something really special. The slow parkour, the weak weapons, the constant scavenging, this makes the game very good. If somehow this element of uniqueness stayed prevalent throughout the whole game, I feel the overall scores would be higher. As such, it does not.The main problem with Dying Light's gameplay is that the crafting, parkour, and combat elements become way too easy by the 2nd half of the game, a.k.a Old Town. By that point, you are one hitting most enemies, dropkicking undead off countless rooftops, and destroying mini-bosses. While this is fun in its own way, it is brain dead fun. It isn't fun for the specialty or for even playing Dying Light, it is fun because you are playing something else.Dying Light's combat was, again, very interesting at first because there wasn't very much of it. You were running and climbing ledges like that fat kid in gym class. Narrowly avoiding quick infected and diving and weaving past obstacles while being chased by Nightcrawlers is very fun. Once any of these enemies can be quickly dealt with, it loses that sort of fun. Sure, using parkour and mobility in fights can lead to a bigger advantage and potentially more fun factor, you soon realize that this weapon you got earlier before this fight can deal with your problems just like that.Dying Light's components are not original. Almost everything in the game was made by someone else, or in Techland's case, even brought in from a different franchise, *cough* Dead Island *cough*. What makes it fun is the way Techland decided to combine them and use them to make a fun game. The only sort of original feature is the hunter to prey mechanic that is advertised quite heavily.Every now and again I boot up a really underdeveloped save to relive that shock and intrigue and hype I felt when I first played this. If it sounds like I hate on Dying Light, I don't. I really liked Dying Light, even the 2nd half mostly. Like with most games, I guess after playing 144 hours I can say that I feel it could've went in a different direction. A different direction that would've, for me, made for a better game.Dying Light could've been a totally different game, one more focused on actual survival and scavenging, that sense that you cannot take on an entire zombie horde, that at most times, whether day or night, you are being hunted, yet you do not know it.~~END RANT~~

_childDocuments_.review: Dying Light is an open world adventure horror game, developed by Techland and published by Warner Brothers, releasing in January 2015 for PC, PS4 and Xbox One. This game sort of came out of nowhere, it didn’t have very much hype behind it prior to release and it came as a welcome surprise to a usually quite month of the year for big game releases. The game play in Dying Light reminded me so closely of Dead Island. You play in first person view as you explore the world. Of course, the world has been overrun by zombies. One of the changes to the “Dead Island” gameplay style is the parkour system. We have seen parkour systems used in games such as Assassins Creed and Shadow of Mordor, but Dying Light’s version knocks them all out of the park. A third of the gameplay is based around the running and jumping across the landscape – you are able to hide from the zombies when you are jumping rooftop-to-rooftop so it is really in your interest to get to grasp with it as soon as possible. There are times when you will be thrown into the combat situations; this is where the Dead Island mechanics come in – melee weapons are going to be your primary source of damage and they work exactly the same as DI. Your weapons take durability damage each time you hit, but you can repair them on the fly with the required parts. Once you get your hands on a gun, the odds swing dramatically in your favour, but you do get the downside of the noise it creates, and it possibly attracting even more zombies to your location.  One of my favourite mechanics Dying Light introduced though would be the dynamic day and night cycle. During the day time, zombies will act in their usual manner, whilst they are still a danger, they can definitely be managed fairly easily. Once it is night time though; boy oh boy, you better have your running shoes on! The zombies transform into a much more dangerous form, they can sprint, and see a lot further away, as well as their heightened sense of hearing – meaning you will find it very hard to by-pass them.  The day night cycle lasts for about 70 minutes in total, about one hour in daylight, and 10 minutes at night. Graphically, I am very happy with the quality of graphics on show. I was nowhere near able to push out the game on 4k, even on the menu screen my frame rate plummeted, and I even struggled on 1440p, so I had to make do with just 1080p with all of the settings ramped up.  The lighting effects, explosions, and scenery all look absolutely stunning. Textures are all high resolution and the animations of everything in the game are faultless. Whilst there is a lot of animations that can be annoying after the first few times, such as when you open a chest, you have to wait 2-3 seconds whilst the animation plays out of you opening it; personally I would have liked this to be skippable but it is a really minor issue. Dying Light starts out in a very easy fashion, allowing you to get to grips with the game mechanics, and the tutorial at the start of the game introduces you to the game very well too. The parkour mechanic can take a little while to get used to as sometimes you will probably fall whilst climbing buildings because you aren’t used to the way it works and feels, but it just takes practice. The only time I had real issues with the combat difficulty would be the later stages in the game, when you are just getting hammered by hordes of zombies over and over again. Little tip; conserve your ammo!!!The vast open world you are playing in very rarely leaves you with nothing to do; there are tons of side missions, collectables and loot to find. There are over 100 different melee weapons, and they can be modified in different combinations (over 1000 of them!). The side missions do seem a little but samey after a while. I completed about 13 or so out of the 44 before I finished the main story and this was because they are very repetitive. A few other optional objectives consist of finding relief packages which is where you race the opposite faction to get a supply drop, saving survivors from the opposite faction’s men attacking them, and the same for zombies. You can also go out of your way to find collectable items such as trophy’s and notes around the world. Completing the main story and about a ¼ of the side missions has taken me just over ten hours. Right now I don’t have a dying urge to go back in and complete the rest of the missions, purely because of the repetitive factor, but I will be keeping Dying Light installed so that I can in the future as well as the anticipated DLC which will be releasing soon. The devs have reports that with all of the current content in the game, you should be able to push 50 hours. I struggle to believe that, I would say you can get about 20 hours out of Dying Light at the time of writing this. I didn’t have any technical issues. The game ran very well at 1080p at a steady 60 fps, the only time it dropped sub 60 was in extremely hectic scenes with hundreds of zombies and lots of explosions but that is to be expected. I played the game with keyboard and mouse, and should be strongly recommended you do not attempt to play with a controller.To sum up, Dying Light is a really nicely done zombie adventure game. Personally I feel it is a much more rounded off game compared to the Dead Island series, and adds plenty of depth to the genre rather than re-hashing content that’s already been done before. The main story and core gameplay mechanics make’s Dying Light one of the standout games to be released in 2015 and I would strongly recommend this game to any open world genre fans out there. 1) Stay away2) Not Recommended3) Only recommended when on sale4) Recommended6) This is a must playIf you found this review helpful, please consider giving it a thumbs up. You can also find more reviews over at

_childDocuments_.review: An open world, parkour based zombie survival game with crushing close quarters combat, awesome scripting, and great production values. I should love this game--But I don't, after giving it a couple chances I concluded with great reluctance (as I said, I really wanted to like it) that despite all the things that Dying Light has going for it, it is missing the most important thing a game has; fun game play mechanics.The parkour, with a notable few exceptions is just running along roads, and jumping on a bus when your character gets tired.The combat? Bashing a partially decomposed and severely malnourished zombie six to nine times in the head with an enormous pipe wrench only to have the PIPE WRENCH break. Yeah, don't get me started on the durability system, everything in this world with the exception of the zombies is (apparently) made out of cheap plastic.The quest scripting is interesting, but consistently ruined by frustrating follow-ons. A quest  that should be completed in an hour inevitably turns into an all day affair of traversing the same routes through the city as you run (often ridiculous) errands for the NPC that gave the quest. This makes it hard to portion out game-play into satisfying chunks for those of us who have to get off our butts and do real life stuff.In summery: frustrating combat, repetitive parkour routes, and bad quest scripting ruin what I wanted to be an incredible game.

_childDocuments_.review: Dying Light is a zombie game that focuses on atmosphere and player movement. If you have played Dead Island you already know the basic mechanics; craft melee weapons and bash zombies while collecting supplies. But Dying Light employs numerous changes that improve on this.Atmosphere is perhaps its best asset. The day-night cycle is a crucial component, as there are major changes to mood and gameplay as the sun sets behind the horizon. At night, the tension elevates as you experience reduced visibility and face zombies that are nimble, fast and deadly. You will be tempted to venture out at night for extra rewards. During the day, you battle hordes of shambling zombies that are fun to eviscerate with a broad selection of weaponry. The difference between night and day provides a genuine rollercoaster ride.Parkour movement makes navigating the world immensely enjoyable. You are able to run, jump and climb over buildings with ease. You just look at a ledge and hold the jump button to climb. As you come upon zombie hordes you analyse the area quickly. Do you attack or use the environment to avoid danger? Various slides and kicks make dealing with zombies, and human foes, quite interesting. Traps placed around the world can be triggered to slow pursuers or distract zombies, giving you an edge as you learn the world around you.The single player is surprisingly entertaining and lengthy, with side quests that are often better than those in the story. Characters are well-defined and memorable, with more effort given to justify the game world. You run between areas, clear safe zones, rescue people and collect items. Story missions might even feature shootouts in indoor levels. Progression comes via a skill tree that unlocks significant character upgrades. You will also learn to craft items like Molotovs and flares to make you more formidable against the various zombie types.Dying Light is also a cooperative game and playing with others is easy. The basic cooperative action works well, aside from rigid animations, and you can undertake just about every quest from the campaign. You can even open your game to a 'zombie invasion' where another player joins and takes the role of a dangerous night-hunter zombie that can instantly kill survivors with a pounce. Your goal is to destroy zombie nests before you lose a certain number of lives. Whether playing alone, or with a group of four, this versus mode is actually good despite its relative simplicity. It gets hectic when four players are battling tougher zombies and running all over the open map while being pursued by a night-hunter that can summon exploding zombies. Dying Light is a terrific zombie game that greatly improves the core mechanics from Dead Island. It emphasizes the world and how you move around in it. The changes between day and night are refreshing and memorable. There is a healthy amount of content that will provide dozens of hours of entertainment in solo or cooperative play. Dying Light mixes intriguing elements to craft a zombie experience that is entertaining, atmospheric, visceral, and frenzied.

_childDocuments_.review: “It was perfect. Perfect. Everything. Down to the last minute details.”Dying Light is a game that is never going to be lost to time, its simply just impossible to forget to those who hold it in high regards. I've never truly enjoyed a game so much as I have this one. Techland managed to nail everything that makes this game so great. The scariest sound design and atmosphere I've ever experienced and a beautiful and diverse setting, with amazing contrasted day and nights. You go from vibrant daytime, to one of the best sunsets in gaming history, all the way to one of the most terrifying, thrilling nighttime experiences to-date. The story, though considered by some to be mediocre, isn't as in depth as some other AAA games, but it still delivers and engaging story line with characters you don't just sit there and hate, they nailed the one thing that makes video game characters great, being "real". If you've never played this game please do, not only will you get likely close to 50 hours of main/side content, playing 1000s of hours is a very do able goal between repeatable "end-game" content and a story that you find yourself *WANTING* to replay. This game has become a staple for me and I can't go more than a year without replaying it, I hope someone else finds this game and enjoys it just as much as I have.

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE: Reach the second map. Quit and uninstalled the game after a dream sequence followed by a boss fight where they prevent you from using any of you equipment but a machete.Some notes on my review, I payed $20 for the title and have all DLC. I played exclusively on hard mode, never touched anything else. I played 17 hours solo at time of review. I only used guides to find police vanes on the map and when trying to figure out how to cross the bridge otherwise played blinded.First of all let talk about something that impressed me about this game and that is how well it handled alt-tabbing. As a user that frequently tabs out to change music, turn on netflix, answer emails and of course bring up guides I was very happy to find that the game doesn't suffer any issue while doing so. The game alt-tabs out quickly and returns just as fast without hitching or stuttering. I also noticed no problems alt-tabbing while in loading screens, which cause alot of games problems. Alt-Tabbing ability is a 10/10.Fast load times for an open world game, I am using a Samsung 850 Evo so your milage might vary, I am usually in the first load screen for about 5-10 seconds. All subsequent load screens are near instant. Also loading after death is instant allowing you to get back into the game right after consumption by zombie. 10/10Lets talk about game flow. This game flows a standard open world zombie formula. There are lots of zombies, you gather supplies, you can craft items (primarily weapons and medkits), fallout 3 style lock picking, first person parkour system, trap activation, safe house clearing, quarantine zones that act as pseudo-arena and range/melee combat. Dying Light features no thirsty/hungry meters and only has health, stamina and weapon durablity as perameters to manage. Weapons can be repair but only limited number of times. Stamina is regain by waiting. Health is regen small amount naturally with large chunk being recovered over time by using medkits.Zombies, Zombies, Zombies. During the course of the game the primary enemies you will face are zombies. They come in several types, most common as the slow walking(occasionally, jogging forward) zombies. The fast moving 28 Day later zombies with the ability to climb structures. This zombies are normally handled by simple using the parkour system and traps to escape the horde. You rarely feel threatened by them and the normal infected as essiently unable to the kill the player who is being vaguely cautious. Most death to these zombies come from trying to press your luck or ingaming in trap baiting or combat for fun. Otherwise they are mostly teethless.Outside of that we have the standard Left 4 Dead special infected. A few large high health tanks, spitters and boomers(minus the attracting goo). The special zombies only occasionally require a change in tactics. With running away being a fairly safe tactic in most cases. With the exception of the Volatiles, which are basically hyper fast hunter zombies. They move faster than you and deal extreme damage. While the tactic of running and avoidance still occurs when encounting Volatiles the franctic and immediate pressure of escape make these encounter the most enjoyable. As the player try desperately to jump building to building, change direction constantly to break line of sight, and avoid certain death.Crafting in this game is simple and to the point. Supplies were plentiful in hard mode and I never had trouble crafting what I needed in the moment. The game allowes the creation of new melee weapons and melee weapon mods. Because of the limited number of uses melee weapons have and the number of hits it take to kill zombies, even with mods, made the crafting system unrewarding to invest in, I never felt attached to my weapons or creations. I usually end up using basic weapons as electrifying weapons or adding poision damage didn't make a noticely difference to the combat for me. As of 20 hours in I haven't found very main weapon blueprints and of the ones I do have none of them add much to gameplay for me.The craftable throwables suffer from the similar problem as the melee weapons, simply being too weak taking nearlly 20 throwing stars to kill some enemies because of this I mostly stick to the tactic that works the best, firecracker(noise maker) and molotovs to kill most hordes of zombies. This leads to a rather boring but effective strat of throw firecrackers then molotovs till the horde is cleared but then that begs the question why bother? when running and avoidance is more effective then fight.Finally we have firearms. There extreme rarity in the early game makes them increabiliy important in early encounters. I remember finding my first hand gun with 10 bullets. I know exactly where I put those 10 bullets. 5 went into bandits to clear an early mission and the other 5 went into a tank like zombie who was guarding a supply crate. When faced with tough enemy I had to make a conscious decison to use my bullets here or not. The uncertainity of how long it would take to find more ammo and the pressure to make each shot count add tension to the game and made firearms feel right. However this tension is thrown out during a story mission 1/3 the way through where I left the mission with 8 rifles in my backpack and maxed out ammo for pistols and rifles. After that ammo wasn't an issue to gather for me. I still mostly use the ammo on human enemies and super zombies making ecounter that are clearly designed to be difficult a 5 minute walk in the park.Next I need to address the parkour system which is focused on 1 button, space bar, much like Assassin's Creed. Like all games that feature a single button doing too many tasks you will run into an occasional problem but over all the system works well when you are free running in the over world. The system involves either hitting space bar to jump or holding space bar and looking at a ledge to grab. Often the character grab ledges outside of what is preceived to be possible to grab(i.e. grabbing a ledge a clear foot highier then his make jump). This leyway with ledge grabbing allows the games parkour to be forgiving however sometimes the character will fail to grab some ledges, air conditions, while grabbing unintend ledges like, window seels, this creates an occasional inconsistent feel when trying to be precious with your free running. I have discovered in my time playing it is often best to just follow developer intended path through areas (stair step roofs or duke of hazard style ramps) to traverse the over world.I wanna take a brief second to discuss the lockpicking. Lock picks are plentiful and you will never run out. It does a fallout 3 style lockpick system but it is real time, no pausing. If you loath this style of lockpicking prepare to cry as it is used in several story missions, usually done will surrounded by zombies, and is used to acquire guns, ammo and supplies from various caches. I would call the lockpicking a major game feature since it appears so often. I would have liked to see more innovating ideas or features attached to lockpicking. Maybe skills or a different style as the Fallout 3 style is nearly a decade old and the game uses a carbon copy of it.Finally lets talk story. Its a standard video game story mode featuring simple motivations, cardboard cutout quest givers and black/white morality. Stuble isn't a language present in Techlands story department with the evil guy being a standard issue sadist and the good guys being underdogs who just wanna help. You got hotheaded younger brothers, sister who are forced to become parental figures, double crossing seen from a mile away, and you, player characters the hero(aka errand boy) of the whole country. Luckily all of this can be skipped by hitting your trust space bar.Despite flaws and critisms I can't deny the game is fun and enjoyable. What other meteric do you need to rate a game on so thumbs up.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is definitely a riot and it deserves to be played on the harder difficulties. The human enemies on higher difficulties in late game however seem way too tanky, taking over 10 arrows with multiple to the head to bring down. Progression through the skill trees is highly rewarding however, with virals being a really big threat early game and in late game they are still a threat but you have more tools to deal with them. All in all, it has some of the best atmosphere I've experienced in any game, especially at night with the shifting weather effects and the outstanding audio design which keeps the experience tense, even if you do have many means of escaping if you're caught at night. _childDocuments_.review: For it's concept it seems like a really cool game, Dead Island but with Parkour were my first impressions. Unfortunately though this game misses the mark with bad combat, clunky mechanics, and droning exposition. If you have the patience to hit an enemy 6 times, break your weapon, repair it, hit them 3 more times and then get grabbed by that enemy and stun locked to be killed by 1 other zombie, then this is the game for you. Not exaggerating, that literally happened to me on normal mode. I got 2 teamed 10 hours in by the most basic enemy the game. For a parkour game the fact that you need stimulants to perform any meaningful traversal is disappointing  to say in the least. Opening any kind of container having it's own animation is also really annoying. I've been hit by enemies while opening drawers that I wasn't able to simply walk away from.Accepting a fetch quest also shouldn't take 2 minutes to explain. There's med supplies over there. Go get it. That's literally all I need. I don't care that your daughter who I haven't met is sick and might die because she got cancer before coming on vacation to this weird place. Just tell me what to do. I don't need the life story of an NPC I'll never interact with again.Cool idea. Not fun.

name: Crypt Custodian
detailed_description: Crypt Custodian is a charming metroidvania/zelda-like about cleaning up the afterlife. You play as Pluto - a mischievous cat who has just died, and landed in the afterlife's palace. After a brief and disastrous meeting with the Afterlife Guardian - Kendra - you are banished from the palace and sentenced to clean... FOREVER!! Explore the vast grounds that surround the palace, battle beasts with your trusty broom, and gain new abilities to expand your map. Solve puzzles, discover secrets, and… organize an ambush to break back into the palace! A Charming Cast Of Characters Meet and befriend all the other bad ghosts who live outside the palace. Learn how they died, and what caused them to face eternal banishment! And then head on over to the local haunt- The Sinner’s Inn- to chat with the ghosts you meet, and upgrade your gear. Tons of Upgrades Complete puzzles, battle epic bosses, and clean your way through ruined dungeons in order to collect new upgrades and abilities. Customize your play style by mix-and-matching your upgrades, and use the abilities you collect to expand your world. A Lively Interconnected World Traverse a vast landscape with secrets hiding at every corner. Form your own path and discover the afterlife’s many secrets at your own pace.

_childDocuments_.review: I recently (within this year) completed Islets, another game from Kyle Thompson. The week after I beat it, the trailer dropped for Crypt Custodian and I knew I needed it. Just like Islets, this game is adorable and engaging, with fun mechanics and it seems like a ton to do. I love the world and the characters and while I'm not very far into it yet, I feel like it's really important to support small developers doing really, really exceptional work. This game feels very polished and extremely fun. I've played exclusively on my Steam Deck and it's the perfect deck game. tl;dr if you like fun mechanics, cute stories, and metroidvanias, plus supporting the little guy, check this out.
_childDocuments_.name: Crypt Custodian

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first game I've played where I made extensive use of the "assist" options, and though I had mixed feelings about it at first, I'm glad I did. I really liked the atmosphere and exploration in Crypt Custodian, which to me are the best parts of a Metroidvania. On the other hand, I have a rather low frustration tolerance for pattern-memorization and bullet-hell-type dodging, so when I got to the first boss, I wasn't sure I was going to keep playing.But I still wanted to explore, so I switched to easy difficulty and gave myself extra life, and eventually beat the boss, even though it still took a few tries. After that I switched back to normal difficulty and life, and just turned off fall damage. I kept up that pattern for most of the bosses, though I did manage to beat a couple on "regular" settings.And then something odd happened. I tried Boss Rush mode on "Easy," and found that the first boss wasn't as difficult as I remembered. After several tries, I managed to beat it without taking damage. "Huh. I bet I could do that faster." And I did, until I was fast enough to get S+ ranking. So I went up to "Normal." And then "Hard." And pretty soon the boss that I had so much trouble with the first time around was completely trivial. Which I certainly would not have anticipated going in.I guess what I'm trying to say is, "Thank you to the developer for making a game accessible on my terms. In doing so, you also made me reconsider my own capabilities and what types of games I might enjoy."ANYway. If you're still reading this, thanks, and buy Crypt Custodian already. It's well worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Crypt Custodian

_childDocuments_.review: Each game by this dev feels better than the last, while still retaining a lot of the same feel and vibes.Like Islets, this game is very smooth to play and explore.  There's paths branching out in every direction and it was pure dopamine uncovering every last room and collectable.  If you're struggling, there's a shop where you can pay to reveal a missing item or important location to visit.  It is very easy to 100% the game because of this.  I got stuck on one puzzle and one cryptic bit at the end though, which I had to look up, but otherwise I was able to figure everything out pretty easily.  The only QoL issue I ran into was that scrolling around on the map screen was too slow.The pet owner in me loved the cutesy pet-centric storytelling, it was wholesome and at times sad.  The plot had me wondering what was  going on too.I wasn't fond of the composers work on the previous games but he's finally won me over with this title, with plenty of chill tunes that stuck in my head.I'd recommend this to all fans of metroidvanias & Zelda-likes, it's one of the best games to come out this year for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Crypt Custodian

_childDocuments_.review: A first look:At first, I was a bit afraid it might have been too hard, but I've been doing surprisingly well on normal. Yet the nagging feeling that I'll get stuck somewhere soon rose again. Then I discovered it has a lovely range of accessibility options that make it pretty much so anyone can tune it to their taste, making it as hard or as easy as you like. I was in heaven—no pun intended!This means I can enjoy this cute game to bits in my style and feel, aka just laid back and enjoying it to the fullest. I would have already thumbed it up just for that, but there is so much more to it.The fact that I can turn off photosensitivity is a massive plus for me, too; ever since my brain tumour surgery, I have been a bit sensitive to flashing, especially when I'm tired or having a bad day. Now, I don't have to interrupt my gameplay or flee for a while when it acts up, and I'm so thankful for that. It has to be said that the art style and music are amazing, too! The characters I've met so far are super charming. Kendra, for example! She gave me a few laughs, so calm and collected, while casually banning friends to the afterlife. Totally normal, no biggie! I think she secretly wants the whole palace to herself! And it's not only their personality but also their design and style that I like a lot. It just all feels so delightful, and I'm here for it. And Pebbles is so cute, too. It all excites me to meet everyone else (and their stories)!Of course, the hoarde... euh, I mean... The collector in me is very satisfied, too, since I already found a few of the collectables, and I'm thrilled to search for the others. I hope I can find and collect everything! I can't wait to see what other abilities I can acquire and collect. The puzzler in me is super happy, too; they're enjoyable. This whole game has been, so far, actually.And don't even get me started on the hack-and-slasher within me. I got a broom, and I can slap it around like there is no tomorrow, which kind of got me in trouble in the first place... But I think it's fun to have something else for a change, then yet another sword. Plus, it kind of really fits my janitor role, huh?But for now, I'm back to exploring since I have RL stuff to do soon and want to spend as much time as possible in the game until then since I won't be able to return for a while.
_childDocuments_.name: Crypt Custodian

_childDocuments_.review: Crypt Custodian is the perfect cozy game while still leaving room for challenge. While other metroidvanias try to implement ways to make convenient features work through charm systems Crypt Custodian opts to not waste your time with needless grinding or equipping of such features. I love that I can fast travel from the start by opening my map from ANYWHERE and selecting a fast travel point and POOF I am there. I feel like my time is being respected.  I've defeated two Major bosses, saved a couple cats and made friends along the way. The humor is refreshing and the world is mysterious. I can't wait to discover what lies beyond what I've already uncovered!

_childDocuments_.review: The Thompson Brothers have outdone themselves with , their third outing. For me–and I love –this is the greatest Metroidvania game I’ve ever played. You can read through my detailed list below if you’re interested. All that I can express to you at the top here is that playing this game was the single greatest gaming experience I’ve ever had. Buy and play this game immediately if you like Metroidvanias!Here’s my breakdown advocating for  as the greatest game ever made:Game Controls/MechanicsEverything about the gameplay is incredible. Combat and platforming feels extremely fluid and responsive. Look, you can warp to a save point at any time in this game, but moving around and exploring the underworld felt so amazing that I skipped on using fast travel a good chunk of the time. It’s that good!AccessibilityBetween this title and , Kyle Thompson is killing it with accessibility features. The almost granular approach at which you can adjust the difficulty settings ensures that everyone will have an enjoyable experience. In a game that’s all about gatekeeping on multiple levels, Kyle has been so thoughtful when it concerns the player’s time and quality-of-life specs. Every game should have the fine-tuned accessibility features that Mr. Thompson provides in his welcoming Metroidvanias.Art Style/MusicFor me, hand-drawn video games are where it’s at. Sure,  and  are striking and beautiful, but their aesthetic is one of literal darkness. Trying to navigate through such dim/murky biomes gives me a headache sometimes. Kyle Thompson can create dark and gothic backdrops too, but his art style and animations are unmatched in the industry. The ultra bright color saturation that Kyle has basically trademarked in all of his games is simply gorgeous. All of the animations are crisp, sharp and beautifully rendered; truly a visual feast. And Eric Thompson’s musical scores are phenomenal. He manages impressive versatility with pieces that shift from whimsical, ambient, pleading, somber and spirited. The melodies are infectious, too. I found myself repeatedly humming certain biome scores after finishing some sessions. Both Kyle and Eric have left recognizable signatures in their artistry, and I am totally here for it! Check out Eric’s sky battle composition from  standing in for the gated battles in . And there’s nothing more pleasing to my dopamine hitbox than Kyle’s light-shattering spiral effect that blooms across the screen every time a character gets an upgrade. The Thompson Brothers are true masters!Metagaming GeniusWhat sets Kyle’s projects apart from every other game on the market is that he continuously subverts player expectations when it comes to interacting with modern gaming tropes. He clearly understands genre requirements, the role of NPCs, how UIs work, and all the rest of it. But all of Mr. Thompson’s games like to play tricks on us in the best way possible: by going against the formulaic nature of video games. He knows we don’t like grinding for currency, even though a certain NPC shopkeeper has set some nightmarish prices for items in his store. As the game progresses, though, you’re relieved to discover that grinding won’t be in your future play sessions because of a surprising narrative twist. This is just one example of Kyle’s metagaming genius. Mr. Thompson likes to bring us up close to the pitfalls of gaming that we’ve all come to expect in the Metroidvania genre, only to suddenly change the mechanics/narrative of the gameplay. Sure, the joke is always on us, but I love it!  is so refreshing and engaging because it knows how to manipulate our game sensibilities in the most delightful way possible. Quick shout-out to “Ghost Slaughter 3,”  the best metagaming boss fight that had me laughing for days. Pure genius!The StoryIf the controls are stellar and the level design is innovative, I think the last element that makes a great game is the story and  definitely delivers. Kyle Thompson’s absurdist comedy and sarcasm are spot on, and the character interactions/dialogue are highlights in all of his games. But this installment elevates the humor and unexpected plot developments, and the payoff is huge. Yes, the humor is tremendous here, but I was also moved by the other characters’ backstories (the photo section of this game is so beautiful and devastating, holy cow!). When the game was over and I had unlocked everything, the themes of the story really struck me as being subtle, powerful and very timely. Yes, the critics always write that Kyle’s games are charming, and they are. But this game has a level of subtext to it that allows for so many interpretations, and I find that remarkable. I think Mr. Thompson is going for something deeper with , be it messages about stereotypes and assumptions or exploring the importance of empathy. But that’s all surface level analysis. I won’t share my interpretations about the characters or the story’s conclusion, but I will say that the larger themes are dark, complicated, and political. None of this bad, by the way. In fact, it’s the opposite. Putting vitally important issues into a video game can be tricky. I understand that a game’s legacy doesn’t want to be known for being preachy or having an agenda. But the best video games out there have very strong messages, and they tackle uncomfortable issues–but they accomplish this through subtlety.  has a very strong moral center, and I believe that it has brilliantly coded messages buried deep within itself that are left for players to unearth. I will stress here that these are my thoughts and opinions; they are not the thoughts/opinions of the game developers. Anyway, I think it’s sophisticated storytelling that’s riveting, satisfying and poignant. You add fantastic humor back into the mix and you get, in my humble opinion, the greatest video game that’s ever been made.I’m so happy that I live in a world where this game actually exists, and that you can play it right now!

_childDocuments_.review: Crypt Custodian is such an awesome Metroidvania. One of the best I ever played. None of the achievements are missable, there are 3 very challenging achievements. I guess that completion takes around 14 hours.  14h+ 7/10 1 You don't need a guide No No No No Yes, in "boss rush" mode the time in which you defeat each boss matters No No Yes, but only for 1 achievement in "boss rush" mode NoYou're a cat and just died at the beginning of the game., You get sent to the afterlife where you first will be judged on your actions to determine if you go to the temple or are doomed to clean the afterlife forever. On your journey, you'll meet a lot of other ghosts and learn about their lives and how they have been doing down here. Crypt Custodian is such a great Metroidvania with a lot of quality-of-life features. It is one of THE BEST Metroidvanias I have ever played. The movement feels so good, the abilities you unlock are fun and the system to choose which power-ups you want to have active and the amount you can choose between are just awesome. I'm very impressed with Kyle Thompson's work. The game feels so responsive and the combat/movement just feels good. Furthermore, the game looks so good as well. I fell in love early on in the game already with the presentation and how the movement felt in the game, but my love for it only grew from that point on. You have a map on which you can mark with symbols things you saw but couldn't reach yet, but you even don't have to do that. There is a specific jukebox in the game that will sell you map markers and that way even if you didn't find them yourself it is very easy to clean up all the side objectives later on. Another amazing QoL feature is that you don't have to be at a warp spot to warp to somewhere else on the map. You can just open the map in your menu and warp to any warping spot. And it feels like there is always one close by. This helped during the game but also when cleaning up after beating the story. The achievements in Crypt Custodian can be separated in 2 groups and none of the achievements are missable: - 45 of them are for finishing the story and finding everything. As stated above, this is quite easy at the end of the game after finishing the story by buying map markers. That way you can easily see which items you haven't found and where to find them. There is one challenging puzzle on the NorthWest side of the map, but you might want to look around in your menus to maybe get a clue on how to solve it. - The other 3 achievements are for boss rush mode. You have to beat boss rush mode for every boss on S+ on every difficulty. This is a real challenge and tbh.. I wasn't able to get S+ ranking on easy on the first boss, let alone later bosses and higher difficulties. However, I know I'm not good at games and normally don't even try stuff like this. So I'm not a good indicator of how hard this really is. I give Crypt Custodian 4.5 out of 5 stars.

_childDocuments_.review: Crypt Custodian is such a great new game from Kyle Thompson!  About 10 hours to 100% main game, it has way more to explore than you'd expect. _childDocuments_.review: Crypt Custodian has been a really great game experience, of the kind I have craved for for a while. I was seeking for a Metroidvania that I would enjoy playing with a history that would move me. Promise kept!Of course, the gameplay is not really inventive, but it does its job (very) well. The controls are pleasant, the bossfights represent a decent challenge, and the upgrades are satisfying. It is a well-done Metroidvania.The quality of life is also quite impressive for such an indie game. As a boss fight enjoyer, I am always disappointed when there's no boss rush to extend the duration of the game. Crypt Custodian provides a very nice one, simple to navigate, with a decent amount of challenge to get the maximal grades for each level of difficulty, You can skip much dialogs and cutscenes by pressing Y, and this is really appreciated when you try and retry the bosses. You can adjust the difficulty anytime (I recommend to set it to the maximum and, if this is too challenging, to adjust it until the game represents a fine challenge for you. I have played maximum difficulty all along, and it is not insurmountable, but I would get that players less familiar to this kind of game or who just want to enjoy some nice visual style while wandering prefer to avoid tryharding). Also, you can buy some markers for your map when you are out of leads to make progresses in the game (in-game backseat, so to say, but only if you want).But the main reason that kept me so late at night in front of this game is the visual style and the atmosphere. behind the cute design of Crypt Custodian lies a melancholic but also heartwarming tribute to our beloved pets. As simple as it was, I really was stirred everytime I discovered what the life of the animals I met was before they passed away. I also feel that there's an innuendo about the impact of human activities on animals, given the backstories of many characters. But maybe it is not the case. The music has this kind of Adventure Time Vibe as well: The world seems cartoonish and goofy at first glance but it really holds some depth if you take the time to explore the world around you. And maybe I'm the softhearted kind, but I had my tear to the final cutscene.Crypt Custodian does have some flaws. And the negative comments I've read covered them quite well. The regular mobs are not really a threat and have very similar moves, the level design might be considered too convoluted, which made it boring to some people who played. I also agree with one criticism about the use of the abilities, some of them are highly contextual and will be of no use in places that have not been made for them. To add to this, I would have enjoyed more music. They really have the kind of vibe I enjoy and there was simply not enough of it (e.g., one song per boss would have been so great). I also found weird the fact that some cutscenes/dialogues in the boss rush modes can be skipped, but not some others.  However, I really think these negative aspects should not dissuade anyone to give this game a try. There's much love and work put into it and it deserves to be appreciated. Much games that yet benefited from more resources do not even compare to that. Please, give Crypt Custodian a try!

_childDocuments_.review: This one requires an informational review, because the game comes with some potentially unexpected design decisions for the genre and presentation. So what follows won't be glowing, but hopefully helping you decide if this is for you. You start with exactly 4 hit points and can only ever upgrade to 5. Health is only replenished at save points and little fountains in between. And the majority of challenges are all about taking as few hits as possible. Be it the general game play, where you can only take 4 hits in a boss fight or between landmarks - or one of the many different bonus challenges like curses that lock your ability to heal until you've defeated a certain number of enemies (while adding additional hazards) - or chests that ask you to defeat a gauntlet without taking any hit whatsoever. The difficulty setting only affects enemy attacks (reaction times and patterns) as well as how tightly timed optional platforming challenges are. "Easy" is by no means actually easy. (conversely, "Hard" doesn't make the game much harder)Only the assist options will actually make the game easier. Here you get up to 200% attack damage, 3 extra hit points, no fall damage, and more leeway on timed challenges. (I forgot these options existed until now - but definitely recommend using them, if you are struggling on easy - hell, these might be the better settings to use in general, so you still get to experience more attack patterns) You always have fast travel to any visited save point available on the map. Health replenish points have infinite uses. You cannot walk off ledges. No hit challenge chests replenish the one hit point you can loose from them on a retry. You can speed up and skip death animations and cut scenes. Map markers for both items and quests can be bought (although item markers require that you have uncovered the respective room). Boss fights are always very close to a save point. There is an upgrade that can disable falling damage outside of boss fights. And outside of boss fights and combat challenges that lock you onto a platform until you have defeated a wave of enemies, you can easily ignore and sweep past all threats. (at least in easy mode - this is how I completed the game 100% in exactly 8 hours getting the majority of achievements except for the defeat 1000 enemies one) And there are probably more details like this. The amount of care taken to streamline everything is astounding. And from what I can tell, absolutely every feedback from the demo was taken into account without compromising on the intended design. Your goal in this game is to make 10 friends. And while the very first one may suggest the formula is one per area and defeating the areas boss will somehow make them your friend, the game actually shakes this up significantly beyond that. First of all, while the characters do have their main area, they will still appear all over the map. And making friends is not always tied to the boss fight. (those do give you required abilities though) Speaking of boss fights, I really like how uniquely the majority of the boss characters are tied into the narrative. I think there are only two that feel like they are just a random unique enemy you only fight once, without any relation to the friends you are making.Dashing around the map and the dash and jump attack feel really good.The game has a speed run mode. (auto skips all dialogue and adds a timer)It unlocks a boss rush mode the moment you defeat the first one.And it unlocks a randomizer mode on completing the game. (shuffles all item locations) The game unfortunately very quickly felt somewhat bland beyond the first area. While every area does have a new look, new enemies and new mechanics - it still all seemed mostly reskinned or very single purpose. It's been challenging to figure out why I got that impression, but I'll try to nail down things that contribute.Every room in this game is floating islands. I imagine this is very much needed for the kind of platforming challenge the game intends to deliver (you can easily swoop out and back onto solid ground to cut corners and avoid attacks), but never being boxed into physically closed rooms certainly added to every area feeling like a reskin of those floating islands.There were only 3 boss fights I remember as mechanically unique. (Spoiler for those:) All the others (many many more) were just bullet hell damage sponges to me (and I imagine the extra attack patterns on higher difficulties will further drive that home - I didn't have the patience for that).New area enemies are largely variations on their basic versions: melee, ranged (targeted or omnidirectional), flying and jumping. Apart from the area where all enemies share the unique mechanic of the boss, the challenge always felt the same. You never defeat enemies with something other than whacking them several times. (there are no weak points, pushing/reflecting/blocking interactions or required combat abilities)And all the abilities you get are mostly single purpose to cross larger gaps and gain access to new areas, which then often let you hit a switch to lower a gate or extend a bridge, rendering your ability unnecessary there in the future. This is good in service of smoothing out traversal, but it also speaks to the abilities not being very fun to use repeatedly. For most of them there are no clever ways to use them in combat or combine them with environment mechanics other than their intended ones.(there are upgrade perks and special attacks to find, purchase and equip besides the main abilities - but all of them only alter the mechanics in small ways such as changing your attack damage/speed or adding projectiles to your existing moves - I always opted for anything that made me faster)The only ability that can be used in more than one way as well as in combat requires you to hold the attack button to charge it up and later does not allow you to choose between an upgrade to it or the original (also very useful) behavior when used over ground. Because of these limitations I ended up not using it very much, even though it is the best among them. (aside from the dash, you get that one first and it feels so fundamental that it's easy to forget it was an upgrade)Alright, I think that covers most of it. It is a very well polished game. Everything works exactly as it should. It achieves what it sets out to do. So I can fully recommend it, if you like what you see on the store page and the details I described are either exactly your jam or won't stop you from having a good time.

_childDocuments_.review: * The artstyle is really nice and some of the music is very engaging. I especially like the challenge room music.* Many upgrades that you can mix and match. These meaningfully change the gameplay as opposed to just applying a small bonus to some stat. * The atmosphere is nice and cosy* The combat is simple yet tedious with no environment interaction. There are some upgrades along the way, but in the end you still have to wail on even the basic enemies for too long. Since there is minimal reward for killing enemies you can just run past them, but often times a random attack will get you and remove one of your precious few lives. Special attacks exist, but there are mostly two that are strictly better than the others so there is little use for switching to different ones since you can only have one active at a time.* Enemy variety is weirdly minimal. There are lots of different looking enemies, but they all seem to be formulaic combinations of one attack trait plus a movement mode. There are jumping, flying and running enemies and they either shoot projectiles at you, do a short range area attack or an explosion of spikes around them. Sometimes more than one of those together. This makes the individual enemies pretty forgettable and boring to fight.* Tedious Leveldesign. The rooms feel like they have been assembled out of very basic tiles. Every biome has it's own tileset, but they mostly differ in look not in function. This makes every biome feel very samey apart from some biome specific but often underused puzzle elements. This gets worse because the individual biomes feel pretty big while not actually containing that many interesting things apart from some challenges and a boss. * Underused abilities. Some of the abilities that you collect have only very specific usecases and while they can be activated outside of those usecases they have no other utility or are too slow and weak to be useful.* Lacking reward structure for bosses. There are quite a few bosses but they often pop up suddenly without buildup. After defeating them sometimes you gain a new ability, sometimes a new friend and sometimes just nothing. The friends don't have mechanical impact so often times there is neither a form of emotional connection to the boss nor a reward for defeating it. They are just a roadblock. * Not a fan of the trend towards bullet hell style difficulty. Boss battles can be quite challenging but mostly because of the amount of projectiles on the screen. Similarly to the regular enemies bosses are mostly mix and match from a set of basic attack patterns. * Some of the music was very jarring to me due to the high metallic sounds used and short loops. Very uncomfortable to the point I had to turn it way down. This may well be a personal thing though. * Lots of challenge rooms. Either as a gate of progression through the map or for a reward. These I mostly dislike because the combat is not very interesting and they feel overused to me. The combat statues, challenge chests and curses were very repetitive to me. * projectiles often travel only slightly faster than walking speed and continue indefinitely which means you sometimes get hit after defeating an enemy or by an off screen enemy.
_childDocuments_.name: Crypt Custodian

_childDocuments_.review: Crypt Custodian is not the best Metroidvania you'll ever play. It's combat is very plain, and I found myself not very interested in the world or characters. I think the areas you explore have neat concepts that are explored well, but accompanied with upgrades and abilities that are too situational to see their full potential. However, I do think Crypt Custodian is better than the sum of its parts.While there are elements that are sometimes weak, the entirety of the game is still a good time. Crypt Custodian is a chill Metroidvania and excellently paced. Its not too difficult and yet you're always making progress and seeing new ideas. I blasted through most of the game all of the way to 100% completion and never found myself getting stuck or too lost. It was honestly refreshing to play a more simple game that's focused on you wandering around and having a good time. Would recommend to anyone looking for a laidback adventure that still provides enough challenge to be engaging.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good metroidvania. The world feels almost too open--not entirely sure at any point what's the next location, I keep running around wherever seems interesting and there's often something new that isn't locked. The writing is cute and funny.Combat is not very fun, which is kind of a problem for a game where you're constantly murdering things. Mostly the enemies throw a bunch of bullet hell at you and you either dodge through it or jump over it while you're trying to melee (and mostly it's just bash-bash-bash-dodgebash). Everything is just a little loosey goosey with the sprite hitboxes unfortunately, plus there's no healing whatsoever except at campfires(!!). On the other hand, there's zero penalty for deaths and the ability to teleport to any campfire at any moment. The end result of both these negatives and positives mean that combat is kind of a chore that doesn't ever matter that much. If you're really bad at it, you may have to take 4-5 tries at a boss, but the retries are so quick you won't notice.The story is also kinda weird. Maybe I missed something obvious, but I did not see any explanation of why there's a bunch of random enemy mooks and bosses in the afterlife? I get that we're in the bad part of town, but there's at least a dozen ghosts that don't want to murder you on sight, so.. why do most of them? Or are the baddies manifestations of garbage in some way? I honestly don't know--the fact you're killing the ghost population seems to go entirely unremarked by your friends.All in all it's fine!

_childDocuments_.review: One of my favourite Metroidvanias of the year — and I've played more than a few. I'd recommend Crypt Custodian to fans of either genre, as well as to fans of Bullet-Hell-Lite experiences.

_childDocuments_.review: Another excellent metroidvania style game from the dev here. Despite the camera perspective change up and a different style of platforming, it still is one of the best out there. Fast travel to save points (from anywhere), optional markers for missed collectibles, challenging curses, charming characters, satisfying smashing of stuff, frogs, I dunno what else you really want. Some of the fights definitely stray into bullet hell territory which isn't my favorite thing but I still managed to have fun (it's probably why Sheepo is my favorite of the 3, because no bullet hell, but still they're all amazing).In my opinion all 3 of these games so far should be quintessential examples of the metroidvania genre. They do so much right and don't forget what makes it fun like a lot of other games.If I had a criticism of this one, I would say I felt like the characters and dialogue in Islets was more fleshed out and enjoyable - it's not bad here, just feels like there is less of it.Edit: I wanted to edit to just emphasize how amazing the level design is. I did things way out of the seemingly "default" order but it wasn't through any cheesing or sequence breaks, it's just you often can go to one of several biomes and go about your business there. It can be fun going "back" several levels with the upgrades you get as you just fly through platforming and puzzles.

_childDocuments_.review: A very fluid top-down metroidvania with a sharp focus on exploration and small combat arenas that reminded me of a mix of Zelda 1, Hyper Light Drifter and Death's Door (among many other potential references) The game's main strength is how freeform player progression can be, as many paths are available at any given time, and the game supports figuring out new pathing through a speedrun mode (and later allowing to shuffle some upgrade locations).Traversal is very fast and pleasant thanks to an array of motion skills that chain well into each other (as it was with the developer's previous title, Islets). Most rooms are simple to solve but the process remains engaging throughout, thanks to an enemy attack design that keeps you in motion at all times and some occasional conditional battles, such as "don't get it" or curses that you lift by meeting specific criteria for rewards.QOL is laser focused on keeping you in the flow at all times, with fast travel between all unlocked points always available, no penalties upon death and generally no loading screens (anything resembling a non-playable sequence can be skipped). The atmosphere is poetic and soft, a lighthearted children's tale with pangs of melancholy, and while the narrative is light, the aesthetic is striking with well differentiated vistas, beautiful colors and cool animations.Performance on Deck has been excellent throughout with no hitches of any kind, and achievements are mostly exploration based, apart from the three tied to the buss rush mode, which feel slightly overtuned for S+ ranks.The whole feels lean and elegant, "simple and effortless" even though game development is anything but, and that's the best testament to how good the game is. If you enjoy top-down traversal challenges and dash-avoid based combat, you'll find plenty to love here.

_childDocuments_.review: Crypt Custodian is a top-down metroidvania that surprisingly ended up among my favorites in the genre. The difference in perspective from the typical sidescroller is used extremely well here, and this is a full metroidvania and not just something that takes small elements from it. The exploration is top-notch, taking elements from top down games separated by overworlds and dungeons like 2D Zeldas or Hyper Light Drifter, but combines that in a very unique way with a more open flow between areas. You'll be exploring what feels like a closed off dungeon, and then suddenly a side path opens into a wholly new dungeon, and then you find more areas connected to that. These also differ from typical top-down dungeons in that they're not one-off locations, there is a lot of backtracking as you unlock new abilities, which thankfully is never too tedious with being able to teleport to checkpoints from anywhere.Combat starts off simple but evolves very quickly and does enough to stand out in this area as well. While individual enemies are almost always very easy, most encounters combine them and juggling a lot of enemies and projectiles on screen gives a very light kind of bullet hell experience. A small but very notable feeling bit of design is the lack of a healing system, you get a set amount of life at each checkpoint and that's it. I enjoyed this a lot, it makes even simple encounters something you have to pay attention to how you approach. There's also an upgrade system that works a lot like the charms from Hollow Knight, but you notably can get a lot more slots for them than in other games I've seen use this system, allowing you to experiment a lot more rather than just sticking to the most powerful upgrades. Boss fights are quite fun and there's a good amount of them, my only real complaint with those and with the combat in general is that boss HP is a bit low even on the hard difficulty, people experienced in this type of top down action game will likely first try a lot of them, and it's easy to burst down a boss without seeing its full move set. There is a boss rush mode where you can refight them, and I am interested in replaying it with self-imposed challenges to up the difficulty, but it could do a bit better there with the built in difficulty options.The pacing of the game is a real strong point as well, you're constantly seeing new areas, enemies, mechanics, and abilities. Those abilities are really unique feeling as well, you'll see the typical metroidvania signs of jumps you can't make and walls you can't get around, but almost always the ability you actually get here isn't what you'd expect, which I found really cool. There's a lot of interesting challenge rooms as well, including plenty of one-off fun ideas, very nice variety there. The game doesn't overstay its welcome either, it took me around 9 hours to get 100% completion, and the amount of backtracking to clean up missing items at the end was very manageable. I liked that length a lot, as it allows the pacing to stay snappy and no area overstayed its welcome. Overall had a fantastic time with this. It kept surprising me throughout my time with it, and I have very little in the way of complaints at all. Exploration and combat are both great. The story and characters are cute and simple, does a nice job of adding to the game without getting in the way. One of my favorite metroidvanias and I've already recommended it to my friends.
