_childDocuments_.review: I've started and restarted this review quite a few times, because I'm having difficulty putting my finger on what I don't like about Dungeons and Degenerate Gamblers. It felt off from the first few moments I played, and that feeling only continued as I kept playing. There's a sense of clunkiness to the controls (I'm on Deck) that made a bad first impression, but the loose threads continued to unravel.I think the thing I think is actually bad is, sadly, the core gameplay loop. Man, it's just tedious. You're fighting through two layers of RNG (your own deck and your enemy's deck), and, especially with different shield and healing effects, it can be quite a few hands before either you or the enemy takes any meaningful damage. This can make fights, even with low-HP enemies, drag on for a while if you can't manage to get a good hit on them while they're bust, and it causes the pacing of the game grind to a halt. Unlike other deckbuilders, like Balatro or Slay the Spire, you're not really making decisions about what cards to play - in D&DG, you only hit or stand, and that's a much less interesting decision matrix than most other games in the genre. You're just hitting Button 1 or Button 2 without much thought, waiting for your RNG to align with the enemy's RNG so the battle will end and you can continue.I also don't think the deckbuilding aspects are very good. I distinctly remember the first time I came across Card Sharp, or Demon Form, in the respective aforementioned games; there was a distinct "OH, this is SWEET!" feeling to discovering cards, jokers, and relics in those games. I'm not really feeling any of that in D&DG; most of what I've seen so far in terms of buildcraft falls on a sprectum of "kinda useless right now" to "hmm, okay". There's no real wow factor to the decks, or the chips, or the cards. I tend to believe roguelikes live or die on the quality of their items/cards, as that's what provides both variety and excitement in a run. So far, D&DG has not impressed me on this front. I know I haven't played very long, but I kind of feel like I've experienced all I need to experience. I give props to D&DG for having an original idea in terms of the fundamental mechanical loop, but I just don't think that loop is very good. The moment-to-moment play is meh, the deckbuilding is meh, the AVFX are kind of meh too. I'm a huge fan of roguelikes/lites/whatevers, so I'm very predisposed to like this game, but D&DG just did not hit (blackjack pun) for me. It's a lot less impressive than its genre peers in pretty much every respect, and, considering you can play those games pretty much forever, a new game has to offer something really striking to warrant playing. I didn't get this spark playing D&DG, so it's back to the tried-and-true games for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Great concept and you can tell that a lot of care went into this game. That said, from a mechanics and gameplay perspective, on release this still has a lot of balancing and reworking left to be worth your time + money.Check out this list below instead of this game:BalatroSlay The SpireCobalt CoreGriftlands (Underrated)WildfrostMonster TrainInscryptionDeckbuilders live and die by their synergies and giving the player meaningful decisions to make. This game does not have enough synergy to allow the player to consistently find decks that are fun. Specifically, there are not enough things to do with advantage which is one of the only non-rng mechanics the game provides. Moreover though there's just not enough cards that go together well and you don't have enough opportunity to find those cards.One example of this is that you can't see what choices you will have before you make them, i.e. Slay the Spire's map.Basically, this game is Blackjack, but more frustrating because you feel like you should be doing better and should be able to manipulate your deck to find fun builds, but you can't. It's not the player's fault. There just isn't enough opportunity to find the fun in this game.

_childDocuments_.review: The game has a cool vibe. The problem is that the core gameplay mechanic (pvp blackjack) misses what makes blackjack fun. The adrenaline rush in standard blackjack comes from doubles  and risky hits. In this game there is no doubling, and the risk/reward is so skewed that risky hits (hits that might cause a bust) are basically never worth it. So essentially it plays out as an ultra-cautious version of blackjack.

_childDocuments_.review: Firstly, you don't build a deck, you just toss cards into the wind and see what sticks. It's blackjack. There's no strategy involved, you're letting the deck play itself. The other cards you add don't really do much except either add or subtract to the underwhelming feeling of 'strategy' the game provides. To add, there's so much RNG that if you want to have a strategy you never actually get it:Want to do a hearts build? Want to build something with advantage? There's too much RNG in this game to warrant any sense of valid of strategy to the point to where if you're facing down opponents with actual decks, while you have a hodgepodge of cards that somehow 'work', and then you bust. If I wanted to slog through a 1.4hr session of literal brainrot copypasta for a straight hour because we're just trading cards back to back and not progressing anywhere, I would rather play against 3 stax players in a mtg commander match at my local tcg and hate my life that way. _childDocuments_.review: Chaotic, unfair, extraordinarily fun. A true old-school roguelike, not every run is winnable, not every fight is fair, but by playing carefully and well you can stack the odds (mostly) in your favor. The way so many zany mechanics interact over a simple premise is incredible. Do you have a good head for numbers, patience for rng, and like carefully reading mechanics and theorycrafting? This is the game for you.If you get mad easily, give this a pass. You have to laugh at the dumb stuff that happens sometimes. But that's the spirit of blackjack, right? Just like regular blackjack, sometimes your luck runs sour - and there's always another run!

_childDocuments_.review: D&DG is a VERY good game that takes blackjack and says "what if you could play your credit card against a goblin." The cards you use can either be used to attack if your cards are higher than the opponents, or defend if they're lower, to negate as much damage as you can.There's a lot of really fun cards that you can build a very synergized deck with, and a lot of cards that can really be added to any deck. People may look at this and think it's some Balatro-like but I assure you it's very different. (Also, this game released demos before Balatro even existed.)I love creating a deck, whittling it down to perfection and with the right set-up, beating the opponents in 1 or 2 fell swoops. Though I love it, it's by all means not perfect.It can, at times, through LOTS of BS at you. A deck that might've been cruising through enemies CAN and WILL be cut short by either the boss, or some random powerful enemy. At it's best, you can get through it scratched up and learn new things and predict the game before it predicts you. At it's worst, one of the final bosses of the game outright DENIES THE USE OF SOME CARDS. (And no, it's never explained to you that any enemy can do that, they simply are able to.) It's a bit disheartening to get all the way to the end and get bodied by something sort of out of your control.And the last thing? To even unlock a single other deck, you HAVE to complete the whole game. And to get another, you have to beat it again with an even HARDER starting deck. I'd love if unlocking new starter decks were based on beating chapters instead of beating the entire game, which may take around 30 minutes just to get to the final level. And there are 18 decks to unlock, which... doesn't sound fun.But besides those two relatively big things it's a very fun game to play. I'd love to see what new updates bring to the table, with new cards and maybe even routes to take-- hell, a multiplayer mode kind of like Super Auto Pets could be really fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers

_childDocuments_.review: Funny and ridiculous, even if it means it's very random.All the card and most opponent appearances are based on some pop culture reference, usually funny enough, at least the first time. Finding combinations is very fun and the game usually gives you some chance of victory at least. You mostly work with what the game gives you rather than planning much upfront.This game has no patience for "balance" or "fairness," it's randomness on top of randomness. Maybe your winning card will be at the bottom of your deck. Maybe you'll get a foil library card and wreck the bosses. It's a fine line between funny and annoying and D&DG mostly lands on the good side. When you do get unlucky it doesn't feel too bad, runs are short enough.Each area has certain set events/encounters and you have to do most of them to get to the area boss and continue. There are only a few generic shop events and all the enemies are unique, with predetermined decks. Each enemy also adds their own sounds on top of the area soundtrack. It works out well to make each battle unique and to make it possible to win by going taking those events that can work out for you.The demo is close enough to the full thing. If you don't know if you'll like it, play that first.
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers

_childDocuments_.review: I really wish I could put it as mixed here. I'm very conflicted, since I beat the game for the first time, and there is a bunch of good and a bunch of bad.Graphics: Better than the demo, a lot of polish went into this area, everybody who put effort into this should be given a raise. Music: Starting song is good. I really do not like the music changing. Mainly since it sounds directly like from WolframTones, which is very low quality until the VIP section, and it made me want to mute the game. It's extremely mixed. The sound effects are good.Gameplay: Pretty mixed in general. The stuff in between card battles is really creative and fun. A lot of effort must have been put there. There are a lot of different cards. The actual card game itself is extremely luck based and unbalanced. Getting to 21 has a bunch of risk vs reward, so being in the middle of 12 and 18 is the best. Starting with the VIP section, doing that without lots of healing behind you is death, since they have decks made to always go close to 18-21. In the Hope area the first guy starts out always getting 21, forcing you to manipulate his max number count to win. If you do not have any cards for that, you lose. Even if you do, you need to draw it quickly or else you won't be able to counter. So the counterplay is much more limited, even before this. The advantage system is very mixed in general and feels like not a lot of thought was put into it. Mainly you have to get cards to use it for it, enemies cannot gain any advantage, and many things are infinite as long as you have advantage to spare, like the credit card blade where you can win instantly if you have any advantage to spam it, since there is no con for going negative chips. No cards that scale off the chips you have that I encountered. This leads all enemy decks to have one counterplay: screw over their win condition. When your whole win condition becomes based on how much you can screw over the opponent, it become much more limiting and everything in game feels directed to this one idea of screwing over the enemy deck and hand. And you can only do things when you get good draws, which impacts 90% of if you win turn one or turn 50 after lots of chip damage, and if you have no healing cards, you are screwed due to chip damage since enemies after the third section will mostly end at 18-21 unless you screw them over. So game design wise, it really doesn't feel good to play and is very one dimensional because of being forced into a single playstyle to get far. Compared to the Demo, when I played it, where it felt like there was a lot more than could be done, it's very disappointing. Card Designs/stand outs: Mostly putting this here since there are a lot of references to other games. Hell, I paid over 1k on Hearthstone when it was good, and 4 mana 7/7 is a great card. But visually the reference cards have more polish in the coloring to stand out, which makes the rest of the cards not stand out as much. _childDocuments_.review: This is one of those rogues that doesn't give you quite enough control over how you play the game. Essentially, you always want to be building a deck aiming to get blackjacks, because many of the fringe cards that have random effects are only consistent when you have very many of them. You can almost never accumulate enough of these cards in time before dying. This sounds obvious because it's a game based around blackjack after all, but when so many cards have values lower or higher than 10/11, you don't really feel like picking any of them ever. Because picking one means you've got to go for ALL of them, and there's absolutely no guarantee that the ones offered to you will be beneficial with what you already have. Going with just a few of these cards almost always puts you in an awkward spot every other hand.Roguelikes, especially deckbuilders, tend to be popular for how you can take advantage of the systems available to you to weigh the odds of winning in your favor, using the strategy that you like. It feels like this game only allows one route, and every other option is pretty stupid to lean into. Especially considering your opponents are almost never playing normal cards themselves. Many of your effects actually tend to be beneficial to them. So why pick them at all?On the contrary, there are also too many cards that have absolutely no risk to add to your deck. These are mostly handy's and cards with 0 value. That's not even including the tarot cards, your reward for beating a floor. They pretty much immediately invalidate all the other options you have when you have to choose what to add to your deck, which is very often.In my opinion, you should be able to start the game picking what your max number before bust is. At least let it go up to 26 or something. There are many cards with values slightly over and far under 10/11, and even some that will bust you immediately if played. They are not beneficial enough to be worth picking, the benefits are minimal compared to the almost guaranteed ~20 damage you'll receive for taking the risk.The process of unlocking new decks to play with is also kind of annoying. You shouldn't have to win games just to be able to play the other options. You should be at least somewhat rewarded for doing good regardless of if you beat the entire game or not, that's kinda how most rogues have been for a long time for a reason.Gambling is fun when you can play in different ways, or there's a payoff. There's almost no payoff here, and you'd be actively throwing to not always go for blackjacks. You just play the game, the same way every time. Or not, if you want to consistently lose early.

_childDocuments_.review: I was excited to see a Blackjack game, similar style to Balatro. Choosing cards between rounds doesn't feel like you are making yourself stronger. It's more like having an extra "ace-in-the-hole", but they don't really make you stronger, worse case scenario they just ruin your run.Some opponents are designed to screw you over unless you have a few specific cards that consistently make them bust. In poker even a bad hand is a hand (naturally), but here it's a choice between "Do you want to take 5 damage, or risk going for Blackjack and take 17 damage instead?" Then at one point you finally get a 21 and stand, but then your opponent pulls out a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ card that removes cards from your played hand, so suddenly you stood at like 7, and the opponent gets an instant 21 and gets massive shield so you have even more hands to catch up to. Watching opponents slowly gaining shields that you can't out-damage is quite demoralizing.Also sitting on a stalemate is really boring, doing 1-3 damage to each other and then healing/shielding between is really frustrating and starts to feel hopeless, especially when you know that multiple matches like these are on the horizon.The game is about blackjack, but the blackjacks seem to happen pretty rarely (for the player at least, the opponents are favored) and when you do get a blackjack, you barely get rewarded for it. Having the Hearts deck for healing when you get a blackjack is like the only good option out of the decksI would give a mixed review if it was possible, but I can't quite recommend the game due to the frustration it causes.I keep trying the game again multiple times but I just end up closing the game frustrated in the end.The satisfaction of Blackjack is missing for me.

_childDocuments_.review: So, on first glance this game is "Balatro but Blackjack", but I'm not sure that's a fair comparison. I'm also not convinced of the "randomness" in some situations, though with an admittedly small number of games played, this could just be down to bad luck. There also seem to be a few things which are underutilised or underexplained in the game, such as the chips you get offered at the start of a run.Don't get me wrong, this game is fun, the card design is interesting, the audio is sometimes a little difficult to listen to with so much "ambience", but it works most of the time, and the gameplay loop is generally pretty fast and satisfying. I don't understand the complaints personally about card descriptions, but then I have a lot of experience in the genre, so maybe that's why. Anyway, I do quite like the game, I just feel like it needs a bit more work, and, ultimately, it's not quite as enjoyable as Balatro.

_childDocuments_.review: Man it's tough because I came into this game after a positive experience with the demo which has only soured with the amount of hours spent with the demo. I'm going to focus on what made this game a negative for me rather than writing up a full IGN review of what the game does well and what it does not do.The update felt like a hail Mary in order to make the game easier which doesn't address fundamental issues like super limited ability to craft and manipulate your deck or fish for specific synergies. Decks feel unimaginative, it feels so irrelevant that my deck heals or shields me on max score if there are only a very select few cards which synergise with them and half the time I'm playing to minimise damage from the AI which bust scarcely.The whole currency (chips) system feels unfinished, most my runs I never have to look at them unless I am trying to force a synergy/get a specific card. A lot of events do not feel adequate to the floor I am on. There is no point starting runs with so many options to remove cards from your deck when you yourself have no idea what the deck is going towards and only having options to bloat your deck with random cards later. Feels like something that should be at least slightly the other way around.The game likes to make references to other games so let me draw an example from slay the spire. STS constantly allows for your deck to take shape because shopkeepers can remove cards all the way throughout the game, you have another option which isn't adding or removing but upgrading your cards which again adds another dimension of priority within your deck building. Slay the Spire, just like balatro let the player take control and create a feeling of advantage in encounters through artifacts/Jokers. It feels so barebones being stuck with just one tag you get to choose at the start and have no reliant possibility of changing the tag itself or forcing a deck archetype in order to utilise the chip. The fun from the aforementioned games come from being able to utilise synergies and combinations as best as you can in a given situation. D&DG has striped that ability from the player and is my suspicion of why the game feels more like a chore than it's competitors.

_childDocuments_.review: Good visual, music and feel. It's blackjack, with lots of references, broken cards and broken people. Once the strategy clicks, it's extremely addictive, as you can tell from my hours played at the time of review.This is where the review could end, but I want to address the two elephants in the room:While the concept of "fake casino game" is similar, the execution is completely different. We are not even in the same category here.The formula of the game is really much closer to your classic deckbuilder formula. Construct a deck around a strategy, play encounters against with a particular theme (they heal a lot, they steal your cards, they make easy blackjacks, etc...). Health loss is also permanent between encounters. We are much closer in terms of feel and difficulty to a game like Slay the Spire. If you buy this game thinking it will be like Balatro, you will definitely be disappointed.Rather, the difficulty of this game relies on encounter knowledge, mechanics and some deckbuilding sense. This comes with playing the game for a few runs and getting a feel for the kinds of builds you can make, and knowing what comes ahead. You know... like in every roguelike in existence. In this sense, the game will feel very unfair at the beginning (and it is, in some ways) as the enemies can and will do some extremely dirty things against you if you just let them. This can range from taking more damage than you should to you literally being unable to play the game and forced in a continuous losing state. Bad deckbuilding can also more commonly result in much longer fights, akin to a battle of attrition. These gotchas are definitely frustrating as you start playing, which explain the negative reviews. While that is a thing, I am here to tell you that these elements definitely lessen as you play more. As you get better at the game, you find more and more ways to have game-breaking decks and strategies to take care of every encounter coming your way. This also happens to be the strongest element of this game for me. The payoff of making a good deck is extremely satisfying. The game's paths and encounters are also almost entirely the same between every run, so you can more or less plan ahead what your ideal build looks like, and what you are exactly looking for. There is a surprising amount of depth in this game, you'll find more and more interesting and wild synergies as you play along. You are definitely rewarded for your experience and knowledge, and that is all you could possibly ask from a game like this.So, yes. This game is awesome, and if you are a deckbuilder or roguelike fan, and that this review resonated with what you are looking for in those, you definitely should grab it. On top of that, the developer is active on discord, and already has updates planned for the future. Here's to many more hours of gameplay!

_childDocuments_.review: Tough one to enjoy. It's really less about making blackjack and more about not busting. The difficulty, where it exists, is in grinding it out against opponents who play decks that functionally only go to 20, 21, or bust. Yes, there's the occasional bit of "ah ha" when you see a way to break that pattern for your opponent. But you actually have very little agency in the game beyond deciding when not to push your luck. Building a deck with a strategy feels impossible. Chips feel very useless; the pricing makes your choices very easy, and your opponents can go negative with absolutely no consequences to them, making me wonder why they're there.It has potential, but something about the gameplay loop needs work.

_childDocuments_.review: Really disappointed because the demo was a great premise for a game, but unfortunately, they pretty much didn't add anything when they made the full release. Yeah they cleaned it up, added more floors (which are extremely similar to the existing floors), added starter decks (which are as lame as possible, literally just different suits), and added extra difficulty modes (which don't actually explain what they do? Like the first one is just "advantage is harder to get". How do I get it now??), but they didn't add many new cards (seriously not sure if I've seen a new card, they might not have added any) or mechanics (besides advantage/exploit which is really just like bare minimum making the game function).Ultimately the problem does not lie in the failure to expand the game between demo and release. It lies in the fact that the core gameplay loop is just not there. You're just not building a deck the same way other games in the genre let you do. The cards don't really synergize, they pretty much all just make your deck better is some small way. There's a little bit of synergy in regards to the fact that you want to make 21, so your cards should combine to get there, but that's not really how that works considering you have extremely limited options to control card draw order, so two cards don't really synergize, unless each of those cards synergize with themselves too (e.g. a 13 of spades doesn't exactly synergize with an 8 of hearts because you can only put one 13 in your deck without ruining it). Its fine for roguelikes to have unconditional bonuses/perks/etc., they don't all have to depend on situation or synergy, but those boons almost always exists outside of the deck (e.g. relics in slay the spire, or jokers in Balatro), so they don't warp your deck into a meaningless direction. For example there's a card that's got this interesting ability about dealing damage when you hit at 17+, but its really clunky to add to a deck because its a 4-score card. Nothing about the ability really makes it have to be 4-score, but its a card so it should have a score I guess. Most other cards like this are just 0-score cards, making them effectively not cards, but this slows down the game A TON. Imagine if you had to draw all your relics in slay the spire, but each of them let you draw an additional card. That's just a bunch of fishing for no reason.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, and after 12 hours of playtime, I feel like I’ve given it a fair shot. Unfortunately, it didn’t quite click with me for several reasons. While I can appreciate the attempt to add a theme through the different opponents, locations, and events, it often feels forced. Personally, I would have preferred a more streamlined experience focused purely on match after match.There are definitely some clever card mechanics, but many of them seem included just for the sake of variety. Some card descriptions are also quite confusing, making it harder to strategize effectively. Overall, the game gives off a sense that you could almost watch someone else play and still get the same experience. There's minimal planning involved, and it often feels like taking risks isn't rewarding. Luck plays such a significant role that matches can feel inconsistent — one minute you're winning in three turns, and the next you're stuck in a 30-minute battle against a similar opponent only to lose.The control you have over the matches feels very limited, and the choices you make between matches don’t feel meaningful. I’m not opposed to RNG or luck being factors in a game, but when you invest 45 minutes into a run and lose due to one overpowered card that locks your opponent at 21 points every round, it’s hard to enjoy the experience. Unfortunately, this has left me feeling frustrated and disinterested in continuing to play.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game, that I think might be marred from it's very high difficulty from the get-go. While both Slay the Spire, Balatro, and other roguelikes have difficulty modes (e.g. acensions, stakes), DDG doesn't. So the higher, or deeper you go into the rooms, you get faced with exponentially tougher decks that rely solely on you knowing their strategies and pre-planning your deck before you encounter them. This means that manipulating your foe's deck is always extremely high value, and seems to reduce the value of cards that simply make your own blackjack easier to obtain (I don't have that many hours yet, and I might be wrong here). That being said, I do think this is a fantastic game with a lot of thought and love being put into it's development, and considering it just released yesterday (from time of review), I think there's so much room for patches to be developed. An absolute buy for anyone that loves to spend time thinking and calculating the gamba.---After winning my first run:This game is cracked. This game is so good.

_childDocuments_.review: I went in expecting to love this game, and I was really disappointed. By the nature of the main mechanic (blackjack), combat goes very slowly. Ties are frequent, meaning even simple battles early are a game of chance on who busts first. Card mechanics in the game feel ignorable or have effects that are detrimental to a wide variety of builds (burning cards on play, forcing stands, shredding cards for little benefit, etc). I think the archetypes are built pretty narrowly, with little overlap. Card removal is difficult to come by, meaning creating consistency is tough. Tarot cards, while an interesting concept in the spirit of boss relics in Slay the Spire, often feature abilities that force your deck into a certain archetype. I played around 200 hands before refunding, and I often had to take tarot cards that made my deck worse, causing me to lose on the next floor. They are not skippable (I may be wrong, but I could not figure it out) and do not get re-randomized after each boss, meaning you must take one of the ones you skipped the first time, muddling again the focus of your deck.I think the core idea of the game is interesting, and I think that the card designs and theming are great. After playing the demo for a few hours, I guess I expected the full release to be more polished. Hopefully, I will come back to this game in a year and revise my review, but for now I can not recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: D&DG is a pretty interesting game but it’s one that I think would only appeal to a very specific type of person. The most obvious game to compare it to is Balatro because Balatro came out half a year ago, was really popular, and is also based around a casino game (poker). So, I imagine a lot of people that liked Balatro will look at this and be interested. The problem is that D&DG is almost nothing like Balatro. Balatro is a fast and simple game that’s pretty carefully balanced. None of the cards do anything too crazy, at the end of the day you’re usually just getting more points. No matter what, you’re always playing something that resembles poker, even if it’s a lobotomized version of poker where you just need a pair to win.D&DG has a blackjack theme, sure, but if you’re playing the game correctly you aren’t going to be playing blackjack past the first few enemy encounters. There also isn’t even a semblance of balance in the game, with the focus in most cases being on flavor instead. The best cards are those that have a low value and disrupt the enemy in some way, for a few reasons. First, if your deck is all low-value cards you can play a bunch of cards in a round without worrying about busting. Second, if you stand before your opponent does (because your deck has a lot of high-value cards) they can play a disruptive card and force you to bust or lower your score. Third and most importantly, late game enemies can almost always hit a 20 or 21, so if you just try to play basic strategy against them without disruption you can easily end up in an endless war of attrition where busting once knocks out a fifth of your health. In most cases your goal should be to force the enemy to bust since that drops their defense to 0. Cards like Geraldo, Yellow Card, Break Limits, and 4 Mana 7/7 are absurdly strong, then, because they either remove important cards from your opponent’s deck, force them to bust, or clog their deck with trash. On the flipside, basically every card with a random element to it or a value higher than around 5 or 6 isn’t worth taking because boosting your own score should always be ancillary to trying to disrupt your opponent. What this means, in technical terms, is that like 80% of the cards in the game suck.I imagine a lot of people would look at the number of bad cards in the game and go “Wow, there sure are a lot of bad cards in this game, they really need to balance them!” Again, however, the focus of the game clearly is on flavor more than balance. A 21 of diamonds is a funny card and there isn’t really a way to make it less useless without ruining the joke. All the cards that are king, queen, and jack puns don’t work if they aren’t kings, queens, or jacks. The design philosophy in many cases seems like the devs said “Wouldn’t it be funny if…” and then added a card without really caring if it was balanced or not. As a result, there are a lot of amusing references to other card games or just types of cards in general (like a “Get well soon” card or a credit card) and they don’t feel forced because they fit with the game’s theme.So, I suppose you need a certain type of mindset to enjoy this game. You shouldn’t expect things to be balanced and you shouldn’t expect to play blackjack. There is a lot of RNG at certain points depending on the starting deck you pick (the Birthday "deck" can literally lose to the first enemy encounter without you being able to do anything), but in a way I feel like this is more of an experiential game in the vein of something like Inscryption. Sure, all of my wins have come from abusing the same pool of 5 or 6 cards and I’ll probably get bored of that soon, but I appreciate the game for what it tries to do. Maybe you won’t, maybe you’ll hate it and refund it. So, I’m basically trying to prevent that from happening by writing this review. If this game doesn’t sound appealing to you don’t buy it, because you might hate it so much you’ll send a bomb threat to the devs and get sent to prison, then in prison you might get sodomized by a big black bull named Tyrone, or maybe a guy covered in Nazi tattoos named Ralph. You’d basically be ruining your life all over a video game. So think carefully, okay?

_childDocuments_.review: In it's current state, there's still a lot to be desired. By 'desire' those things seem to be very basic things that should have gone into the game from the very beginning. Some of those things are:- ability to properly manage the deck- ability to heal outside of random healing events- more opportunities to explore the game mechanics before losing a run quicklyA lot of the game is based on RNG to the point where it doesn't seem like a game of strategy but a game of chance.The gameplay formula is similar to the childhood card game most know as 'WAR' where you and an opponent each shuffle a deck of cards and blindly pulling the top card with the highest value card winning.You can't base any strategy around the RNG or 'trap' the opponent into anything as your only 'strategy' in the game is being made only after the initial cards are dealt in which you have to attempt to plot a tactic around that falls apart instantly as the next card is dealt.A lot of times it feels like your opponent has complete control of the rules for the encounter and you don't with the opponent presenting weird and obscure 'debuffs' that aren't explained and with the complete randomness of the cards being given to you you'll be praying on the 'Heart of the Cards' like a vintage Yu-Gi-Oh duel hoping the ONE card that can counter the madness shows up in a manner that you can actually use.For example:There's a card that creates an instant blackjack but it can ONLY be used if there is already a Jack present in your hand.That card is literally useless unless RNG favors you a Jack before that card is drawn randomly off the deck. So 9/10 times, this card's effect is never used.Another Example:A card that swaps your hand with the opponent's hand. Sounds nice, right? That could be helpful if the opponent has a winning hand, right? NOPE! Because RNG can play that card and its effect is INSTANTLY activated the moment it's drawn without giving you ANY choice in the matter so you'd end up swapping YOUR good winning hand with the opponent's losing hand which results in whatever diabolical strategy you attempted to create to be used against you which in a lot of cases the damage you've been building against your opponent gets used against you.Some cards are absolutely confusing you get. There's a card called Memory Card that memorizes a card to be played later. But... the game doesn't explain how to recall the memorized card. Another example of confusing thing is that some cards are automatically 'locked' when you play them (meaning they don't get discarded and remain in play until they are unlocked or discarded) but here's the silly thing: you need a card to be drawn to unlock them or you have to wait for the opponent to destroy it. So lets say you have a card's value at 14 and it's locked. 14 is a low number to STAY on so you decide to HIT and 9 TIMES OUT OF 10 you will always bust on the very next card. So RNG has handicapped you the entire round and your perk turns into your punishment.ALSO, if you're using a controller then most of the time you're trying to figure out at which angle do you need to move the left analog stick to select an certain option and a lot of times I just found myself reaching for the mouse because the game just doesn't understand what it is you are attempting to select with a controller.

_childDocuments_.review: At first I kind of thought this game is... not good. However, after few attempts I have realized that there is something here. _childDocuments_.review: Edit: Here's an edit I'm happy to make. They fixed the game! No, seriously, the update they did to balancing makes this so much more enjoyable to play (and really highlights how odd some of the initial balancing was) but its an absolute slam dunk and I can happily say this is worth your time with NO caveat. Rest of review remains unchanged.So I initially threw this a positive review with a promise to update, and here's the update. This is good, really good, actually. But it does definitely have some problems. You should buy this game and support it, because its already very fun, and with some balancing changes it'll easily be a classic. Lets start with the good before the bad. The aesthetic overall is fantastic, its grimy and gross and as you move through the zones the board you're playing on and the music you listen to reflects the area you're playing in very well. Also, references galore. There are so many subtle (and not so subtle) references to other popular media. It never feels like too much, but there was a lot of little "oh no way" moments I had. To touch on the music again briefly, I love it. There's a little trill or change in the music for some of the opponents you run up against (I love the tune swap when you face the bard) and its the kind of thing that you could leave on forever and not be bothered by. Its a bop, and thats a good thing. Now the bad.I think if I had to pin down the main issue, it really feels like the game ramps up the people you're playing against much quicker than you can ramp yourself up to a "build". Blackjack is a game of playing the odds and chance moreso than poker, but by the end of the *first* floor (of five) you are already encountering people with like 5 cards in their deck and a specific playstyle you have to beat. That's fine, but by that point for you, you still most likely have almost all of the cards you started with plus a few more you picked up after wins. The opportunities to trim or focus your deck are few and far between and really expensive. I actually don't have a problem with the opponents, they are all clever fights and demand that you actually counter their mechanics, but I do think that the player's ability to fight those mechanics can be really difficult to manifest. The 4 starting decks all don't feel fantastic to use because they only activate powers if you deal damage at Blackjack (meaning if you hit 20 and win the head to head, no deck powers. Has to be 21 and cant be a tie of 21). There's also way too few options or opportunities to heal, and what is there costs too much. I'm not saying make the game easier, but at least give the player the tools to forge their way to victory. At the moment it really does feel like random chance on the players part if they end up winning or not, which is part of blackjack, sure, but if I get a 21 and stand and then the AI steals my ace... well thats not chance anymore is it?I love what is here, genuinely, but the balancing isn't quite right as of right now. I would recommend you wishlist this at the very least and keep an eye out for a big balancing update. This is good as is, but it could very well be great with some tweaks.

_childDocuments_.review: This game shows promise, but several design flaws hold it back from being enjoyable in its current state.Firstly, the lack of randomization severely limits replayability. Enemy and boss encounters are static, with the same enemies appearing in the same locations every playthrough. This directly contradicts the core principle of roguelikes. For instance, encountering  downstairs every single run eliminates any sense of surprise or need to adapt.Secondly, resource management feels restrictive and hinders build diversity. While many builds seem viable in theory, the scarcity of resources renders them unattainable. Successful roguelikes often allow players to manipulate game mechanics for near-infinite resources, enabling "god runs" and rewarding creative strategies. This game's limited resources and underwhelming opponents prevents such experimentation and powerful builds from happening.This game has the potential to be enjoyable, but until these issues are addressed, I cannot recommend it in its current state.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll give it a recommend because I want to support Indie creators, however I doubt I will replay this a lot unless substantial updates come. First of all if you want to buy this because you like Balatro: this game has nothing to do with Balatro. The joy in Balatro comes from "seeing the number go up" and getting progressively more insane combo's to see the number go up. Whereas this game is more about defeating bosses. At least I think so because I honestly don't really know. In my opinion it lacks depth in both the deckbuilding aspect, and in the "writing" of the bosses. The bosses and opponents should have had more themed decks and some more flair in how they engage with you, if that's what the developer was aiming for. The cards and decks are not interesting enough to really get into them and several aspects are either missing or I'm too dumb to have noticed them. Card rarities would have been nice, so you have an indication as to whether "this is something you might want to try and build around". Also, runs are too short I feel to really build a deck. It's more: take stuff that you think kind of works and try to cut out the 6 and 5 from your deck. By the time you feel your deck is halfway decent you're at the final boss. When you start the game you have absolutely no clue what your opponent is doing, there's no "slow mode" that shows you exactly what is happening. You can obviously take the time to read every card in their deck, but even then: there's some keywords and mechanics that are explained, but often not really adequately, so you still don't really know what's going to happen/what's happening. I'm pretty disappointed because I really wanted to like this game, but like I stated at the start: unless a lot is added I won't be. I've beaten the game twice and I'm already not interested to boot it up anymore. On the other hand it's cheap and the developer clearly has love for their game and video games in general, so if you want to support someone who deserves it definitely buy, you'll get a few hours of fun out of it at least. Very last point of criticism: this is very personal, but I'm kind of sick of the whole "let's make our games look like it's 1974"-vibe. I'm not a graphics-dude AT ALL, but being able to read the text on the screen without hurting your brain is nice, and what's the point to the avatar you can mess around with on the top left corner, if it's just adding some random pixels that are supposed to represent a hat or a haircut? You could have spent that time writing some funny dialogue for a boss or, I don't know, developing another card. I'm sorry if this is very negative, I really had high hopes for this and imo it just failed to deliver.

_childDocuments_.review: While I admit I expected a more Balatro-like experience, I have to say that even trying to hamper my expectations and thinking "not every gambling deck-builder is a roguelike", I still feel intensely disappointed. In short, I feel like this game lacks in everything it promises and that I expected from it: the roguelike aspects are hampered by the lack of meaningful unlocks, the deckbuilding is lackluster at best and downright useless at worst due to the absence of any outside influences on the deck, and the core mechanics turn blackjack from a quick little gambling game into a luck-based not-really-strategic slog against opponents that are at a fundamental advantage against you, both due to the strength of their decks, but also due to them having access to gimmicks the game pretty much doesn't allow you to have.I just think the game fails at almost everything it tries. Clearly monumental love and effort has been put into designing the pretty fun minigames, into designing the characters and the excellent soundtrack, the cards and NPCs... but it all falls short due to fundamental failures it has mechanically. There isn't much to strive for or play with, besides just clicking hit, and not only praying that you don't bust but also that your opponent doesn't play some card that triggers a condition that instantly kills your family dog. It just is not satisfying.In long:I do not have a problem with the luck-reliance or randomness aspect of blackjack, but I feel two things really made me just not want to play this game: the fact that this game doesn't feel as satisfying due to how it treats blackjack, and the lackluster "deckbuilding".On the satisfaction of playing blackjack, I feel like this game failed to deliver (perhaps only to me) by really heavily amplifying it's extremes. Unless your opponent busts, the damage you deal (unless they score very minimally) is going to be lackluster, but if they do, it might win the match instantly. Also, none of the suit bonuses activate unless you actually hit blackjack. I feel like it feels unrewarding to play unless you get a 21 (and then only situationally) or your opponent busts: I've had rounds drag on and on and on for what felt like ages because I kept outscoring my opponent (or the opponent kept outscoring me) by 1 or 2, and we kept gaining shields or regaining health from the occasional 21s that popped up, only enhancing the torture, to the point where I just up and closed the run to start a new one. However, even this is only a relatively minor gripe, and my issues with the game reach far deeper.The deckbuilding isn't satisfying. You just get one card to add to your standard deck after every encounter beaten, with the occasional shops mixed in, as well as minigame events (which are usually glorified shops anyways, not that there's anything wrong with that). It doesn't feel like anything you play changes anything at all, though, since (at least with the standard decks I've tried) you just don't get the ability to alter your playstyle. There's no meaningful upgrades to the cards, there's no meaningful changes to how a deck is played depending on external factors like Balatro's jokers or Slay The Spire's relics, in fact there's not even an equivalent for them. It genuinely feels super dull, like a contest of hitting or standing depending on the number, and also praying, while seeing your AI opponent play a genuinely interesting gimmick deck.The closest comparison I can make, knowing most people come here from Balatro's sphere of influence (myself included) is... imagine if, after beating a blind, instead of a shop you add one playing card to your deck, and nothing else. That is genuinely what it felt like playing, and I hate it.Don't get me wrong, the interplay between cards is there for sure, as evidenced with one enemy on one of the last floors I was quite impressed by, who had the gimmick of constantly playing a card that ties whatever you have, and a different card that deals damage to you when you've tied; or the Wizard that plays 1s and adds more and more 1s to his deck until he just gets a guaranteed 21 so you have to rush through him before you just bleed out. However, these are all just NPC decks, and you only get to unlock them (and mind you, you get pre-built versions of them, instead of them being some kind of build you can go for) after beating the game many times over. It feels impossible to get that one King that turns to an instant blackjack if you have no other faces, because the cards that sound like they could have interplay with it (like a different King that burns all other face cards) don't play together, they actively ♥♥♥♥ gimmicks over. It really feels like you're at a disadvantage both mechanically and fun-wise, since you have to probably be dipped in the river Styx to actually get a gimmick deck working. The part I mentioned about this not being a good Roguelike in my eyes is the unlocks. Every other Roguelike I've played or seen being played and have been captivated by is always the quirky achievements that let you play the game in new ways. For an expected example, it's a new deck or joker in Balatro, new cards and characters in Slay The Spire, new items and characters in Isaac, new characters and pathways in Tiny Rogues, etc etc. They keep you playing, keep you engaged, and once you got them, you're there to try a new playstyle and get a new outcome with them, only to have the cycle repeat. This variety is, in my opinion, is what gives Roguelikes their amazing replayability. Here, your reward for the incredibly luck-based and honestly grueling challenge of beating the game for the first time is... a deck filled with card that do nothing. That's honestly baffling to me: the reward for actually completing the full challenge set before you is a downgrade from everything you've had before. And I feel like that mentality follows through to the rest of the game too, because besides lackluster new decks (like just 2 starter decks mashed together, or two other starter decks mashed together, or random cards...), there's... no unlocks. No new special cards or gimmicks to orient your deck around, no alternatives to anything. This isn't just because most of those things are unlocked by default, but also because there is simply nothing meaningful to begin with. In other Roguelikes, getting an item can shift, curve or instantly flip the direction of your build. Here, this is not the case.I mean absolutely no offense to the solo dev of this project, who as I stated must have put tremendous love and effort into this. But I also think the issues with the game run incredibly deep. Take everything I said with a grain of salt, but I simply do not enjoy this game, and I would not recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: The game has serious potential, but it is balanced so poorly that it makes me question the design ideas behind it.As the easiest example, you boot up the game, you begin your first run. You are matched against the bartender. Cool, this is a tutorial enemy! He's only got 5 health. he pulls a 10. You hit, you get a 6. He hits, and pulls an ace. Ouch, bartender blackjack is rough. You can now hit without much worry about busting, you do, you get a 9 and you're at 15. If you stand, you take 6 damage. If you hit, you might bust and take 21 damage because the bartender's blackjack will not be blocked by your 15.The next hand rolls around, your bartender got 19. then he gets 20. then he gets 17, stands, and you hit him with a 21. he's now at 1 health, but you are at best in the 80s. This was the tutorial enemy.This is a game where it is extremely easy to get bad RNG and die before ever meeting the first boss.Why do i say that this makes me question the design rather than just saying "game hard, git gud?"Because there's no player interaction with this extreme RNG slugfest. I've had HP in the 63/100 range coming out of the tutorial bartender fight, on the lowest run difficulty. I could not choose cards, I could not build my deck, I could only have played strictly to mitigate damage and not hit above 13, but that would only have saved me a bit of health.One of the game's first major updates was an adjustment of the difficulty. This definitely means that the devs are listening. Unfortunately, the change that is needed is more of an overhaul than a balance adjustment. Compare to a solid analogue like slay the spire, where even on a high difficulty you have real choices about the path that you take from screen 1, advantages built into your choice of class, and the game opens with the option to change your build in serious and meaningful ways (unless you've just lost, when it offers you a strong catchup mechanic!)Or take the comparison with Balatro, where the first few rounds are easily and smoothly winnable with a single hand, often without a discard. The game allows you to see a shop, get jokers, and start working towards a build in an early ante before the difficulty ramps.A balance adjustment will not provide the kind of change to give the player any kind of meaningful engagement with the very early game, and this sets the tone for the entire run. The game is currently in a very playable state, and has a lot of potential. It's just not good enough to be worth sinking in the time, not in its current state.

_childDocuments_.review: Criminally underrated game. As a "rogue-like deckbuilder" it is interesting and unique with extensive content and character to make it a worthwhile experience regardless of your experience with the genre. There's an impressive amount of depth in the decision-making during every part of the game, with chance being a surprisingly minor factor for the most part (aside from a few pain points, like certain overpowered cards). To compare this game to Balatro (which was conceived after this one) would be doing it a disservice, though unfortunately it is a relevant comparison: D&DG unlike Balatro is a highly dynamic game, with buildcrafting and gameplay being engaging and demanding. The cards themselves encourage more active participation in the games systems, and are consistent in their adherence to a style of theming and direction that provides for a strong identity in the game. Beyond that, the enemy, world, music, and art design are quite strong and make for a game that's enjoyable even just for navigation of its setting. That said, the content in this game is designed to played in a more arcade-y style than similar games that encourage completionism and long-term time investments. You can try to play this game to 100% collections, but it isn't built for it. If that sounds fine to you, then I highly recommend D&DG.

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of people see a deckbuilding game based on an actual card game that uses goofy variations on cards right now and think "oh, that's like Balatro"... In fact in writing that I am perpetuating the issue so let's just get this out of the way first: if you're looking for Balatro and that crazy thrill of card combos leading to insane high scores as the dopamine floods your brain... This is not that! It's its own thing and I'd say it's all the better for it.So what this is is blackjack, draw cards, try and get a score 21 and not over, but instead of money being your driving goal, instead you are always playing blackjack against someone and are trying to build decks to be stronger, more adaptive, reactive, and to completely mess with your opponent's play. Like blackjack luck is a huge factor and (thanks to being able to see what's left of your own deck at any time) so is educated gambling through card counting. And that luck factor is something you cannot escape; you can do a lot to reduce it and recent updates have helped massively in giving you power over your own deck but that aspect of gambling is built into the design itself, it's a game about taking risks, the thrill of a great plan and deck paying off, and the pain of losing everything to that 1 card you didn't want to see. If you prefer chance to be a less prominent factor in your game then this game is not for you.But say you're still reading this and think that you don't mind that thrill of chance at all, then what you got here is a great game that has a surprising amount of personality for as simple as it looks. your opponents are just 2 text lines, a portrait, a deck, and a value that they'll hold on, but through that the game gives them a surprising amount of character. When an opponent holds and how their deck interacts with that can lead to some interesting strategy but also just gives these people personalities that are fun to see. Stuff like how the wizard's deck starts as nothing but grows and grown, how a knight prioritises defense, or even just the comedy of a dog that has a deck consisting mostly of 2s, while also standing on a 2, it's silly, it's funny, and it's incredibly charming; especially with these characters all adding their own little sounds to the backing soundtrack that makes them even more distinct in their own little ways. These are seemingly little things but they're appreciated, they didn't have to be there but the game is so much better and more charming for it and is something that does a great job of separating it from the dry exercise of "just blackjack but roguelike" that this could've become.So yeah, it's a great little game that has been paired with many a long-form video recently and has been wonderful to have, I really recommend it (unless you happen to be my friend who was a blackjack dealer for many years and, because of the rigid way casino dealers are made to play blackjack, finds this game weirdly infuriating for breaking literal years of forced habit xD)

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game concept let down by the core design not taking enough risks, which feels like a crazy thing to say for a Blackjack game where you can play a Charizard card. The basic decks are boring, highly limited by doing nothing whatsoever unless you pull a 21, offer no alternative win conditions (Balatro manages this because it has a bunch of other hands which score points and can win you matches in different ways) than "Score 20/21/22 and hope your enemy only ever busts" and offering little to no synergy with the Advantage chips and the more creative cards you can purchase and receive as rewards. And of course, as always with non-Slay the Spire deckbuilders, there's too few nodes that let you remove cards, leaving you stuck with a bloated deck of cards with awful values that make it harder for you to reach 20/21/22 (depending on if you modify your hand value cap). Moreover, if you ever do manage to remove a single card from your deck, good luck winning with that card's "pair" (6 and 5, 8 and 3, etc.) gone when you want to reach 21.Overall, I really like the concept, and I even really like a lot of the execution. I would really love to love this game because it is right on the cusp of actually being a rewarding partner to Balatro's earlier success. However, as it stands now, I do not plan to play the game any further until the core decks, advantage chips, and gameplay loop receive serious top to bottom reworks and cannot recommend it to anybody expecting anything more than about thirty minutes of going "Haha, that card doesn't belong in Blackjack! Funny!"

_childDocuments_.review: before i start this review, i'll preface it with thiseveryone is talking about how they can't control the rng enoughguys, have you ever played blackjack?have you ever played any game with cards?what did you go in expecting?"but muh balatro" this isn't balatroyea, the balancing needs some work, especially high value cards, but you can't complain about rng in a card game.maybe it'd be cool if you could spend 1 advantage to draw a card even after you bust, in hopes of getting something that saves you, that would probably help the high card situation, and some cards are just objectively waaaay better than others, like everyone's gonna pick business card over club of 3's, and that's a fair complaint.don't go in expecting this to be "balatro, but blackjack", because it's not. the gameplay is entirely different and that's not a game issue, that's a you issue.overall, some changes i'd suggest are1) as mentioned previously, balancing higher cards to be better. i think a "high risk, high reward" system works, which is what some cards go for, but it doesn't hit the "high reward" mark very well on most cards. a card that does this successfully is valentine's day, which gives you 14 health, but in return, is a 14. the risk of this card being a 14 is made up by the health you get from using it. the risk/reward is very clear and the card is actually good. however, it fails for cards like green card, which is worth 13, as the reward of using it is very low in comparison to its high value, as it puts one of your cards into your opponent's draw pile. you could theoretically use it to give your opponent a really bad card, but that also means you'd have to have it in your deck to begin with, so the reward is very low.2) other ways of using advantage, because it's given to you kind of strangely and feels like it should be a bigger feature. you are given an advantage chip after beating the first enemy, but only a few cards actually use advantage. i think there should be some other ways to utilize advantage. like i said earlier, it'd be interesting if you could continue to draw after busting if you use one advantage. alternatively, maybe you could use 1 advantage to increase/decrease your bust limit. i think advantage, as a system, would be more interesting if it could be used to "break" the traditional rules of blackjack in this way, or similar ways. this isn't a huge issue by any means, and i enjoy cards that do use advantage, but i wish it had a bigger role, and i wish managing it was more complex and required more thinking, because as it stands, it's just something to use and abuse whenever you have it, with not much foresight into the future of the match.3) a high contrast mode for the 4 basic suits, similar to the one in balatro (yes, i know i said "don't compare this game to balatro", but this is different, because it's an accessibility thing). i have bad vision and somtimes it makes it kind of hard to notice what suit i draw without looking hard at the cards. it's worse with hearts/diamonds, and that's an issue because heart and diamond blackjacks do 2 *very* different things.4) instead of a cigarette, add an easter egg that makes you hold a tube of chapstick, just to remind the player that their lips are dry as they are playing the game, to berate and to make fun of them (jk)overall, this game is super fun, and i hope that i die to the wizard for the 3rd run in a row

_childDocuments_.review: I remember liking an earlier demo version, but I can't say I enjoy this game right now. Roguelikes are one of my favourite genres and I like a healthy dose of RNG. Unfortunately, this game largely lacks meaningful player agency.You are at the mercy of the order in which you draw the cards, which would be fine if you had any reasonable tools to mitigate bad luck. Special cards with effects can manipulate your cards, your opponent's cards, the cards you draw, etc. But then you have to actually draw those cards, and often times you need to combo multiple cards to trigger any sort of  impactful effect. This furthers the reliance on RNG giving you the cards you want to perform the special card effects that separate this game from normal blackjack.The game also has a mechanic called Advantage that allows you to spend it after generating it via a few means to "exploit"  cards, triggering their effect, as well as to play cards from hand. However cards only go into hand if they have the "handy" keyword or through the effect of another card. Playing cards from hand feels like it is supposed to get you out of a tough spot by playing your "ace in the hole" so to speak. However, since it requires generating advantage to do so, you can easily end up in a situation where you need the ace in the hole but don't have the advantage to use it. What this game truly suffers from is the culmination of all these different RNG mechanics that could potentially be fine if not for the fact that there are so many of them that you need to rely on. Needing to have the "handy" keyword to put something in hand to use at a later time. Then needing advantage to play it from hand. The individual card effect not being that powerful so it needs to be played with another card that you have to draw. Needing to actually be offered those cards in a shop or from rewards to begin with. It was all just extremely unsatisfying to me when the few times I was offered cards that I felt like could work in my deck, that the draw order or other cards in play didn't allow me to make use of them.The cherry on top is that you might have to slog through combat if the game didn't see fit to give you effective cards or just not in the right order. Damage is dealt through the difference between you and the opponent's scores, with going over 21 (in most cases) making your score zero. You can have round after round of chipping away at each other. Sweet! You got 21. But your opponent got 19, so that's 2 points of their 50+ health gone.It feels like the problems with this game are inherent to the limitations of blackjack, as the attempts to change the formula outside of the zany cards fail to make your actions feel meaningful and therefore, worthwhile.

_childDocuments_.review: This concept feels like it has alot of potential, but unfortunately it does not seem like the potential was used wellThe core mechanics are very simple (I mean its literally blackjack) and the extra mechanics (mainly cards with special effects) and each suit having a different effect on playing a perfect 21 are a nice addition; While still keeping the mechanics simple and easy to grasp. The effects of the games cards are however not interacting well with each other, alot of the cards I thought would be fun, seemed hard to fit into a deck. And it feels like the deckbuilding is so much more RNG based in the first half (?) than it should be. Only with luck in events and pulling cards did it feel like I could actually starting building up my deck somewhat.However thats not the main problem, the main problem is the enemy design: They might just be basically perfectly immune to whatever deck you are building or have some crazy synergy immediately beating you into the ground. I assume after playing the game alot it would be possible to figure out how to build your deck, to make sure that cant happen - but thats not a way of progression I could recommend. You should have a fair chance from the getgo. Additionally they seem to always have the same deck, which would probably make this game feel boring and repetitive quite fast. (Especially if you have to replay the beginning cz a enemy youve never seen before just has a perfect counter to you) Also bonus (Might be how I played, instead of a issue with the game itself):The fights (atleast with the way I built one of my decks) can drag on. The fight against "Celubutante" was her pulling a 20 every single round. My deck at that point was good enough to get 20 or 21 every round...but so I needed to use my 1/3 chance for the 21 to win the fight slowly but painfully (As it was literally not possible for me to lose) - The fight has a mechanic which makes her easily beatable...but I wasnt able to use that with the deckTl;DR: Good concept, lotsa potential - but needs polishing before I can recommend it; Once its polished I think it will be a very good game

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like Balatro will be seen as a blessing and a curse in the coming years.  Just like we see every year with the plentiful seasons of offspring of “Soulslike” games birthed from Dark Souls and Bloodborne, and the many roguelike card-builders spawned from titles like Slay the Spire, we will eventually see the increased traffic of “Deck of Card games with many twists in them to make them something completely different” games to hit the market.  Some will be good.  Some will be bad.Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers takes a lot of what makes Balatro such a tantalizing piece of gaming and combines the storytelling of Dungeons & Dragons with the money-sucking casino game, Blackjack.  You walk into a seedy tavern with a deck of cards and your wits and your task of discovering who runs the seedy and shady casino is masked by a litany of patrons to combat against and several floors to traverse.  What starts as a small deck of numbers and face cards soon evolves into a cavalcade of boosts and rule changers as you dip and dive through the house-of-mirrors' worth of encounters.  But if you bust your HP: you’re out.  And back to the bartender with you.Your starting deck means a lot to how you start your run, as each suit provides a different buff when you hit a blackjack: hearts heal, diamonds cash out, clubs shield, and spades hit harder.  Whether you want to play a more defensive and reactive build or a more forward, hard hitting style, the options are there for you.  You start with 100HP and a couple chips in your pocket, used primarily for acquiring new cards, playing minigames, or spending on certain abilities.  After a friendly spar with the Bartender, you’re shown after each victory you’re awarded a choice of one of four cards, the fourth requiring you to pay chips to see.  This is the start of where you can acquire one of the over 300 cards to unlock throughout the game.The range of cause and effect on these cards is an immense undertaking where if you think of something whimsical and ridiculous to do with a blackjack hand, there’s a good chance the card exists in its portfolio.  Most cards will be activated on different set situations, aptly colored in red and politely given a definition at each notice, but almost always needed a commonly used D&D term: Advantage.  Advantage is a finite resource that allows you to do a multitude of things to gain the edge against your opponent, such as playing cards from your ability-made hand or activating secondary buffs and debuffs on your cards.  Advantage is gathered through one of three random passive buffs of your choosing provided at the start of your run, and it would be wise to work your deck into making as much Advantage as possible because you’re going to need it.When engaged in combat, your goal is to hit 21 for a blackjack or get as close as you can as it is the same for your opponent.  You will Hit to add more cards and Stand to end your turn, with you and your opponent taking turns adding cards to your hand until both have stood or busted by going over 21.  Whoever has the highest number at the end of the hand will take the difference between the two hands and deliver that amount in damage: rinse and repeat until you have a winner.  Hitting a blackjack will not only provide the most amount of damage, but will activate the suits on the cards used in your hand allowing for any of the four buffs to proc, giving you life, shields, cash, or damage.  If you’ve ever played blackjack before, you know that it’s like that one Fort Manor song but instead it’s 80% luck, 10% skill, 10% concentrated power of will.  D&DG does little to this formula because you will live and die, a lot, on your ability to hit 21.  It’s how you heal, how you crush opponents, how you mitigate damage, and how you cash out for better things.There are several stages on each floor for you to build your deck out with battles, but there are optional events that can happen in place of a good ol’ fashioned throwdown.  Pay some chips to take a nap and restore some HP, play roulette to change the number value of cards in your deck, rob a sleeping man, pay taxes, channel your inner Shawshank Redemption, the list goes on.  Each game has the ability to provide you with extra cards or set you up for success for your next fight, but some can also financially ruin you or dwindle your HP or burn cards in your deck, the only way to know is to go into the event and coin flip some trial and error: a recurring theme within this casino.While your HP is higher than almost any opponent you face, your HP does not regain after a fight, so you will have to pick the right events or work your deck to gain more HP while you fight or use cards that provide shields to mitigate damage as it happens.  But get ready to be peppered with some tailor-made shenanigans when you see what the CPU can accomplish most of the time, because your opponent’s hit 21 a lot.  There’s no shame in losing a hand, so smart play is rewarded with small losses instead of big chunks if you bust.  You will have to play steady and not be reckless or the game will punish you for it.The issue with each of the 60 characters, all come with specific decks they’ll use to put you in the dirt but the later game foes have truly evil setups that are flat not fun to fight.  Each enemy will have a glaring weakness within their deck for you to find, which can be a fun test to see how you can handle the deck in front of you, but certain decks require certain cards to exploit that weakness, and if you don’t have that card there’s a very very low percentage chance you’re going to win.To go full circle, Balatro avoids the problem of “randomized instant death” by giving you two opportunities, the Small and Big Blind rounds, to cycle the shop and give yourself a fighting chance to overcome the obstacle in front of you.  D&DG does provide two choices per floor, minus boss encounters, but no way to see what is ahead so if both the choices are two enemies you don’t have the cards to fight against: you lose and there’s no going back.  Nothing is more debilitating for a game than to provide the enjoyment of the fruits of your labor only to lose to something you can’t control.And this feeling will follow you throughout your playthroughs.  There are plenty of times where I misplayed a hand and put myself in a scenario to lose, or I didn’t clock my Advantage correctly and didn’t take the shot when I should have, but it’s mirrored by your opponent tossing out 21s like they’re fun coupons or you run into a foe who’s deck is so blatantly powerful it’s clear you’re headed for a restart because you didn’t grab that one card 3 floors and 15 fights ago.  D&DG revels in the fact that you will go on losing streaks so you can unlock more of what is to offer but where games like Dark Souls or Lies of P counterbalance these losses with taking what you’ve learned and using it for the next fight, you’ll leave most losses just hoping the next time they don’t get the House Luck as much as they did this time.Which is a real shame, because the labor of love to provide a near infinite amount of deck combinations, the instilled humor of the characters and situations the D&D style setting travels you through, and the pure card-comboing shenanigans that you can pump out within a run is fascinating and can be really fun when it clicks.  But there is, and I shouldn’t really be surprised in this, a frustrating amount of luck involved with having a good time, and no game’s final outcome should have you winning but feeling like a loser.Aw, dang it.

_childDocuments_.review: Many reviewers are focusing on the state of the gameplay but I only want to highlight one thing: This game has no Borderless Fullscreen option. This wouldn't be a massive issue if it weren't for the fact that the game crashes when entering fullscreen. Not for everyone, but for me, and for many other players who started/replied to threads about this issue. I bought this game on launch and haven't been able to play it once. I tried everything. Updated drivers, edited the user settings file, restarted my PC, launched the game at the native resolution of my display, tried it on a TV and a monitor. I made a thread in the forum, waited, bumped it, waited. Nothing so far. I haven't had this issue with other, far more system-intensive games. I'd recommend avoiding this game for a while and maybe checking back in a couple of months, especially given the other reviews re: player agency and decision-making within the game's systems; and the news that the devs are going to try and address these problems. Proceed at your own peril until then.August 19th Edit: The beta update didn't fix this, but if you have this fullscreen issue, try this, it worked for me (with an AMD graphics card):Open your AMD Adrenaline software, navigate to the Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers entry in the Games section, go to Graphics, Radeon Super Resolution, change from Enabled to Enabled (Borderless Fullscreen) and the game should launch. Hope this helps someone. Now that I can actually play the game I'll update my review with thoughts later.

_childDocuments_.review: Honesty I really want to like this game. I've been through the gauntlet a bunch of times now and its very apparent that there is one successful way to play this game. It however is not a git gud game, due to the heavy reliability on RNG mechanics for YOUR random deck. The opponents decks are all catered to synergize together and work incredibly well against you. You will have an incredible run only to be met by a hard counter to what you were able to throw together throughout play. Losing does not feel like a step forward for next time it feels incredibly cheap and will eventually show you the only way to build a deck to win the whole game. If this is a deck building game with multiple choices on how to play, then why is there really only one way to succeed. This game has a great potential to be really good and I have had fun playing it but overall I will be waiting for some game play changes or balances. I cannot recommend the game in its current state. I think if the developers added options to the game to create a balanced game then I will happily continue to play. (such as removing healing factor for enemies)
