_childDocuments_.review: I have played this game for 250+ hours and I originally did not like the game for many reasons, there are some positives but massively outweighed by negatives for me. I continued to play due to friends who have now stopped playing and quit so I am now also free to do the same.The PositivesDungeon bosses have mechanics that are good/engaging but not so hard pugs can't do them.Variety of choices in build (weapons/skills/passives)Multiple loadoutsReasonable levelling speedArena - small scale pvp is good just needs some balancingThe NegativesDesync - The game moves you to places you never even moved to and can put you in boss mechanics, it also desyncs Peace bosses and you see them alive when everyone else has already killed it (you cannot cast abilities due to this lag) and it disconnects you.Running over rocks might rubber-band you for 30 seconds straight, don't run on rocks.Grappling - Again grappling with lag causes you to teleport or for nothing to happen, sometimes when you need to fly after grappling it just doesn't work and you crater into the ground taking damage or dying.Large scale pvp, WHY. It is just bad, skills stop working, half the classes are obsolete in large scale or play a minimal role at best, It is just a bunch of mindless drones following 1 guys orders. 1 Guild always seems to have way larger numbers and just dominates which ruins the point/fun of the pvp because there is no competition.Arena - Exclusive: limited to 1 SnS and 1 Wand, A paladin fills both those roles and means no one else can use either of those weapons - instead of balancing these weapons and possibly making them less appealing to run multiple of but allowing it they instead just outright banned multiple of them which means friends may not be able to even queue together.Grinding: this game is extremely unrewarding, it takes forever to achieve anything outside of the battle pass or the contracts/weekly stuff to the point it is almost pointless to even play.Gearing: feels designed the way it is just to make you want to swipe (you can just buy the traits/items you want for stupid amounts of money), you need to find the it with a good trait, then find more good traits to unlock other trait slots then feed more items with those traits into it to upgrade the traits with lower quality items being a 10% chance to succeed (and a small pity mechanic)  Trait unlock stones is the only other option to unlock traits and they are extremely limited (time gated).Bosses drop a lot of the BIS items and most of the time 1200+ people show up to them and 1 maybe 2 people get loot from them, a lot of that loot not even being the good loot.They have events every hour most of the time, some of these events may last almost the entire hour taking you into the next event, some may last 5 minutes at best, this makes it really hard to do things you want to when you want to as they are constant throughout the entire day. (makes it hard to get into a grind mindset when constantly interrupted)Time gating: You cannot just lot in and do what you want since everything worth doing is time gated behind a currency or timer, contracts, dungeons, open dungeons, guild contracts.Guild: Constantly expected to do things to benefit the guild instead of yourself, (I am not talking about helping other members of the guild) I am talking about contributing to the guilds level/reputation which is a huge daily grind in itself that is expected of every member in any meaningful guild.Guild contracts are also a once a day thing, for some people they are complete before you even log in and due to that you cannot participate in them, some guilds look at contribution and frown upon you if you did not contribute enough, this makes the guild contracts more important and punishing for people who don't get a chance to do them.Alliances: 70 man guilds with 3 allied guilds makes 280 people that do not even have an alliance chat to form groups or communicate in game, you have to use an external method making it harder to form groups across guilds for pve and pvp for no reason.Tagging mobs: It uses the tag first method for loot which promotes toxicity, people with bows just running around tagging stuff and dumping the threat on others, just poor design, this also encourages guild members not in the same group to compete against each other.Bugs: you will sometimes be thrown into terrain while grappling and unable to move (have to teleport out), you can be spawned underground or in the ground, there are probably more but I haven't experienced many bugs that I did not contribute to lag or desync.In short, the game is pay to win, time gated, grindy, laggy, buggy, constantly interrupting you and tries to force non character progression activities on you constantly.

_childDocuments_.review: Its early.At first it looked like it had all the typical tropes. The story typically high fantasy candy. The combat a lot like Guild wars 2. But at its core it incorporates all of the old designs of past MMOs. Its not skimping on how full on that could be before everything was streamlined, simplified and dumbed down. This is actually good.  But it demands a lot from you. The battle pass is pay to win in my books. I don't like the shop. I'm not a huge fan of the monetisation but what the hell I'm playing it free so far. You CANNOT get anything for free and if you're playing it you should pay for it somehow otherwise there will be no good games or gaming companies left. This type of monetisation is aimed at whales who spend way too much on games in order to get ahead and its great for short term profit but that's about all. Otherwise it's poison for gaming and games.It's a pretty game graphics wise. The combat seems very average to start with but it grows on you in a retro way. The original design requiring team work is there harking to a time when games were designed to bring people together and not a disconnected and lonely toxic experience. There's so much to do and the UI is extremely overly complex. So many key binds and keys to press. Standard UI with mini map, quest log, skill bar, potions etc. But the gear and skill progression systems are beyond complex. They're almost stupid. And yet it is celebrating all that was good in games like WOW and FFXIV to start. Before WOw became a sea of quest marker exclamation marks for mind numbing boring collect quests and FFXIV became an anime CGI movie interspersed with one or two raids.It'll crash and burn once all the dvmb-assed players race to level 50 and experience the end game they're all in such a rush to experience so they can flex. The story line alone gets you there way too quickly and the rest of the things to do on the way are too time consuming and complex to do. Requiring the game to consume your schedule and the making of appointments to fulfil achievements. Players who want to flex will be flexing to no-one in a month because flexing isn't worth the time of day, we've seen that before in games such as New World. It's the completion ism, exploration, theory crafting and levelling journey that's fun. Once that's done the game is over. I can only give a thumb up or down. It has to be thumbs up because this game deserves a higher ranking than 65 % approval. It needs more people playing it. The game is  pay to win. The monetisation is toxic. You need to work out how much you think a game is worth and only pay what you think is right.  If Diablo 4 gets panned for being $110 here in Australia and Elden ring is seen as great value for $86 then you have a guide. Why cant someone make a game that's fair in terms of monetisation, using the action combat of a FROM game yet make it is busy as this game is in terms of things to do to stay busy?Rich whales shouldn't win by spending money. That adds to a game that's basically toxic in terms of community right out of the gate.The text chat interface isn't great. And the measure of this type of game i.e. the co-op dungeons with random players is a toxic affair mostly. Button mashing and inadequately telegraphed boss ins-ta kill abilities make for lots of deaths and lots of frustration. Often its a stun or push that's required but the best indicator of when to use these is the voice audio of the boss. Often this is out of sync with the ability. The ability itself is hard or impossible to see due to design. The MMO game genre NEEDS a success story or it will die. It is dying. Yet Throne and Liberty is doing okay for at least a few days

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: The designers have probably never played any PVP-Focused MMOs before.- The PvP combat is stun-lock heaven.- Ability cooldowns on average are greater than 20-30 seconds.- Time-to-kill is very low.- Zerg-fiestas dominate, as this is primarily a numbers game over anything else.- Multiple servers and server transfers mean that politics are useless, anyone can just leave at a moments notice, whether it is because you dominated an enemy and they left and now your server is boring, or you got dominated and want to leave your server instead of trying to turn things around.- Localization is some of the worst I've seen in many years, though I didn't play Lost Ark so I can't comment on that one but I hear it wasn't great either.- There are no raids. You cannot setup raids in an open-world PvP game where they expect groups of 280 to fight each other over a castle. - Physics-based gameplay (pushes, pulls, gliding, grappling) is notoriously buggy and glitchy, causing both combat and non-combat to be frustrating and unpredictable. It's a horrible show of Unreal Engine's capabilities.- Most combos in the game are self-driven combos, and will not work with other players even using the same abilities or combos. Debuffs belong to the player who caused them, and in most cases can only be combos with that same player.- Content for solo players is unremarkable and there is no endgame for solo players or small guilds. This inevitably causes the death of PvP MMOs as the game only bleeds players and never retains small groups.- Group based PvP isn't capped, meaning whoever is more active in a particular timezone wins.- Scheduled events for everything, including at times that don't make sense. This is a theme park at its finest, and not a Sandbox MMO.- Alliance system exists without an Alliance chat.- PvP occurs every 2 hours for 30 minutes, and if you die in PvP zones in most cases you can't go back, or have to go through a chokepoint to participate again. This will be slightly remedied with further content coming out later, including a 24/7 combat zone, though details are sparse on that. There will be more battlegrounds as well, from 1v1 to 48v48, but I expect those will be scheduled events.- Min/maxing daily coins you get to get the best RNG possible for drops for your time is annoying and frustrating.- Combo possibilities between different selected weapons are minimal if non-existent between most choices. It's less about combos and more about playstyles- one weapon usually helps with utility and/or survivability while another is your damage, that sort of thing.- In most cases, player stats in the game are not obvious, and it's not due to localization, but rather intentionally hidden information from the player.Now the things I don't really care about myself:- Heavily limited customization options.- No real concept of housing or life skilling to any meaningful degree.Now for the things I like:- My friends are playing so I guess I'll keep checking it out for the mean time to hang out, and hopefully issues are remedied. However that's just about everything keeping me here.

_childDocuments_.review: After 4 hours in, Throne and Liberty just hasn't grabbed me the way other MMOs do. The world feels bland and lacking in personality, and I’m still waiting for that hook that usually pulls me into games like WoW or FFXIV. Those games have an instant draw—whether it's the immersive storytelling, unique world design, or engaging combat—but here, everything feels kind of flat.The pacing feels off, and nothing about the gameplay has stood out as particularly exciting or memorable. While I understand that MMOs often take time to reveal their full potential, the early game experience is usually where you get a sense of what’s to come, and so far, I’m just not feeling it.Maybe things pick up later, but for now, I can't help but feel underwhelmed. If you’re looking for an MMO that grips you from the start, Throne and Liberty hasn’t done that for me yet.

_childDocuments_.review: If you don't wish to read a thorough analysis: Pointless, a waste of time and a money grabber masked as a game.If you have time to read a thorough analysis:I have been playing mmorpgs for more than 15 years at this point. I have tried almost every mmorpg out there. Throne and Liberty is nothing more than a money grabber that tried to follow a mmorpg formula. Unfortunately it fails miserably on every single level. It's a game without soul, without an essence. By february next year, probably will plummet to 10k players.The pros:- Visually good game.- Decent optimization when not in mass pvp, with minimal loading times.- Good soundtrack.The bad:- Classless system- 2 weapons to swap. What is this?- PVE and PVP builds. Why? Just to make more money.- Only human race- Auction House with real money currency- Not a social game. _childDocuments_.review: AGS and NCSoft, you've managed to turn Throne and Liberty into yet another pay-to-win cash grab that leaves most of us feeling frustrated and ignored. This game’s loot system is a nightmare, it only rewards high-spending DPS players, while tanks, healers, casual players, and anyone not in a top guild are left with nothing. By basing loot on damage contribution, you've made it nearly impossible for essential roles like tanks and healers to compete, which destroys any incentive to play these roles at all.The top guilds here can manipulate events by switching from peace to conflict mode, gatekeeping world bosses, and hoarding all the rare loot while the rest of us are left with scraps. It’s like you designed the game to give whales everything and leave the rest of us behind. This setup turns what should be a competitive MMO into a monopoly where only the richest players thrive, and the gap between them and the rest of us just keeps growing.AGS’s track record makes it clear why this game is going downhill fast. Remember Crucible? Pulled back to beta and killed off in no time. Or New World a promising game that you quickly ruined with unbalanced, money focused mechanics. NCSoft is no better, having run games like Aion Classic and Blade & Soul 2 straight into the ground with ridiculous pay-to-win mechanics. Time and time again, you’ve both shown that you care more about squeezing out profit than about delivering a fair, enjoyable game.If you actually want Throne and Liberty to survive, you need to throw out this predatory loot system and make it something that gives everyone a fair chance, no matter their role or spending level. But if you’re going to keep this “rich get richer” model that only rewards the top 1%, then prepare to watch your player base walk away, because this game won’t be the first one you’ve killed through sheer greed and incompetence

_childDocuments_.review: Throne and Liberty is a free-to-play MMORPG developed by Korean developer NCSOFT meaning yes - you can whale your game into “Winning”Once inside the game, wielding your credit card like a sword you make your way through a relatively alright tutorial and introduction sequence that tells you that you got Starlight within you, Paimon 2.0 and the ability to transform into your favourite furry friends of nature. After that you find out that not only are you absolutely nothing special amongst the thousands of other special Stardust sniffing furry transformers, you also can morph into other ♥♥♥♥. Like crabs, Goblins, Spiders, overly monetized battle pass miniatures.Yes this game has a Fortnite Battle Pass and YOU are going to not only be tempted to buy the premium battle pass, but it also has a LEVEL PASS - in which you can also buy a premium version of it. But that’s aside the point, you got to choose a primary and a secondary weapon with individual skills and passive skills to equip. There are a few weapons to choose from but ultimately it boils down to Tank, Healer and Damage Dealer, amongst which you got Sword’n’Shield, the wand with book which both can have whatever as secondary to compliment them and for Damage Dealer you got Bow and Daggers. Seriously I wasted a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ materials to find out what to run and even though most DPS builds use the daggers, the only true damage dealer class is Bow and Daggers. Everyone else is a clown with a funny hat.Hold on mate! I hear you say - I don’t see this advice on build pages and all that I do have other options, right? Pfft, yea, if you play the content up to level 50. But honestly, once you hit endgame content, you’re going to realise how difficult it is as a black mage in a white neighbourhood.So you might as well say that you have freedom to do whatever you want in that game and sure, more power to you. Lifeskilling in this game can be summarised up to Fishing, Cooking and taking bigger Ls than your little brother does at playing Tarkov. You don’t have a little brother? See, that’s what you get for living in Ohio.Fishing is…self-explanatory. Get a hook, get some bait, throw the hook, yank the pole until the fish is tired and then be happy that you got materials for literally just cooking or a bag with materials that increase your fishing pole. You fish to fish in order to become the fish but I digress, cooking surrounds itself around materials you can fish, gather in the wilds, buy from the local shopkeep and Salt.These highly marketable plushies you can collect in game and also through the MIGHT of your credit card, you can go into your whimsical home and send these plushies on expeditions. Preferably once to get Salt. The more Expeditions they finish, the higher their level and eventually you can send more plushies out.And then you cook. For buff food. audible breathing - Expedition is the third life skill which is the most fun one to do because you can go outside, walk around [getting hit by mobs] and gather materials from material points you can see on your map. They are not bound to the person so whenever you see a tree stump you wanted to cut down being cut down by another player, the material node will disappear and you have to move onto another node, making those materials you gather truly your own. What a wonderful and fun experience!Speaking of, did you ever want to know how it feels like to be playing online from the actual Amazon Forest? Well now you can, simply join a European server and over short or long you will see the funny internet connection error notification as the nice invisible people with black suits carry you back to the main menu or even make your client crash completely. Truly kiss a 40 bucks free-to-play gaming experience.Let us not forget to mention the vast amounts of wonderfully nice comments this community gives to the developer on their discord! But I digress, my friends. Let’s talk about something more interesting to the rough core of MMORPG players, the part that wants to know….THE ENDGAMEThere’s this stigma about Korean MMORPGs and specifically MMORPGs either developed or published by Amazon that they are pay2win. I am here to debunk that theory in the most truthful manner. For you see, the endgame of Throne and Liberty consist of creating or becoming part of a Guild, join organised guild events with other max level players and grind for gear in dungeons.In that aspect, Throne and Liberty really isn’t too much different from your average MMORPG, you got Co-Op Dungeons, Abyssal Dungeons to loot, you got day and night changing time changing abyssal Dungeon areas from PvE to PvP zones, world bosses that are also PvE or PvP respectively depending on whatever the schedule feels like marking them as and if that isn’t enough you can also grind contracts and PvP events for gear.Or you could just wield the combined might of credit card and auction house and just $$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$Trading in this game is probably the most fun mechanic that ever has graced the digital landscape as trading with other players is virtually impossible without the auction house. In order to trade, you need to set a price for your item, pay the registration fee and on top of that also pay taxes. And all that with the game's real life currency. SO GET YOUR CREDIT CARD READY LADS! HERE COMES THE MONEY BAWHWAWHAWHHAHAs we have established this game has a lot to offer. I spent about 30 hours in this game and you, too, can grind for max level in even less than that. The speedrunning record so far lies below 4 hours, so long as you manage to not count in the frequent disconnects and server crashes, however, the game is nice to remind you as well, if you have played for way too long.So it is up to you, my dear reader, to decide if I have failed or succeeded in this task to debunk this game as pay2win. Because I honestly paid 40 bucks and all I won was losing my will to keep going and a rising interest to figure out if you can legally sue video game companies for selling a piece of labouring, unentertaining entertainment media. But oh well...Good luck and have fun!

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot honestly recommend this game.It's incredibly generic - everything from the graphics, the storyline, the music, right down to the game mechanics all feel like poorer iterations of things that other MMOs do far better. Even the morph system (when you sprint you turn into a mammal, when you swim you turn into an water-based creature, when you leap from a tall place you turn into a bird) as a unique selling point feels completely half-cooked.The crafting system is incredibly basic. The cooking vibe feels like a direct rip-off from the Monster Hunter games. Even your magical little companions, Amitoi, are a rip off of the Palicos from the MH games.The biggest issue for me though is the loot system is designed in such a way that the strongest keep getting stronger so if you're late to the game you're going to have to spend real-time cash in order to drag yourself out of the doldrums. Which is likely part of the plan from the devs.The journey to 50 is "ok" but after that it really struggles because your progress absolutely falls off a cliff - you can't do enough damage to bosses to reach the contribution required for the good drops so those that are already strong keep getting the good gear to sell or to transform into beneficial traits. You'll get completely wiped on PvP events for the same reason.My one line summary would be; it feels like a jumped up mobile game.

_childDocuments_.review: The controls in this game are abysmal. I can't set basic attack to be held, the only option is always on (WHY EVEN HAVE A BUTTON FOR IT?) or toggle (VERY MUCH not preferred). For my own preference, I hate this. Why even have a basic attack if by default, you can't even turn it off without enabling it in the menu? Just do what WoW does - have it on by default while attacking an enemy, and don't even have a UI element for it at all. It's basically invisible in retail WoW because you always have a filler to use, or an ability that takes priority over it - but if you don't have fillers, and using abilities interrupts it, it really should have the always on/toggle/hold to use option. This is an issue of skill expression that cripples my own enjoyment quite a bit. It means that essentially, core gameplay revolves around hitting buttons as they come off cooldown - creating a piano of cooldowns that you need to watch over. Watching 12 timers go down is NOT fun, no matter how you spin it.Following this - air movement. There's basically 0 air movement when jumping. This means you're locked into whatever direction you jump in. At that point just remove jumping or make it auto jump. No point in having a jump button if there isn't some degree of air control. I get that later on you can glide, but the heart and soul of any good movement is having some ability of control while in air. In WoW, you can stifle your jumps and shorten your jump - or double jump, or use movement abilities like blink or disengage, all depending on your class. In Gw2, you have complete air control, allowing you to do some really difficult platforming and jump puzzles. In Archeage, you have air control, gliders, and magithopters - essetially flying machines with a whole scale of movement, and if you cancel using a magithopter when you pull it out, you keep your upward momentum and can use it to use more movement abilities in the air - like backdrop (WoW's disengage), or Teleport (Blink). There's 0 skill expression in the movement here, and it hurts. You have what boils down to bird gliding, and that's it. It feels terrible.In combat, I discovered a horrible thing as well. For whatever reason, despite changing the button for auto run, if I press a certain combination of buttons - I'll start blinding auto running in a straight line. It honestly feels like I have no control of my character and that half of the decisions are made for me.The combat in this game feels okay when you use abilities, but the atrocious "auto attack" removes you from the experience right away. They expect you to bind roughly 12 keybinds for skills, 4 for items, 3 more for quickslots - I'm never coming back to this. Gw2 did it right. 5 buttons per weapon, swap between weapons to access the other five buttons. Then you have a dedicated heal button - simple and intuitive - and 3 utility slots, with one elite slot. Perfect, I only need 10 buttons in total, with one more button to swap weapons. Anything above 12 is already a lot to keybind, especially with targetting and control schemes this terrible requiring not just one button to target, but a button to target and switch targets (why can't you have simple tab targetting?) In classic WoW, I have around two or three main buttons I had, and a million situational buttons. Most keybinds there are for opening something like say, the leatherworking menu, or using a potion - sure, it's a lot, but the core of the game is hitting at most 5 buttons, and then having roughly 3-5 buttons for emergencies, and then the rest is optional and to reduce clicking. In retail WoW, it's roughly the same situation. You have 3-5 buttons for your core rotation and fillers, then around 7 situational buttons, and maybe 2-3 buttons for self buffs - it's a lot, but it's manageable. You only need two buttons for healing (self heal, potion), and the rest I can place on buttons that make sense to me. (My Disengage, for example, is on Shift+S, which feels super intuitive to press).Here, I'm instantly hit with the issue of having 8-12 rotational buttons to hit. It's not a few core buttons and some bloat, it's roughly a dozen buttons you HAVE to hit - it's button bloat. Like for example - I have like, six buttons with my bow that are required, passive buttons, elite buttons, then six buttons with my wand, some are situational, then I have potions on buttons, all in all you're pushing around 18 buttons that you have to find room for. Now, I have 5 buttons on my mouse. I have a good chunk of space on my keyboard. But I also need buttons for setting a target then changing a target, a button to parry, a button to morph, a button to grapple, a button to talk, buttons to access UI - it's too damn much. It really is too damn much. It's bloated.To really put the nail in the coffin, you basically can't use any weapon ability without an enemy targeted and in range. This feels absolutely abysmal. In Gw2, which has proper action combat, you can use your skills whenever, wherever, unless if it's something so niche that it requires a target to even activate (which is like, 1/30 moves on average, and it's often something like "reveal the enemy and prevent them from using stealth"). So not only do you have 0 control over your basic attack, you have no control over when you use your abilities unless if there's an enemy specifically right in front of you. But T&L has a lot of action combat abilities and clearly shows itself as an Action Combat game. You have a block and parry system, a dodge, you even have *action cam mode*, but you have essentially none of the core aspects of action cam, and you have terrible default movement. Couple this with excessive keybinds, and this game is a chore.And looking at buffs and debuffs, I already know for a fact that this game is going to have 10,000 UI Icons you'll want to memorize for specific events. Oh, this is a Dagger bleed - but THIS is a greatsword bleed that will make me vulnerable to greatsword 5, and this bleed is actually a bow bleed - but it's not REALLY a bleed because it's a target, so it doesn't actually benefit Sword and Shield 3, but it works for Greatsword 3 - it's going to be hell to understand intuitively. Watching this game WILL feel bad for anyone not intensely aware of the game's mechanics and every type of buff and heal applied. And it will quite literally - only get worse, especially if the game starts adding more weapons and bloat.I feel like I need a piano to play this game. I've played both classic and retail WoW, Archeage for thousands of hours, and I didn't feel this much pressure to have this many buttons keybound, because each button in T&L is vital. If I can change weapons freely and with 0 cooldown, why can't I just share the same button slots? Because I can use attacks from the other weapon with my main weapon equipped? I would honestly prefer weapon swapping because it makes far more sense and it's less button stress. Or make it an option in the menu. But don't pigeonhole me into playing with a piano because it's optimal for a 3% DPS increase.I do not recommend this game in its current state and I already know these issues will NEVER be addressed, because it's the developer intention. Playing beyond this point doesn't seem smart, but I should at least give it like... at least 5 hours in total to see if I can tolerate it until it gets better. I have a feeling I won't. But I should at least try. Oh, and I didn't even touch on the supposed P2W. So just take this as my own ramblings about gameplay without even thinking about store content.

_childDocuments_.review: By CuatroThis won't scratch your MMO itch. TnL is a massive cash grab with its in-game Lucent ecosystem and 22% tax, and Guilds as first-class citizens system.This is a pay-to-win PvP game masquerading as an MMO. Combat is stale in PvP and PvE settings; the targeting system isn't robust and can sometimes be non-obvious where your character is targeting. This goes up a lot when you are in mass PvP balls.PvP boils down to the biggest group with the most whales. Some creators have touted this game as 'you can't become a raid boss', and it's been the opposite. Play a healer, stack evasion, and buy your gear. You'll most certainly be a raid boss. For anyone outside of that category and isn't a tank, the PvP is stun and nuke. No counterplay, just few shot combos to delete a player.End game is guild PvP mass content where all of the interactivity boils down to who's showing up with the biggest numbers. Guild alliances can deadlock conflict zones, and cater to folks with endless time.There is no end game PvE. It does not exist, and bosses are unchallenging, but somehow extremely punishing for noobies as the mechanics are non-intuitive to players that aren't good at MMO bosses. It's a paradox, I know.The tl;dr of the cons list is: the PvP is bad in a game that's solely about PvP, and a lot of that is caused by P2W and guilds as first class citizens.Now for the positives -Game looks good, and the animations are appealing. The optimization is a bit on the weak side, but DLSS helps a lot with that. I'm running the game on 4k with a 4090, and outside of PvP mess halls it runs OK. 2k resolution is probably the sweet spot here.Weather effects are awesome. They have a dynamic effect on the world, and are used to determine accessibility to some content. Players at the top of the kill boards get world altering skills that can force rain or darkness.World dungeons is something more games should be doing, and TnL's implementation does a great job at making things feel massive. They haven't capitalized very well on all the cool things that could be done with world dungeons, but it's a step in the right direction.Contracts are a nicer version of dailies, and have some randomness baked in, but you get to choose where you do the dailies which is nice.The many different chat options are a good add. Allows people to communicate freely and makes for some fun interactions.The overall takeaway is that the game looks good, and has some seriously cool mechanics in place in terms of world building, interactivity, and semi-dynamic events. However, a profound amount of this good gets overshadowed by the terrible group PvP optimization, clunky combat system, no end game beyond 'take castle and tax', and the obvious P2W environment that many have touted as being a non-issue in early stage reviews prior to NA release. There are better ways to implement PvP, and there are many other MMOs out there that are miles ahead in this category despite having been out for a decade or more.Would I play this game again? Probably. Would I recommend it to anyone else after playing it? No.

_childDocuments_.review: A Fresh Take on the MMORPG GenreI've been playing Throne and Liberty for a while now, and I must say, I'm really impressed. It's not often an MMORPG manages to balance a beautiful open world, engaging combat, and deep progression, but this game truly delivers on all fronts.Graphics and EnvironmentsThe world is incredibly beautiful with stunning landscapes and details. Whether you're exploring ancient ruins, vast forests, or snow-capped mountains, it feels like every area is alive and carefully crafted. The graphics engine does a great job of creating an atmospheric experience.Combat SystemThe combat is smooth and responsive, with a good mix of action and strategy. Each class feels like it has its own identity, and finding the right combination of skills and gear for your playstyle gives a real sense of progression. Boss fights and world events are also thrilling and challenging.Community and Social GameplayOne of the game's strongest points is how it encourages cooperation. The guild system and the opportunities to collaborate with other players in both PvP and PvE events are well-designed. It feels like the community is central here, and that adds to the dynamic, living world.Exploration and FreedomThe ability to shapeshift into different animals to explore the world is a really fun and unique feature. It gives you a sense of freedom and access to areas that would otherwise be hard to reach.ConclusionIf you're looking for an MMORPG with depth, stunning visuals, and a dynamic world that evolves with your gameplay, I highly recommend Throne and Liberty. It definitely has the potential to become a favorite for both veterans and newcomers to the genre.

Worlds events are pretty much only for the top large guilds due to the "Conflict" scenario which is really stupid.  Sure lets make the boss event a massive pvp arena, really dumb design idea.Character design is your typical holy trinity of tank/damage/heal which is nice.  And you have decent freedom to create your character which can be rare in some f2p games.Don't spend money and you'll probably enjoy it for what it's worth, which is a time sink and break from reality. _childDocuments_.review: The game is the classical Korean RNG based game: the goal is to farm and raise the combat power.Content wise there are instances, group content, pvp content, pve, bosses, many (redundant) other mechanics... there is "a lot" to do, but you must follow strict rules and timings. Many almost all the PvP is instanced or scheduled and limited to fixed areas.Player trading is strictly moderated (devs say they do this cause of goldseller, meh...), in the auction you can trade a limited assortment of objects with a currency that you can buy in the shop for real cash. You can't even trade your crafted items (unless you "crit" them) or loot.All other mechanics are really the condensed concepts of themeparked game with an overly complex combat system with dozens of different undocumented and somethimes mysterious parameters.The only things that limits the grind are the time and quantity limited amount of items that enable for part of the game content (scrolls/points for contracts, points to drop from certain areas, points to unlock chests...)Overall i find it a very repetitive product, that requires an everyday effort (cause activity points recharge daily basis and there is a cap for the amount you can stack). Some may love it, but I think that the majority of westerner users will leave in a couple of months. If you want to raid bosses for a (small) chance of higher level drop, you must enter in a guild, learn to play and tryhard gearing accordingly to standard optimal builds until the next expansion that will of course change the meta and force you to start all over again.I already feel a bit tired, now that I understand the endgame and I'm not sure I want to repeat the same instances with ridiculously low drop rates, so I'm just casually playing.The pros? Well... it's free.Technically the game is fine, some areas are very well made (like the initial town) but others are really boring and less insipred consisting in just fields full of packed mobs with fast respawn rate. Textures and models also are not consistent in quality.The engine (UE4) works fine but you'll need a powerful CPU to manage large crows of players. My Ryzen 5900X limits the GPU to 60-70% in cities with many players. Maybe a series 7xxx or 9xxx X3D can behave better, not sure.A final suggestion: if you are not an hardcore player, DO NOT RUSH the game. Take your time, follow the story, do the side quests and watch the cinematics. The lore is not that bad and you can enjoy at least 30-40 hours of decent gaming before entering the demonic endgame loop.

_childDocuments_.review: To preface the review, I'm not a huge MMO player. I have played some over the years, but never gone all in one MMO and played it for years and years. I find the MMOs in general to have a lot of fundamental flaws that makes them not fun over the long term. Also, my experience has been mostly focused around PvE. Now, to the review of this game itself. I generally liked the game. It's not a masterpiece by any stretch of the imagination, but I'd say it's a solid 7.5-8 out of 10 for the content that is there. The good:- Graphics are really nice, visual effects are cool looking, the locations are pretty nicely done in general. - The combat system feels quite fluid. You have a limited set of active abilities, making you choose which build you wanna go for and give up certain abilities in favour of others. You have 2 weapons, all of which have their own skills, and you pick and choose what to use depending on what you're doing. A really good thing is that you don't need to swap to your other weapon to use that weapon's skills - you can easily run around with greatsword and use crossbow abilities at range without hassle. - The levelling is completely fine, you don't need to grind mobs 24/7 to hit a max lvl cap. I think you can get to level 50 in just 9-10 hours, provided you know what to do and generally just follow the main questline. Min-maxing starts at max level, though. - There's a variety in activities which you can do, both PvE and PvP. There's fishing that can net you some rare gear, there's pretty barebones cooking. There's non-restrictive crafting, in the sense that you don't have to level it up to craft max level stuff, just need the materials. All of these act like supplementary activies to get you more powerful either temporary, but they aren't the focus and aren't very deep. - Decent boss design - there's a plethora of bosses to fight, by yourself - in a Secret dungeon, with a group - Co-op dungeons, and with a lot of people - world bosses/guild bosses. Overall, some bosses are very straightforward, some have fairly complex mechanics that you need to follow otherwise they're varying degrees of impossible to complete. - Parry/Block - nice touch overall, because every weapon has its own block ability that gives you benefits for perfect parry. For a tank (sword and shiled), you get a pretty sizeable self-heal + temporary shield with some mana restored on a perfect block. These timings are very generous (unless you're stunned) and are super clearly telegraphed by both a visual cue and a sound cue. The more devastating the attack, the more time you have to perfectly time it. Even if you don't time a block perfectly, you still have some window to defend against the damage, but you're not getting the special ability bonus, as you would if you perfect parried. - You get 3 presets for abilities, allowing you to tailor your build depending on what you do. You can easily switch between them unless an ability is on cooldown. So you can't swap ability sets during battle easily, making you commit to a preset you chose. The annoying thing here is that you can't just copy your current present onto a different slot and change some abilities, you have to build it from scratch. - The game can be played completely for free and you don't need to pay to get rare stuff. An active guild + quite a bit of item grinding can get you all the same gear + you can sell some of your items (with restrictions, though) to get Lucent, the premium currency. For high-end PvP you need a lot of grinding to be on the same level as those who put a lot of money into the game, though. The very best stuff is insanely pricey. For 95% of PvE you can make do with much less expensive stuff and still be very useful. - The game generally describes most of the mechanics and prepares you for the late game, but it could still use some work in my view. - The game tells you exactly where a certain item gets dropped and the exact chance of it dropping, making hunt for specific items a lot less frustrating. - People actively look for guild members, even if you're new, so I advise you get into a guild and ask for various advice, help with dungeons etc. People have been generally friendly from my experience. The bad:- Parkour system needs a lot of work. It's quite inconsistent and requires being super precise in the least important segments sometimes. Also, when you have connection issues, it becomes infuriating. Thankfully, parkour isn't essential in most of the areas, so it's not that bad. On the face, the system is interesting and I think it could be good after some improvements are made. - Plethora of enchanting mechanics that are quite confusing initially. I'm not going to explain them here because I'm not 100% sure on all of these mechanics myself yet. - Some areas have times of forced PvP due to events, or open-world dungeons just becoming hostile during the night. It might screw you over if you have a main story quest in the area and you're forced to do something else for 20-30 minutes until the night or the event is over. This is sometihng you can definitely work around, but can be annoying when you're just about to complete a quest and get killed randomly. I'm not a PvP fan, so for me it was a negative, for others that might be a positive instead because you do get plenty of opportunities of open world PvP. - A good guild is a must. Guilds provide you with the opportunity to do weekly guild boss battles, that are instances of world bosses (so you don't compete for them), in which you can obtain valuable gear. The higher the guild lvl, the more attempts per week you can do. Also guilds frequently have high-level dungeon parties which you'll need if you want to farm some rare items/resources in the dungeons. You can just as easily assemble a party with randoms on the spot, but with the guild you can plan your composition a bit and ensure you have a tank and a healer. The guild also gives you some passive bonuses like 2% extra EXP, some mana regen etc. Those aren't massive, but they do add up with your items' stats. Without the guild, you will struggle to get the rarest stuff. - There's not that much content yet. Once I got to lvl50, got a few decent items, I was able to run all of the dungeons and vast majority of bosses with the guild in like 20-30 hours. So the content is fairly limited, however, there are updates coming increasing the amount of content, so now could be a very good time to get into the game. - The story is nothing special. It's there, but it's not a masterpiece by any stretch of the imagination. Overall, the game is fine and you could definitely enjoy the grind for quite a bit of time. _childDocuments_.review: This is my first time writing a review because I’m genuinely concerned about where MMORPGs are heading.You log in to the game in the morning and start with dungeons - after all, that’s where you have the best chance of scoring some valuable loot. You’ve finished the dungeon three times and want to go for a fourth, but unfortunately, you’ve run out of points.So, you move on to farming open-dungeons. This is your favorite part of the game; the drops are rare, so when you finally get something, it feels incredibly satisfying. While farming, you can chat and laugh with your friends since beating mobs in open-dungeons doesn’t require much focus - it’s just laid-back clicking. You’ve been playing for half an hour and are having a great time, but suddenly… you run out of points. The mobs won’t drop anything more for you.Then comes the part of the game you despise - using contracts. You get 10 per day, with a maximum limit of 60. The rewards are mediocre, and you hate doing this every day. But what else can you do to push your character forward? After all, you’ve run out of daily limits for the things you actually enjoy in this game. Begrudgingly, you go back to doing contracts. Day in and day out.Someone might say, that’s how every Korean MMORPG works. I agree. But is that really an excuse for poor game design? By playing this game and spending real money on it, you’re supporting this type of game. You’re supporting these 'daily' systems and the P2W model. This game had 300,000 players online simultaneously at launch. The developers have already made a fortune off of it. What does that mean? It means that other developers will create similar games - because it’s profitable.Now, someone might argue that this game isn’t truly P2W. Everyone’s entitled to their opinion, but I find it hard to believe anyone would defend their favorite game so blindly. For me, the definition of P2W is simple - if paying gives you any advantage over a non-paying player, it’s P2W. A game can be more or less P2W. Can a game have an acceptable form of P2W? In my view, yes. If a non-paying player can fully max out their character within a month and then compete on equal footing with someone who paid a fortune to max out on day one, I’d consider that acceptable P2W. But in this game, you’ll never catch up to the whales. By the time you do, tier 2 gear will be introduced, then tier 3.So, I’m reaching out to all MMO players with a plea: support only games that are not P2W. We, the players, determine the shape of the MMO market, not the developers. They’re only doing what’s profitable for them - because players pay. Of course, developers’ greed plays a role here, but if we want to, we can take complete control over the P2W aspect in games.The game has also other issues, but I don’t consider them significant compared to the ones mentioned above, so I won’t list them.

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't get very far in the game and although this game has some unique ideas and definitely has potential there were cons that definitely outweighed the pros for me; one was big enough for me to quit and uninstall the game. Below are some of those pros and cons; it's my experience with the game so don't let it keep you from playing it if you are really on the fence.  Pros: 1. Interesting and unique combat mechanics and controls, including pretty seamless controller support.2. Great graphics 3. Monsters. Everywhere. And they don't all aggro.4. Quick loading screensCons:1. I don't like the sprinting mechanic. It's unique, but I just want to see my character run.2. The over world gathering points are a first-come-first-serve. If someone else gets there first, you're SOL.3. No real gear progression. You do have to unlock traits and move them around, which is a progression, but I just want my character to look good with available gear in-game at item breakpoints. I also didn't get this far in the progression.4. This is the big con that made me quit the game. There is no incentive for newer players to play and experience the game:I went into a level 20 dungeon at level 20. Other players queue'd in and rushed the boss. I went to provoke the mobs away from them so they could survive. They went to the boss and killed it. I was outside of the arena and couldn't get in, therefore could not participate in the fight. I was not able to loot the chest. I was later told by a friend that there isn't any sort of level sync or gear sync in the game and that I likely queue'd in with level 50 players. I started the game about 2 weeks later than him and realized that there weren't real incentives for new players to play if they could not participate in in-game content with a level requirement since all players will be higher level doing the same thing, effectively giving them an intentional built-in disadvantage. This is the deal breaker for me. I don't mind free-to-play games having microtransactions since the devs need to make money too, but when in-game mechanics gives new players a disadvantage, it makes me feel like it was intentional and is a bad business decision. If the game continues like this without addressing it, I can see it not appealing to new players.If you didn't play this game on release, I wouldn't recommend playing.

_childDocuments_.review: Throne and Liberty: Yet Another Pay-to-Win DisasterI came into Throne and Liberty with some cautious optimism, hoping it would break away from the ever-growing trend of pay-to-win MMOs. But after spending some time in this so-called “next-gen” MMO, it quickly became clear that it’s nothing more than a shiny facade masking the usual greed that has plagued the genre. If you're looking for a fair and fun experience, prepare to be sorely disappointed—because Throne and Liberty is a pay-to-win nightmare that epitomizes everything wrong with modern MMOs.Let’s start with the obvious: the cash shop. Instead of being a place where you can pick up cosmetics or small conveniences, it’s blatantly designed to siphon every penny out of your pocket if you want to actually compete. Progression? Forget it unless you’re willing to pay. The best gear, upgrades, and even essential items are locked behind absurd paywalls. Sure, you can theoretically earn them in-game—but it would take you years of grinding like a robot to get even close to what the whales can buy in an afternoon.MMORPGs are supposed to reward skill, time, and teamwork. Throne and Liberty completely dismantles that concept. Why bother investing time and effort when someone else can drop a few hundred dollars and outpace you with ease? It kills any sense of accomplishment when every challenge you face is trivialized by people who spent their way to the top. PvP is a joke—you either get obliterated by wallet warriors or you become one. And good luck in dungeons or raids, because your gear will always be second-rate unless you shell out real cash.What’s worse is that this pay-to-win model erodes any semblance of community. MMOs thrive on the bonds players form through shared experiences, struggles, and victories. But in Throne and Liberty, all of that is overshadowed by the glaring inequality between those who spend and those who don’t. How can you build a sense of camaraderie when everyone’s aware that no matter how good they are, someone else can just pay for an advantage? This isn’t a game world—it’s a virtual marketplace disguised as one.It’s not just the monetization, either. The gameplay itself feels hollow and repetitive, designed to keep you on an endless treadmill of mediocre content, all while waving shiny microtransactions in your face. The questing is stale, the combat is uninspired, and the world is lifeless despite its high production values. The developers clearly focused more on ways to get into your wallet than on creating an immersive or engaging experience.The worst part? This isn’t an isolated incident. Throne and Liberty is just the latest in a long line of modern MMOs that have abandoned what made the genre great in favor of quick profits. The days of truly immersive, player-driven worlds—where skill and dedication mattered—are gone, replaced by games that only care about how much money they can squeeze from their player base. Every time a game like Throne and Liberty comes out, it feels like another nail in the coffin for the MMO genre.In the end, Throne and Liberty is nothing more than a flashy, pay-to-win trash heap that spits in the face of what MMORPGs are supposed to be. It’s a reminder that greed has taken over, and unless we start demanding better, we’re going to be stuck with more of the same hollow, wallet-draining experiences. My advice? Don’t waste your time or money on this garbage.

_childDocuments_.review: Throne and Liberty is a breathtaking game that truly delivers on visuals. The graphics are gorgeous, and the immersion is enhanced by the sheer number of players online at the same time. It feels like a classic MMO, with solid gameplay and a lot of farming. A huge plus is that it doesn't seem to be Pay-to-Win—only cosmetic items are paid, and you can grind to earn premium currency, which is great.Edit: The game Auction House is pretty much mandatory, to keep up in pvp please insert Credit Card :)However, there's one major issue: the game is clearly optimized for Nvidia cards. Owning a RX 7600, I can say that while it’s not top-tier, it's still modern and comparable to an RTX 4060. Unfortunately, it struggles with Throne and Liberty. Nvidia users have access to DLSS 3 and Frame Generation, which are essential in crowded player zones or during PvP. On the AMD side, there’s only FSR 2.0, and it doesn't work well. If you don’t have a high-end AMD card, you're in for a rough experience.Another thing to note: go for a powerful CPU, ideally an X3D model, because the game is very demanding. And aim for at least 32 GB of RAM, or you’ll face performance issues.In summary, a great game, but non-Nvidia optimization is disappointing.

_childDocuments_.review: A review from a casual player:Knowing that you will never please everyone, and that everyone has different tastes, I would start by saying you just need to try this game. It's FREE, and the most you will lose is some time you could have spent on another game.I personally think this game is really great. Not perfect by any means, but still really great. I have had a lot of fun and honestly have very little complaints as a casual gamer. There are qualities this game implements from old school MMO's like grinding for gear, and there are plenty of new qualities as well. The biggest complaint from others: First, its worth mentioning again that this game is FREE (no upfront cost or subscription at all), and they need to pull money from somewhere. If whales want to spend their money on this game, let them if it means I don't have to pay for anything.People complain about it being PW2, but I have yet to come across an instance where I have been forced to open my wallet to obtain a piece of gear. However, I know the correlation they are trying to make. There is no direct trading in the game between players. Instead, if you want to get items, you have 3 choices: farm it, craft it, or buy it off the auction house(server wide trading post between players). Now, I will say, the major downside of the auction house is that it does not use the default in game currency, or 'gold', that you obtain from quests and killing monsters. Instead, you have to purchase a 'premium' currency to buy anything off the auction house. This is where the majority of the P2W belief comes from. So from this, yes, someone could open their wallet and spend hundreds of dollars and buy top level gear right away, but at the same time, most of the top level gear isn't even on the market. And how did that gear get there in the first place? Yep! Someone had to farm/craft it! So if they can do it, so can you!I do not believe this is P2W, but rather, nobody wants to play and experience games anymore. They want to be max level, max gear, max everything ASAP. They dont want to take take to actually play the game. I for one enjoy the aspect of having to put in some time to get top level gear. They act as if there is literally no other way to get the max gear (crafting/farming). I have spent time farming gear and thus far, I have not experienced any atrocious rates where I have had to sit at one location for several days. At most, I spent a few hours at one spot trying to get a staff drop. IMO, thats fair. The crafting system is unique and different as well. Mats can be obtained through a variety of ways, and only after crafting A LOT of gear did I find myself in a dry spot of little to no mats on certain items, making me head back to questing/farming mobs.The overall aesthetic of the game is 10/10 for me. Graphics, sound, narration, story, it all comes together really well. You can definitely tell its a Korean based MMO, but they have English sub/dub for the entire dialogue/narration of the game. There is a night/day cycle and a weather system, all of these aspects can affect certain skills/monsters, or what type of dynamic(world) events are going on. There is also a giant flying whale, so 10/10 there.The combat offers a unique take as well, basing your skills off what weapon you have equipped. You're able to have 2 weapons on at once, and can choose from both of their skills offerings how to load our your available 12 skill slots(ex, you could have a greatsword and staff, with 4 greatsword skills equipped and 8 staff skills equipped). Each skill also has around 2-6 upgrades that can enhance or completely change how that skill works or what that skill does. I enjoyed the story line and followed it all the way through. Not too long, not too short. It offers the best way to level up, and throughout the entire story you are gaining free rewards such as gear and mats for crafting.This is just my opinion, and again, an opinion of a casual player.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall the game is enjoyable until you attempt to gear for end game content.  Dungeons can only be ran three times per day with your allotted daily tokens, so getting equipment there is extremely slow.  World bosses spawn in either PVP mode or PVE mode.  PVP mode is just mass zerg fights between the top pay to win guilds on the server.  The PVP mode is the most effective way to get gear though, as your guild has the option to assign the gear to whoever they deem worthy to get it.  PVE mode has a small chance to drop one epic piece of gear, which is currently assigned to the highest DPS roles that participated. This means if your a tank or healer you have zero priority for gear from world bosses. On PVE bosses, they sometimes spawn in conflict zones which get griefed by the pay to win guilds, who activate an ability that forces the zone into a PVP area.  Once this happens they basically gatekeep the instance entrances and only allow their alliance members to enter.  Finally, if you are not wanting to spend a bunch of money on the game you are always going to be at a massive disadvantage to the people that spend thousands maxing out their epic gear.Overall I would not recommend this game to anyone I play with having experienced the massive pay to win aspect of the end game.

_childDocuments_.review: I really love how the reviews that tell you to not play the game have less than 6 hours of playtime. The game itself (pros):-Beautiful game-Nice community during the day-Entertaining endgame loop-Easy to understand UI, leveling and crafting systems, but they're nothing to talk about at this moment in time.-Rewarding gameplay to an extent.-The PvE content is enough to keep me entertained since I'm not big on PvP-Everything can be obtained without pulling out a credit card from my experience. -Lucent (premium currency) can be farmed in game. Cons about the game:-Heavily PvP oriented, but it's to be expected considering the thematic of the game.-Combat can feel clunky at times and there are a few bugs here and there-Farming can sometimes take you hours or days for you to obtain something (not really a con for me, but may be for others)-Story is decently mid and if you skip it you still feel caught up, characters are not memorable. -Crafting system is very bare bones, you'd expect to have the New World crafting system, but nope.-Resources are limited (players can steal resource spots from you if you ain't fast enough). -Life skilling (fishing and cooking) is very bare bones as well and needs improvement as well as more life skills. -Classes are very limited in their skills and what skills they take. (I like having bars full of skills). -Zergs are annoying and pretty awful to deal with if you're just questing in an area and no interested in the event. -Peace and conflict is a stupid mechanic, peace allowing F2P to not get killed while doing a world boss and conflict being PvP for a world boss as example, it applies to many other things in the game, just make PvE and PvP servers. -Customization is P2W and there's no transmog as of today.-Team based content sucks to solo since you can run into a team that can clear a dungeon in 10 minutes, meanwhile a bad team can take 2 hours, join a guild. -"Dungeons" and "Deep dungeons" have limited currencies that refresh daily, (it's a good thing for me since I work my 8 hours during the day, may suck for hardcore grinders), you can do the dungeon without the currency, but you can't open loot chests. -Skill books once you finish the story are hard to come by and can be difficult to come by specially if you want to swap to another class. -Class swapping is punishing due to the lack of story fed resources, it might be better to make a new character and start over. I have not tried the PvP content yet so no opinions on that.Overall the game is a solid 6/10 for me, it does a few good things right, but others need to be improved, if Amazon treats the game kindly and listens to the community this could be quite the gem.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like TL a lot. The guild content is fun, world looks great, and the story, while fairly basic and cliche, wasn't total garbage. The issue the game has as a result, is that there isn't much of anything you can really do outside of this content. There is no lifeskilling, fishing/cooking aside, and there is no real mindless grinding. I'm a grinder, I used to plant my ass for 8-12 hours a day in BDO and just farm out gear. Or in Archeage I'd slam my face into grinding purses and running packs back to back. TL at best allows you to grind very spaced out mobs in the open world for middling pieces of gear.Then the actual grinding is extremely limiting. Dungeons are capped at 3 a day (or you can save 15 runs up across 5 days) and open world dungeons are capped at a much less easy to quantify number, but still way too short. As a smaller gripe, the pity system for dungeons forces you to run dungeons you'd otherwise not need and that will cut into your daily runs a fair bit.Next issue is the PvP and to some extent the P2W nature of the game. PvP itself is more restricted than even New World, where every few hours it turns night for a little bit and then the open world dungeons turn PvP. Boonstone sieges happen every two days or so iirc and sometimes bosses are pvp on. This means the only on demand pvp are arenas. Random 3v3s where your gear matters, making p2w feel worse than it would normally. The rare moment you get a fair-ish array of players, the pvp is quite fun, which makes this even more disappointing.Even when you manage to get some open world pvp, the game heavily encourages top guilds to band together to stop any other guilds from participating. Which is the name of the game, I get it, but it doesn't feel great having no chance because all the top guilds have allied. Quick aside on this one, I can only speak for my server, but I have heard most servers that aren't dead, as well as KR, has had this issue.Top it all off with the p2w player market and you get a game that I wanted to love, but ultimately only ever had frustrations with. In conclusion: The game doesn't feature much on demand open world pvp, grinding is restrictive and gated far too much, there is damn near 0 lifeskilling or casual brain-off content, and P2W is rampant.

_childDocuments_.review: I had fun for hours but god this game is shallow.For a MMORPG like this I can't believe they restricted trading so hard in fear of bots and RTM which still exist. Or divide up tasks with friends and share consumables mats etc. You can barely sell your crafted items on auction house because it needs to be a great success (%10 chance), plus auction house trading is premium currency only.Probably no one cares about story but it is so damn cheesy after one point I just skipped all of the dialogue and rushed main chapters to level up. Some quest markers are so far apart and carefully placed in the middle of waystones it becomes annoying to constantly go from point A to B 5 times to finish a single quest. Yeah, MMORPGs have lots of fetch quests but at points this just becomes a walking simulator.There were interesting events on some of the quests but either it felt like it was poorly executed or just dragged on too much to the point of leaving a bad taste after completion. See all those trailers and gameplay footages of turning into wolves and eagles? It SUCKS. They are quite slow and lack stamina especially the eagle which only lets you "glide" some distance. Some areas you need to reach are annoyingly unreachable without first climbing a high point and gliding. It's also annoying to travel through elevation as the character rolls down slopes quite a lot.There are grappling hook rings around the map but they are not in the places you would expect and annoying to use. It is hard to aim to for one, but the wonkiness of movement makes it so difficult to land and not get into a glitched state on ledges. Those hook rings don't even chain properly which makes it even more annoying to use, and at some places it doesn't chain to ANYWHERE AT ALL where you are just stuck at someplace. Also god forbid you try to fall down from any ledges the game will just put you back where you were in a glitched state where you keep falling down.I'll probably keep playing for a little more then just say goodbye.

_childDocuments_.review: Throne and Liberty: A Game Review That's Half Laughter, Half TherapyWelcome to Throne and Liberty, a game that’s as visually stunning as your ex’s Instagram feed but with enough clunky mechanics to remind you why you should stick to browsing cat videos. Let’s dive into the pixelated world of thrill and frustration—because what’s gaming without a sprinkle of chaos, right?The Good Stuff (Pros)Visuals That Wow: If you’ve ever wanted to feel like you’re frolicking through a digital wonderland, Throne and Liberty delivers. The graphics are breathtaking—think of it as the game equivalent of a fancy artisanal latte. Every environment is beautifully crafted, making you forget that you just spent an hour stuck in a bush trying to find the exit.Character Customization: Ever wanted to create a character that looks like a warrior but fights like a toddler with a plastic sword? You can! The customization options are so extensive that you might spend more time tweaking your character's jawline than actually playing the game.Large-Scale PvP: There’s nothing quite like the thrill of watching 500 players try to crush each other like overripe grapes in a giant wine press. The chaos is exhilarating, albeit slightly terrifying. Just don’t expect to be the hero in this cinematic masterpiece—unless you have a death wish.Progressive Low to Midgame: The early game is like that satisfying first sip of coffee in the morning—great rewards, a sense of growth, and a hope that maybe today you won’t screw it all up. It feels like you’re moving forward, and that’s a refreshing change from staring at your screen wondering why you still don’t have pants.Fair Upgrading System: Unlike that friend who always takes the last slice of pizza, the weapon, armor, and skill upgrading system is fair and balanced. You actually feel like your efforts matter, which is a delightful surprise in a game that often feels like a hamster wheel.The Not-So-Good Stuff (Cons)Endgame PvE: Time-Gated and Repetitive: Once you hit the endgame, you might feel like you’re trapped in a never-ending episode of a reality show where the only plot twist is more waiting. Time-gated content can feel more tedious than watching paint dry—on a rainy day.Solo PvP Woes: If you thought playing solo was empowering, think again. Small-scale PvP can feel like bringing a spoon to a knife fight—good luck with that. You might just end up as a statistic in someone else’s highlight reel.GvG Meaninglessness: Joining a small to mid-sized guild in large-scale GvG is like being the tiny boat in a sea of battleships. You’ll feel more like cannon fodder than a brave warrior. Don’t forget your life jacket!Top Guilds: The Economy Monopolizers: If you thought capitalism was rough in real life, wait until you see top guilds running the economy like it’s Monopoly night. Getting a seat at the table feels more like a job application—complete with a resume and a cover letter explaining why you’re not a total noob.Guilds = Job Tasks: Being part of most guilds is less about camaraderie and more about completing daily tasks. Forget about fun; it’s all about checking boxes, meeting quotas, and wishing you had just stayed home.Daily Activity Requirements: You better be prepared to clock in every day, or you’ll find yourself on the irrelevant bench faster than you can say “pay-to-win.”RNG is King: In Throne and Liberty, luck is less about fortune and more about how many times you can roll the dice before they start laughing at you. If your luck is worse than a black cat on Friday the 13th, prepare for a long, poor road.Weapon Class Rerolls: Need a different weapon class? Good luck with that. You might be better off creating an alt character. It’s like playing the lottery, only to realize you just bought a ticket for the wrong game. Theres no way of previewing how a class will play like. So its either hit or miss.Clunky Movement and Combat: Navigating this game can feel like trying to dance in a phone booth—awkward and utterly frustrating. Especially if you’re a melee class. Seriously, who thought combat on elevated terrain was a good idea when it has not been optimized yet?Dungeon Mechanics: A Mystery: Ever joined a dungeon and felt like you were the only one who didn’t read the instructions? Good luck with that! The game’s mechanics can be none to so vague that you might as well be trying to solve a Rubik’s Cube blindfolded and get roasted or expelled from the party if you fail.External Resources Required: You’ll find yourself searching for guides on YouTube like a lost child in a grocery store. If you don’t, you might just get flamed, roasted or expelled from the party for not knowing or researching anything externally.Free-to-Play Struggles: If you’re a free-to-play player, expect to feel like a hamster on a wheel, chasing that elusive power. By the time you catch up, the goalposts will have moved, and you’ll be back where you started.Chasing Power for Whales: While you’re grinding to keep up, it often feels like you’re just fodder for the whales, whose swiping behavior encourages this endless chase for power. It’s like being the sidekick in someone else’s superhero movie—where the hero is too busy swiping to notice you.In conclusion, Throne and Liberty is a wild ride filled with beauty and frustration, camaraderie and competition. Whether you’re battling it out in PvP or desperately trying to figure out the mechanics of a dungeon, you’ll likely experience a range of emotions—mostly wondering why you signed up for this. So grab your sword and a therapy appointment or just skip this MMO.

_childDocuments_.review: I tried it because I've been on a 10+ year search/wait for an MMO to release that isn't pure unrefined steaming garbage. I have thousands of hours in GW2, GW1, Runescape back in the day, New World and it's early beta, Elder scrolls online, DCUO, SWTOR, the list goes on, if this game is meant for anyone, it is meant for losers like me. That being said, my god I could not maintain interest in the game for long enough to even get passed the tutorial. The combat is just so astoundingly clunky and has no feedback or weight to it. I consciously am aware what my skills and attacks did, because I read them, but it didn't look like I was doing anything, and it felt like I was just pressing buttons and not experiencing combat in a game. The fact that you select the hotbar, even if you switch out a weapon, and you keep the same hotbar skills even when switching between 2 active weapons, is entirely redundant, GW2 did weapon based skills and hotbards much better and understood that you switch weapons, your skills should also change, there you got specific skills for the weapon you had equipped, you switch to your other weapon, now you have a new hotbar and new skills, you get 2 full hotbars of skills with 2 separate hotbars, this game you get one hotbar, all the same skills no matter what weapons you switch to or equip, even if you fully change weapons and no longer even have access to the skills anymore you have to manually change the entire hotbar skills. I could get past the hotbar issues, if the combat felt in any way satisfying, but it just isn't, and while I generally don't care about graphics, especially in MMOs, this game looks like it is trying desperately to be new gen while failing and looking like a 2010s uncanny valley attempt at realistic hair/skin on characters, as well as the environment looks very clearly to be flat textures and assets with no real texture or depth to them. All in all, I didn't play nearly enough to give a full review of the game, but the fact is I love MMOs, and even for crap like New World I invested hundreds of hours into it and level capped, this game I couldn't get past the tutorial...

_childDocuments_.review: At its core, the game presents itself as a free-to-play experience with PvP elements, but it ultimately hides its lack of substance behind charming graphics. While the combat system is enjoyable, it remains simplistic, relying primarily on gear upgrades rather than complex mechanics or player skill. Exploration, despite the game's beautiful landscapes, feels lackluster; there are few rewards like hidden chests or engaging discoveries to encourage adventuring.The interface is cluttered with numerous menus, many of which are poorly explained. Housing feels like an afterthought, you receive a room but have no meaningful interaction with it. There’s also a room for adventurers, but its only purpose is to send them on missions to collect resources, making it a missed opportunity for deeper, engaging content.Another major drawback is the time-gated events. Missing an event forces you to wait three hours for the next one, and since some of these events are linked to quest progression, it feels like a mechanism designed to keep players logged in, disregarding their time outside the game.In short, the game feels like a hollow experience, a visually appealing surface with no real depth or structure underneath.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played the game quite alot in the Beta, so dont mind my playtime.The game is a really great MMORPG. _childDocuments_.review: So, I played the open beta and found the game was not really for me.  I tried it again today at launch to see if combat had improved in a way that made a difference.  Seems not.The game tries too hard in all the wrong places.  The graphics are amazing but there are too many cut scenes - too much sitting and watching.  The story is a jumble with no light and shade - the emotional pitch is too high.  There are way too many systems and menus. The tutorial is confusing - way too much is thrown at you while you have the story pushing you to save the world before it's too late.  You start with quite a few skills - many of which come with a number of paragraphs of interdependent effects to read through.  That said, for the purposes of getting through the tutorial it seems not to matter which skills you use - auto-attack is enough.  You get the feeling that the game is at once overwhelming and empty.Once in the game proper, the combat feels much the same as in the open beta.  It is somehow unsatisfying.  The systems and menus are still bewildering.  Again, there is a lot of visual noise but when it comes down to it, there is much less to do than it seems.  I don't think I can work up the enthusiasm to push through the main story again.

_childDocuments_.review: A Solid Leveling Experience, With Room to Grow in EndgameAfter playing for several months on the KR servers, I'll keep it brief: Throne and Liberty offers an excellent leveling experience, though the late-game content feels a bit shallow. However, I have hope that future updates will address this gap and bring more depth to the endgame. Overall, I'd recommend giving it a try.Now, let’s talk about concerns around monetization:It's not pay-to-win. Traditionally, pay-to-win (P2W) meant gaining an exclusive or early power advantage by spending money. That’s not the case here. Best-in-slot gear is available to all players, regardless of spending. Yes, you can spend large amounts of money to buy gear, but you can also earn premium currency in-game to acquire those same items without paying. And just having the best gear won’t guarantee success—you’ll still need to build a viable strategy and execute it well.

_childDocuments_.review: Throne and Liberty isn’t a bad game per se, but Amazon Game Studios has once again demonstrated their incompetence in managing an MMO, as they have with every other title they’ve published.The game is definitely p2w, but it's a pretty managable and non predatory aspect and it's possible to be on par with whales just by playing. The real issue is that the game is plagued by guilds, mostly Russian, that abuse scripts and exploits without facing any consequences. The Siege event, the most important in the game, further highlighted this issue, turning into a complete clown fiesta where the winner was whoever could exploit the most. Amazon not only wont punish the offenders but even promoted the exploit on Twitter, stating it wouldn’t be fixed in time and advising players to simply ‘be on the lookout and defend against it.’Throne and Liberty has its qualities and is a decent MMO, but its severe flaws and poor management make it hard to consider it a truly enjoyable experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Tab targeting, no skill based combat besides stats crunching, auto attacking, and single target combat. Basically WoW/FFXIV mechanical combat.
