_childDocuments_.review: Game has possibly the most obnoxious and awfully implemented level scaling system I've ever seen.I've always hated level scaling, even when done RIGHT it's bad and unnecessary and punishes the player for growth.Here it's not done right... You'll go from an enemy being manageable one second to getting absolutely one-shot by that same exact enemy type in literally the next encounter and you'll say? "What gives!?"Well... "What gives!?" is that a magic number in the game's systems incremented because, unbeknownst to you, you got "too strong"... Fought "too many battles" and now the Goblins that were tough but manageable have become giga Goblins that treat your attacks like a mosquito bite and one shot your mage despite trying to keep them in the backline (where the game tells you they're "protected" ... Yeah... No.)Speaking of being "One Shot" this game f***ing LOVES one shotting you. The bosses will one shot you, the Goblins will one shot you, almost everything will one shot you."Well... I just need to gain some levels!" You'll think to yourself. "I'm getting one shot because I need better equipment and higher HP!"So... You go about trying to raise your HP and get money for your Equipment upgrade, only for the game to say "Gee, nice prep work, it'd be a shame if level scaling showed up and ruined it all."Then level scaling will show up and ruin it all and next thing you know you're back at the bottom of the totem pole getting one shot by Goblins again.Maybe that wouldn't matter if the game didn't give you an LP system where every time a character goes down they lose LP (which is IMPOSSIBLE to recover) and upon losing all LP they just die.No... F*** this game, F*** level scaling in all its grotesque and miserable forms and F*** the developers who use it.Stop. Let ME decide how hard the game will be by deciding how much time I want to spend grinding levels. Don't go "Oh look, he's trying to grind levels to get more HP!? Because he's tired of getting ONE SHOT! You know what he must want!? For every single enemy in the game to just magically get stronger for no reason thus rendering his attempts to correct the One Shot problem totally null and void."I want games that have level scaling to advertise such in big, bold, beautiful letters so that I can know to absolutely not purchase them.

_childDocuments_.review: Game has some really great aspects that blow my mind when I think its from 30 years ago. But it has a fatal flaw in its design. The game wants to actively discourage you from engaging with its battle system. The more you fight the harder the game becomes, and on classic difficulty this can quickly become all of your characters being one shot by random mobs. There was a game called the last remnant that had a similar concept back in 2008 and the mechanic was not well received there either. It adds nothing to the game, it punishes the player for playing the game and is such a severe detriment that I cannot recommend the game. The game is fairly light on narrative for a JRPG, its narrative is very much dated and simple and thats ok because its built on a fun gameplay loop. Until of course you are punished for engaging with that gameplay loop incorrectly. The game never tells you how any of this works, and it obfuscates how exactly and when exactly it punishes you. Youll have to go to online forums and discussion boards to even learn about this mechanic that is so crucial. The optimal way to play this game is to fight as few battles as possible, running past enemies and only engaging with the most efficient and lucrative fights and only when absolutely necessary. Which fights are the most lucrative? You just have to know or have a wiki up on the second monitor. This just severely hamstrings the game and unfortunately it just kills the fun. The game is popular its a cult classic so people who liked the franchise will of course say its perfect. But in being honest the game needs a better way to scale enemies or to make managing your number of encounters more fun and more intuitive. Its really close to be a great game but especially for a modern audience it unfortunately shoots itself right in the face with this baffling design choice

_childDocuments_.review: It has been one of those ultra rare games that had me hooked from start to finish. While the story is pretty linear, it’s split into different regions, giving you some flexibility in where to go and which quests to tackle first. This setup makes each playthrough feel a little more unique and lets you carve your own path.I have to say, the enemy designs are absolutely outstanding. Combining different existing models to create new monsters is a brilliant touch that keeps things fresh. A bit of character customization for your party would have been nice, though—like picking from the already available RNG hairstyles and colors—to make it feel a bit more personal, so you're choosing your look rather than just adapting to what the game gives you.The progression can get a little unbalanced. Finding new weapons in the early and mid-game can take absolutely forever, so it feels like you’re constantly adjusting your party around whatever you pick up, rather than the other way around. The damage scaling is sometimes really weird, too. For instance, martial arts scaling is pretty wild and doesn’t even require any equipment, which can get a bit frustrating at times.Then there’s the PC port, which really misses the mark. Square Enix once again fell short here, there's multiple Unreal Engine crashes, very minimal support for ultra-wide displays, and a messed-up FOV. These issues are a real shame in an otherwise brilliant game.

_childDocuments_.review: I will be writing this explicitly for how it plays as a Generational game and NOT just as a JRPG.In Short a Generational game is a game in which by some mechanism you move forward through generations and play as new characters as this happens. Think Crusader Kings, Agarest, Fire emblem 4, Godhood, and Wildermyth.This games main mechanic is around appointing new emperors, which on its own would not really be much of a generational game, but it is tied to time skips and the such so it fits quite well. Story wise the memories and powers of the previous emperor are passed down to whoever is chosen as the new emperor. Unlike others of the Genre there is no Familial component, aka you do not play explicitly as your children. This felt bad at first, I was not seeing the story of a family line of emperors and there was no connection between emperors at all. However the game is very vague about who the characters are so you can easily imagine that whoever you chose is a Descendant of the previous emperor. Nothing in the game says this to be the case, but nothing in the game really implies otherwise either.Firstly there is no genetics or romance mechanics (despite the name). You will not choose wifes or do any sort of family building. Which is extremely rare for this genre, as often the reason Generations pass on at all is to serve playing as offspring, see even Fire emblem 4 where even though marriage is technically optional it is a major factor in your runs. The execution of the lack of offspring is interesting. Since your emperor's skill levels and abilities are carried over directly from memories being passed from emperor to emperor. So there is a sense of “inheritance” but through memories and empire development.As for your non-emperor characters there is inheritance for them as well. As you use weapons your weapon levels will increase globally in a sense, so when you time skip and pick new party members their levels will be close to your other characters. If you brute force a class to learn a weapon they don't specialize in that carries over as well. Speaking of the timeskips, they are handled quite adeptly imo. Every few major quests, usually every 2 major quests the game will jump you forward 58+ years. The previous emperor will be gone and you will then appoint a new emperor, if anything changes over the years someone will tell you and you will get new quests like monsters rising in areas you already cleared or pirates throwing a mutiny, then you rebuild your party in the castle.After every time skip, anything made in the smith, all skills learned, and all magics become available to all characters at the designated facilities. It helped create a sense that your empire's military is learning from its “heroes” over the years.The Length of generations felt very good, not too long and not too short. You spent enough time as an emperor to care about them and their story, but not so long that you only get 1-2 time skips. I found each generation took me personally about 5 hours.This game is not using an infinite model (which I don't think anyone would expect as this game is a remake of a snes era game). But this does mean that the quests that happen over the years are not randomly generated, which means you will only see a handful of them ever. This game does have a strongly defined ending which I will not be discussing here.Final note, there are a lot of small details with each of these systems and some I probably missed/didn’t talk about partly because of char limitations.I was considering layout out the pros and cons but I would write a pro and there would be a corresponding con to go with it. For every step this game took forward it would also take one backwards or sideways.So, this game's generational mechanics are very non-intrusive. Great for JRPG players who don't really care about such systems. To summarize, when you switch someone into your party, they will have near identical stats to the previous generation. So let's say you have a knight, you made him learn axes this generation. Next generation starts, if you pick a knight again, he will have the same/similar level in axes. This is awesome if you have your favorite set up and just want to ride it out till game end, since you can keep remaking the same party over and over, since who you can recruit is always the same, you will always be able to recruit a class you recruited.Why is that a problem? Well what is the purpose of having your party reset every so often in the first place? It gets you to do new things, it forces you to adapt to your new options rather than relying on one strategy, it can also let you relive fun parts of early progression assuming you design the game with the intent that early progression is fun. This wouldn't be a problem if only your emperor was like this, but EVERY class will scale up, even on weapons you don't use. In the later generations you barely discover skills too, which was a great part of the early game.As such this game loses out on a lot of the fun parts of this genre. For example you never do anything to set up the future generation, bar building facilities or smithing. Which all progresses naturally as you do encounters anyways. This hurts a lot actually as making decisions that help you in the next generations feels great in this genre, things like picking up young recruits in Wildermyth since your best 3 are getting old, or things like picking who will marry who in FE4. This sort of “Generational Planning Play” is borderline nonexistent.This might sound very negative, however this game succeeds as a generational game. Despite having a system that mechanically doesn't engage the player in the generation side of things, this game's thematic and contextual wrapping of the system hits home a lot of the time and makes you feel the generations for the most part. Things like new quests showing up in eras you liberated, the main antagonists being immortal monsters helps, one town being built *during* the game, but the biggest one is just a lot of facilities and tools open up over time as you do more things and progress. Plus even though functionally the characters are similar it felt interesting to defeat the many bosses with different protagonists who had subtly different feels because of character design. Honestly respecing into a party of guys who look different was enough for my brain to feel like things changed despite nothing really changing for most of the game.The cherry on top is that there is a post game role call of all of your emperors and the things they accomplished. This felt so good.This game as a generational game nails the feel, does a lot of unique things, and does absolutely execute on what it's selling. However mechanically if you are looking for the things generational games often do, such as encourage you to adapt to your ever changing tools, let you optimize genetics, or make you re-experience unit building/early progression, then you may be disappointed to find a JRPG that only has a thematic and contextual feel of a generational game. But if you are after a JRPG that has some systems you may not have seen, and that does cool stuff with time then this might be exactly what you're looking for.If you like this style of generational game, my go to recommendation would probably be Agarest: Generations of war, since their system is also non-intrusive and serves a more Linear-narrative focused JRPG.As someone who loves this niche genre its a solid entry and does alot of great things, and does alot well. Very happy with it despite my gripes with the systems.

_childDocuments_.review: This takes the parts of the original game and turns it into something truly great.  I'm a giant SaGa fan but the original RS2 was one of my least favorite games in the IP.  This, however, is an open-world JRPG for the ages.  It cribs a bunch of concepts from the Octopath battle system, and reduces the overall number of encounters to make something far more engaging and strategically interesting.  Every new mechanic is a great addition.  Every UI improvement is a welcome improvement.  Every balancing tweak is for the better. All of the possible spots to brick your file have been cleansed away.  The new story content is good and adds the Japanese-only stage play to the game's canon.  The dungeon design is generally great.   The postgame content is meaningful and satisfying.  The core difficulty levels span are suitable for JRPG fans, SaGa fans, and players that really want to push the game mechanics in satisfying ways. The two NG+ difficulties add a bunch more replayability as you can see all of the variations to the main campaign across multiple playthroughs.  This is the new gold standard of how to remake a Super Famicom RPG.

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing Remake done right!For those who loved the series this is a must. For those who are new or unsure due to worries of scaling, no linear-guiding, grinding, and LP perm death, they do a really good on balancing how you want to move forward. (Mechanic spoilers**) The "Perm" death and LP concerns are refreshed by successions, so you're party never really "dies" forever. They just get a makeover ever 200 years, and you keep all your stats. Plus all your stats from your previous emperor is now part of another party member, so you'll gain a buff on one member each time. I myself have gotten a couple of characters pretty close to 0 but by then It was time to time skip anyhow after i spent an extra 2-3 hours grinding in each dungeon before moving on.Only into my 3rd succession, and I''m really loving the polish and having fun.Story, voice acting, and sprites have been all just solid. _childDocuments_.review: Oh man... I actually knew about this game several years before the remake was announced, because Hyadain made a banger song, and I eventually picked up the switch port because I... Didn't realize it was for Romancing SaGa 3, not 2. But that was no problem because it was a gem and I immediately fell in love! Wasn't able to finish though due to life. Years later, I by chance see the Nintendo Direct announcing Revenge of the Seven and was both super hyped and TERRIFIED... Square has been dropping the ball left and right on anything that isn't final fantasy 14 or 7 for the longest time, and the last thing I wanted was for them to make a mess out of RS2. 22 hours later, I can happily confirm that the dev team knocked this out of the park. I've gotten way farther than I originally did and keep getting pleasantly surprised with the stream of new unlocks. There is just so much stuff to choose from that the amount of customization of party goes crazy. The gameplay is so much fun too, I've developed a strong allergy to turn based RPGs about a decade ago, but this game is like 90% gameplay and 10% story, and I'm still having fun blasting everyone away with fun classes like martial artist and corsair (pirate). I also really love the empire management simulator where you deal in mass amounts of money, "imperial revenue from taxes", and fund development of magic, technology, and education for the betterment of the empire. I swear they also yoinked the vocational school quiz minigame from (Yakuza) Like a Dragon 7 and 8 hahahaha. Also very cool to see some towns literally change appearance because of consequential decisions you make. I actually chose to do some other quests instead of this important one, and it came back 100 years later where they got wrecked because I didn't help oops... It's very "choose your own adventure" and feels refreshing that your choices actually matter for onceAnyway I'm kind of glad I didn't get to finish the remaster, because the play experience on Revenge is so good and modern feeling. Please play this game, the generational skill transfer system is one of a kind and will probably make you mad that no one else has ever done it again, not even other SaGa games loool

The enemies also seems to scale with your grind, so there will always be enough challenge, from every single enemy blocking your way. _childDocuments_.review: I've played several SaGa games before, but had never played this. Having completed it, I can now see why it's considered the iconic crowning jewel of the SaGa series.It's impressive that this was a SNES JRPG because it captures the kind of breadth and freedom that a lot of games aspire to today. The game does have quest markers, but won't discourage you from going somewhere completely unknown or out of your depth if you feel up to it. Honestly feels like it was a bit ahead of its time in that regard, especially for JRPGs. In terms of SaGa's signature "open scenarios" this feels like the best version of it, which is strange to say about a game that's decades old in a series still getting entries.Definitely a "gameplay first" experience. If you're coming in here looking for deep narratives or super developed and compelling story, you'll be disappointed. Character designs are nice, though. THAT SAID, if you're the type of player that wants to build characters, craft teams and strategies, and engage in challenging encounters, I can't recommend it enough, as long as you can put up with a bit of an old school turn-based JRPG heavy on the encounters.I did my first playthrough on classic and honestly enjoyed it so much I plan to do another on Expert, and maybe move on to Romancing after that.

_childDocuments_.review: The remake is good, it has the same magic as the original game <3. It makes me happy going around and completing quests and recruiting allies. The same as the original ^^. The original you could blast with magic until you run out of magic points and then switch to weapon skills, now you need to work out characters to specialise in a specific role to make your BP last during boss battles. This is good too because the game forces me to think about who has what spells and weapon skills before I add them to my party.   The music is amazing, I haven't changed it off of the remake soundtrack and everything sounds perfect for the original! Kenji Ito did an amazing job transforming his old MIDI OST into HD <3. _childDocuments_.review: The original Romancing SaGa 2 is the game I enjoyed playing the most this year, by far. It gave me a feeling I hadn't felt in a long time playing a video game, and I wondered if I would have a similar feeling with this remake, and I believed that I wouldn't, since the magic of discovery would no longer exist here. Well, I can admit that I got hooked in the same way, but not exactly for the same reasons. It's hard to say without being too redundant compared to my review of the original game, but here we go.Square Enix has been focusing a lot on reviving its more "B-side" franchises for a general audience, and coming from the same team that made the remake of Trials of Mana in 2020, you could expect a game made with love for the fans and to attract a new audience. It's a difficult task with SaGa because it's not such a standard franchise, and it was actually easy to break the barrier: QOL, QOL EVERYWHERE, QOL FOR EVERYONE.Come on guys, they just fixed OG's biggest flaw and it's now possible to change your party with enormous ease! The revitalized combat with weakness indicators, united attacks and more assertive formations is good, but nothing compares to seeing a lightbulb next to a skill tech and a glimmer happens right after, man, it's extremely satisfying and without having to be blind all the time, and with all the tracking of what you still need to learn, not to mention the famous "global level" fully visible. The game constantly seems to be saying: "We have a lot here, but don't be scared, you can explore everything in your own way." I believe that this whole obscurity of mechanics is what most drives away potential new fans of the series, but the remake has taken this to an extremely impeccable level.What initially seemed strange to me were exactly the indicators for the quests. Okay, it's predictable that there would be this, but the game loses a lot of the sense of discovery that the OG has, since you can easily take the best routes for the quests without any problems. But I reached a point where I no longer felt like this was a problem. There's so much to do, the battles are so enjoyable with very well-made bosses, and the quests are individually so cool that I just kept thinking every day "hm, what can I do today?" I definitely felt like a drug addict.The game does a good job of making it clear that our goal is to help the world and eliminate the threat of the old heroes, maintaining the same identity as the original, but with beautiful cutscenes, giving more identification with the characters and the situations. It's still not for everyone, those who are very attached to having an epic narrative with great continuity will be displeased, there's no way. Not to say that there's nothing additional about the story, I loved the heroes' past, it's good to understand how they got that way, who they fought against and also to get closer to them.They continue to have the biggest face in the game for me, the fight against each of them is incredible and the ending, despite liking the OG design more, is still challenging. The post-game bosses are dope af, much better than the remaster four generic dragons.Romancing SaGa 2 ROTS has certainly shown its credentials and told everyone that SaGa can indeed be bigger than it is, that it's possible to introduce the series to new players and I believe that many of the next games will use this as an example. It's an stunning remake, it leaves practically nothing to be desired from the original, except for some "sensations", but wins on so many, but so many other points. It's a lesson in how it's possible to revitalize a 16-bit JRPG without needing that much of a budget.

_childDocuments_.review: The Good:In general, RS2 is unique and very ambitious. I haven't played anything else like it.All of the old content was kept intact, even where it would go against "modern decision making". There are some changes to balance like merging defense types, separating some weapon types, adding new spells, and Dantarg doesn't roam anymore.They added in a lot of story content around the Seven that was previously tucked away in a play and manga.The battle speed is very fast in general. Animations don't drag on and encounters are quick.I like the art style a lot but that's subjective.The game is well optimized for low end hardware.Lots of QoL:Quick travel has improvedIts much faster to set your spells and skillsYour moves have their potency listedAt least 2 new classesMinimapThe voice acting is really good dub and sub. The Bad:Like the original, there's a low amount of unique music for areas. Many towns share the same BGM.No quick way to end a battle that you know you're going to lose. You will have to wait until the enemy kills you if you don't want to altF4.I would have liked more information for Formations to be in the game. i.e. "Increased Physical Damage" should tell you how much  the increase is.

_childDocuments_.review: Would I have ever played this, had it not been for the awesome demo? Nope. THIS is why every expensive game NEEDS a demo! Why would people fork over 50-60 or even 70 of their hard-earned bucks for something that they might not enjoy? Steam allows for refunds, yes, but if you refund too often, your account will be flagged and you won't be able to do it anymore for a while, so really, demos are the ONLY solution. Now, onto the game itself, it's really good. My favorite thing about the game is the absolutely insane variety of monsters you run into. I did not expect that in a 3D game, not when most dungeon-crawler JRPGs (think Etrian Odyssey) struggle with that. It's a bit sad that the first monsters you fight look so... harmless and cute, when 90% of the rest are grotesque, weird or even nasty-looking, some people might have an issue with that.As someone who enjoys playing only female characters when given the option, it did bother me a bit that I had to play male characters a lot just to unlock either their formation or masteries. It's only at the very end, when I mastered everything else, that I was able to finally have the party I wanted.And sure, the character customization isn't great, and the fact that you can't upgrade older gear more than once to keep it relevant throughout the game means that most cool weapons with nice abilities that you find early/mid game will become obsolete in the later part, but if they can improve on these things, I can see the next game being even better.It's one of those games where I did not want the game to end, and after 70 hours, I just want more of it!

_childDocuments_.review: I've always had some pretty mixed feelings about SaGa games since they tend to punish you for doing the one thing their mechanics seem primed to allow you to do: relentlessly grind. Legitimately, 90% of the SaGa games I've played try to counter the player grinding by just ramping up the enemy difficulty for every few battles you do. The remake of the first Romancing SaGa game had that problem, and it also really punished you for spending time doing anything besides specifically completing quests. Not a great feeling for someone with grind-heavy and completionist tendencies.This game doesn't really have those problems. There's no side quests, just story paths. Every "generation" of your lineage ends when you complete one of several "main" quests and then the quests you don't complete carry over with the fallout of not doing them. For example, early on I could either save a town from the monsters coming out of a mine or I could take back a fortress from the fiends. I chose the town, and I lost my easy access into the fortress because my easy access I had found before changing course had been blocked off and even more monsters were plaguing the fortress.The grind is also good too, because the game doesn't ramp up as maddeningly as previous SaGa games. The leveling system is also pretty kind with the weapon and magic experience paired with the inheritance system. It basically allows you to no longer be punished for eventually party-wiping.The story itself is still... basically non-existent. It's just a major plot beat per location to retake it that's affected by which ones you do in order, and none of them are bad. It's basically just a VERY basic device to get you to fight the main 7 bosses and complete the End Goal™ for the story. I'm pretty sure there's a secret ending/final boss but I'm not far enough to tell yet.If you've always wanted the grind of SaGa without getting slapped on the wrist for doing it, play this game. This is a game for JRPG mechanics lovers, not JRPG story lovers. Which is fine! Both have plenty of place in the market imho.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr:  parading around in the skinsuit of .This game blends a lot of the Square Enix RPG franchises, while losing much of what makes the SaGa series unique, resulting in more of an Octopath Traveler game with a few SaGa series influences.It uses the structure of , but introduces many changes to combat and exploration.The game remains good, but it sacrifices a lot to become a "greatest hits" of Square Enix mechanics.The combat system is a notable downgrade from  and . It's a bit of a downgrade from , which is more SaGa-like than this.The SaGa series usually has a turn-based combat system where you choose all of the actions of your party before the turn plays out in its entirety. This introduces a lot of the Kawazu chaos that forces the player to rely on preparation, knowledge of the systems, and a bit of luck. With SSG and SEB, seeing and manipulating the timeline could provide for some varied and dynamic encounters.The turn-based combat in this game is much more traditional and you can always react to the last move from an enemy, so it plays more like Final Fantasy or Octopath Traveler than older or newer SaGa games.I got tired of the weakness system in , and I don't enjoy it here. In fact, after 15 hours of this game, I can say that I'm finding it boring and tedious, just as I felt  was after dozens of hours.It's an alright combat system that wears out its welcome.You'll encounter new enemies, then have to go through static  combat sequences.- Poke at enemy with every weapon/element to discover weaknesses- Hit enemy with its weaknesses- Build the Overdrive meter- Heal and Overdrive as appropriateThen every time you see that enemy in the future, you'll play out the exact same strategy to exploit weaknesses.The Termite Queen doesn't spawn adds in the original. It could stand on its own as a very difficult boss that you had to prepare for.In the remake, it seems to spawn 1-2 termite/termite soldier adds every few turns.This is a   mechanic.Battle Rank in this game is something you immediately feel. Experience gained after combat will double and enemies will take four times as many hits to go down. There's not a ramping up, but a stepping up.However, most enemy encounters will be fairly easy even with a BR spike. Combat just takes longer until your party levels up to meet the current BR.Armor is also a downgrade, with generic Physical and Magic defense numbers. Rubber Soles no longer seem to protect against lightning-based attacks, for instance.This is a big step down from the original and every game in the SaGa series, where equipment preparation was almost as important as having the right formation.The collect-a-thon aspects of the game are imported from the Mana series and are out of place here. But with full 3D environments, the areas need to have something worth exploring.I love the Mana series, but my fondest memories of those games don't include looting towns of Candy and Chocolate.This aspect alone takes the game from being Kawazu's closest take on  to being a very generic RPG where the "hero" comes into town, robs everyone, and continues on his quest.The more I play of this remake, the more I don't like it. It's just , and it's boring me the same way I felt bored playing .If you like , you'll probably like this game. If you like this game, you  like other SaGa games, but possibly not.Other than glimmering techs and Battle Rank, there's hardly anything left of SaGa series mechanics.Alright, Square Enix, I bought , , and this game in 2024. Give us the rest of the games.

_childDocuments_.review: I love JRPGs, and this is my first experience with a SaGa game. The game runs smoothly, and the art is nice—it actually reminds me of Dragon Quest XI, and I wonder if it might even use the same engine. Initially, I was excited about the unique inheritance system, as it’s new to me, but it turns out it’s just not my cup of tea.The basic premise is that there are seven corrupted heroes you have to defeat, and the story seems to end there. There’s no real connection with the characters, which makes it feel more like a turn-based combat simulator than a fully fleshed-out RPG.The first few hours were fun, but then, out of nowhere on a random mission, the game suddenly skips 143 years into the future, and I had to start over with a new party.I’m playing on hard mode, where combat feels more punishing than challenging, but I guess that’s just how the game is designed. A character’s death doesn’t mean much, since you can go back to town and recruit another one—it feels almost like Darkest Dungeon. Any enemy can one-hit KO any party member, even the tankiest one. I don’t understand why my tank can’t withstand more than a single hit—what’s the point of having a class like that? Plus, there’s no way to manage aggro, so defensive formations (so far) don’t seem useful.I clearly don’t fully grasp the mechanics yet, and maybe it’ll click if I pick it up again. For now, though, I’m setting it aside.

_childDocuments_.review: BEFORE YOU PLAY, READ UP ON HOW TO UNLOCK UMBROLOGY!  I ended up playing this game all the way through twice in a row because I did not know there was a choice between unlocking dark magic or recruiting Salamanders and I ended up skipping both quests.  I love this game and there is so much replayability!  I had a blast playing this game twice in a row and I will probably play it a 3rd time through in a few months to see how Salamanders are.  This game has tons of hidden secrets, lots of unique items, and so many recruitable characters!  Its fun to mix and match spells, techs, and abilities to get the most out of your party.  As a JRPG fan, this may be my very favorite title in the genre! The way that your main character dies of old age and you constantly have to change your party out keeps the characters fresh and is a great way solution to how JRPGs can sometimes fall into the "meta party" pitfalls.  Why would I use Charles when Jane is so much better?  Well, Charles just died of old age... time to switch him out!Really innovative and can't wait for playthrough # 3!

_childDocuments_.review: I recommended this game but only by a little bit. I wish I could give it a so-so rating. This may contain minor spoilers about game mechanics. This is my first time playing a Romancing Saga game. I played it on Original(Hard) difficulty. I found the game pretty challenging but not unbearably hard. If the game is too hard for someone the game offers difficulty that can be changed in the options at any time which is quite generous. The only time I lowered the difficulty was for the final story boss. Thank you difficulty change setting.The game is good but it is also very grindy. You build a party and a character throughout the game as you travel along a timeline. There are certain events that will move the timeline forward(example given: a party wipe), therefore some of the events(quests) may be missed if the timeline moves forward as they were time sensitive to the previous location in the timeline. Because a party wipe moves the timeline forward it doesn't seem to incentivize party wipes(recommended to reset the game if you wipe). Although I did eat about two party wipes, i was able to continue onward to through the game. The major plot points of the game do not get locked out (the main objectives) even if the timeline moves forward a lot. The enemies scale with the player levels. Because the enemies scale with the players you may feel incentivized to run pass them (and I did do a bit of this). Leveling a bit may give  you the edge as you may have more HP or that needed ability. The enemy density is way too high. I felt like the game needs less enemies for balancing. Sometimes there is a small room (very small) and like three enemy encounters in there alone. I really enjoyed the plot and crafting my party but the game was bogged down with the heavy enemy density/encounter rates. The game also felt a little too long for me. Took me about 50-60 hours. I was really enjoying the game for about the first 25 hours (it was a 8+ rating at this time) but after that it kinda fell off for me (down to a 6/10). Overall I still enjoyed it. I never played the original but I guess it also was a very grindy game because it was a Super Famicom game from 1993. I would like them to take a few more liberties next time in the development. I hope for the next Saga game they remove enemy scaling and reduce the enemy density. I also hope they work with a bigger budget to work on the cutscenes . The series could use a little more love. 6/10

_childDocuments_.review: Here is my Review for First time playing Romancing Saga 2, never played any of them before.  I do love the story it seems cool.  But there is some glaring obvious flaws in the game and they don't get better.  I am not writing this Review to slam the game.  Just what I have observed and experienced in playing the game.  Combat is fun and enjoyable, I love the turn based combat and the Glimmering for skills, spells and etc is nice.  Something different I never experienced but do like.  Now here is the bad.    There is no Levels, Stats, or anything outside of your character.  Yes you can equip Different Weapons and learn a lot of Skills, Spells and the Like.  But the only levels I can see at the moment are based on how much you use said weapon, skills, spells, or anything.  An then there is Items, Weapons you buy from the Shops.  It's not a normal shop.  It is "limited" on how much it will sell you and when you reach that limit your ♥♥♥♥ out of luck.  There is NO WAY to reload and get more of said items.  So use them sparingly.  Concerning items also, when in battle or outside of battle.  You can ONLY carry 2 items per each person in battle.  When they are gone your ♥♥♥♥ out of luck, there is no way to replace them.  You can have 100 in your inventory but when you use them in battle the 2 you have.  That's it hope your Luck Carries you to whatever you are doing.  Then there is Combat, from what I have read will screw your game up.  Which is seriously a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up game play mechanic, cause people love to Grind.  But this is what I have learned " Every fight you engage in will increase the amount of battles you have fought. As you fight more battles, monsters will gradually increase their strength.  What happens when you grind is that you functionally strengthen monsters; without acquiring new equipment to help enhance your team's attributes, excessive grinding can leave you at a severe disadvantage. Naturally, you will need to fight in order to acquire better techniques, so never fighting isn't a great answer either. I'd recommend trying to avoid most fights, but going after the different treasures you'll see. This will inevitably lead to you running into monsters here and there.  Enemies increase their strength depending on the number of encounters you have engaged in. That means you are in a constant tug of war, attempting to build up your pool of techniques, while not engaging in so many battles that your foes outpace your party's strength. If you run from a battle, however, you will increase your encounter number, strengthening your enemies, while not gaining any Technique Points. That's the worst-case scenario."  That is from    An Honestly the Two Battles that made me write this Negative Review is before you even get to the first Boss.  There is a Treasure Chest that reminds me of a Mimic but call it a Dopplaganger.  It ruins your formation and Honestly one shots all of your characters.  An that to me it really damn impressive cause I did some grinding to try and get stronger for it, but no matter what my first battle it took Gerald out with one attack.  So I did some Grinding for it and on the second fight it was doing 100+ damage to my characters.  So here is my Advice don't but the game at $50 wait for a sale or if you are going to try it anyways, be warned it is not a very forgiving game and you maybe lose a keyboard or controller.  Cause it will piss you off no matter what.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't let the low play time fool you.  Having played the demo helped.I played the original back on whatever console - SNES, I think - and it was interesting but I clearly remember getting absolutely smashed and having to abdicate, unable to beat the first Hero.This time, he was challenging but not overly so.  There are so many QoL fixes that it made it a much more enjoyable play experience.  The 3D and voice acting also helped quite a bit.  I'm taking a break so I can get some progress on Ys X before I forget how to play it (with those terrible controls).I recommend this game...but understand, it's a bare basic story.  It's not going to wow you.  But it's accessible to everyone and you have the freedom to advance at your own pace and style.If I had to call out one negative it's the time skip.  There's no story, no cutscene, nothing to at least show the passing of the throne.  Also, the newer Emperors have no voice acting; you're choosing their answers but they don't speak them out loud, which is jarring given the beginning of the game (quest NPCs are all voiced).Still recommended, just manage your expectations.  It's not a AAA game nor does it pretend to try to be.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Between DQ3HD and RS2's Remake, RS2's remake is the better choice.Square Enix is such a bizarre company. It seems like DQ3HD was handed off to a B or a C team, while Romancing Saga 2's remake was handed to a main team.Let me break this down for you. DQ3HD should be the regional equivalent of $20-30, but it's at full price. There are fade to blacks/loading screens for area transitions, even for buildings and rooms in towns. The only customization for your player characters are hair and voice. It also has some censorship, which is pretty gay, but at least it's not something major, like changing a character's personality or a major story arc. If DQ3HD was at least done entirely in 3D, and had decent visual customization for your player characters (height/body sliders, hairstyles, etc.), then there wouldn't be much to complain about.Meanwhile, RS2 got a full 3D remake. It appears to be that they went in the opposite direction in regards to censorship because it's like they got porn addicts to make the game. There's a lot of attractive men and women, even ones that don't have to be. The English dub is also pretty solid.For those of you who don't know, and why an autist such as myself is taking the time to lay this information out, it is because Dragon Quest is one of Japan's largest franchises. It is what The Witcher series is to the kiel basas. By comparison, Romancing Saga, for the jelly donuts, is that guy playing Battletech while most of his neighborhood is playing Dungeons & Dragons. DQ is also way more accessible than the RS series because DQ doesn't punish you for grinding.With all that out of the way, I'm a newcomer to the Saga series, and this is a pretty solid game so far. Combat is more tactical than raw numbers. Characters level up weapons to unlock better skills. You have to prioritize hitting enemies with weapons and elements they're weak against to maximize damage. However, this is a game that will bust your balls or stretch your clit if you're playing on normal or harder. So, this may not be the game you wanna play if you want to sit back and relax or maybe turn off your brain. Kzinssie wrecked me so hard, I had to bump the difficulty down to normal.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite how it looks after remake, it's based of oldest type of jrpg iteration, the notorious 8bit era. It's an acquired tasteStory's not bad, it is cheesy and somewhat predictable. As you progress trough the story there are branches and events that may lock you out of content, or timed quests which completion requirements are in area you have not unlocked. That kind of stuff, feels a bit unfair in that regard.The main selling point "Ancestry and heritage system"It's watered down and poorly executed. It lets your character stats and weapon/magic masteries to be added (inherited) by next heir (actually a random existing character) you choose. Random character generator would prosper in this type of game or at least some sense of relatability with descendant, but instead its just some random pre-existing mercenary you could of hired as part of your party or has been part of it already ... it's dumb. Supposedly there are time skips and age mechanic of over hundreds of years, but all first area mercenaries available from start are still around like nothing happened. My gripe and deal breaker is with combat and technical aspect of hiding numbers. Enemy levels, mastery level exp, enemy health or damage/defense levels. Any type of quantifiable power representation or progress would have been nice, but it just feels so underhanded. As you go trough battles and level up, mobs scale up with you, but you will have no idea that's a thing ... if you got in a tough fight and lost many LP points or some characters died, you might be inclined to restart save, go grind somewhere easy and come back, but now, due how mobs scale, its even harder than before. In some instances my party members would get hit for 60% of their hp in single attack (this is, apparently, normal. Often 3 mobs ganging up on one character is guaranteed death even in favorable fights ...) and then next enemy i fight literally same enemy and composition they are one shotting my party with no chance of counter play. Block or parry skills are pointless as you can't see enemies intent, which essentially is giving up on turn for potential stalemate or loss with no benefits. No effective ways of cc, everything is chance base with addition to getting resisted, blocked, dodged, missed or straight up nothing. I tried lowering difficulty down, but eventually power creep kicks in and it turns into one shot situation either way.Solution, unfortunately, is to grind high enough till enemy reaches their cap. In order to do that you have to invest several hours running and refreshing same area. Combat wise, i feel square enix jrpgs are at the bottom of the barrel. Didn't see anyone complaining about it so i thought this title was different, but it's just smidge better than final fantasy ones.

_childDocuments_.review: This is easily one of the worst RPGs I've played. It has some interesting mechanics, reminiscent of The Last Remnant, and sharing a LOT of problems with that game. But the mechanics are completely at odds with each other and they do not give you fun choices to make. In this game, EXP from battle goes into every skill you used in battle. So defeating enemies optimally (quickly) means you will not learn and level your skills. To raise and learn your skills you need to purposely be extremely inefficient at killing the monsters. For instance the best way to grow your characters is to equip the weakest equipment, use the worst attacks, and make sure you at least use one of each kind of attack you have. It is not at all clear if this consequence is intentional or not, but it is incredibly bad game design either way. But OK fine, but it sounds like the player can at least exploit that to get a good outcome right? Nope. Because the game is balanced around your HP coming back every single fight, every enemy has the potential to kill your characters who have limited lives (after which they permanently leave your party).So, on on the one hand you desperately need to power up your characters so that they can perform well and not keep losing lives, but if you do that the inefficiency in combat will lead to you losing an insane amount of lives, and you'll soon permanently lose the characters you worked to build up. OK so just play perfectly and you'll be fine right? Nope, enemies will literally 1 hit your characters anyway, even Defensive characters who are defending and have your best armor on. (unless you play on casual maybe).So sure, if you play optimally you'll beat the fight in the quickest way and you'll lose the least number of lives (but you'll probably still lose a lot because of the random instant-kills) but you'll also get terrible character growth and they won't be able to scale well enough to the enemies and will start losing a lot of lives anyway.The real "challenge" of this game isn't in the combat or building the characters, it's in managing your LP. I.e. choosing when it's OK for characters to lose lives, which ones, and when. Because of this, every single trash mob fight in the long grindy dungeons applies 100% pressure to your entire retinue, because losing a life in those fights is not unlikely and it's just as consequential as losing a life to a boss. There are no interesting choices in regards to build or strategy in this game, because everything is subsumed by this meta challenge of balancing character growth vs spending lives. Not to mention that on normal and hard modes enemies will literally just instant kill your characters over and over. No there is nothing you're doing wrong, that is just how the game is. They want to apply pressure to you by stressing your life point economy. Basically, this game is completely balanced around the LP economy, much like how, say, XCOM is balanced around the limited time system. Its game over when you're death spiralling on LP, much like XCOM is game over when the timeline is getting away from you.The game is stressful and unfun in all the worst ways, and the choices you have in your direct combat gameplay are boring as ♥♥♥♥. I also got to the castle management part and at least initially there are no interesting choices. Not sure if I'll even play long enough to see these mechanics fleshed out because the game is so mindnumblingly boring and stressful to play. Even if you have the most well reasoned approach to the game, it can still just decide to spit in your face for fun (i.e. instagib your character despite a sound strategy, or not give your the new skill even after 100s of uses! There is no build up it's just 100% random).That is the core issue of the game, but there are many other issues. It doesn't help the game that the environment art and storytelling is incredibly bad and doesn't make any sense at any point in time. Plus, I'm hours into the game's prologue with absolutely no end in sight. I have no idea when I'll get to play my the MC I chose, so as of 4-5hours in I'm still stuck playing as characters I don't want to play.I genuinely would not recommend this game to anyone unless you just want to play on casual mode and spam the A button and have pretty pictures on a 2nd monitor while you're doing other things. The flow of the game is genuinely that horrendously designed and it doesn't respect the players or give them interesting choices, so I wouldn't recommending giving it any of your attention.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolute masterpiece of a remake that stayed true to the soul of what made the original great, while making things more accessible and appealing to the average person. I was pretty checked out of video games prior to playing this. Especially RPGs, which seemed to have forgotten what made the genre great. Imagine my surprise when Romancing Saga 2's classic design gripped me right away. Story: Fast, succinct, conveys good timeless values. Easily skippable and unintrusive. Combat: Turn based, but doesn't waste your time. Your moves have immediate feedback and each effect is clearly conveyed. It's the perfect challenge on Classic mode and will make you actually think instead of relying on one boring team comp. Exploration and Progression: The name of the game is player freedom. You choose where to go, who to use, and what to do at all times. Your builds are highly specialized based on choices you make throughout the entire game.Visual style: Solid anime esque. Nothing mind blowing but very good.Voice acting: Some of the English voices are kinda cringe and you will notice the elitist actors that pop up in everything. Mostly fine though, and Japanese voices are available.Performance: No issues whatsoever. Runs consistently and has a medium amount of options.This is the best game Square has made in a long time. I won't just play once, I'll likely play it several times. Take it from a jaded cynic that's played hundreds of JRPGs. This is a special game.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start by stating the obvious. The game is beautiful. It has such a faithful finishing coat applied to it that playing this remake of RS2 with any knowledge of the original game becomes an almost surreal experience. Since it has become commonplace to rag upon old school JRPGs over the past decade, most developers continue to streamline newer game IPs into interactive movies and move away from the formats commonplace throughout the golden age of gaming.And yet out of nowhere comes RS2: ROTS. Perhaps it's just easier to remake a classic game which never truly had mainstream appeal so long as you stay faithful to the source material. Perhaps it's series producer Ichikawa's design to use this as another entry point into the series for a new generation of fans or those who just don't like what's been going on with more recent SaGa entries.There's a lot of fun to be had here if you're a fan of combat heavy RPGs and general experimentation with different party setups. The quality of life issues addressed with the new coat of paint make what was already a more forgiving SaGa entry into a great game that will allow anyone to grow familiar with the SaGa format without punishing regrets.

_childDocuments_.review: Game's fine.   A perfectly serviceable 7/10 RPG.Probably the most accessible SaGa game in the series.  Original game came out in '93 - and was WAY ahead of its time.  Remake applies a very decent coat of paint, but still feels like an old ass RPG at its core.  While they added several quality of life features - there was way more that they could have improved upon:   Needed more music variety, battles dragged on overly long, and as far as I could tell there wasn't a way to disable battle animations (watching the full animation of the same tech 400 times gets super tedious).Game at several points allows you to 'fail' by not doing things in the proper order, or wandering away from a quest.  Finishing one quest has a tendency to -end- other quests that you had in progress.  The original intent seems to be that they want you to play through it several times to see all the possible conclusions to quests (including 'fail' states) - but its a long enough game as is, and the payoff amounts to a 'hm.. I see.  so that happens.'  Not worth an extra 50 hours of playtime.If you're like me and really only plan on going through it the one time, save often - rotate your saves - and be prepared to lose several hours of progress when you didn't realize dancing with the mermaid was something the game wanted you to do with a male emperor, but let you start the quest with a female because F* you I guess.

_childDocuments_.review: May be one of the greatest JRPGs I have ever played -- I said that about the original, but this remake is a worthy inheritor of that accolade. I am constantly impressed with both how faithful this remake is and how elegantly they've integrated some of the revised mechanics. Romancing SaGa pushes you to maximize your decision-making both in combat and in how you approach the world, you are rarely grinding through "easy" combat and getting too complacent is going to result in unexpected failure. The game does an excellent job of penalizing failure while still allowing you to "fail forward" by allowing most aspects of character progression to persist through the generations of Emperors, but blocks you from simply grinding your way past challenges with the enemy rank system that progresses the more you enter combat. You will always need to be thinking and playing smart.There's more that can be said but if you are a fan of JRPGs you need to play this game, it's legendary. Here's hoping for a Romancing SaGa 3 remake in a few years!

_childDocuments_.review: The Saga series always put me off with its dense and ornery ruleset, along with needlessly vague navigation. I dropped Saga Frontier and Scarlet Grace Ambitions after a couple of hours each.  But this game changed everything- it's the first Saga game I enjoy.  This remake added UI indicators for a lot of the progression systems that usually happened behind the scenes.  You can now see how close you are to your next HP up or proficiency increase.  You can also see which skills have a chance of Sparking a new move.  It makes the battles more rewarding because I can see what I'm building toward. It also added unambiguous quest markers.  I don't care if it's hand-holdy, I'd rather not shakedown every NPC for directions.  I'd rather not run in circles navigating to the content.  I'm all for the new system. If you liked the demo, go ahead and buy the full game at full price.  It only gets better from there.  The demo stops right before the quest options and major power-progression systems unfold.   You're a king, so you can spend money to open up new shops that outclass everything else.  You can build a magic academy so all your soldiers learn new spells.  The quests have some fun, unexpected interactions.  For example, a nearby town is having a monster problem and the local Luchador martial artists are helpless because the Slimes resist their physical attacks.  You can kill all the monsters yourself, including two boss fights, or you can come back after killing the slime boss.  If you do that, the Luchador will instakill the second boss for you.  PSA:  SAVE BEFORE COMPLETING SIDEQUESTS OR FIGHTING BOSSES, THERE ARE SOME WEIRD TRIGGERS FOR TIMESKIPS.  Sometimes you can go right up to one trigger, do some other stuff, then carry over.  Final word of advice: don't lose sleep over the Life Points system.   At the end of each generation, you transfer everything to new characters whether you make it with 1 LP or 16.  I finished my first generation with at least 9 LP on each combatant and I would've had to try to spend ALL of them on the timeskip boss.   If you're just getting one or two deaths on each boss, you're in great shape.

_childDocuments_.review: The remake of Romancing SaGa 2 is a brilliant reimagining of the classic Japanese RPG, finely tuned for a new generation of players. The game retains its deep strategic gameplay, while also introducing several improvements that make it more accessible for newcomers without losing its original charm.One of the most exciting updates is the enhanced game balance, which smooths out the notorious difficulty spikes from the original, making it easier for beginners to enjoy the adventure without compromising the rewarding challenge for which Romancing SaGa is known. This version has refined mechanics and more user-friendly features, ensuring a smoother gameplay experience that doesn’t feel overwhelming.The character designs are also a highlight in the remake. They capture the charm of the original sprites, while adding a new level of detail and expressiveness that makes each hero memorable and visually appealing. Fans of pixel art will especially appreciate the care put into these visuals.Whether you’re a long-time fan or a newcomer to the series, Romancing SaGa 2 offers an enchanting, strategic, and rewarding RPG experience that’s hard to put down. This remake preserves the original’s legacy while making it more accessible and enjoyable than ever, making it an ideal entry point for international players who are ready to explore the iconic world of Romancing SaGa.

_childDocuments_.review: A solid remake.  I was pleased to find that even on "Normal" difficulty which is apparently easier than the original, the early bosses Kzinssie and Termite Queen required planning ahead, an understanding of the Formations mechanic, and so on - the challenge feels true to the original.  The extra info you get about how glimmers work feels helpful without being too much of a spoiler - sparking a new tech is still satisfying.  I think the very start of the game could feel repetitive for a new player not knowing what's to come.  The voice acting is pleasant enough, though is repetitive in battle.  Save-anywhere is gone, but given how easy it was to softlock yourself in the original, this is probably for good reason, and anyway there are save points all over the place.  The writing is bare-bones, but the interest is there when it comes to making major story decisions.  Configuring your retinue is less time-consuming, with recruits from all jobs available at any pub and a single contact for learning magic.  The option to abdicate the throne, and to swap out team members without having to kill them off, is much less punishing if you make a bad choice.  I'm not crazy about gathering crafting materials for the smithy, etc., but, it's not significantly different from the original.  Overall, I'm having terrific fun with this and I'm so glad more players will get a chance to play RS2!

_childDocuments_.review: For a remake of an old game, the different approach it takes toward the jrpg genre feels very refreshing. Something like Baldur's Gate 3 or Dark Souls give you many items that inspire ideas for future builds, but this game is more about the order you tackle quests in and the consequences of those choices. Hopefully the 30 classes and passive abilities will make things feel different enough. I recommend it if you're tired of the genre being too easy in modern times and want a challenge.

_childDocuments_.review: Way better than any modern remake of a SquareEnix title has a right to be.Pretty much everything from the OG was left intact without a hint of "modern audience" pandering, interfaces and menus were overhauled to provide a tremendous amount of information at your fingertips without having to consult external guides for every little thing, a bit of extra content has been added (including badly-needed backstory cutscenes for the Seven Heroes, largely derived from the lore established by THE STAGE productions and various supplemental sources), and difficulty options for those raised in gentler days and unable to handle the OG's punishment ("classic" difficulty is still included as the hardest option of the three choices available at the start, plus two more NG+ difficulty levels which will make you cry).All of the QoL additions and cleaner overhauled systems mean that this release has become the go-to starting point for anyone new to the franchise and looking to test the waters without immediately being pulled under by a merciless shark, and is by far the most newbie-accessible SaGa game available anywhere.That said, SaGa gonna SaGa, and it is going to have a field day with you if you try to go in facerolling at it like it's some generic RPG. Exploit weaknesses, tweak your party setup and comp for the challenges directly ahead of you, and don't be too reckless and you will go far; mindlessly push buttons because you're too cool to care and you will get the beatings you deserve.Missables are still a thing, along with the same mutually exclusive quest paths and such from the OG. The game is pretty good about giving you hints to avoid doing the dumb, but I know dumb tends to be the default state for a lot of people so consider this your warning to be less dumb. New Game+ is a thing, replays are encouraged to take different routes to the end, experiment with various party setups, and basically redo all of the things you missed out on and/or screwed up on when you were still learning.Bonus: Sensei and Sensei's shapeless butt are here, this time in the form of the same sort of scavenger hunt target as Lil' Cactus from Trials of Mana, which as it happens was made by the same team that did this remake. Maybe that's enough to persuade you to give the game a try. Maybe that's your thing. I won't judge.Much.

_childDocuments_.review: By the time I'm writing this I only have 3 heroes defeated but I already think this game is great.I've liked everything this game offers so far, combat is fantastic for someone addicted to turn based combat like me, I love the character design, I love the areas and how different they can be from each other and the details in the towns, the game is not next gen or anything but it looks and runs great (you can turn off the motion blur by adding some lines to a file btw), I like how hard the game can be on Classic difficulty, I really like how your choices matter and how they change the world around you or give you a new class if you do it right and I really like how much customization there is for your party with formations, equipment, techs, spells and abilities.I came in with no knowledge of what the romancing saga series was about and I can say I'm very satisfied with this game.

The more you level with that tech the more damage you do. Game gives you a beginning setup and then when you get to your third emperor you go about it your way and how you find the game most comfortable with your strategies. You might end up having a horrible setup, you might end up with a way better one. But love the game... its a excellent remake of the original.

_childDocuments_.review: Super fun, and I love the challenge. The game already looked really cool, but it definitely surpassed my expectations. I like that the game has weaknesses you can exploit/visually see like in Octopath Traveler. The combat is difficult because the enemies seem to scale with you. _childDocuments_.review: I didn't get a chance to play the original, but this remake is phenomenal. I haven't loved all the saga series I have played, but my favorite was Saga Frontier. I did play some Romancing Saga 3 and quite a bit of Mistrel Song and enjoyed them as well. This remake really hits the nostalgic old school rpg factor for me that I haven't felt from many of the new jrpgs out there. I thought I wouldn't like the time skipping and character changing, but it's awesome and while the game shows you where quests can be, this game isn't linear at all. _childDocuments_.review: This is my first game in the Saga series and man... Playing on the classic difficulty is brutal yet rewarding at the same time. Considering that the backbone of this game was set years ago, this was a game truly ahead of its time with its game systems. The order of which you do things matter, and your decisions matter and has consequences. I can't describe how rewarding playing this game with how you build your empire, your emperor and your progress. It's a very classic game that feels modern and it's just such a joy to play. I can't recommend this enough to people looking for a great JRPG.
_childDocuments_.name: Romancing SaGa 2: Revenge of the Seven

_childDocuments_.review: Romancing SaGa 2: Revenge of the Seven - Review"Romancing SaGa 2: Revenge of the Seven" is a fun and immersive experience, though it would benefit from clearer guidance on how to switch between enemies during battles and manage healing for companions. Coming from an MMO background, I found the mechanics took some time to master, but once I got the hang of it, the gameplay was engaging and enjoyable. For anyone who needs a break from solo play, there's always the option to return to a multiplayer title like SWTOR. Overall, this is an entertaining RPG with a unique charm that keeps me coming back!
_childDocuments_.name: Romancing SaGa 2: Revenge of the Seven

_childDocuments_.review: After beating everything, including the post game, I can honestly say this has been one of the greatest JRPG experiences of my life...and that's not hyperbole either. The fine balance between being so hard it makes you want to tear your hair out to finally rewarding you when you formulate a winning strategy that annihilates the boss that was owning you...it's orgasmic.Everything about Romancing SaGa 2 is so perfect, for an old fart like me anyway. The simple story, the endless combat, the hundreds of unlockable skills, about 30 different unlockable character classes, punishing dungeons, non-linear quest progression, a 10/10 soundtrack, and this BEAUTIFUL early 2000s Playstation 2 aesthetic that I can't keep my eyes off of. This game was 50 hours of pure joy and I feel like I owe Square even more money for how great it was. Yeah, sure, it won't please most people either due to the flimsy plot, retro visuals or high difficulty, but for people who are into these sort of things, well, your holy grail is here waiting. Come get it.
_childDocuments_.name: Romancing SaGa 2: Revenge of the Seven

_childDocuments_.review: As a longtime fan of JRPGs, I couldn’t be happier with the game. It gives me everything I love about old-school JRPG with a very welcomed refurbishment. The graphics are nice (disable this awful motion blur tho), the OST is an absolute banger, the multi-generational storytelling is simply brilliant and makes every decision feel meaningful. IMO this game is a rare gem that (for once) respects the player’s intelligence while staying true to its roots. If you appreciate classic JRPGs with depth and replayability, this one is a must-play!
_childDocuments_.name: Romancing SaGa 2: Revenge of the Seven

_childDocuments_.review: Just incredible, first time playing a saga game, it's dazzling. I believe everyone should give it a try only to comprehend all the concept displayed because it opens a lot of outlook on games conception in general ( and also on the history of video game since the original game released in 1993).

_childDocuments_.review: This remake takes the story of the original Romancing SaGa 2 and develops it in more detail while remaining true to what the original game portrayed. The quests, characters, places, items, monsters, skills, etc., are all here with a nice new 3D coat of paint, and the game mechanics have a few tweaks while still remaining mostly the same and being recognizable from the original version. Playing the game so far, I kind of felt like I did when I played the Trails series and I went from the old school Trails in the Sky to the current Trails Through Daybreak series because I'd just played RS2 and RS3 not too long ago, so it's been really cool to see all these familiar faces and locations no longer as pixel-art but in 3D.Gameplay-wise, it has a ton of Quality of Life features to make things easier and less confusing than the original games, such as quest markers and progress bars to let you know just how far along you are on your way to level up a given skill or attribute and the game has three initial difficulty settings ranging from Casual to Hard (Classic), so it's far more forgiving and accessible than the original version. Having said that, you have the option to deactivate all these QoL features and play in the classic difficulty setting to roughly approximate the experience or playing the previous version.So far, I've defeated two of The Seven and expanded the Empire to three territories and I'm only starting to play as my second emperor after Gerard and making different choices than I did when I played the previous HD pixel remake so that I can have a somewhat different experience, and I can say that I'm having a ton of fun. If they decided to do a similar remake for RS3, I'd buy it on release date too.Edit: I finished the whole game and the extra endgame content I could find, and I have to say I'm very impressed with how faithful this game is to the original version while still tweaking some details so that things would make sense in a 3D environment and updated gameplay. Pretty much nothing from the original game was omitted, except for the optional dungeon where you meet the Ninja and the Diviner and fight the Dread Queen, but all the important elements were integrated into other quest lines anyway. On the contrary, instead of removing stuff, there's a couple of new recruitable classes, most places and characters get a bit more detail, there's more abilities and things to unlock at the various facilities you build, and, most importantly, through a series of collectibles known as Memories of the Seven you get to find out the backstory of the main villains and why they went from being ancient heroes who saved the world to immortal demons bent on destroying it, and you also get to fight them in their original human forms as post-game content.This is what all remakes should be like. It was basically like stumbling into an alternate timeline where this game was made today instead of back in the SNES days, and I have to say I loved this one just as much as the original HD pixel remasters. Once again, I hope this does very well so that they remake Romancing SaGa 3 in the same style. I'd love playing that game.

_childDocuments_.review: Phenomenal remake, really good, if you're on the fence go for it. Top quality game.How does it compare? The remake from the 2010s was better on every level but still quite rough. This however is perfectly fleshed out and modernised right from the get go.

name: The 7th Guest VR
detailed_description: Experience the most spine-tingling VR mystery adventure of your life. The classic game that chilled you to the bone in the 90s has been brought back to life, with cutting-edge VR technology that delivers an atmospheric story like no other. Six guests have been welcomed to the foreboding mansion. But something sinister is at play. The wealthy recluse and toymaker, Henry Stauf, hides in the shadows, and there is a dark power here, shrouded in mysteries. Who is the 7th Guest? What does Henry want with them? And who will live to tell the tale? As you explore the eerie mansion, the puzzles become increasingly challenging, and there are dangers lurking around every corner, with every shadow, creak, and flicker of light adding to the haunting tension. Unlock new rooms and uncover hidden secrets, all while trying to keep your wits about you against the eerie horrors. The 7th Guest VR is the ultimate adventure for fans of mystery-puzzle games and those seeking a new and terrifying VR experience.

_childDocuments_.review: The game seems just as great as I was hoping for. I'm using an RTX 3090, i9 10900K (10 cores/20 threads, 3.7-5.3Ghz), 32GB, Win10. And the Valve Index hmd.The game is a 24GB download (25GB installed), twice the size of the Quest version. The PCVR version is greatly enhanced with high-res textures, great lighting, highly detailed dynamic shadows and polygon levels are fine (the latter probably generally same as Quest, but some models have increased polygon count, like the chandelier in the main hall). It's a dead world like Red Matter 2, and npcs are shown like movie characters - this works great, and also does not require tons of rendered polygons. I've taken several screenshots here:Performance is great, but might also reveal the Quest origin. Using an insane Index res 400% (36 mill pixels combining both eyes) I get 80 fps in 80 Hz with maxed in-game settings - for 90 fps I need res 350%. That's inside the mansion using 4xMSAA - but you can just use 2xMSAA instead, looks the same with that res. In short - most should be able to play this game in high res. Devs say you need a RTX 2070 for the game, I would be surprised if this does not work with a GTX 1060 6GB (or at least 1070 8GB). EDIT: It has been confirmed that the game works great with GTX 1060 6GB and Quest 2 in the Discussion Forum. You can teleport, slide or both. Smooth and snap turning are available - controls are great. I played the original 7th Guest a lot of years ago. This feels so much better. I've solved a few rooms, still have much to do. The game feels like an 9/10 rating for the PCVR version right now - within its genre. It's a high-quality game. Puzzles seem well-balanced, not too hard, not too easy. I'm in the start of the game, and so far the puzzles did not make me feel like a chimp trying to solve a Rubik's Cube - maybe later :-) I'm normally not into puzzle games, but this game feels like being in a league of its own - much like Room VR (and you get many more rooms in The 7th Guest ;-) Note that the game is almost too bright with the Index, consider reducing brightness to 70% for better blacks. I also tested the game with my Rift CV1, and the game looks great, even if slightly too bright for oled panels. The game uses OpenXR drivers, so users of Meta and other hmds - with no native SteamVR driver support like the Index - will get optimal performance too.
_childDocuments_.name: The 7th Guest VR

_childDocuments_.review: It's going to be easy to dismiss this as a VR remaster with identical puzzles, script, and so forth. I'm pleased to report after initial impressions this is *not* the case. Quick nostalgia bit: I was 8 when the original game came out. It was one of the first and only games that our family, for what it was worth, played together. The atmosphere was incredibly spooky and genuinely terrified my young self - for being pre-rendered mostly static images on a CRT screen. This is not that. This is a reimagining of vast swaths of the original game, complete with new mechanics (no spoilers) and way better immersion than I would have expected. Jump scares? No, just a genuine feeling of dread as you fumble around the mansion  one more time. + Feels totally new while retaining callbacks+ Spatial recording looks pretty good+ Various types of interactions make it feel made for VR- You will get stuck!- Shader bugs - By default, post-processing is set to Low. I assume that is on purpose, as increasing it to high caused some bad artifacting with the ghost scenes.- Seated mode is not very accessible. Puzzle pieces are manual, so if you have trouble sitting up or reaching high things, you may not be able to do some puzzles at all With a patch or two to fix the visual artifacting and accessibility issues this is a 9 / 10. Everyone who has played the original and doesn't have a VR headset should be jealous.
_childDocuments_.name: The 7th Guest VR

_childDocuments_.review: As an avid 7th guest and 11th hour fan, I've been really really looking forward to this. And it doesn't dissapoint on the actual game play, the game itself is really well put together. Puzzles can be challenging, the atmosphere is superb and the music takes me right back there. Of course there are a few things I am upset about. The first was Stauf, I would have liked the original or near as, but in this he is a completely different person. And the other biggest one for me is the house. It's not the Stauf Manor, the layout downstairs is fine, but if you go upstairs it's completely different and I was really looking forward to going around the manor in its full and first glory. I also wanted to walk through the clock... But I can understand why they did it, there's more rooms now.But even with those bugbears, I am enjoying it immensely and would definitely recoment it if you enjoy puzzle games with a haunting atmosphere.
