_childDocuments_.review: Visions of Mana feels like a game made by several teams, none of which knew what they were doing and why.At its core, this is a team-based action RPG with simplistic hack and slash controls and separate menus for magic attacks and a few dedicated buttons for other types of special attacks. Just like in Secret or Trials, you control a team of three characters and can switch between them at any point during the fight, though during the city exploration you always revert to the main character of the game (or another character, if the story requires). As you follow the story, more characters join and the game allows you to create a team out of any combination of characters. And characters themselves have a selection of classes to choose from in addition to their default starting class. Unlike Trials, the classes are unlocked by equipping special artifacts tied to one of the elemental powers and can be swapped at any point outside of the battle. Each class has its own linear selection of skills you can unlock, with some becoming available for any class the character equips and some remaining exclusive to when you have said class active.Unlike Trials of Mana remake, that played very much like a fun “Ys-lite” hack and slash game, where everything was super fast and to the point, Visions returns to a more traditional “enter the battle state” format when you attack enemies on the field and when in the battle you can then rub against the edges of the battle border to escape the battle (if the game allows it). And the combat is… primitive. It’s less of a hack and slash, and more of a jRPG game with direct controls, although your control over character actions is a bit more responsive than, say, Scarlet Nexus or Final Fantasy XV. But it doesn’t play like Trials of Mana (even less so Ys) and I’d say Final Fantasy VII Remake is also a far more interesting recontextualization of what the original Secret of Mana was aiming for, in case developers didn’t want it to be like Trials. Nothing about this combat system is outright bad, but it’s extremely boring, with “harder” fights usually being more long rather than difficult, which is also the case for the Hard difficulty. It’s simply designed in a way, where making this “challenging” is not possible.The story, while suspiciously reminiscent of Final Fantasy X in more than one way, is also a mixed bag. On one hand, it has some really good emotional moments and characters aren’t always as one-sided and cliche as they usually appear during most of the game. On the other hand… well, that – most of the game story is exceedingly simple. Which isn’t a bad thing if it’s exciting and adventurous, and it sometimes is, but that’s where the rest of the gameplay issues completely kill whatever this game is going for emotionally.The world looks beautiful. Really, it does. It’s as if concept artist made wonderful watercolour and oil concepts of locations and then magically made them 3D assets. It’s the art from Secret of Mana come to life. But as a gameplay space, it’s extremely boring and lifeless. Unlike Trials (and Secret), which created the illusion of  big forests and fields via clear defined paths you run through, as is very common for action RPGs, Visions makes most of the locations work as a modern type of wide open world spaces. And probably because of that and the real chance of getting lost or not being able to find things game wants you to find, it’s full of markers that clearly show where stuff you might need is. Which, in turn, turns the entire game into running to markers on the map with no regard to the context of the action. You don’t need to read the dialogue, you don’t need to know what’s going on – run to the marker, do the clear thing, go to a different marker.Which is also the entire formula for the side-quests in the game, of which there are about 120. Why so many? Because. Most of them are just “go there, kill enemies, go back” or something that sounds as exciting as that. And some have storylines of sorts, but those storylines are extremely boring and uninteresting. Meet a character who’s very nice – here’s a series of 5 side quests, between which you need to reload the location so the next one appears, at the end o which you will learn that the character is indeed very nice. Exciting.And it brings me to that lack of cohesion and understanding of what the game is. It genuinely feels that story was written by one team, combat done by another, main quests by another, side quests by another, locations and mechanics that get their own long explanation only to then never be used again was made by another… And many other teams, none of which actually played the game and saw what their combined efforts bring. Characters get experience separately with each of their own XP bars filling in post-combat menu one by one. But it’s always synchronized across the entire team, so the more characters you get, the longer the post-combat screen lasts for no reason. Equipping a class gets its own intro cutscene, but you always get all artefacts by the middle of the story and can always unlock all classes for every character. Yet, when you finally get the last character, if you want to unlock their classes (which you obviously do), you need to sit through about 8 unskippable class intro cutscenes in a row. And every character gets an achievement for “unlocking all classes”, separately, even though you can’t not get all of them unless you’re too lazy to equip the artefacts. Some of the interior locations get a weird prompt if you want to enter them that looks like a last minute crutch, while some don’t…I’m not even talking about how technically messy this game is. I had one fight almost become unwinnable because the enemy got flung high into the sky by one magic attack and couldn’t go back down. Objects on the locations might stay invisible. Map markers glitch constantly. Half of the cutscenes render at the gameplay framerate and look fine, half are rendered at a lower framerate and look like they’re constantly lagging for no apparent reason. Some of the already mentioned on-off mechanics barely function or require you to perform incredibly illogical and inconvenient things. The way controls are assigned is ridiculous and you cannot rebind any action to any button – for whatever reason, only select buttons are available per specific action. Also the game has about 4 different types of “currencies”, with 3 of them being almost entirely pointless for the majority of the game. Again – as if someone had an idea, put it in the game and no one ever played the completed product to realize that most of it could and should be cut or changed.For the first dozen of hours or so I thought that I’d end up being carefully recommending the game. It had already shown most of its aforementioned problems and lack of cohesion or understanding what game is it supposed to be, but at least it was a simple adventure that could be enjoyable. But then the game lasted for way too long, for absolutely no reason. I could easily see cutting about half of everything in this game, locations, mechanics, story beats, characters and etc., and getting a far superior title. It would still be not something you’d love and remember forever, but at least it would be approaching the entertainment level of Trials of Mana, just without all of the fun crazy ambitions of that game. But as is, Visions of Mana is a boring confused mess that doesn’t do anything too badly, but also doesn’t have anything to justify spending the time on it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is gonna be a long one. Unfortunately, I can't recommend this unless it's on a pretty steep discount. This is probably the most disappointing release of the year for me.To preface this, one of my all-time favorites is Seiken Densetsu 3 (Trials of Mana). I have fond memories of, like many folks, playing a fan-translated ROM on ZSNES or whatever back in the day. That game aged very well, and I'm glad it finally came out over here! You should play that! If you play the remake, use the Japanese dub.However, this game ain't it.First, the positive: This is a super pretty game which, at least from an aesthetic standpoint, pays a welcome homage to the classics. The way the music blends in-and-out of battle is a nice touch. Careena and Morley are fun characters.Sadly, it only goes downhill from there.The first thing I noticed was that it failed to bring anything original to the series. An early boss is a literal clone of an early boss from Secret of Mana. At first, I thought, "Oh, cool, a throwback boss! That's fun." However, several boss encounters in this game are essentially recycled bosses from other Mana games. This is weird.A major character/story event is blatantly telegraphed, constantly, for hours prior to it happening. Once said event happened, I rolled my eyes so hard they nearly fell out of my head. Mana games have never really been "known for" their story, but good god, man. There are multiple cutscenes where an antagonist or other major character does a climactic thing, the party responds accordingly, and then for some reason the character in question just... goes away somehow? A major character death is followed by the killer just... going away somehow off-screen. Then the party's like "oh no, he got away" ...like, what?Outside of the previously mentioned Careena and Morley, the other three characters have insufferable voice acting. The child character, oddly enough, was the least annoying of the three. I don't believe this is a fault of the actors but rather bad direction. Why does Palamena refuse to speak any contractions, and why does she sometimes speak in alliterative sentences and sometimes she doesn't? I can't stand it. There's a part where she acts completely out of character and that's the only time I enjoyed her. Again, not the actors, but the direction. If I have to hear Val shout "GRRRRRRIZLYYYY!!!" over the game's pretty music one more time I'm going to drink bleach.The side quests in the game are absolute trash. They are nearly 100% MMO fetch quests. Go here, kill thing, come back. Go there, get 5 rabite steaks, come back. After about 20 hours I started to skip them entirely. The rewards are almost always nothing to write home about.The game incorporates an active/passive ability slotting system using "ability seeds." This, if it were done with more care, could have been an interesting idea with a lot of potential for synergies. However, aside from "this gives you more crit chance" + "this lowers their defense when you crit" you won't be doing much. I would just stuff stats into most of these slots. This is just another disappointing missed opportunity.While the job system is interesting on the surface, there isn't very much variety to it. Many jobs play very nearly identically.The party AI is absolutely dreadful. Just... awful. Your party will not heal you unless you are nearly dead unless you explicitly set them to "only heal/full defense" mode. They try to sneakily side-step this by sometimes tossing in guest characters that you can't control, won't die, and will toss heals now and then. This just feels like a lazy band-aid solution. This came to a head on a late-game, otherwise boring mid-boss that would fire off slow-moving projectiles that sleep on contact. If the character is asleep, the boss would perform a massive lifesteal on them. However, because the AI is so braindead they would just stand there, get hit, fall asleep, and heal the boss. I got past it but only after being stuck in the fight for nearly an hour. If you Google the "Vampire" boss you'll see that I'm not alone on this one.The environmental traversal starts quite promising. Early on, many of the environments are quite vast and open. They even give you an adorable land mount! After the first act of the game, however, you get the ability to travel by sea. This results in the game losing all of the large explorable zones. Things become extremely formulaic and boring: Zip to a town at light-speed, watch some cutscenes, do the dungeon. It's a really weird shift. It almost feels like someone else entirely took over this portion of the game halfway through development.Speaking of environments..."Grizzly Syrup" is an absurdly stupid collectible. Whoever thought it would be a good idea to pepper the pretty environments with bright orange floating egg-shaped blobs should rethink their life choices. I feel like I'm playing freakin' Crash Bandicoot or something. The game is full of chests that contain absolute trash, so why couldn't they just put the Grizzly Syrup rewards into these chests? The rewards aren't all that crazy.I was beginning to lose my interest in this game in the latter part of the third act. I began a very tedious dungeon with a lot of unnecessary and, again, tedious traversal mechanics. There was a pretty easy and kind of pointless mid-boss. No save point. Weird. Okay, so I continue through the dungeon. I get to what looks like the boss arena at the end of the dungeon. Still no save point? Well, I start fighting the boss, get it down to 20% HP remaining, and then it freezes in place before blinking out of existence. Boss music kept playing, health bar was on the screen... but nope! He was gone for good.I reloaded my save and I was at the beginning of the dungeon. 45 minutes lost. I was fed up enough by that point that I uninstalled.I can go on and on:- Environmental traversal mechanics are a couple unique ideas iterated repeatedly with different color schemes/elemental themes.- Controller input lag is irritating and makes using the menus frustrating.- If you sell your weapons, they are removed from your transmogs. This means you'll have a clean armor inventory but a cluttered disaster of a weapons inventory if you want to keep all the weapon styles.- You can't double jump or dodge in towns for some reason. This makes towns feel like a huge drag because when you're out and about you can usually double jump and dodge.- Many cutscenes and lines of dialog are just characters repeating the same thing over and over. While I wasn't skipping story cutscenes outright, I was getting to a point where I was buttoning past things.

_childDocuments_.review: Visions of Mana is a wonderful game in the Mana series of games. It draws a lot of design choices from the game Legend of Mana, which is my favorite game in the series. As a long time Mana fan, I can say this game is a very enjoyable experience for fans and newcomers alike. However, it's not without its issues.This game isn't perfect by any means, but what it does wrong is way overshadowed by what it does right. Being part of the Mana series, it's an action JRPG with a focus on character relationships, and story. Below I'll list my thoughts and feelings on some of the things to be experienced in the game. For reference, I have nearly 40 hours, and I'm midway through chapter 7. I know that there are a total of 11 chapters.PresentationThis game is gorgeous to look at. Just amazing colors used, and the models are very clean and crisp. All of it feels like it does fit into the world. Sadly the character animations in scenes are a bit stiff and sometimes lifeless, and the voice acting sometimes isn't the best. Some lines do fall flat, but most of the time they work really well. Careena does sadly have a bad rep when it comes to the quality and direction of her voice over. She's very heavily southern in English. Sounds like she's from Tennesee or something. While I'm not one to get nit picky over voice overs, she does sound a little out of place, especially considering no one from her village has the same kind of accent. But as you play the game, you get used to it, especially since Careena as a character is actually enjoyable.StoryThe story of Visions of Mana doesn't do anything new. It follows Val a Soul Guard appointed to help protect and guide the new Alms of the world to the Mana Tree so they can offer their souls to the Mana Goddess to keep the world's Mana in balance. Along the way, Val meets many different characters who all have different motivations and personalities. My personal favorites are Morley and Careena. Morley is a well spoken man who is a traveling blade for hire. He's kind hearted, motivated, and determined to bring his homeland back from the dead.Careena is a young woman from the country who is headstrong, stubborn, and quick to anger, but at the same time, she doesn't hesitate to stick to her convictions and tell people how it is. She travels with her little beast cub named Ramcoh, who is like a sister to her.CombatThe combat for Visions of Mana is, as I said before, action based. It's fluid, fast, and can get kind of frantic, but it always feels great. There are a total of 8 classes PER character, and a total of 5 playable characters. Each class is assigned an elemental attribute, and each attribute can only be assigned to one character. It takes the usual ring menu from previous games and expands on it rather well, allowing you to assign items to one ring, skills to another, and both items and skills have their own shortcuts which can be assigned to a smaller ring of 4 slots each. It's similar to the Trials of Mana remake in terms of it's fluidness and speed, but I find it a lot better. The AI of the characters, which can be somewhat customized, is also much better than Trials of Mana's AI. The characters actually try to do things and will buff, debuff, heal, and attack as needed. However, they do have difficulty dodging attacks, especially AOE attacks.World BuildingThe world of Visions of Mana is a vibrant and beautiful world. It's filled to the brim with flora, fawna, and people from all walks of life. It never once felt empty or lifeless, and everything in it always felt like it was there for a reason. Just a fantastically beautiful world.ContentAs I've stated, at the time of writing this, I'm nearly 40 hours into my journey. Midway through chapter 7, with at least 4 more chapters to go. The game never feels like a slog though, at least not to me. Getting to explore the world as I'm going from location to location feels really good to do. There are also loads of optional side quests to do, all of which grant you money and gear in some from. There's also a ton of things to collect along the way, from Grizzly Syrup, to completing the Aeries. There's just a ton of things this game as to offer. Lil' Cactus also makes an appearance, and by finding him in each zone, you are awarded different bonuses based on how many times you find him, which a special reward when you find him 35 times.Price/contentI think that Visions of Mana is worth the price tag. It's clearly a game that has had a lot of love put into it, and I do feel that the amount of content you get out of the game is enough to make that cost worth it.Overall thoughtsAll in all, Visions of Mana is a very enjoyable romp through a lovingly crafted game. If you're a fan of the Mana series, especially Legends of Mana, you'll enjoy this game. If you like fast paced action JRPGs, with a decent bit of skill customization, you'll also enjoy this game. Out of all the Mana games, this one is definitely one of my favorites, right up there with my all time favorite of Legend of Mana.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite having very pretty environments, good art direction, and fun character designs, this feels like a big disappointment compared to the Trials of Mana remake and I have very little motivation in continuing.My main gripe with the game's structure and gameplay comes down to the new "open world" system. Gone are dungeons and a compressed world to lead the player to new dungeons or towns. Now it's replaced with bloated open world areas and an almost Ubisoft styled checklist progression. """Exploration""" boils down to either looking at fat waypoint markers on the minimap/HUD indicator or staring at the mini map more than the actual environments for blue marks of interest to find really inane rewards or activities (treasure chests mostly with pitiful gold/items, elemental crystals for a very small number of points for leveling up skills, bootleg time trials a la Chadley trials from FF7R, etc.) Due to dungeons being out of picture, the player is obligated to interact with these areas for leveling up and getting money to buy things. For me, they simply weren't interesting to explore or interact with. The fact there are so many fast travel markers the player can teleport to at anytime once they're found felt like the furthest thing of a sign of confidence from the developers about this design decision.I'd like to emphasize that Trials' dungeons are nothing to romanticize and very much a, "They get the job done," ordeal to me, but that style of controlled progression simply worked to the benefit of pacing by having the game not outstay its welcome with specific areas.As for the story, I have two issues. First issue are how the main cast are handled. Trials of Mana limited the player to picking three playable characters from a cast of six and I think that worked to its benefit because each character had unique struggles, interacted with each other in fun ways, and affected what story content the player would see (which gave the game some replay value). Comparatively, Visions is much more by the numbers and you will get all five playable characters in your party (which is NOT a bad thing on its own). The much bigger issue is how any personal struggles they have are wrapped up within the hour you meet each of them and from there, they all become static in terms of any character growth because their entire focus becomes getting to the Mana Tree. Comparatively, each Trials character got individually introduced and had their distinct, personal struggle that got taken care of throughout the story. It also doesn't help a lot of the cast have muted personalities unless they're Val or Careena (aka, dialogue interactions are a lot less interesting).The second problem is how the "self-sacrifice" angle of the overarching plot has been handled. I'd like to emphasize this second point is a lot more shaky due to not completing the game and if it does something clever with it down the line, please ignore. The game establishes that every four years, the world needs "alms" to sacrifice their souls to the Mana Tree, or else, different towns and cities will suffer and eventually collapse due to an element not having a sacrifice represent it. Some people are making big reaches and saying the writers are promoting suicide with this. I do not think that's the case at all, I simply just find the subject matter of self-sacrifice to be severely undercooked and brings up more questions than needed. The game makes it very definitive that the world is screwed if the sacrifices don't happen which is fine on its own, but then immediately introduces Eoren, a tragic antagonist whose entire purpose is to try and find a way to change the system to stop people being sacrificed. Unfortunately, the character feels like a giant, walking contradiction, not even because of how it's established that sacrifices are culturally engrained in the world, but more that his action during the intro cause a town to get completely decimated because of wanting to run away with an alm he was in love with. The game has raised the stakes so comically high on the matter that it's hard to really sympathize with him in any capacity even when he has a point. Along with that, the idea he's the ONLY character in the game who is seemingly trying to come up with an alternative solution is ridiculous. It makes the world feel incredibly tiny despite trying to be this globetrotting adventure with unique cultures and ways of life. Unfortunately, this simplicity also applies to most of the playable cast where they all have made up their mind in advance that they're 100% okay with being sacrifices and makes their interactions even duller because the only character being slightly swayed by it all is Val (who isn't even a sacrifice, he's basically just a bodyguard for them all). Some people would probably argue that I'm overthinking this plot, but I'd argue back that the game does not need this baggage in the first place if they didn't want to develop it meaningfully. Trials of Mana did just fine with its standard fantasy plot thanks to good character development that made me care enough about what was going on and affecting people.Look, if the game has a DQXI tier "pull the rug under the player" moment that I didn't get to, I'm sorry for my ignorance, but ultimately, I'm nearly 20 hours into the game and I just wasn't engaged by either the characters or main plot (and even when DQXI was by the numbers, it was still way more entertaining thanks to its distinct cast of characters).There are other niggling things (like Trials, the combat is very easy even on "Hard", the player can't double jump and dash in town areas for some reason, the cutscenes are locked at 30 FPS and tend to look visually scuffed compared to the regular game parts), but those are minor compared to the previously mentioned stuff. I feel ♥♥♥♥♥♥ for writing this review considering what happened to the developers, but I can't recommend the game for amateurish open world design and the subpar plot. If you haven't, pick up the Trials of Mana remake on a sale instead (also nobody in Visions is "Suffocate me with your ass" tier as Belladonna from Trials is so rip).

_childDocuments_.review: I wish Final Fantasy XVI could be like Visions of Mana. It is a well-scoped, grand adventure in a gorgeous art style, one where you follow a party of characters with different classes, skills and abilities, and different struggles. They really are the highlight of this game. When the plot focuses on their arcs, the narrative really hits its stride. Each character has their shortcomings, backgrounds and challenges. They are all relevant to the plot and get plenty of development and love. Customizing them for battle is really fun too. I really enjoyed mixing and matching their classes together with the non-class-restricted ability seeds for some OP builds.I also enjoyed the exploration. They confidently gave us a stupidly OP Double Jump right from the start and delivered maps that let us make full use of it. Together with some janky movement tech, you can really break the game early if you learn the systems, which is a good indicator of a confidently design JRPG.Really enjoyed this game. Shame about what happened to the studio. Palamena is hot.

_childDocuments_.review: A long-awaited return to the Mana series that is a bit of a mixed bag. The graphics are stunning and the soundtrack is captivating, while the combat starts a bit simple but offers depth as you unlock new classes (for me it picked up after getting the fire vessel). The game is fun to play and the characters are great and compelling, however, the pacing is erratic, as some segments are enjoyable while others are boring and a chore to get through. The game does get bad near the end with predictable plot twists and backtracking in areas that were beaten before. ✔️ Stunning visuals and a compelling soundtrack that immerses you in the world of Mana.✔️ An engaging combat system that is dynamic, fun, and offers a good balance of simplicity and complexity. ✔️ Diverse roster of characters and classes that offer a lot of options.❌Terrible pacing, like a roller coaster, is a pattern: amazing for two hours and tedious for one hour. ❌Weak story compared to other Mana titles.While the game is decent, it falls short of the greatness of the previous Mana games. Is a solid entry if you can make it to the end or are a big fan of the Mana series, but for newcomers it might be a pitfall of frustration or boredom by its flaws. Some areas like the desert one or the prince one are boring, while the story progresses slowly and changes it's focus too much, making it less compelling. If you enjoy and find the review helpful, please follow my curator!

_childDocuments_.review: this game is great and fun, if you know what you are getting.. i like to compare this to trials of mana, as this was basically a prototype for this game. this game holds your hand heavily, technically you can just run from star to star and rush through the story if you want to. however, to me the star is the last thing i go to, which is why im not that far in the story even after 6 hours. personally i prefered it in the old games, where you had to figure things out yourself by talking to people and things, but oh well. BUT, the maps are more open here than they were in trials of mana.the music is good, the graphics are good, the menus are not too overwhelming, as they were in the demo, where you just get everything thrown into your face at once. generally everything is explained well enough, you can choose a difficulty for the game, you can later choose the character you want to play and the gameplay you prefer.all in all this is your usual mana game, you have the elements, you have the fairies, the same items and everything you know.i wanted to play this on the tv and had huge issues getting this to run on a second monitor. the resolution just kept changing no matter what i set it to in the settings. i choose window mode it goes full screen and vice versa. and on top of that it ran the game with 30 fps. could only fix this by mirroring my pc screen because all other options failed. but aside that the game runs smooth now.i must mention that i play using a controller. i cant possibly imagine using the menus with a keyboard.one "bad" thing that at least the demo had but wont matter for english users, the english and german translations are completely different. yes, in the end both tell you where to go and what to do. but especially in the cutscenes the characters said very different things. its a little annoying, so i changed to japanese voice.i did not regret buying this game. im looking forward to more hours of brainless running through maps and collecting things until eventually progressing the story. it is what a mana game nowadays is, it was like that in trials of mana and i doubt itll be different in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: Visions of Mana is the latest entry in the Mana series. Like its predecessors, it has a very vibrant and whimsical atmosphere and extremely addicting action combat. Although it's a AA game in its budget, it really stands out and makes an impression compared to most other JRPGs on the market. Although decades have passed, the series is extremely faithful to its roots and this game is definitely a JRPG at its core.The artwork in Visions of Mana is phenomenal. The main cast of 5 characters are all very uniquely designed to be a variety of races around the world. Each of these playable characters have 9 job classes, which is a unique outfit for the character. These class designs are some of the best class outfits I've seen since Final Fantasy Tactics or Disgaea. These classes are based on elemental magic in the game, namely fire, water, wind, earth but also more interesting ones such as light, dark, wood and moon. Each character and class has its own nuances and as you unlock more passive and active skills in each class you can then keep them as you change classes, somewhat like Final Fantasy 5's job class system. The system makes it very fun to experiment and it's never overly complicated. Characters each generally have 3 different kinds of weapons (depending on their class) but they each have only 1 armor and you can purchase better gear as you progress through the game.The premise of the game is simple. It's about representatives of each element (called Alms) going on a pilgrimage to sacrifice themselves to the Mana Tree along with Val, their Soul Guard, so they can prevent a calamity. It's very similar to the premises of Tales of Symphonia or Final Fantasy X. The introduction to the game is very boring and cliché, with characters acting extremely one-dimensionally and being fine with the culture of their world. All I can say without spoiling is that the game does subvert this in Chapter 3 and there are amazing twists afterwards with characters actually having personalities afterwards and the plot really picking up. Unlike Trails of Mana, you don't have to pick a protagonist. The story you experience will be the same no matter what with Val as the protagonist. It was disappointing in the previous game because your plot would change depending on your protagonist, meaning you'd have some plot arcs that would be introduced but not concluded - like if you wanted to see Belladonna's conclusion you'd have to pick Hawkeye or Riesz as your protagonist in Trails of Mana. I was saddened at first that you couldn't choose between different protagonists, but when I played through the game I realized that the writers wanted to narrow their scope and focus on writing a story on Val. The gameplay is the high point of this game. It's action combat where you choose your character's class, upgrade their class abilities and level up, as well as increase your level. In battle you can do simple combos and it's fun to juggle enemies. The game is on the short side, taking us about 30 hours to get through the story including an extra chapter of post-game. The game didn't require any grinding and generally you'd get a full level up or two from just defeating each boss.The Japanese voice acting is amazing. The English dub is somewhat poor such as Careen's country accent. I can understand why the developers did this because in Japanese you can dialects that sound like country accents as well (like a Kansai dialect). The lip-sync in certain scenes can be bad for the English dub as well.I was disappointed there were only 5 party members. Although it's impressive there are so many possible classes for each character and all kinds of abilities and builds, I really would've liked to see more party members. There was one important character who tags along who I felt could've definitely been a full-fledged party member. The dungeons and cities are colorful and fun to explore. Unlike most games everything is marked on your map such as treasure and elemental job points, meaning you don't actually have to search every nook and cranny - but you can turn off the hints and maps if you don't like this. I found this to be amazing because I wanted to get all the treasures to build my characters but didn't necessarily want to explore everything. The dungeons have a lot of soul and it was fascinating to see the ideas the developers came up with - this game had no bland dungeons at all and the gimmicks are easy to navigate through without feeling labyrinthine. The world is connected together and you can eventually unlock a boat and an aircraft. This is one of the few modern JRPG releases that actually has a world map to explore! The developers really did remember the roots of this franchise.The soundtracks are great, though the sound effects can be loud during battle. We had to turn down the sfx in the audio settings so the combat sounds didn't overwhelm us. One big criticism we had is that the game does nag and handhold you a lot. For instance, the cast of party members tell you too frequently to check your equipment and buy items when you have a chance. Often this is integrated in the story cutscenes as well. I felt that they could've just done this in the beginning and endgame portions instead of all the time. Sometimes the gameplay loop would involve going to a story NPC, having a cutscene, then going to another story NPC, back and forth several times. I think that the flow could've been improved because it felt very annoying to keep getting the gameplay interrupted every few minutes. It sounds like a silly complaint, but if the cutscenes were group together and longer instead of going back and forth it would've been more fun to play.The NPCs and sidequests are bad and generic. We tried a few sidequests and they're just generic "kill 10 monsters" and most of the NPCs don't have any plot relevance. You don't need to play any of the other Mana games to understand this game's plot because it's a stand-alone plot with only a few references to the previous games such as the flamingo-like birds and the mana tree. It's neat that the developers included references to Final Fantasy, such as having a moogle status condition and black mages as enemies. If you played the demo of the game on PC in the past it had stuttering issues, where any time the game loaded something new it would freeze up for a few milliseconds to load it. But the full release of the game runs flawlessly with no stuttering issues because it preloads the shaders when you start the game. I didn't like how the endgame recycled assets, such as the levels and the bosses. The endgame has a boss rush where you fight leveled up versions of old story bosses and it can be repetitive. The endgame level curve is bad since it's so compressed. The final region is recycled and you keep fighting bosses to get guaranteed levels, for us it was level 50 to level 66. The ending is extremely satisfying, but it does take some repetitive gameplay to get to that point. There is an extra chapter that is post-game with fully voiced cutscenes that is a side story taking place before the ending that was fun to play through - this post-game recycles bosses again but in this case since it's extra content it's fine. Visions of Mana does have a limited budget and does make a few mistakes, but it's still a very fun JRPG to play and the action-based combat is very addicting. I think its stand-out points include the job system, where you can make so many different kinds of builds. Although the graphics aren't cutting-edge, the visual direction is astounding and this game has some of the best character designs and beautiful landscapes I've ever seen. The story does start off generic and will make you want to roll your eyes at first, but when the plot gets going it really gets going. If you love JRPGs and are willing to overlook a few missteps, I'd strongly recommend checking it out.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit for a couple of additional thoughts after playing another 18 hours since the original review. I still think the game is great and would still recommend it but it is a really scummy move by NetEase to sack the entire studio behind this game and on the day this released no less. The team behind this did a really great job and they deserved much better than being unemployed. Sadly, this means there also likely won't be any further updates which is a shame since there are a few minor issues that keep the game from being as good as it could be. My biggest gripe besides the lackluster side quests is that fast travel in the game is a bit crap. You can fast travel within the zone you are in but still have to manually walk to the next zone even if you fast travel to the exit between zones.  This makes traversing the span of a few zones much more tedious than it should be and traveling across the world a big pain. This is something that could absolutely be fixed through a patch that will likely not happen. I also ran into a weird bug where I got the cut scene for a boss fight and then the boss never spawned. This put me in a soft lock but thankfully I was able to re-load my save and it worked the second time. Really hoping this is something that doesn't repeat, and again, something that would be patched in a perfect world.Despite those negatives though, I am having a blast with the game (the combat is a lot more fun than the demo once you start unlocking class abilities) and I am really enjoying the darker and more thought provoking turn the story has taken versus earlier mana games. Still recommended.------------ Original Review Below------------Highly recommended. This is the first game since the 16 bit era to really nail everything that made Secret of Mana (and to a slightly lesser extent Seiken Densetsu 3) such charming and fun experiences. And seriously, I would put emphasis on the word "charm", the world and characters all ooze charm and it is clear that the team putting this together wanted to make something that stands out. The colorful aesthetics, cell shaded graphics, and the music really has a lot of the charm that made Secret of Mana such a hit and that subsequent follow-ups have lacked to varying degrees (I still like Seiken Densetsu 3 and Legend of Mana but they are just different experiences). The game really is the mana format brought forward without feeling like a simple remake or something tied purely to nostalgia and "remember this", Visions of Mana is it's own game.The combat is solid action RPG fare with a job system, customizeable skills, and even different weapon types depending on your job so it scratches both the character building/customization itch as well as different play styles based on your current weapon. Jobs and weapons all change your appearance as well. The world also has unique named enemies scattered around, some of which are quite challenging, and there are also enemy wave type challenges scattered around the world to take on.The music is a nice mix of tunes that call back to the pipes, steel drums and various wind instruments that made Secret of Mana's soundtrack standout mixed in with some fairly typical RPG fare. Overall, I dig it.I think what I am most intrigued about is the story. It is not entirely the happy go lucky bare minimum of story telling that Secret of Mana and Seiken Densetsu 3 had, there are some really interesting things going on with the plot and character interactions and I like what I have seen so far. I'm looking forward to seeing where the game goes with the story a whole lot more than any previous mana game which is a huge plus for me. With that said though, everything is presented as very positive and upbeat so please don't take that to mean that the story is dark or negative, it is just different and I hate to spoil anything so I'm going to leave it intentionally vague.Performance has also been great. I'm running a Zen 2 processor and a Radeon 6800XT  and I am playing the game at 4k with visuals maxed and have not seen a single hiccup. No bugs or crashes so far and my controller worked just fine without having to mess with anything. Load times are also fairly minimal which is appreciated.If I absolutely have to list a negative, I would say that, so far between this and the demo, the side quests are pretty basic fetch quests and "go kill X of enemy Y" type fare and definitely the least interesting part of the experience.So on balance I'd easily recommend this to anyone with an interest in action RPGs, the mana series or just anyone interested in a fun upbeat RPG with a very cool world that seems to be very well built with a lot of attention to detail and lots of nooks and crannies to explore and unique enemies to fight.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd like to start with the fact that there are two distinct categories of players approaching this: longtime fans, and players who are newly or more recently introduced with the series.For returning fans, there's a lot to appreciate here. Music and art are well realized. While not the most complex narrative entry, it holds true to the themes of the series. Classes and weapons from various entries are included. I would say the development team did a fair job identifying what is important to the series and it's fans and delivered well on creating a new main entry for the series.For those not as familiar with the series, I hope you enjoy it, but honestly, it's not for everyone. The series usually has strong focuses on music, art and story. The story this time is a bit simple, but touches on themes that have been a part of the series for a long time.If you're here for achievement farming, I'd recommend setting that aside until NG+ or accept that you will want a walk-through from the start. There are a lot of sidequests, and they're intended as optional narrative, not achievement obstacles.It is an action RPG and has a legacy to that, which will probably vary from expectations of more recent entries to the genre.Regarding critics, people can make their own choices based on what's available. Millions of people will still not generate any interest on my part in a title featuring a monkey.

_childDocuments_.review: Tons of fun, great combat system, lots of strategic customization. Visions of Mana should be the gold standard when it comes to JRPG shortcuts and QOL systems:You can teleport, change class, and save whenever needed. The map shows all unlockable chests and points of interest, and you can TELEPORT to most PoI's on the map instantly. They give you a glowing light to show you where to go, and many other unlockable QoL perks throughout the story,All of those features above allow you to focus on the story and combat without any slog.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd Like to formulate this in a way that fairly depicts what I played without simply just saying Don't buy this.The Good------------------------------ The Combat was actually pretty solid, Especially on hard I felt like nothing was too difficult once I understood shields and such. I never failed fights unless I was just fully unprepared. Part of the difficulty is resource management with the items which was interesting.- The Exploration was pretty fun, I felt like there were plenty of opportunities to just spend time running around without having to fight constantly- Leveling grind was very fair, I never felt under leveled but i also rarely felt overleveled either.- Custom class builds in endgame and newgame+The Bad-------------------- The character art was just, not really good. characters couldn't look flatter or duller unless careena was on the screen. most of the npcs and even player characters just felt like hollow husks with barely any attitude or emotion in their face.- The voice direction was... not great... I don't feel like its on the voice actors fault except a few scenes but overall the director seemed to have next to no idea what they were casting for. Once again, aside from careena, most characters were never directed in a way by the voice director to give more than flat barebone near emotionless dialogue. Maybe the story limited the voice directors choices, but I think things could have been better here.- The Ai fighters did Not understand the fights. If your going to use AI fighters, they should be coded to dodge mechanics at the bareminimum. 90% of the end game fights i was baby sitting them or burning 10 revives a fight on them (on hard). This is insane, burning all of your resources on near incapable ai that do 15% of the dmg per fight is insane. They did literally nothing but die in the final boss fight anytime there was any mechanic (and trust me there are "a few"). No dodging was coded into them whatsoever apparently.The Ugly----------------------------The story can only be described as a company not knowing who they're trying to target with their game. If they were targeting a Mana series audience they missed, if they were targeting a preteen audience they missed, if they were targeting an adult audience they missed, if they were targeting general jrpg audiences they missed. I Have no clue who they were making this game for. The dialogue was basically for 8 year olds, the combat was near souls like half the time, it didn't follow anything in the spirit of older mana games, no acknowledgement of how dark the sacrificing was, no twists, everything predictable and OFCOURSE, we beat the game with the power of friendship. TLDR- wait for the game to be on hyper sale- mod it or play newgame+ right away with custom classes- get prepared to drag 2 ai through hell by their hair

_childDocuments_.review: Had high hopes for this one after having a ton of fun with the Trials of Mana remake a while ago.Unfortunately this doesn't exactly live up to what it promises.The Good: + Runs fine. No crashes, no notable glitches. Fine.+ Gorgeous, colorful environments. + Occasional genuinely funny bits.+ Combat is fun (with caveats mentioned below).The Bad:- The writing ranges from "eh" to "what the hell were they thinking?". From basic premise to sidequest dialogue it's just going from one cringey moment to the next. - Characters are more flat than they used to be in the 2d era.- The one and only interesting NPC gets killed off halfway through the game.- Seriously, I can't emphasize enough how bad the writing is.- Many maps are way too big with way too little going on inside them. This is not a game that needed to be open-world(-ish). Far too often you just run or ride through beautiful landscapes with nothing to do for ages between groups of monsters that die in under 5 seconds. Just ditching the open-world elements would have helped this game a lot.- The game doesn't really show what it can do in terms of dungeons until about 2/3 of the way in. Most of what you do before that is one or two rooms and a boss fight.The Ugly:# The music...exists. That's about all you can say for it. It plays, it's inoffensive. It's also a big disappointment considering what this series has had before.# The level curve is broken. If you do any exploring of the needlessly big maps at all, you'll quickly outlevel all enemies so massively that even at maximum difficulty you'll stomp bosses without ever noticing their mechanics. Only at the very end does some kind of challenge return. I normally don't like level-scaling enemies in games, but this one could have benefited from it.# The game just throws names from real-world history and myth at things without any regards to what they actually represent. Many abilities and weapons have utterly nonsensical names as a result. Would have been better to just give them completely made-up ones.# Interface could use some work. Inventory sorting options are extremely basic. Switching out moves takes way too many steps. # Character designs are...eh. Cute, yes. But also incoherent.Overall verdict:It's okay at the best of times, deeply disappointing at the worst. Save your money, play the absolutely excellent Trials of Mana remake instead.

_childDocuments_.review: Visions of Mana! The long awaited next entry in the oft forgotten Mana series. As much as I love Final Fantasy and many other JRPGs, I can't forget the colorful high fantasy of the Mana games. Visions of Mana is like if you took a cozy blanket and turned it into a game.There's a few things that are wrong, and it's ONCE AGAIN with the mixed english voiceacting and writing. You're either going to get sick of it fast, or get used to it. I got used to it in Trials of Mana, so of course I did for this game. It's not entirely bad, some of the voiceactors give it their all, and there is some heart to the story. The plot is pretty standard, but bursting at the seams with charm, and I definitely like the themes it tackles. There are a few surprises in the story that almost made me cry, so be prepared!There's an extensive class system that has dizzying depth. You can learn abilities that can be used with any class, along different "elemental plots". But there are some abilities, like class abilities, that can only be used when a character becomes a class associated with an element, by equipping an "elemental vessel". The sheer number of classes is absurd, and I love it! No character shares the same class, and it's quite unusual to see this sort of variety, but it exceeds Trials of Mana's class system in every way. Unique and beautifully designed outfits for every class, and at least 2 to 3 kinds of unique weapons that each character can use depending on class. You can also get more abilities by equipping "ability seeds", They're spells, abilities, or passive bonuses. When you remove an ability seed, the ability is removed.The locales are pretty huge, probably the largest in any Mana game to date. Well, besides Dawn of Mana. The places you go to are breathtaking in Visions of Mana, and I want to explore them as much as possible. You'll sometimes run into enemies that are too powerful to defeat, encouraging you to come back later, and they're often in ruins. Elite enemies keep you on your toes and up the challenge. "Elemental aeries" provide a timed combat challenge that will test your skills. There's tons of items and collectibles just laying around, even in towns. It just activates some kind of kleptomaniac gremlin within! I did hear that these areas "lack personality". Sometimes, there's plenty of fantastical landmarks and regional uniqueness, such as the windswept pine trees of the wind elemental region, to the gloomy fog and bizarre architecture of the dark elemental region. Your mileage may vary, but I find many of the towns gorgeous beyond belief and bursting with detail. The best looking and biggest Mana game to date! It's only hurt by one thing. You'll eventually find incomplete terrain and holes in terrain geometry, but it's rare and in out-of-the-way locations. I'm just surprised they even put in this much effort!Side quests aren't good in this game and they're not interesting, involving collecting a certain amount of items, killing a certain amount of monsters, or finding an item/location/person. However, even if the side content is throwaway, they can be done QUICKLY making them an okay excuse to explore the breathtaking locations for awhile longer before leaving.The combat isn't remotely sluggish. It was a concern I had during the demo. But it appears they have enhanced it, and attacks combo together more fluidly, and even into spells. The battles aren't as tight as the combat in Trials of Mana, but there is a lot of class and ability expression in Visions of Mana that keeps the action exciting. The bossfights are fantastic and present us with the same kind of MMORPG-style mechanics I enjoyed so much from Trials of Mana.Once you beat the game, new game plus is unlocked and there's an entirely NEW endgame chapter unlocked with powerful gear to get, just the cherry on top of a pretty cozy JRPG!Also, if you love dragons as much as I do, Visions of Mana will appeal to you with the dragonfolk, Ramcoh, and also Flammie. There's more than one sacred beast dragon?! Well, now I've seen everything and I love it! Ramcoh is a sweety after my own heart!Visions of Mana is a fantastic return of a neglected JRPG series. People tend to focus a lot more on what else Square creates, such as Final Fantasy or Kingdom Hearts. So it's great to see this B series return in such a beautiful form! Adventure awaits!

_childDocuments_.review: The plot is good, but the writing is terrible. This becomes apparent as the story progresses, despite the well-put-together opening. The characters, with the exception of a few tragic scenes, feel more like commentators of the story as opposed to those that are effected by the arduous endeavors presented in the plot.  To make matters worse, Careena is the most insufferable character that I've ever had to endure in gaming; I mean everything from that over-compensated, extreme southern accent to the stupid, vain, useless soliloquy that poured from her ever-flapping gob. Believe me, if I could have killed her to close that trap, I would have. As far as combat goes, it's okay but felt limited in ways. For one, the move sets were plagued with redundant copy-and-paste projectile maneuvers and lack-luster, elemental power ups. It was definitely inferior to both Trials of Mana and even Secret of Mana for that matter. I mean, Secret of Mana didn't limit a character to 3 weapons that are involuntarily fixed to each of the eight classes. For instance, concerning the main protagonist Val, the only way to play with the smaller sword was to choose either Gnome's or Dryad's class. Unfortunately, those aren't available til the last half of the game.Also, there is a certain degree of --- LEVEL SCALING --- that one becomes increasingly aware of as they progress the main story. For me, that is a deal-breaker.  When monsters level-up with the characters, it totally defeats the purpose of leveling in the first place. I mean, just remove the levels and add earned skill-points. It's, literally, the same thing.With this being said, for me, this is the worst of the Mana series. It had potential, but quickly wore out its welcome with its limited factors and its vain grindyness.

_childDocuments_.review: It's good. Feels like "My First RPG" gaming. Everything works, looks nice, mechanically, it's great! TLDR-At some point I noticed this could have been a 10/10 game but somebody dropped the ball somewhere.8/10 for kids and 6/10 for RPG enthusiasts.There is however something missing. A LOT of things missing actually. Everything you wanted from classic jrpg greatness is here and has been set up for and the puzzle has been laid out but someone forgot to actually snap the pieces together. I could make an extensive list of things that aren't present and don't technically NEED to exist but feel they should. Examples off the top of my head include, not being able to run around in random houses (whether i find loot or not)Dialogue with random villagers and travelers (walking up and having a short convo with people cuz i can) The 2 story inn that we always rest at and progress stories. Where else am I going to afk my game and fall asleep? Where else am I going to look for the same 6 items that I never need? I don't know about other people but I NEED my arguably useless 2 story Inn! (the pacing and flow of events felt especially "off" to me and i think this is a part of why)Exploring the map for loot and hidden stuff (they just show you the chests on map from the start). I wont get into it all but there's a thousand things you realize while playing that just should have been easy to expand on or fix, things that have been a staple in the industry for years. Oh and bosses? Challenge puzzles? All those little things that are missing are what make the journey a memorable experience and without them the pacing and character development can feel wrong when certain events happen.The maps and zones feel like they could and should be double the size.More side quests, possibly ones that require brain power idk.-STORY SPOILERS-As far as the story goes, I'm personally fine with a cookie-cutter "bring down the system, fight god, save girl". The end goal never mattered to us as much as the journey for a game like this. That being said this game was so easy to read that it was almost boring. Chapter one is just Tales of Symphonia. Like, sure they used different words but....yea, and i know i'm older and i have played a great many games but this really felt like there was no effort or exposition put in to make the story of this world seem believable. I don't need to be tricked into believing that the story is what it is. I do need to believe that the characters believe what they are saying is real and that their world/mission is real and I didn't get that feeling here. This was especially true with a certain event in an earlier chapter where a main character gets deleted. I found myself comparing it to Laphicet (who id known for a much shorter period of time) and it just wasn't on the same level. I was mad when that happened but with Visions of Mana of remember saying out loud "Well that was just silly, you'd have to be an actual child to get into this situation.."I don't think the writing was particularly bad either but i would say that there needed to be twice as much written and it felt that would actually be possible without "filler".Im not a content creator so im not going to ramble but if the devs do see this i want you to know that you all definitely have the talent to make something truly epic and to please not be discouraged by the company situation after launch. we love to hate you but we also love you and if you continue to make good games we will continue to buy them <3

_childDocuments_.review: Visions of Mana is a beautiful Margherita pizza, it's a classic that JRPG fans will love because it stays true to the Mana series and avoids unnecesary innovations like pineapple. Features:- Open zones set up like a platforming game.- 5 playable characters with 8 unique classes each and 40 unique costumes in total.- Surprisingly dark story with twists to keep you guessing.- NG+, post game content and unlockable extreme difficulty at launch, no need to wait for the "anniversary update"- Fantastic graphics and it runs great, it has a shader compilation step to avoid common UE4 issues.Flaws:- Lazzy port, not many options and some technical issues I haven't experienced but some people reported them in the forums. - Slow start, the combat is really good but it takes a long time to get more classes than the ones from the demo.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing a bunch of "serious" game, I needed a light-hearted one. Visions of mana is exactly that, a colorfull and easy JRPG you can play while relaxing after a rough day at work. The world is beautifull, the battles are fun, the class system is great and the game is long enough, though it feel extended by a ridiculous amount of sidequest.The game is far from perfect, it actually seems designed for a very young public. Characters behaviours are childish, story is what you can expect from a game of the mana series, everything is marked on the map (chest, quest, point of interest,... everything) and it's probably one of the easiest game I've ever played in my life, even in hard mode (and I'm no expert, Horizon in normal mode was challenging to me). But I'm having fun. 40 hours playing and it still has that cozy feeling. But do not buy it expecting challenge or a great story, it has neither.

_childDocuments_.review: 17 hours in and just obtained the last party member, been doing all available side content, back tracking for side quests, EVERYTHING. And I am loving all of it. _childDocuments_.review: This is a good game, it's fun, looks nice and runs well. The characters are interesting and not annoying. Combat can be a bit clunky but the systems are good. Although I recommend this game I want to take a moment here to point out some odd issues I have with the translation.I've already noticed a few minor changes that make no sense:1. An item is originally called the "Luna sphere" using English loan words in the JP script. For some reason this is translated as "Luna globe" which just sounds awkward to me. Why translate it? The original was in English already.2. A character was named "Francois" but her name was translated to "Francine". I can kind of understand the motivation here since Francois is typically a male name so they changed it to fit her gender I guess, but why not just leave it? It's weird hearing Francois but reading Francine in the subtitles.3. I saved the biggest issue I've noticed (so far) for last. Val is portrayed in JP as a caring, respectful, and capable young man. You could also interpret him as slightly naive due to his age and optimistic outlook, but he's not an idiot or a jerk. For some reason the EN subs occasionally rewrite him as rude, incompetent, or stupid. It's not consistent enough to make me think it was entirely intentional, but it does change the way his personality comes across. He's meant to be a good, reliable friend but every once in a while the EN translation has him act like an incompetent fool. I just don't get it. Did the translator genuinely think they improved his character somehow?Again, I think this game is overall quite good and I do recommend it, I just want to bring some attention to the poor translation which is sadly typical of JP games. It sucks that if you don't understand Japanese then you get a noticeably different impression of one of the main characters. I'm sure there are other things I didn't pick up on too, since my Japanese is pretty basic. It would be nice if translators would put more effort into preserving the original intention of the writers, since they themselves aren't writers it tends to be a downgrade any time they deviate from the original meaning.

_childDocuments_.review: Visions of Mana? A Nostalgic Journey with Modern Flaws! (ฅ'ω'ฅ)"A charming return to the classic Mana series with a vibrant world and engaging combat, though marred by a few design missteps."Visions of Mana is the latest action-RPG entry in the beloved Mana series, taking players on an adventure with Val and his childhood friend Hinna as they journey towards the sacred Mana Tree. This game brings a mix of nostalgia and innovation, offering a semi-open world full of elemental spirits, strategic combat, and a narrative that delves into themes of fate and sacrifice. Fans of the series will find familiar callbacks, while newcomers can enjoy a standalone story that’s accessible yet emotionally impactful.Visions of Mana excels in creating a world that feels alive with the spirit of the classic JRPGs. The semi-open world is vast and vibrant, filled with lush environments that invite exploration. However, while the world is visually stunning, the exploration itself can feel somewhat repetitive. The game’s decision to embrace a more open-world design, reminiscent of Ubisoft’s "checklist" style, might disappoint those who prefer the focused progression of previous titles like Trials of Mana. The abundance of collectibles and fast travel points sometimes detracts from the sense of discovery, making exploration feel more like a chore than an adventure.Combat is where Visions of Mana truly shines. The game offers a dynamic battle system that allows players to harness the power of the Elementals through different classes and characters. Each character brings a unique playstyle, and experimenting with various combinations adds depth to the gameplay. The battles are swift and strategic, offering a satisfying mix of action and tactics that keep encounters engaging throughout the game. However, some players might find the difficulty lacking, even on harder settings, which can reduce the challenge for seasoned RPG fans.The narrative in Visions of Mana strikes a balance between simplicity and emotional depth. While the story follows a somewhat predictable path, with familiar themes of destiny and sacrifice, it’s the characters that bring the narrative to life. Val and his companions are well-developed, with their personalities and backstories gradually revealed through the journey. Yet, some may feel that the character development is rushed, particularly when it comes to resolving personal struggles. This can leave certain arcs feeling undercooked, especially when compared to the more nuanced character interactions seen in previous Mana titles.Visions of Mana is a game that walks the fine line between paying homage to its predecessors and trying to innovate within the action-RPG genre. While it succeeds in delivering a vibrant world and engaging combat, its open-world design choices and uneven pacing may not appeal to everyone. Nonetheless, for fans of the Mana series and those looking for a JRPG with a blend of nostalgia and modern gameplay, Visions of Mana offers a memorable, if imperfect, adventure.If you enjoyed Visions of Mana, consider exploring other action JRPGs like the Ys series or Ni No Kuni II, which share similar gameplay elements and aesthetic appeal. And if you’re a fan of classic JRPGs, be sure to follow our  for more reviews and updates on the latest in the genre!ヽ(´• ω •`)ノ

_childDocuments_.review: So. Another year, a new Mana game, I see. First of all, before I give this review, this is gonna be an honest as a fan of the series since 2000. This by any means a bad game. It's rough on the edges, but no means a bad game. What I love about this game, is the battle system and music. The music can go heavy metal to charming that everyone loved the series. I mean, heck, I would rather play this game over Dawn Of Mana and  Sword Of Mana any day. The less we talk about those  games, the better. I loved Val and Hinna's relationship. Even though I've seen it many JRPG do that, it wasn't shoehorned or forced. Just right. VM however, feels.... cheap. The graphics are amazing and all, but for some odd reasons, feels like I'm not playing a big budget game. For an example; the game can have tons of stuttering midway when I'm walking or during battles. That even the game's FPS gone and reached peak 1FPS for about 10 seconds. Some of the boss fights I didn't see cause the game kept freezing on me. I have a 3060 RTX and 16GB of ram. Surely this game can handle it. The side quests, God. If you love games that tells you "Bring me this, kill that monsters that." Then this game is for you! I don't mind doing that, but at least give me EXP. Oh? You didn't know? The game has this weird way of not giving you too many EXP unless you're fighting a boss. So if you want to level up, better find some good monsters with the red orbs, and use an item to get 15 or 20% EXP. And you might get 10K EXP. Which by the way, that's not much when you're level around 60 to 70. The game seems to love 30FPS during cutscenes. Which I despise. You *can* make the run at 60 if you press F11. Which is...odd. Final thoughts:Pros: Good Mana game. Probably one of the best in the last 15 years. Pros: Fun characters and pretty diverse.Pros: Great music can make you hype, or calm you down. (Kinda wish Yoko did it, though.) Pros: Class systems are back, can be OP. :P Pros: A good edition to the series. Cons: Feels cheap and rushed. Cons: Lack of EXP. Cons: Can overstay it's welcome time to time. (I hate when JRPG do that. >:( )Cons: Side quests = Blah! Overall, I liked the game, but far from everyone's hype around it. Which hurts my childhood fandom. I would give this game a 6/10.. Not good or bad. Just....it's okay. Wait for a sale around 29.99 or 19.99. Trust me, you'll thank me later.

_childDocuments_.review: Visions of Mana is a faithful entry into the Mana series. The game features beautiful art direction that has almost a painted or watercolor feeling. Perhaps a small nitpick would be about the texture quality on some environmental objects and weapons, but this game was never meant to be a graphical showcase in that regard. Despite that, it has had a number of vistas and set pieces that are simply majestic. Seeing the Mana Tree in the intro alone was like seeing the Secret of Mana Cover Art come to life in Real-time 3D. Truly amazing. The music is quite good as well, providing fans of the classic OSTs with some revised tracks, some songs that have similar motifs to old-school tracks, and plenty of new music that feels right at home within the series. Some new tracks don't really carry the feeling that I've grown accustom to in the series, but they are good in their own right.The gameplay has been quite fun. As you acquire new elemental powers, the system really starts to shine. It also boasts a fairly deep system to control your secondary character. Besides allowing you to switch to characters on the fly, you can also assign specific AI modifiers to finely tune how the party acts (similarly to something like Final Fantasy XII).The Story is serviceable enough. Not being too in depth, but providing enough twists and emotional moments to remain engaging throughout. This is a wonderful entry into a beloved franchise, that I think it will appeal to younger and older audiences alike.
_childDocuments_.name: Visions of Mana

_childDocuments_.review: It is a budget jrpg, so don't expect something as grand as Final Fantasy XVI or as polished as Metaphor ReFantazio.But, for what it is, it is still a gorgeous game (seriosuly, it looks like a watercolour painting) with an alright combat system (which does benefict greatly from the class and elemetal systems) and a entretaining albeit superficial story.It is basically a PS2/PS3 action JRPG taken to our era with (sort of) Modern graphics and a few QoL elements.If you liked games like Kingdom Hearts 2, Ni No Kuni, or Nier (the original), you will probably like Visions of Mana.If you're not fully convinced, wait for it to go on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Sadly I beat the game....             Honestly, this is the WORST Mana game by FAR. The plot was concerning, like they tried to take a page from the Tales series but done poorly, They want you to care for one of the main characters family/village but failed HARD. The whole village was insufferable and I didn't care if they all lived or died with how they acted. A lot of NPC's are copy/pasted throughout the game, which would be fine if they were background characters with no name, but some of those models are named here and there. Two of the are even voiced, but their models are still just used over and over again.           The "storytelling" was interesting in a bad way. An enemy would do something like summon a monster, the Main would defeat said monster, the summoner would run away by going THROUGH the main characters group and they'd be like"oh no, they got away. How are we going to stop them?" like WHAT!!? This also happened MULTIPLE TIMES.           Traversing towns is a slog. For whatever reason as soon as you enter a town/village or a city you can no longer double jump or dash/ air dash. _childDocuments_.review: Usually i'm not a big fan of pro / con list reviews, but Visions of Mana invites this structure very well.Pro:-This game is a visual treat. While not technically impressive, it makes up for it in spades artistically. It captures the Mana series' style to a T. Everything is crooked, crowded, colorful and whimsical. The art direction overall is phenomenal. -The gameplay itself is really fun. Exploration feels great and rewarding. The combat system is great. Not overly complex but with enough depth and customizability to cater the experience towards your playstyle. It also rarely if ever overstays its welcome. Encounters rarely take longer than a minute, rewarding more EXP for shorter clear times. On top of that, encounter can usually be avoided entirely simply by not engaging with them at all. They never feel as if they bog down the experience.Con:-The soundtrack, usually one of the highlights of this series, is incredibly forgetable this time. While no piece is bad, quite the opposite in fact, few of them manage to stick out. Most of them are very quiet, almost ambient background music instead of the series staple heroic, driving tunes. Not the end of the world, but disappointing nontheless.-Sidequest design can be a bit monotonous. There are countless "Go to X and kill 6 Y" quests that don't really add anything to the experience and simply pad out gametime.-Partner AI that lacks any kind of survival instincts. While mostly servicable and thanks to functions to babysit them a little, later regions and bosses show their blatant weakness. Their AI simply isn't good enough to deal with platforming challenges or skill based boss atacks that require more than walking to get out of the way.-Its story is, by a wide margin, Visions of Mana's biggest blunder. It's quite possible the worst written story in its genre. Each and every character, not only the playable ones, operate on room temperature IQ because that's the only way this story even exists. A moral conundrum so hopelessly contrived that the supposed villains turn out to be entirely right in their assumptions and motivations, while everyone else sticks to the script without ever showing agency or a unique thought.Visions of Mana's gameplay and presentation are genuinely so good that they can keep you engaged even if the story needs to be endured rather than enjoyed. If you're only here for the story, this isn't the game for you.If you want a fantastic gameplay experience and can ignore a bad tale? Treat yourself! Ultimately, Visions of Mana is hard not to recommend. The overall package is solid, the gameplay experience is fantastic. But i wish is three writers were awake during their work hours.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best RPG's of 2024.Game-play = 9/10A surprisingly deep and rewarding combat system with up to 40 playable classes (not including non-vesseled).Plenty of ways to customise your group to your own play-style and a addictive monster deleting cycle, adding monster abilities to your own characters skill-set with the use of core-stones. Story = 8.5/10Personally enjoyed the twists and turns in the story, with much of the English voice acting being a lot better than i expected. Replayability = 8/10Plenty of post credits game storyline too! Including an additional difficulty level and New Game Plus beyond that!Music = 10/10I mean, it's a Square Enix game. The music is fantastic.Summary : Probably the best RPG of 2024. It scratches the nostalgic itches you have been looking for if you loved the older games in the series, yet rewards new players alike with challenge, fantastic visuals and a deep experience in customising how battle plays out depending on how far you delve into it, yet not hurting you if you elect to not dabble too much.An engaging series of open world activities with actual rewards that are useful and fun to collect, plenty of side quests and memorable locations, dungeons and boss fights.Feels like we are back in the 90's and it feels good :)Amazing Game. We need more like this!
_childDocuments_.name: Visions of Mana

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:-Gorgeous colorful and lively graphic that tells you "this is a Mana game"-Good atmospheric music-Exploration-focused gameplay with relevant rewards-Fun class change on-the-fly system-Combat is similar to Trials of Mana, but faster-Good story with proper character growthCons:-Cutscenes feel stiff-Music is good and mood-fitting, but are not as eargasm like ones in Secret or Trials of Mana-Terrible teleport system that goes through various loading screens.-Terrible side-quest system that requires you backtrack every time a major event happens and some event require to load out and load in the map.-Combat difficulty is not very well-balanced toward the end-New Game+ feels lacking due to level carry-over, making a majority of the game feel irrelevant difficulty wise even at the hardest difficulty-Price tag is hefty.Verdict: 4.5/5Comment: A love-letter to Mana fans and a good modern entry to the series along with Trials of Mana. Whether you are long-time fans of the series or just someone who is attracted by the game's colorful breath-taking art direction, the game would be able to provide dozens of hours of immersion into the world of Mana.What comes with Ouka Studio is a shame, but you should not let that deters you from this wonderful game. After all, Square-Enix has no power regarding the sunset of Ouka Studio which is under NetEase. Still, considering patching still happens (v1.03 is updated one day before this review), I believe the game is not abandoned or anything, so Visions of Mana deserves a chance, whether at full prices or discounts.
