_childDocuments_.review: Review of Sonic X Shadow GenerationsI will be name-dropping a large number of Sonic games for comparison in assessing this game. This is supposed to be a nostalgia trip of Shadow the Hedgehog’s best levels and moments in the Sonic franchise, as well as the inclusion of the Sonic Generations title from 2011. Sonic Mania, a title from 2017, introduced the Drop Dash and somehow managed to be a brand-new Sonic game that looked and felt hardly any better than the original trilogy. Need I remind you, games like Sonic Advance came out in 2001, and its entire trilogy is objectively better in every sense of the word. The animations and unique playstyles introduced in that game are absolutely unfathomable and amazing, and it is crazy that they have not touched upon it ever since.In my honest opinion, Sonic Superstars comes much closer to achieving the quality I should expect from a Sonic game than the majority of modern Sonic games. Sonic Superstars is the most fun I have had in a Sonic game since Sonic Generations from 2011. Sonic Frontiers from 2022, (not to be confused with Sonic Forces from 2017), was a significant step up in the 3D Sonic genre. Its open-world segments overstay their welcome, and the bosses were sadly lacking aside from only a few. Sonic Forces, as you know, was incredibly short and atrocious in a vast majority of ways.Keeping these things in mind, we can now move on to Sonic X Shadow Generations. I will be naming many Shadow the Hedgehog moments throughout the Sonic franchise to keep consistency and flow in this heartfelt review. To be honest, the Drop Dash does a lot for the Sonic Generations classic mode but actually causes a lot of fluidity issues in the 3D Sonic mode, making it an even plus and minus scenario. I find that Sonic Generations does what Shadow Generations does not. Captivating the entirety of Shadow the Hedgehog’s history in a single game would have been one of Sonic the Hedgehog’s greatest achievements in their entire history, and sadly they fall incredibly short, only achieving a quarter of what I expected from them. An insane amount of Shadow levels from past games are absent here, and even some of the levels in Shadow Generations are technically Sonic levels. This broke my heart to see because at first, it was amazing, but then upon completion, I saw that it was taking up a third of the levels and some of my favorite Shadow the Hedgehog levels that I considered to be on legendary status are completely absent here. (ex. White Jungle isn't here. SAD.)Shadow's 3D hub world is significantly better than Sonic's 2D hub world, though it is a mess and confusing, and I don’t enjoy it. Similar to Mario 3D World Switch's added DLC mode, except it might be worse than that. I could sit and compare Sonic games to Mario games for the rest of my life, and you would be amazed to see that I find a lot of Mario games to be quite terrible. But at times, Mario will achieve gold star titles, and sometimes I wish Sonic could do that a lot more often. Sadly, the Sonic Generations portion, aside from some quality-of-life features and mild new mechanics, does not feel as good as it once did. Instead, it feels like it’s trying to push itself to be faster than it was originally intended to be, or possibly a frame rate issue, it is unbeknownst to me and it really made me sad, wishing that I should have probably bought Sonic Generations backwards compatible on the Xbox Series X or S. It is nearly identical and does not appear to have any resolution increases whatsoever. A sad occasional chug can be found at peak speed moments throughout both Sonic and Shadow Generations. I would say that not only do they only have a quarter of the Shadow levels that I was expecting, but 50% of them are not ones I asked for and references to bizarre levels, etc. I could go on for quite some time. However, the levels they do have that I like, I love very much and have already played through at least five times each.Now, I would like to move on to something that is going to be hard to describe easily. Shadow's new abilities are rather cringe and unnecessary and could have easily been replaced with Hyper Shadow or Super Shadow. The weird goop one, not the manta ray, but the goop one completely negates the ideal structure of going fast to the point that I would compare it to the werehog segments in Sonic Unleashed. However, unlike Sonic Unleashed, where it was specific levels that played differently to add what is the only alternative to a Sonic playstyle that there has ever been here, the snake goop thing is overabundant, hyperbolic, and is the number one thing that you are guaranteed to screw up. It adds nothing but pain and suffering. I could probably go on forever about all the picks and gripes I have that are slowly eating away at my soul. The more I think about my disappointment and how I start to realize that my list of excitements is rather very small and self-contained. Radical Highway makes its return as the final level just before the boss and is absolutely bastardized down to the point that I cannot even fathom what was going through their minds. It is objectively broken and obscene.Which brings me to the last huge complaint, the Doom Wing. Yes, you see that Super Shadow ability to fly that everyone loves has been replaced with goopy wings that are copy-pasted onto Shadow's back and obnoxiously jammed into all the levels as though you unlocked Super Shadow at the end, but he’s hideous and dysfunctional. The most adds is a goofy ah mode that just breaks the level so you can literally fly over it and I guess that’s cool or something. I don’t know. Upon beating all of these levels and collecting the vast majority of collectibles, I have found that this is all the content that the game has to offer and it only totaled the tour absurd 11 hours at most and this was me really playing and enjoying it like eating a cheeseburger slowly. I’m pretty pissed off and I feel like I deserved something four times better. It reminds me of the DLC from Sonic Forces. That was really cool with Shadow, except here, they aren’t even original levels. I am severely disappointed, and surprisingly, this might be my least revisited Sonic game for the next decade to come.

_childDocuments_.review: If you were worried about this being a Sonic Colors Ultimate situation, where it attempts to remaster a good game but completely loses the plot (in more than just the story of that game), leave those worries at the door. This is a straight upgrade from the (now kind of delisted) Sonic Generations from 2011.Sonic's campaign is still just as beautiful as the 2011 release to look at, while stuff like the cutscenes are sharper to look at and some have gone under some re-animation to fit the new script of the game, which I will go into a bit later. Not all of them are winners, as you can tell they were animated around the original script, so you would every now and then see some character gestures not line up with the tone the lines they are speaking are saying, kind of taking you out of the actual story.The actual gameplay of this game is also a step up, at least from the initial PC release. The original felt like it was held back and could not use the resources your PC had, especially if you have had a gaming PC of the past 5 years, where no matter what you did, the game would always find a way to stutter or suffer from pop-in. Largely, the latter of the two would be isolated from the actual gameplay, and only affect background details or cutscenes. It was never like Frontiers where it would pop-in critical bits of the environment that you would need to react to to play efficiently. Framerate problems were constant though. Especially in Chemical Plant. Thankfully, these issues have been ironed out, and it is a smooth 60 fps for Sonics campaign with no compromises.While I am not too deep into Shadow's campaign, I am really pleased with it so far. Levels are longer than Sonics, averaging about 5 minutes rather than Sonics 2-3, but they never overstay their welcome, and the Chaos and Doom Powers are fun to use, and while they take some getting used to, you can tell Shadows levels were really built to use both of these toolkits. Compared to something like Forces where stuff like the Wispons were a complete afterthought, where the one they gave you is practically the best one, and you have very little reason to switch off. Here, you are met with knowledge checks and need good reactions to know what Chaos or Doom Power to use, all while it can feel slightly automated at times, those moments are very few, at least so far. If I had to describe what it is in the simplest way possible, imagine a mix of Generations and Frontiers. Generations because you get two acts you need to complete and needing to get Boss Keys from Challenge Acts, but the hub is an Open-Zone with collectibles and enemies to fight. (There is no combat system in this game though, so take that how you will.)I mentioned a rewrite of Sonic's campaign, as I believe it is for the better. The original was rather self-indulging in the "mystery" of these locations and what they actually are, but the problem was it made Sonic and Tails look not-smart because they should know what these are. Here, the mystery shifted from what they are to why they are grayed out in a white void, which I think is a much better route to take. It raises a question that anyone would reasonably ask themselves if they see their home, or otherwise comfortable and familiar location, suddenly look all drained. I get that this is a touchy subject with rewriting stories of the past, but given how the story was a common criticism of the original Generations, I think this is a net positive for the end user. And while I cannot speak too much on Shadows story itself, I do appreciate how it is recognizing more about his history than just Maria, as that is a common trope in his character and stories that center him. Even making characters like Black Doom, one of his original creators, be the antagonist for him and his runtime. I also like how they showed him "moved on" from Maria. Another trope that is easy to abuse for his character.I have been pretty positive about this game, but that is not to say I think it is perfect. That being said however, my complaints are either exclusive to people like me, or just nitpicks out right, as I do not represent the whole playerbase. One issue I have with the game is how it ties your graphic settings to your save file. This means that if you play on a proper gaming PC, then decide to pick this game back up later on your Steam Deck, the game won't configure the graphics to fit the Steam Deck, insisting that it is just your initial PC like you never left. This isn't a huge deal breaker for the Sonic campaign, because the Steam Deck is well overprepared to run this game at 60 fps, even at max settings, just to be sure to reset your resolution when you go back to your proper 1080p/1440p/4k PC. The problem lies with the Shadow campaign, as that part is way more intense to run on the Deck. Meaning that on each switch off, you have to go out of your way to fix it for your current PC. Yes, if you have just one PC this is not an issue, but it is an inconvenience for people like me who use both. If I want one thing addressed in the future, it is this. I am also ecstatic to report that you can freely swap displays in this game without running into the dreaded "Invalid Graphic Config" error. This was an extra big deal on Steam Deck if you had a dock, as you had to delete the initial Graphic Config file, run the tool again, adjust your settings, and then you can finally play the game. But since this game does not have a dedicated launcher, and can handle swapping displays, this is an error that can stay in the past, and I couldn't be happier.I haven't even gotten to stuff that is an objective upgrade to the original release like implementing proper save files for multiple runs or what the Chao do. I fully believe that SEGA/Sonic Team really did want to treat this game like it deserves the love and attention that it has garnered over the years, bringing it to new hardware while fixing what was broken in the initial release. This is how you do a remaster, people. Honestly the only reason I can think of to even look at the original is if you really want to mess with mods, but even then I would give this game 3-4 years before it catches up to the original's modding potential anyway.If it wasn't clear enough, if you haven't played the original Generations, this will do you wonders, while earning some more bang for your buck like offering hefty QoL fixes and even a whole new campaign that did not even exist. And even if you have played the original (like I have), the Shadow campaign is already earning so much of its keep to justify the price tag, at least as far as I am in now.

_childDocuments_.review: Without a shadow of a doubt, this is one of (if not) the best 3D Sonic game in recent years. Sonic Generations itself is practically untouched in terms of gameplay, the only additions include the extra hidden Chao and Drop Dash ability added to both Sonic's movesets which are incredibly welcome additions. The rewritten story, while ultimately a little meaningless, gives the game more references and tidbits for long time fans to sink their teeth into. And the game felt great with 60 fps and 4k resolution, it gives you so much more time to react accordingly to the level's challenges. Complaints about this remaster is, again, the rewrite felt a little superfluous to me. The story, while it had no stakes or anything like that, was completely inoffensive and the same can be said about this rewrite. Some of the actors playing these characters are really starting to show their age from the jump from 2011 to 2024. And I'm not sure what caused this, but there were a handful of times where I came across minor hiccups when it came to collision, camera movement, and other things that weren't present in the original release. Nothing game-breaking, just a small nitpick as someone who's spent way too long playing this game over the years. Regardless, it's always nice to come back to this masterclass of a game.But the real highlight of this game is Shadow's campaign bar none. The movement feels like a great blend of the loose controls of Frontiers while maintaining that breakneck speed you've come to love in Generations and other Boost titles. The level design is incredibly well thought out, offering those who'll go out of their way to explore and take different paths rewards. Whether it be through the Collection Keys, ways to shave time off of speedruns, or anything else. The graphics of the levels themselves look amazing, it's so great to see levels like Rail Canyon and Kingdom Valley in such beautiful high definition. The story in Shadow's campaign is one of the best in Sonic history, offering flashy and downright awesome moments with strong emotions to boot. And you already know it's a Sonic game, so the music is going to be amazing no matter what, and this game is no exception. My only complaints with this portion of the game is the map the tedium of collecting the gears for Orbot and Cubot. The map only offers where the level and challenge gates are, boss gates, and collection box locations which sounds useful, but for some odd reason, the boxes that weren't collected didn't always appear right away. Some only showed up after being collected, which one hand incentivizes learning the map's nooks and crannies, but it's also just unintuitive since you can't mark locations like in Frontiers' map. And those machine parts were such a CHORE to deal with. They don't have an icon on the map so you can't track them down like the boxes, and some of them are either in the most obvious spot in the world or somewhere you would NEVER think to look. But regardless, finding everything and eventually 100% completing this game was an amazing experience through and through. Sonic Generations by itself was already an amazing experience and now with Shadow Generations to go along with it makes this one of my all time favorite Sonic games ever. I'll surely be coming back to this to speedrun all the levels to get a new personal best, look at the hours of concept artwork in both game's galleries, mess with mods, and so much more.If you're either a hardcore or new Sonic fan, I still highly recommend this game. It is the best offering the series has to offer to date. Bow your heads low, all hail Shadow.

_childDocuments_.review: I, like many people, was dubious at the thought of a remaster of Sonic Generations. My trust in Sega regarding this was also particularly low due to the disappointment that was  a few years back - shoddy remakes with technical issues not present in the original games, all the while delisting said original games from digital storefronts forever, alongside developer mistreatment.With Sonic X Shadow Generations, Sega seems to have learned their lesson, at least somewhat. First of all, the original Sonic Generations from 2011  While not the best solution to this, this is still a better compromise than what they did with Sonic 1, 2, CD, as well as 3 & Knuckles.Second - there is actually something new here for everyone. Sonic Generations, surprisingly enough, received new content in the form of re-animated cutscenes or brand new dubs to fit the series' continuity better. This is the first time I've seen them actually rewrite the story of an older game to make it make more sense within the confines of the series' universe canon. The one thing I do not like about the remaster of Sonic Generations here is the nerf to Classic Sonic's movement. The overpowered spindash from the old version of the game is completely gone, making Classic Sonic feel insanely sluggish to control due to years of muscle memory from the older version. Aside from that, if you wanna know what I think of Sonic Generations itself, Now, for Shadow Generations...okay, first of all - I find it very weird that they named it "Shadow Generations" to begin with. Shadow has had playable main story appearances in 4 games total - Sonic Adventure 2, Sonic Heroes, Shadow the Hedgehog and Sonic 06. What I really wish they did with the Shadow Generations portion is decouple it entirely from Sonic Generations & release it as its own separate game, with a longer, more detailed and fleshed out story, a few more levels - preferably with more original theming rather than revisiting ones from older games again - and name it "Shadow the Hedgehog 2".That's just the thing...playing this honest to god felt like a direct sequel to the infamous 2005 game - Shadow the Hedgehog. And you know what? I am so on-board with this idea. I am one of the rare few who actually loves that game, despite its glaring issues with structure, pacing & everything else. And I absolutely adore the ideas they toy around with in the game, be it the new powers for Shadow or fleshing out characters which we vaguely knew about regarding Shadow's past. That whole thing was AWESOME and I genuinely wish they just made it a full blown "Shadow the Hedgehog 2" with it instead.Granted, I understand why they didn't and felt the need to basically shoehorn it into a remaster of Sonic Generations - marketing. Because Shadow the Hedgehog was critically panned & overall receives mixed-to-negative feedback from the community even in 2024, close to 20 years after its original release, I understand that they don't want to make a sequel to Shadow the Hedgehog, at least not yet.What I'm hoping for is that Sonic X Shadow Generations is just the testing ground to see how receptive people are to the idea of Shadow starring in his own games again, and my honest opinion? Hell yeah! I've already mentioned that I love the original Shadow the Hedgehog. I love the Shadow Generations portion of this game so much, just wish there was more of it. And I want to see more dedicated Shadow the Hedgehog games in the future.The game itself is rather short. I completed Shadow Generations in around 3.5 hours - not much longer than Sonic Generations itself. Controls' wise I found it to be pretty much perfect. Aside from the final stage where it's centered around a new ability Shadow gets, everywhere else I found him controlling pretty much perfect. Did not encounter any bugs or anything of the sort in my time playing either. The length of the game though...again - really wish they made it its own separate game & had time to flesh it out, it's so good otherwise!From a technical standpoint, I ran this game start to finish on my Linux machine and it ran beautifully. Steam Deck & Linux people, you're in for a great OOTB experience with this one!Overall, yeah I do recommend Sonic X Shadow Generations. For both people who have never played Sonic Generations, and those who know it front to back. There are enough neat additions in Sonic Generations that will make you go "I wonder what else they changed", as well as a very enjoyable Shadow adventure to go through, albeit both games are rather short.I can't wait to see what the modding scene for this will look like.

_childDocuments_.review: In my many years of being a Sonic fan I've been used to not getting what I want, and having to settle with mediocrity. For over a decade I haven't been happy with a single mainline Sonic game. Even games like Frontiers which I could appreciate what their vision was and what they did I cannot go ahead and say if "A good game". Which is what makes Shadow Generations such a shock to the F#cking system. Its a miracle that Shadow was even given a game with how Sega has avoided other playable characters since 06, let alone one that gets his gameplay down so well. The game takes every controversial piece of Sonic media from 06 to Shadow the Hedgehog and embraces those aspects entirely. All on top of it having the best 3d Sonic level design since Sonic Unleashed. Having 3d levels be entirely 3d and not partially 2d really shows how much effort Sega put into this game. The 2d levels which I usually dread for modern Sonic is also the best its ever been Rivaling Sonic Rush's design. The Doom powers are an incredible addition to Shadows base moveset and Im glad theyre usable In every level. The Bosses although not as grand as Frontiers are a lot more challenging and Id argue better to play. The Hub worlds White Space is the perfect realization of Sonic Frontiers "Open Zone" gameplay. It is not only the best Sonic game to come out over a decade, Its arguably one of the best Sonic games of all time. And on top of all of this? It comes with a Remaster of Sonic generations, another one of Sonic's greats, all for the low price of 50 dollars.Wish it was nominated for game of the year

_childDocuments_.review: Shadow Generations is excellent! I only didn't really enjoy one level and ...unsurprisingly, it was the Frontiers one. (I liked Frontiers but that island in particular sucked and uh, this didnt change that) The Doom powers were an excellent addition that spice up the gameplay real nice. Only real disappointment in this package? Sonic Generations is still exactly like the old game. It's a separate executable using the old engine and all the old assets complete with the old 60FPS cap. It's a shame, because the visual and performance makeover that could have been made possible by the upgraded Hedgehog Engine would be incredible... dare i hope for modders to address this in the future in some way? I haven't tested Ultrawide support but I played it on a 4K TV with a Ryzen 5700X3D and an undervolted RTX 4070 Super and the whole game went without a hitch or stutter in sight at 2160p120- minus the occasional camera flyover in white space which seemed to my eye to be locked to some weirdly frame paced 30FPS? that's literally like less than 1% of the game though.No HDR support from what I can tell.At the time I'm writing this it says I played for 4 hours. I didn't touch Sonic Generations aside from booting it up once to see if it was upgraded in any way, the 4 hours was playing Shadow generations start to finish and getting about half of the collectables. If you think that's too short, then that's up to you. However, I'm absolutely recommending this game! it's a tight, polished experience and nearly ever level is what I would call "peak boost formula" maybe even exceeding Generations and Unleashed's highs. It does share Generations' weakest aspect however: you're forced to do challenge missions to complete the story, which makes this a bit speedrun unfriendly.One last thing. Steam input is not turned on by default and this game says it has native Dualsense support.... it doesn't. Make sure you turn steam input on if you're using a Dualsense. Didnt test any other controller.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the best Sonic game I have played in YEARS. SEGA and Sonic Team are finally putting in some real effort into these games and it shows, especially with this one. Not only is it a perfect port of Sonic Generations with improved graphics and performance, but the additional content is amazing. It is a short, but wonderful experience. It feels very fleshed out, they definitely took their time with this one. The story is good, the sound track is AWESOME (per usual for a sonic game), the graphics look amazing, and the gameplay is phenomenal. And there is a lot of post game content to keep you entertained once you're done with the story.I really hope that every Sonic game that follows builds off of this one. This game should be the new standard. I really had a great time playing.

_childDocuments_.review: Sonic X Shadow Generations is 2 games compiled into one.Sonic Generations is by and large the 2011 original, with some better support at higher resolutions and actually pillarboxes properly in ultrawide. The story's been rewritten and keeps the same beats, but makes things a little more grounded and I think better characterises the cast given the circumstance. The extra chao are a neat little thing to look for but I wish they'd been used to give us some extra concept art or background music as so far they don't seem to reward anything except a photo of where the Chao was found. The Drop Dash has been added as an optional skill for Classic Sonic and a base part of Modern Sonic's moveset, but it didn't feel like it ever really came up for me as being something to use, though that could just be because I'm so used to the 2011 original and it doesn't really harm anything by being here.Shadow Generations by comparison feels closer to Sonic Frontiers than it does to Sonic Generations, Shadow largely plays like Sonic but Chaos Control and Chaos Spear give him just enough extra "stuff" to do that the levels can be a little more experimental with things. Even simple interactions like having to hit a switch or enemy with chaos spear as you approach adds just a little extra dimension to be aware of that I think makes a good run of these stages very satisfying, and that's without the extra moves you unlock throughout the campaign that allow you to traverse water, or glide through the air, or become a squid, or knock certain enemies skyward and launch them away, before teleporting to where they landed. The latter move is very satisfying to experiment with, trying to find places they may not have expected you to aim for to try and skip things and the like.Compared to Frontiers, it's much more condensed and straightforward, you beat levels to progress, and the levels contain keys that let you open chests you find in the open zone to get concept art, music and the like. It's an extra step over Sonic Generations just giving you the stuff via Red Star Rings but I think it helps give the open zone a use that the white space in sonic generations kind of lacked due to how simple it was. In the open zone, you can also find entries from Gerald's journal that was offered as a physical bonus to view in-game, and spare parts which can be handed in to get some more concept art. I think it's done an excellent job of "trimming the fat" from Frontiers and it's got me excited to see where this gameplay style will go next. The port is locked to 16:9 and pillarboxes on ultrawide, but the framerate caps at 120 here compared to Sonic Generations' 60. You can see the bump in graphical quality going between the 2 games as Shadow is running on the Hedgehog Engine 2 whilst Generations runs on the original.Overall, a great package and a must-have for any Sonic fan. Maybe wait for a sale if money's tight as each game is only about 4 hours long going straight to credits. I only hope Sonic Team can keep the momentum for the next entry and beyond.

_childDocuments_.review: You can definitely tell this was directed by a designer from the original Gens team. Not to trash Morio Kishimoto's recent work, but this is an entirely different league of design quality. Shadow Generations is  good.Level design, boss fights, abilities (yes, Morph is fun when you figure it out), all a joy. Sunset Heights and Chaos Island are way better here than their original incarnations, awesome stuff. Story's mostly a retread of Shadow 05, and the characterization is still not quite perfect, but it has heart, which is great.The Gens remaster included is just the same game with higher res visuals, & some questionable cutscene rewrites + awful VA changes. Hud adjustments are also odd, removing button colors was a bad call.Things of note I'd like to see improved in the future:-Shadow is still rather slow,  in some of the 2D sections. Decision making/reaction pace is decent, just the sense of raw speed is lacking compared to Unleashed/og Gens, albeit vastly better than Frontiers. This is done in large part for the sake of lowering controls difficulty & challenge, but I still think it could be better. There's some dashpad segments that crank the speed up, and I wish the game had more of that kind of speed.-The quickstep isn't actually a quickstep here, it's been replaced by a pseudo-drift spin move that can be held down. In theory this could be interesting, but the game never properly explains it, and doesn't make almost any use of it in the level design. In part because the speed is lower, it feels like it just isn't needed, although the limited application it does have (like in the starting corridor in Sunset Heights) is pretty cool, with a sweet looking animation. I'd like to see this mechanic either expanded, or replaced by the classic quickstep again.-Still miss water running-Wall jumps feel kinda scuffed in how they look & feel compared to SU/og Gens. Just some leftover Frontiers jank lol

_childDocuments_.review: A spectacular remaster of an absolute timeless classic Sonic game from the Xbox 360 era that also adds a whole, brand-new Shadow campaign with its own levels. The original game getting remastered is amazing as it is, but we are also getting a new story to go along with it akin to that of Super Mario 3D World + Bowser's Fury. It's a remaster and an expansion at the same time, and it doesn't lose it's luster and is just as fun (and sometimes frustrating) as the original. I am serious when I saw this: this is definitely one of the best remasters in recent memory, because it not only keeps most, if not all of the things about the original Sonic Generations that made it such a hit in the first place, but we also get a whole new Shadow Generations and get to experience a story contrasting to that of Sonic's. If Sonic's story is the Saturday morning cartoon, then Shadow's is the gritty OG Teen Titans-esque anime. Getting the original game remastered was fine enough, but the new campaign with Shadow the Hedgehog is truly going above and beyond. Definitely the icing on the cake.An absolute recommend from me. Definitely someone around a 9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: SONIC X SHADOW GENERATIONS? A Nostalgic Yet Modern Blast Through Time!SONIC X SHADOW GENERATIONS offers fans an impressive double feature, combining a new Shadow-focused campaign with an enhanced edition of the acclaimed Sonic Generations. In this reimagined adventure, players explore Shadow's darker journey as he faces off against his nemesis, Black Doom, while also reliving the classic, high-speed escapades of both Classic and Modern Sonic. Featuring fresh mechanics, a new hub world, and a wealth of unlockable content, this game delivers a celebration of the Sonic series that appeals to longtime fans and new players alike.The standout experience in SONIC X SHADOW GENERATIONS is undoubtedly Shadow’s fresh storyline, which fleshes out his mysterious past and expands on his unique "Doom Powers." These powers bring a thrilling gameplay twist, allowing Shadow to control time, surf across water, and traverse levels with a combination of stealth and aggression fitting of his Ultimate Life Form title. The new "White Space" hub world takes cues from Sonic Frontiers, giving players an open-zone setting to explore, where discovering collectibles, hidden secrets, and background lore adds depth and value to Shadow's side of the game.The remastered Sonic Generations campaign complements Shadow's adventure well. Fans of the 2011 original will find Sonic's levels as exhilarating as ever, now enhanced with HD graphics, optimized performance, and small gameplay tweaks, like the addition of a drop dash move and collectible Chao in every stage. While Sonic’s story remains mostly the same, small rewrites add context, giving both the Classic and Modern Sonic campaigns a fresh feel without detracting from what made the original a classic.On the technical side, Sonic X Shadow Generations delivers in spades. Running smoothly at high frame rates, even on mid-range PCs, the game shows marked improvements in performance over recent Sonic titles. Sonic Team has fine-tuned the graphical elements of both campaigns, with new animations, sharper textures, and improved lighting effects that make Shadow's journey through familiar stages visually engaging. The soundtrack is a nostalgic powerhouse, offering remixes of fan-favorite themes alongside iconic tracks that players can choose as background music for levels, adding a personalized touch.Players looking for a flawless technical experience will be pleased to know that the game has minimal issues. While some controller compatibility and ultrawide support complaints exist, they are minor compared to the game’s overall polish and stability. The game’s high optimization standards are especially notable given Sonic Team’s recent struggles with other titles.SONIC X SHADOW GENERATIONS offers a thrilling journey that celebrates the legacy of Sonic and Shadow. Shadow's campaign provides an emotional, action-packed storyline that gives longtime fans the in-depth character exploration they’ve been craving, while Sonic Generations continues to be an enjoyable romp through the best of the franchise’s past. For those who haven’t played the original Sonic Generations, this package is a must-have; and for longtime fans, Shadow's new story and the game’s quality-of-life upgrades make it a worthwhile addition to their collection.Are you a Sonic fan ready to dive back into the ultimate speed adventure? _childDocuments_.review: I have been a massive sonic fan my entire life. I have played almost all the games in the series and have stuck through even the darkest times in the series. This game makes it all worth it. Graphics:The sonic generations part looks fine. The game never looked bad so there wasn't really a reason to make it look better except some higher resolution textures and such, which the game has. Shadow generations is the best the series has ever looked. The animations are beautiful and everything is extremely detailed. There is so much care just put in the way Shadow moves from him doing a skill roll from a large fall to all the different animations for the ranks you get in stages. This game is incredibly cinematic in everything it does.Gameplay: I feel like i have to mostly ignore sonic generations, not because its bad but because its sonic generations. The game feels great and the level design is mostly amazing. Classic sonic feels a little wonky as always. If you have played sonic generations and liked it in the past than you will still like it, if you have never played sonic generations than if you like fast snappy and interesting gameplay than you will like it. Getting the S ranks is fun as always, so is getting the red star rings. The new chao missions are sadly tacked on and offer nothing in return but gives you a chance to explore the level more. Shadow generations is amazing. Shadow feels incredibly tight and responsive to control. The new doom powers add a nice new dynamic to the gameplay. The levels are truly incredible with snappy platforming that lets you keep up your speed if you do it right. Multiple paths in these large playgrounds that are begging to be mastered. The keys are fun to find and it is nice having only three rather than 5, however with how long the levels are, it can be a bit frustrating to have to search every corner to find them all. The boss fights are the best the series has seen, which is a low bar, but they are cinamatic and fun. Could not recommend this game more just from the gameplay alone. The only big difference I would make is a radar to find the orbot and cubot screws because once you get down to the last few it can be a pain to find them.Story:Sonic generations has never had the best story but the rewrites to add upon the characters a bit better. Shadow generations story is a shadow story so its amazing. I will say nothing more on that but just know I love it.Conclusion:This game is a huge love letter to sonic fans that have been craving a tight and fun sonic experience. They are finally listening to the fans and it must be celebrated. I am excited to see if this keeps up and I am hopeful it will but based on the last time generations came out we have to still be weary. Does not take away from the fact that you have to play this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Sonic Generations is the same game as ever. There are a few changes to the cutscenes, and the drop dash from Mania was added, and a new chao hunting mode. But aside from those small additions, it's all the same as the original version. Which isn't a bad thing; the original game, while not my favorite, was pretty solid and didn't really need much revamping. But the Sonic Generations remaster is really just the side dish to Shadow Generations.Shadow Generations is amazing. The controls feel better than ever, Shadow has some awesome new powers, and the level design is fantastic, being basically as good as Unleashed in my opinion. Shadow also has some cool new powers which help change up the gameplay and make him feel like a distinct character from Sonic, despite their core movesets being the same.The stages in Shadow Generations are fantastic. I love the choices in stages that they brought over (except for Chaos Island -- seems like a weird choice to add a level from Frontiers), and the level design is better than ever. Stages are linear, but pretty wide open with lots of paths to take. They've really refined the boost formula with this game, and it feels better than ever. Control is tight, and it's easy to control Shadow to get him to go in the direction you want, which has been an issue for me in past boost games.The hub world isn't exactly my cup of tea, but I don't think it's bad, per se. I disliked the open-world sections of Sonic Frontiers, and while I do think this is an improvement over them, I still don't love it. I do think the formula works better in a smaller, tighter space like this, but I still don't love the execution. I'd really love them to go back to the style they used in Adventure 1, '06, and Unleashed, where it's mostly just for immersion and connecting the stages together.But despite the few issues I have, I think that this is the best boost formula game Sonic Team has made so far, overtaking Unleashed, with level designs that are just as good as that game, and controls that feel way better to me. To be honest, I've never really been a big fan of the boost formula. I think Unleashed was the best version of it, but even then, I've always preferred the Adventure style gameplay. But Shadow Generations has quickly become my new favorite boost game, and I really think it might overtake Adventure 1 as my favorite 3D Sonic game of all time. If the standard stays as high as it is here, I'm excited for the future of Sonic again.I also want to briefly touch on the story; I know a lot of people don't really care about story in these kinds of games, but I've been invested in the Sonic storyline for practically all my life, so I do care about it. Unlike Sonic Generations' story, which is pretty inconsequential, Shadow Generations actually has some really good development for Shadow's character, which could have an impact on his character in future games. I love that the story takes itself seriously, but doesn't become as melodramatic as Forces and Frontiers' stories do. It feels like it's really very similar to the way Adventure 1, 2, and Heroes tell their stories, albeit the story here is much shorter. I also love how they leaned into the edgy aesthetic again, like they did in Shadow the Hedgehog. I find that over-the-top tryhard edgelord stuff to be really charming when it's pulled off properly, and it is here.I had less-than-amazing feelings about Sonic Frontiers, but Sonic Team has really learned some lessons from that game about what did and didn't work, and they've refined the formula even further. It's taken 16 years, but I think the boost formula is just about perfect at this point. I can't wait to see where the Sonic series goes next, and this is the first time in a long time that I've been able to say that.

Now, in a normal sonic game, when there is a collectable that is tracked on the main hud, that means you get something pretty cool for getting everything.  For these however, let's just say I hope you REALLY like cuckoo clocks.  I also hope you guys don't get too attached to shadows new abilities, because based on what happens, he probably won't have them in the next game he's in.TLDR:  It's a very short, underwhelming experience for too high of a price that should have just been dlc or sold separate from the remaster, wait for it to go on sale or find somewhere to buy it cheaper

_childDocuments_.review: I always thought that, if they were to make a Sonic Generations 2, it would be a pale imitation of the original. Frontiers' Cyberspace levels felt awful to play and the level design was somewhat lacking. Forces was completely braindead in terms of level design and also had fundamental physics & control issues, especially with regards to Classic Sonic. Actually, though, they did an incredible job here.Shadow Generations feels like an evolution of Sonic Generations, with more mechanics that add depth. Even Shadow's homing attack equivalent - which teleports the player next to the enemy - is properly exploited, allowing the player to zap through hazards and obstacles if there is an enemy on the other side. There are some proper deep cuts, too, and I'm impressed by the willingness to call back to games that are generally not well regarded - Rail Canyon from Sonic Heroes was such a weird level to bring back, but I can't pretend it wasn't sick as hell. I will say, though, that I'm annoyed by the lack of a specific Shadow the Hedgehog (the game) callback level. Did we REALLY need a Frontiers level?! I'd have taken a Secret Rings or Black Knight level over that, without question. The bosses are awful. I appreciated the callbacks to Metal Overlord and the Mephiles fight, but these were not good bosses. I didn't think the Frontiers bosses were mechanically great, but they were definitely better than this. Also, simply playing a variation of All Hail Shadow for the final boss was LAME. Also, Sega, PLEASE patch the game so that the d-pad can be used for movement. It's messed up that you can change to a legacy control option in game, but there's no way to use the d-pad to play the 2D sections, except for fiddling with Steam Input. Also, it's unfortunate that the original Sonic Generations is still limited to 60FPS, and still has the exact same stutter issues, and still only has FXAA as an antialiasing option - what is this, 2011?Overall though, if you're a Sonic fan, this is the best Sonic game since the original Generations. It might be better. It's funny, actually, that the callbacks to Generations in this game are as nostalgia-inducing as the callbacks to older games. It feels like a celebration of Sonic Generations more than anything.

_childDocuments_.review: It's just like the olden days really.THIS WILL BE SPOILER FREE RELAX ALL READERSGonna start with the new stuff here, all of the Shadow side of the game is entirely new and that is what the bread and butter of this game is and what most people will buy it for if they owned Generations before. The story is decent enough for very short stories, both take around 5-6 hours give or take. (I didn't 100% Shadow's side but I did beat every level and boss, I didn't play the Sonic Side besides the 1st level). This length is however a lot shorter then many probably hoped for as it's easy to wrap up each story in a single play session espescially if you skip cutscenes and I STRONGLY URGE people to take they're time with it and space it out among other games. There is only 6 levels (and 4 bosses) in the Shadow side, 2 of which honestly don't make any sense in the context of the game, as they come from games that existed long after the time-frame Generations takes place in and both the Sonic and Shadow sides take place at the same time. Sega dropped the ball here however as in all the promotional stuff we already knew basically everything that Shadow's story was bringing stage and boss wise before the game even came out just not the order. Shadow's levels also all take longer then most of what the Sonic side has, 1st level Sonic side easy to clear under 3 min both sides, Shadow's first level will take between 4.5-5 min on a first run through for Act 1 alone. This stuff isn't a negative per-say it just sucks that people who followed the marketing got spoiled for a lot of stuff. What is a negative though is any collectables obtained through the Shadow Story do not Carry over into the Sonic one as, judging by what the game does when you click the Sonic side, plus there being 2 exe's in the folder, it runs an entirely separate game. Another obvious negative is Denuvo, nuf said. I haven't really experienced any performance issues except frame drops in a few places, and only in cutscenes, but what drops I have seen are VERY noticable, and I have a 3070TI and more then enough RAM to run the game so it might not like systems on thee minimum requirements spectrum. The Sonic side from what I can tell from just after the first level (and 100% the original Generations ages ago) is the same thing mainly. The story DOES have some rewrites and its been re-dubbed from what I can tell. Sadly the funny stuff in the birthday scene at the beginning where Amy gets held back by Sonic as she's fangirling, and her sending Knuckles into a tree are both gone in this version, as well as the first conversation between Sonic and Tails after clearing Act 2 of the first level is also changed a little bit. I do not know the level of rewriting and redubbing that's actually in the game fully yet but I assume there will be more in the later stages of the story. The new controls are also somewhat annoying to get used to but you can switch it back to the og Generations scheme if you wish so its not a problem. The game also makes Red Rings unobtainable on the first clear of a stage ACT (least with the 1st level) and there are new Chao to find, hints for them are actually available in the Collections Room which you get access to after clearing Act 2 of the first stage by going left instead of right. The "HD" textures of Sonic Generations is BARELY noticable so there is a chance returning players will not be able to tell unless they look closely. Aside from what I said in this paragraph however, the Sonic Side is the same game that came out all those years ago.The Deluxe edition really only comes with a beta Shadow design which is mid, a Modern Sonic skin that looks off, the early access is nice but again you CAN beat one of the 2 stories very easily in one sitting if you have the time to burn. The extra BGM's are only available in the Shadow side and they are all songs from like Sonic Riders and up in the timeline. The DLC is known to be a movie tie-in with Sonic the Hedgehog 3 and comes out before the movie does in theatres so I can't rate it at all. And yes the Gerald Robotnik notebook they were advertising is in the Shadow collection room fully accessable you just gotta get its pages.All in all this game is a very Solid revisiting of an old 3D classic with a bunch of new flair in the form of a sister game accessed from the same launch. If Denuvo doesn't mess with your experience cause you have a stronger gaming rig or get lucky this game is well worth it as it is effectively a 2 in 1 special. However if you have a computer on the weaker side of the spectrum this may struggle to run at times cause of that dumb DRM. There is no info on how modding this game is gonna go, Sega seems to be ok with it yet they use a DRM that makes it harder to do so I dunno what is going on in they're heads.Is the game worth its asking price? The standard edition is most certainly worth it long as Denuvo doesn't cause too many issues, the deluxe depends on your opinions on what it comes with. Keep in mind there is no longer a way to purchase the original Sonic Generations outside of bundles now. If you have never played the original Generations game treat yourself with this game, espescially if your a long time Sonic fan there is a ton to like in this game, even more if your a huge Shadow fan as that is by far the superior game out of the 2 in this purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: I've already played the original Sonic Generations way back in 2011 on the 360, so my focus wasn't really on that. Don't get me wrong, the levels are still fun for what they are. Beyond some daytime Sonic Unleashed stages, they were the best modern Sonic had to offer in terms of level design. However, it's pretty apparent that its gameplay is dated. Sonic is still incredibly awkward to handle when he's not going 999 mph, Classic Sonic still has a momentum bug here and there when it comes to slopes and curves, and there's a large dependence on having skills make the gameplay tolerable when it should be tolerable from the start. Beyond this it's still a really good time. Shadow Generations? Amazing. Level design is incredible. Shortcuts are just visible enough to notice, but just out of the way where you have to think on your feet to figure out how to get there. The new abilities are varied and all useful in their own way. Shadow controls almost like his Adventure counterpart (can't state enough how good this is.). Bosses are actually fun to fight. And there's just enough side content to keep you busy, even after beating the final boss. My only issue is that, compared to Sonic Generations, there aren't as many stages, acts, and bosses. I honestly wish there was more.

_childDocuments_.review: Sooo, this is going to be more of a small heart-to-heart than a review, but I'm still posting this here nonetheless.TLDR in case you don't want to read: Sonic X Shadow Generations is a complete masterclass in how to both handle a remaster, as well as build upon said remaster with completely new, refreshing ideas.Now onto my thoughts.Picture this - you're a kid who just so happens to stumble upon Sonic the Hedgehog on TV. You think to yourself "Man, this guy is cool!" and you start looking for more and more content. You find out that he has an entire videogame franchise, and he's regarded as a gaming legend in his own right. How cool is that, right?And then, you find out about Sonic's miserable past as a videogame icon - shoddy ports, janky titles, dead air games, the entirety of Sonic 06, it's all there. It makes you sad that the moment Sonic gets a good game is when he does nothing new and only relies on the past - Sonic Generations. So you stick to that game, cherishing it for all its worth. And you sit back, watching Sonic fail time and time again to stick a good title.But then, a miracle happens. Sonic Frontiers releases, paving the way for better future Sonic titles. And then, it releases - Shadow Generations, in all its glory.This game. This ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ game. It single-handedly brought back a franchise which was basically on its last legs. Every single element of this game's design (with a few very minor additions, looking at you rocket parts) sticks the landing tenfold, doing backflips for pure style points while its at it. And while all of that's happening, Sonic Generations endures the test of time, even if showing a very slight bit of age.All in all, Sonic X Shadow Generations is the game that brings it all back. It ensures that the Sonic franchise pumps out better and better titles, and I couldn't be happier to say that.Sonic bros, we are so back.

_childDocuments_.review: In short: it's peak fictionThe Sonic Generations remake aspect of this package is fairly straight forward and does what it says on the tin: it updates the visual ever so slightly, adds a few bells and whistles such as the drop dash for Classic Sonic; what you'd expect from a remaster. Still a classic 10+ years later and Sega largely left it intact save a few minor story changes.The Shadow side of the package though, is what makes this worth grabbing. If you're like me, you were probably expecting this to play just like Sonic Generations with a Shadow skin and a few new levels. However, it's difficult to convey just how more depth Shadow's unique skill set adds to the experience. If nothing else, it's a testament to how much potential the "Boost formula" has for growth and expansion. These abilities are complimented by some of the best level design Sonic Team has released in recent memory and really invites player creativity; a true playground for player expression. Unexpectedly, the story included in the Shadow side of things is also surprisingly endearing and well written (for what it is) and nails Shadow's character in a way that hasn't been done since Sonic Adventure 2.However, with all the high praise that has been given to the Shadow side of the game, it does create an awkward problem where it makes the Sonic side feel a little dated by comparison, still a great experience though and definitely worth a playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: Admittedly, I was a bit skeptical when this game was announced, but after having played it to 100%, I am very impressed with what SEGA was able to accomplish, at least for the Shadow portion of the content. We'll talk about and rate Sonic's portion separately for this reason, but let's examine the Shadow portion first. Shadow Generations is technically impressive, solidly designed, and very well written. I would like nothing more than to see SEGA remove boost from Sonic and Shadow's moveset completely, as it usually reduces the ground and air control of each hedgehog, making steering and control feel sluggish and much less agile, but in Shadow Generations, they managed to create a much more balanced movement system. This time around, the boost is only a technique that Shadow possesses, not the only move the developers expect you to focus on. Boosting destroys enemies, yes, but it is not so over-centralizing to the point where you feel like you are running in a straight line. Chaos Spear, Chaos Attack (in the form of Doom Blast), and Chaos Control all return to Shadow's moveset in this installment, making for a much more combat-focused experience that feels faithful to what Shadow's gameplay strengths were always meant to be. However, these new moves to his arsenal don't feel like extra abilities, they actually feel tested and planned-out. Extensive testing was clearly done with both Shadow's moveset and the levels to ensure that his new and returning combat techniques were not only a fun change of level pacing, but intentionally designed to be used to intelligent and creative new routes and secrets throughout each level. While Shadow's air and ground control still does somewhat mimic the sluggish turning of most boost games, it's not nearly as offensive in Shadow Generations. Moving Shadow around feels agile, and with the controls being adapted from what was used to build Sonic Frontiers, it feels like there are plenty of opportunities to course correct movement and platforming in the event of player error. To put it simply, it certainly needs a few more tweaks, but this is the best a Sonic character has controlled in an official 3D Sonic game in over a decade. It's not perfect, but it's relatively inoffensive, quite tolerable, and dare I say fun, even. As far as the level design goes, once again, SEGA nailed it this time around. These are the most competently designed and immersive official 3D Sonic levels we have seen in an official Sonic game in over a decade. Yes, the levels of Sonic Unleashed were well made, but that's because they were built around the sluggish steering and insane speeds of a boosting Sonic. Shadow Generations also builds its levels around it's main character's movement, but this time, it also takes into account the three key principles that make for an ideal experience when it comes to a Sonic level: speed-based platforming, combat, and exploration. In Shadow Generations, all three of these aspects are present, implemented, and balanced to near-perfection, to the point where it's simply fun to find the fastest possible route through a level, take a stroll to find some secret paths, utilize combat skills or Chaos Control to open up routes that are hidden even more creatively, or simply balance all of these aspects for the perfect run. The positives don't stop there. This game also balances the two key principles of presentation in a Sonic game: spectacle and freedom. These two aspects are also balanced to near-perfection. Too much spectacle feels like Sonic Forces, a playable cutscene. Too much freedom can lead to non-descript level routing, confusion, and player error. Shadow Generations balances both of these. The player is given enough freedom to go where they want, while still being given a general idea of the basic path they need to follow. All of this ties together with spectacle being brought in a just the right time with seamless in-game cutscenes, giving the player a rush of excitement followed by a moment to breath before being put right back into the action without missing a beat. This balanced extends to the bosses as well, which are, once again, some of the best we've seen in an official Sonic game in over a decade. The balance of freedom and spectacle is at its peak with the boss battles, and the developers were even creative enough to put in secret attacks that can be activated by using Chaos Control at the right time in order to interact with certain objects that were out of reach before. I haven't seen level design and boss sequencing this competent from Sonic Team in a long, long time, and it is greatly appreciated. We cannot conclude without discussing the story as well, and the praise continues here. Shadow Generations gives us some of the best writing in an official Sonic game since Sonic & the Black Knight (which absolutely needs a proper remake, by the way). Shadow was written perfectly, and his interactions with Maria and Gerald Robotnik were near-flawless. Rouge and Omega were also present in the main hub, and getting to see their dialogue changing as Shadow slowly restored the hub was incredibly immersive and an absolute treat. Rouge had some powerful dialogue that called back to Shadow's arc in Sonic '06, and some of Maria's final dialogue to Shadow provided competent and emotionally intelligent writing that we have been missing and asking for in official Sonic games for far too long. The voice acting and music was also on-point, which is greatly appreciated, given that the Sonic titles of the last decade have had questionable voice direction. Shadow Generations also gives us an explorable hub world with tons of collectibles and extra content. The amount of legacy content from Shadow's past and previous Sonic games in general as the icing on the cake here. The hub is a blast to explore, and finding concept art, music tracks, and lore from previous games, speaks volumes to how much effort the dev team put into this installment. We are even treated to some new content, with Gerald Robotnik's Journal, which adds yet another profound layer of depth to the collection room in Shadow's campaign. If you're an enthusiast about Shadow's character, lore, and backstory, you're going to want to collect every page. It is well worth your time to read this cover to cover. Where was this level of effort when SEGA was working on Sonic Origins?! Shadow Generations provides better collectibles than the recent "collection" game itself! I could go on and on, but in conclusion, Shadow Generations alone makes the game well-worth the asking price. My only real complaints are that the moveset still relies on boost gameplay, which hinders turning radius, although that is much more tolerable here, there are no levels from the 2005 Shadow the Hedgehog game, (would have much preferred Lava Shelter and Final Haunt to Sunset Heights and Chaos Island, the latter making no sense as to why they were present), and that Sonic Generations was basically an unnecessary inclusion. Personally, I would have preferred two more levels in the Shadow campaign, but even with what's there right now, I can safely give this game a 9/10. It's not perfect, but dang it is both inoffensive and fun to play. More like this please, Sonic Team!Oh, and I suppose I should also review the Sonic Generations portion as well...Base Sonic Gens is fineMost of this portion feels like busy work by comparisonThere are glitches that weren't in the original, which are mildly annoying sometimesREMOVE DENUVO IT CAUSES LAGADD D-PAD SUPPORT FOR CLASSIC SONIC (It was in the original, why not here?!)6.5/10 portUltimately, this does not take away from the Shadow experience, which I am choosing to focus on and give a 9/10. Sonic Team should not group remakes and sequels together for the selling point. Overall, I greatly enjoyed my time with this game and I thought it was very well done. Keep that momentum and keep improving Sonic Team!

add to the story at all most animations are left unchanged lip syncing included I definitely think leaving gens story unchanged would have been a better thing they also nerfed my girl rouge but mods gens I like the added shadow lore and the level design is very good its very open with lots of paths and they have added more natural ramps to ramp off of instead of making fake ramps with dash pads open zone are still different to the levels its frustrating to have the physics changed constantly because it leads to inconsistency tricks you can pull off in the open zone are not possible in the are actively looking for it but 70% of the time the incline will literally eat shadows jump causing you to stick to the ground gaining zero height that is just terrible and ruins the flow of the gameplay for the level physics incline jump boosting seems to be removed I tested in kingdom valley with the vanilla physics and a physics mod jumping on inclines always eat your jump or give no boost _childDocuments_.review: When you buy this you get two things, Shadow Generations and a launcher to play Sonic Generations.What you get out of the sonic generations portion is a nice no hassle no 2011 launcher jank, your options are in-game and you get a bunch of nice bonuses with the Digital Deluxe. You lose (assuming you didn't already have Gens), easy access to modding (for now) and the time to regain all achievements and beat the game again.What you get out of Shadow Generations is about 4 hours of the most well polished and presented sonic levels and hub area they've ever made, with just the right amount of gimmicks, set pieces, and challenges to keep you engaged. (6 Stages, 2 acts each, 4 bosses)The gamefeel in Shadow Gens feels more like an updated Frontiers than an updated generations, the game feel is very similar to frontiers (the way the camera locks, the way boost behaves, enemy and rail lock on, how momentum carries, and how acceleration works). I'm of the opinion this is a test drive for what Frontiers 2 will bring us. Overall, a fun but criminally short ride with Shadow Gens and another run at a QoL improved Sonic Gens. Once modding catches up, you'll have one of if not *THE* best sonic title to own on PC.

_childDocuments_.review: Is Sonic X Shadow Generations worth it? Let's break it down from the perspective of a longtime Sonic Fan / Hater.With the rollercoaster-esque nature of the franchise the passed 10+ years (realistically since 1995), it's very easy to fall into the Sonic Cycle; Anticipation -> Realization -> Disappointment -> Rage -> Indifference yada yada lather, rinse, repeat. Hearing the news about a Shadow Generations type game alongside a reduxed Sonic Generations left me with an extremely cautious disposition. I've been here, done that for almost 30 decades now. I can't be blinded by the rose-tinted nostalgia and memories of my past as it's very easy to hit that stone cold brick wall of reality when you're looking behind into the backseat of your brainmobile. That being said, I'm also hopelessly optimistic about the future of the little blue guy. Against all logic and reason, I've fallen into the mindset that the Sonic I knew 20 years ago could just pop back up into the mainstream as if he'd never left his TB303, Trip Pants, Y2K ridden universe. However, my critical self knows that can't and shouldn't happen. The Sonic I love was on the cutting edge of what was new in culture, technology and sometimes even politics such as saving the earth in quite a literal, civilian type way. That being said, where should he go? Even SEGA can't quite answer that question, as it lingers on philosophical and capitalistic importance.Ever since the bigger, borderline Final Fantasian adventures of Sonic in the mid-2000's, Sonic has returned to a hollow version of his roots. All the cartoony visuals and dialogue lends itself to there new vision of Sonic's gameplay, Boost To Win. While this isn't inherently a bad thing, it does manifest into different experiences as time has gone on. Lots of changes have been made to reduce the boost's importance while trying to compensate in the level design, resulting in a "Boost In The Right Places To Win". However, there's been little progress and sometimes even regression of progress since the original boost game, Unleashed.Generations back in 2011 also put a shackle onto the series as whole. The "Remember When?" nostalgia grabbing became extremely evident. A lot of the story and dialogue, while introducing new characters and concepts, has melted down into a self referential goop that, while back in 2011 it was fine and maybe even warranted for Sonic's 20th anniversary, has left the franchise feeling old and rerun-ish.With Forces barely being on my radar, Frontiers with a shaky start, a strong mid sprint and a face-bashing fall right before the finish line, I wasn't exactly excited for this game. Though, as stated before, I had to try it out as soon as possible. Not only do we live in a timeline where they gave Sonic a rival, then that rival gets a gun and borderline Rated T context, we live in a timeline where they reference it again almost 20 years after the fact.So let's get straight to the ice cream sundae of this package.- - - Shadow Generations Review - - -GAMEPLAYI'll cut it clean and crisp for you, this is the best playing S(hadow)onic game in recent memory. While Frontiers left a weird, copper tinted taste in my otherwise greedy, unsatisfied mouth, Shadow Generations has amazing controls that work the way you actually want them to. While the mechanics may feel alien at first, (because they quite literally are), they very quickly begin to become part of your finger language. Dare I say, the way it's weaved into the levels with quick responsiveness almost, maybe even actually, feels (really) fun.  The levels themselves are set pieces, with a ton of "first level-isms" still showing up passed the first level. While speed is still the name of the game, the branching pathways and reactionary secrets lead itself to extremely replayable levels that make you go "Oh wow, I didn't even know" even many hours into game.The game seduces you into trying out different ideas, especially once you unlock more abilities down the road. There's also a nice difficulty bump to these levels, nothing too crazy but just enough at first to make you sit up in your seat the first few hours. I can't say it enough, the gameplay is next to perfect.GRAPHICS AND MUSICThis game is very genuinely beautiful. Shadow's proportions and animations give him weight that Sonic has lacked...actually I'm not sure if he's ever had in modern recollection. The fidelity is very impressive, for a Sonic game at least. The graphical tricks they use in some sections are borderline psychotic, it's really amazing what they can do almost seamlessly now. With a rock steady 120 FPS on my still fresh as a baby new PC, running an RX 6800 XT glowing with LED lights as I look into the case and type this review, it never cried once. Super well running game.While Sonic has been known for it's golden walking cane alibi of "Well the music is amazing", I can't say for me personally that this soundtrack really speaks to me in any capacity. Even Frontiers surprised me with it's slap in the face induction of post-hardcore after hours of "thoughtful" quiet pieces. The tracks range from enjoyable, but safe to ear blistering or parody-like renditions of passed tracks. I found myself near the end game changing up the tracks for a different experience. Some changes were cool and interesting, while others made me feel a sigh of relief. In my honest opinion, SEGA should really get some experienced talent in the field of music they're conceptualizing for a soundtrack, and I don't mean a metal guitarist Youtuber (Ironically the Biolizard track falls under the not so bad category).STORYNot going to spoil anything here, but it is a very nice and condensed story. Very heartfelt, almost made me tear up. Amazing dialogue choices the franchise hasn't seen in a bit. It won't blow your mind, but if you love Shadow, you'll find yourself smiling.WHAT WERE THEY THINKING?While the post game is still as fun, and sometimes a little healthy challenge, once you stop playing the levels and start looking for the collectibles it becomes a bit tedious, then extremely tedious. The chests contain lack luster art from the vault, pales in comparison of what Capcom offers in their collections, music from other games which is a MUST if you're me who can't stand most of the music but also because it gives each level and boss a different feel, and story elements which might as well be for people who are under the age of 10. You can also get pieces of Gerald's diary which I still have to go back and read, but seems to be scans of the big pre-order one you get if you order the physical.As a warning, and you'll know what I mean by this, the bolts for Orbot and Cubot are NOT worth it. Not even a little bit. I won't spoil the stink bomb present they give you for completing this challenge, but it's a waste of actual time considering the needle in a haystack torture this puts you through.As much I hate the soundtrack, I was also confused to see the pre-order bonus soundtrack is for in game, not the actual new soundtrack in MP3 / FLAC form. I love to study music and revisit it to understand what I hate about it, but also maybe find an interesting bit of something I liked to incorporate into my own work. So yeah, this was a decent disappointment. Just fair warning.WHAT ABOUT SONIC GENERATIONS THOUGH?From the little bit of time I've put into the remaster, I can't say I really give a ^$#&. It's the same game more or less. It's locked at 60 FPS and feels worse than Shadow's side of the game. They would've been better off making this DLC for the existing digital version.The Point? Get it for Shadow Gens. It's a 3 hours campaign (18 to 100%). If you've seen the trailers, you've seen it all, but even with the lack of surprise it's still fun. If you can, grab it on a discount.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is about the Shadow campaign.It's the best thing to come out of Sonic Team in a long, long time. The very few complaints I can possibly levy against this game are incredibly minor and nitpicky, and do not detract from the overall quality of the product. It seeks to innovate upon tried and true ideas and it does so with incredible flair and panache. It's got wonderful visual and sound work, it's cinematic, it's fast, it's bold, it's something more primal and visceral than Sonic's gameplay. I have never in my life had more fun playing as Shadow the Hedgehog than I have here. The story, while relatively simple and somewhat predictable, is very nice and easy to follow, and doesn't really pull from the gameplay at all.I found some of the new Doom Power mechanics to be kind of questionable, but they are fun twists if nothing else. I also encountered several glitches during my run of the main campaign, this is par for the course for Sonic Team, but I won't deny it did detract from my experience at least a little bit. I wouldn't expect big things from characters that aren't Shadow here either though, this is his story and he's mainly the one carrying it from start to finish. I will say I do love this new version of Black Doom, it's likely we may never see him again after this, and if this is how he is to be remembered, then I can't complain at all.Overall I had a blast with Sonic X Shadow, it's a solid experience well worth your time and money. If you've never liked Shadow the Hedgehog before and want to see what all the fuss is about, give this one a whirl and see what you've been missing. Easily 9/10. Wish there was more of it.

_childDocuments_.review: I know a lot of people were mad that Generations got a remaster before Unleashed, and I get it, but look at what we got. Sonic Team took everything they learned from Frontiers, went back to Generations, and COOKED.The original Sonic Generations isn't much different from the excellent original game from 2011, aside from rewritten cutscenes which give much needed life to this game, new low poly skins (which I will ALWAYS be happy about), and extra collectibles to keep you speed running for hours. On top of being fully re-written and re-dubbed, certain cutscenes have been reanimated. For instance, the opening where Sonic would be holding Amy back with his hand while talking with Tails, Sonic now just kind of ignores Amy who is awkwardly holding a plate of cupcakes. While I do like the original cutscene more, this new one is fine.Now, Shadow Generations on the other hand.... HOLY CRAP. Stunning. Simply stunning. Shadow controls wonderfully, his new powers are a blast to use, and the places he visits, while new to him, aren't new to us. Places like Sunset Heights from Sonic Forces and Chaos Island from Frontiers have been rebuilt to be thrilling roller coaster rides that never stop the excitement from coming. The levels we're given are, while only 5 zones before the finale, split into two acts a piece. Act 1 is always in 3D while Act 2 gives us the 2D platforming that's been fine tuned to near perfection.As Shadow is exploring his White Space, he comes across familiar faces from past and present. Orbot and Cubot appear trying to build an escape rocket to get home, Big shows up after you play Kingdom Valley and does nothing, Omega is the first you come across just as surprised to be there as Shadow, and even Maria and Gerald appear from just before the ARK was raided. Sonic even shows up for a tie in for the original game in an awesome cutscene!Sonic X Shadow Generations is MORE than worth the price of admission! If you never played the original from 2011, now is the PERFECT time to hop in and experience 3D Sonic at his finest and giving Shadow an excellent solo adventure that all fans can be proud of! Just be sure to go into the options and change the control scheme back to the legacy controls for Sonic Generations before you hop into the game.Drop the cash on this game as soon as possible to show Sonic Team that THIS is the golden standard we want to see our favorite hedgehogs running at!
